News.title: Uefa preparing criminal legal action against Infantino
News.content:
Uefa claims that the valuation of the stakes to be sold were not independently verified and would have been offered too cheaply, calling the proposed sale "a fraudulently off-market price promoted by Infantino for his own benefit".

The application adds: "Under the terms Infantino announced, those investors stood to acquire a permanent financial interest in Fifa's commercial arm for $4.2bn, implying an absurdly low enterprise value of only approximately $20bn, a figure that was neither the product of an open, competitive auction, nor tested by any independent valuer."

In the application, Uefa is applying to a court in Florida to attempt to access files held by two Fifa businesses - Fifa Americas and FWC2026 - to be used to pursue the criminal charges in Switzerland at a later stage.

The two businesses are based in Florida.

Uefa claims that its 55 member nations would have potentially been harmed by the sell-off plan, and that it may pursue criminal proceedings against other Fifa officials as well as Infantino.

"Uefa and other interested parties are preparing to bring criminal claims in Switzerland against Infantino and possibly other Fifa officials and advisors for criminal mismanagement," the application states.

"The secretive structuring, valuation, financing, and marketing inflicted direct and concrete injury on Fifa's reputation, governance authority, and commercial relationships to the detriment of Fifa as well as its 211 members, including Uefa's 55 member associations."

Uefa insists that the plan was concocted without the knowledge of them or other key stakeholders in football, and that it had been long in development.

The applications says: "On July 28, 2026, without consulting the Fifa Council, Uefa, or any of the other confederations, or any of the 211 Fifa member associations, Infantino, purportedly acting on behalf of Fifa, publicly announced a plan to place the commercial rights to the men's and women's World Cups and the Club World Cup into a new subsidiary: Fifa Forward Enterprise.

"That announcement by Infantino was the public unveiling of a plan that he and a small circle of co-conspirators had conceived and reportedly been developing in secret for more than a year."

Uefa states in the document that there has been "an enduring history of corruption among Fifa officials" and claims that world football's governing body only relents on its plans when pressure comes from outside the sport.

"Fifa's extraordinary power over world football has operated largely without meaningful internal constraint, with accountability coming principally through external forces, including political pressure, public scrutiny, and intervention through international criminal law enforcement," the application adds.

Fifa's headquarters are in the Swiss city of Zurich, and Uefa says that its plan to eventually pursue criminal charges against Infantino is backed up by Swiss law.

"Swiss counsel has confirmed [...] that the proceeding is within reasonable contemplation for purposes of Swiss law and that Uefa has standing, as a complainant, to file a criminal complaint for criminal mismanagement against Infantino and potentially other Fifa officials as may be warranted."

BBC Sport has been told that a separate filing has been lodged to a court in New York, where Uefa is seeking documentation from Thrive Capital, the business proposed to take up an interest in FFE, and its founder Josh Kushner, the brother of US president Donald Trump's son-in-law.

The American investment bank JP Morgan is also named in the application.

A third application has also been made in Colorado, relating to former Formula 1 chief Greg Maffei, who is referred to in the court filings as "the key commercial adviser" on the proposed FFE transaction, and his Bann Ventures firm.

BBC Sport has also approached Uefa for comment.

News.title: Extra 200 police drafted in to aid force investigating wrong-way crash and fire deaths
News.content:
Earlier Brown told Radio 4's Today programme that residents deserved to "feel safe in their own homes" and he understood people from the area might feel "left behind".

"I'm from an estate, from the same ilk," he said.

"You live around people that may be suffering poverty or other social issues, it can be that uniform sort of consciousness that 'we're left behind'.

"But I can assure the people of Grangetown and South Bank they're as important to me as people from any other estate in the borough."

Local Labour MPs Anna Turley, Luke Myer, Andy McDonald, Jonathan Brash and Chris McDonald issued a joint statement in which they welcomed the help of other police forces during the past week, but called for more long-term support to protect residents who had expressed "safety concerns" for "far too long".

Myer said current national funding formulas for the police and fire service did not take into account the "seriousness" of the crime people in Teesside faced.

"We essentially have a metropolitan style of crime and also risk of fire but with a sort of rural-style funding," he said.

"This is why we need to see a real overhaul of the funding formula."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey told the Press Association the events in and around Middlesbrough over the last week were "deeply worrying".

On Saturday, PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough died when a Volkswagen Passat, which was going the wrong way on the A66 at South Bank, hit their vehicle.

The five young men in the Volkswagen also died and inquests into all seven deaths opened on Thursday.

Police said 17 people, aged between 18 and 61, had been arrested across Teesside as part of an investigation into the lead-up to the crash.

They have been held on a range of offences including possession of a firearm and being part of an organised crime group.

News.title: Clean-up of illegal waste supersite costs taxpayers £6m
News.content:
The clear-up of one of England's largest illegal waste tips has been completed - landing taxpayers with a Â£6m bill.

The government has vowed to recoup the clearance costs for the Kidlington dump in Oxfordshire - and seven other sites - from the criminals responsible.

In 2025, around 22,000 tonnes of domestic and commercial rubbish was dumped at the spot, between the River Cherwell and the A34. It is one of nearly 30 so-called "supersites" first uncovered by a BBC investigation.

The government, which launched a crackdown on waste crime last week, said it would do more to force criminals to pay for clean-up operations by confiscating their money and assets.

But figures obtained by the BBC show that, in the past five years, the Environment Agency has so far managed to claw back just over Â£7m from waste criminals using Proceeds of Crime Act (Poca) confiscation orders.

At the same time, the agency says waste crime costs the economy Â£1bn a year., external

Campaigners have labelled the amount taken from convicted criminals as "derisory" while the Country Land and Business Association (CLA), which represents rural landowners, asked: "Where is the deterrent?"

The amount paid by criminals so far was revealed by an Environmental Information Regulations (EIR) request to the Environment Agency by the BBC.

It shows there have been 66 confiscation orders between January 2021 and March 2026, totalling Â£7.3m.

Fourteen orders have yet to be fully paid, leaving around Â£1.4m still to be recovered.

The figures cover those larger illegal sites for which the Environment Agency is responsible, and do not include confiscation orders for smaller fly-tipping offences, which fall under the remit of local authorities.

News.title: What we know after the big Grand Theft Auto 6 preview
News.content:
After more than 18 months since the last official glimpse of Grand Theft Auto 6, developer Rockstar has shown fans a 26-minute preview of the upcoming blockbuster video game.

Its "extended look" debuted on Netflix, six hours before going live on YouTube, and was the first chance players have had to see detailed footage of the title in action.

The montage, with no commentary or explanatory captions, showed off improved graphics, detailed environments and a selection of car-chases and shoot-outs from the sequel.

The broadcast followed a week of unauthorised gameplay leaks, which the developer said it had been "heartbreaking" to see shared online.

After it got its chance to show the version of GTA 6 it wanted the world to see, here are some things we learned, and some things we still don't know.

News.title: Trump signs order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America
News.content:
US President Donald Trump has signed an executive order seeking to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America.

The move comes after trade talks between the US and Canada collapsed late last week, and the US imposed new 50% tariffs on $20bn (C$28bn) worth of Canadian goods. Canada will implement "dollar for dollar" counter tariffs next month.

Trump has repeatedly posted threats about renaming the lake, one of the five Great Lakes that straddle both countries, on social media amid the trade dispute.

He said on Thursday the move was "official, effective immediately" and that his administration has "filed all the necessary papers, documents" to make the change.

Text of the executive order says it gives the US Department of the Interior 30 days to update the name change with the Geographic Names Information Service - the official repository of domestic geographic names in the US.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney noted the name Lake Ontario can be traced back more than 400 years, adding in a social media post on Thursday that preceded the formation of the Canadian Confederation and the US Declaration of Independence.

"We know that the United States is changing. Their trade relations, their foreign policy, their national monuments, their hydronyms," he wrote. "Canadian women and men also know that things must be called by their name, and this lake is called Lake Ontario â today and forever."

When Trump took the White House in 2025, he signed a similar order that changed the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. Mexico has rejected the name change, arguing a single country cannot rename a shared body of international water.

It also led to a legal dispute between Mexico and tech giant Google, which renamed the gulf in its maps application. , external

In that case, Google Maps users in the US see "Gulf of America", while those in Mexico see the "Gulf of Mexico". Those in other countries see the "Gulf of Mexico (Gulf of America)".

The White House at the time also blocked Associated Press reporters from presidential events over the news agency's refusal to adopt the name "Gulf of America" in its coverage. The AP sued the Trump administration in response, and that legal battle is ongoing.

News.title: NHS bosses warn of chaos in ADHD and autism care
News.content:
Autism and ADHD care is at risk of descending into chaos, NHS bosses are warning, as costs spiral out of control and unregulated private providers capitalise on the huge demand for help.

The NHS Alliance, which represents health managers, says the current system represents a "bad deal" for patients and taxpayers alike.

It points to big variations in what the NHS is being charged for assessments and care - in one case, a local health board was paying Â£300 to Â£3,000 for similar services.

The group says there has been a rapid expansion in new providers â both private firms and charities are involved - and NHS managers are struggling to ensure the quality and safety of care being provided.

The government said an independent review into services would be published soon and it would act on the findings of that, promising a ânew national approachâ for autism, ADHD and mental health.

Ahead of that, the NHS Alliance has been gathering information from integrated care boards, which hold the budgets for local services, about the current state of care.

Under the right to choose policy, patients can decide to opt for care from both NHS and non-NHS autism and ADHD services.

The initiative is aimed at helping patients bypass the long waiting lists that have developed in recent years.

The NHS Alliance said the policy has led to an influx of new providers, helping to reduce some of the longest waits for adults and children, but at a cost.

It found a number of boards were reporting sharp rises in spending, describing it as "out of control".

One board saw costs rising 10-fold in a year, to Â£1.5 million a month.

Another saw annual spend jump from Â£4 million a year to Â£30 million over the course of two years.

News.title: Bank holiday weekend to see more thunderstorms and rain
News.content:
Most of the UK is finally getting some rain, in time for the bank holiday weekend.

The weather will remain unsettled across the next few days with showers, longer spells of rain and thunderstorms all likely at times.

By Monday the focus of the wet weather is likely to be across Scotland, with sunny spells developing elsewhere.

The RAC estimates that 20 million trips by car will be made across the weekend in what could be challenging driving conditions.

News.title: King 'heartbroken' by deadly Nepal flash floods
News.content:
The prime minister and the Foreign Office in the UK have urged people to follow local guidance and remain alert to the changing situation, as officials in Nepal warn of a possible secondary flood risk near the Bhote Koshi river.

The Foreign Office added it was working closely with Nepalese authorities.

A British woman from Slough, Leena Bector, has been confirmed by Fishtail Tours and Travels as missing. Her husband, Bhupesh Bector, told the Times he is flying out to the country.

"I know that she's in Nepal for sure, so even if they find her today or tomorrow, I need to be there," he said.

British resident Pramod Pudel, who lives in East Sussex but is originally from Nepal, told BBC Radio Sussex on Thursday that "nothing remains" where his family lives and he is flying back to search for his wife, mother, brother and uncle.

"It's a very, very difficult time for me and for my family and my country at this moment, but obviously I have to go and see what's happening there," he said.

"A lot of people are missing and there is no information regarding who is missing, where they are. Nobody can contact each other and all the bridges are broken, so you can't cross the land.

"There's no power, no electricity, so I can't contact anyone, so it's a very difficult time not knowing what's happening."

Essex nurse Rajendra Pudasaini said his relatives were "swept away" by the floods.

"My wife's auntie and uncle, and their granddaughter and her husband are missing, and my godson as well," he told PA Media.

"They're gone. The speed the water came, they couldn't be saved, they were just swept away."

Meanwhile, a Nepalese man living in Aberdeen Barun Lamichhane, 26, told BBC Scotland News his brother, uncle and cousin all died in the disaster - but his mother, father and grandmother managed to escape.

Lamichhane said they got away by "crawling like a baby" into the hillside.

Other families are waiting for news, including Tatajana Phillips, from Folkestone in Kent, who said the last known location of her sister Julija Jakovicka was in the border area an hour before the flash floods struck.

"We are really hoping that people hear us and try to find and locate [my sister]".

Phillips said her sister, a mother-of-two living in Germany, was in the country for a yoga and meditation retreat.

"We are terribly worried," added Phillips' husband Ben. "We just know where they were and that's really tough."

News.title: Rape and sex offence specialists on all police forces by 2027, PM says
News.content:
Investigators specialising in rape and sex offences will be introduced to every police force in England and Wales by the end of 2027, the government has said.

Ministers are speeding up the rollout of the scheme, previously announced by Sir Keir Starmer's government, by 18 months as part of efforts to tackle violence against women and girls (VAWG).

They are also offering more money for some forces to boost protection orders.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the previous plans were "too slow" and ministers should be "laser focused" on tackling such crimes.

One charity has welcomed the measures, but says they represent "only a small portion of what is needed" for victims.

The Home Office initially announced the plans last year and was due to have teams in place by summer 2029.

Burnham said: "The scale of violence and abuse suffered by women and girls in this country is unacceptable.

"We're taking action to accelerate the roll out of specialist rape and sexual offence teams, who will go after perpetrators, enforce strict new protection orders to protect survivors, and invest in programmes to intensively manage offenders to break the cycle of abuse."

Up to 10 police forces across England and Wales will also get a share of a Â£13.3m pot to boost the teams managing protection orders, where offenders are subject to electronic monitoring, exclusion zones and other measures, the Home Office has said.

Minister for Safeguarding Satvir Kaur said violence against women and girls was one of the "most critical challenges of our time" and the government was strengthening its response by "relentlessly pursuing perpetrators and helping victims live their life without fear".

The charity Refuge welcomed the changes, but suggested the government should go further.

Its head of policy and public affairs Ellie Butt said the measures "represent only a small portion of what is needed to ensure all survivors can access timely and effective support".

She said the charity hoped the announcement would be the "first step of many" in Burnham's plans to tackle VAWG, adding that protection orders were "highly underutilised" and "enforcement is often inadequate".

"Survivors often avoid reporting the abuse they've experienced to the police for fear of being disbelieved or undermined, so for protection order teams to increase uptake of these tools, genuine efforts are needed to build women's and girls' confidence in policing and ensure abuse does not go unreported," she added.

In December, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood described violence against women and girls as a "national emergency" as she announced plans for the specialist investigation teams.

She told the BBC at the time that the way police forces investigate cases was "too much of a postcode lottery".

The accelerated rollout comes as the prime minister has been facing pressure over the early release scheme, designed to avert overcrowding in the country's prisons.

Justice Secretary Alex Norris is expected to reveal the findings of a review of the scheme next week when MPs return to Parliament from their summer recess.

The plans were paused earlier in the summer, and the eligibility for the scheme was also changed, removing the right of those convicted of rape, serious child sex offences and grooming to have their sentences cut.

However, domestic abuse commissioner Nicole Jacobs said not excluding domestic abusers was "wrong and puts victims lives at risk".

She said earlier this month: "It is critical that no abuser is released in October unless I am confident that victims' safety is not being compromised."

News.title: 'Cowboy builders' targeted in new government clampdown
News.content:
People carrying out home renovations will gain greater protections against "cowboy builders" through a new database of trusted traders and a payment system offering more safeguards, the government has said.

Traders signing up to the scheme launching next month will need to demonstrate certain standards of customer service, transparency and dispute resolution.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said unscrupulous tradespeople "leave families with months of stress" as well as unfinished work.

The National Federation of Builders said the changes would not stop rogue operators while the Tories suggested there would be added paperwork for firms already operating legitimately.

Citizens Advice has said home renovations are one of its biggest sources of consumer complaints.

The government said more than a quarter of people who carried out home improvements in the past 18 months have experienced problems, such as builders disappearing after upfront payments were made.

It cited a survey carried out for the Competition and Markets Authority, external suggesting customers lost more Â£10bn in 2024 on home and garden maintenance services due to losses, overpriced costs or unfair practices by traders.

BBC News has previously reported on "bait-and-switch" locksmith scams, where customers were given an initial cheap quote before hidden charges and unnecessary work were added.

Under the new traders' scheme, customers' money will be held in an account and released in parts after certain milestones in projects are completed.

The National Federation of Builders (NFB) told BBC Breakfast there are already schemes in place to find trustworthy builders.

Adas Rico Wojtulewicz-Richmond, the NFB's director of policy, said: "Is this scheme going to stop bad actors operating and ripping people off? I don't think it will."

He said a better approach would be for every project to have a "passport" which records all the work done.

"It protects consumers because you can find out which companies are doing a poor job, and it brings up the industry standards," he said.

The prime minister said rogue tradespeople gave their "decent, hardworking" counterparts a bad name and would be "putting the cowboys out of business".

Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said that, while home improvements can be stressful, "we're taking action to protect consumers, support reputable traders and make sure people can spend their money with greater confidence and security".

Shadow business secretary Andrew Griffith said the announcement looks like "the sort of government initiative that risks the unintended consequence of piling more paperwork onto the majority of businesses who already do the right thing".

He said: "The government would do far better to beef up law enforcement and have tougher sentences for the minority who fraudulently rip off customers. Those who break the rules will keep breaking them regardless of whether there is an app in the way."

Liberal Democrat business spokesperson Sarah Olney said: "Rogue builders cause real harm and ruin real lives every year. The current system is simply not fit for purpose and this half-baked announcement falls frustratingly short from fixing it.

"A voluntary code for tradespeople completely misses the mark. Rogue operators won't voluntarily sign up - they will simply keep exploiting families in the shadows."

News.title: Sports Direct founder Mike Ashley attacks Burnham's 'populist' High Street plans.
News.content:
Billionaire Sports Direct founder Mike Ashley has criticised recent cost of living and retail policies from Andy Burnham as "populist reactions".

In a letter to the prime minister, the entrepreneur accused him of "jumping on 'everyday fixes' or bandwagons", while "disastrous" business rates policies and increases to the cost of employing workers were causing businesses to struggle.

He also described a previous proposal of increasing business rates on large warehouses to help reduce them for pubs and clubs as "delusional".

A Downing Street spokesperson said Burnham would "build a new economy that backs British business, delivers growth in every postcode and ensures the essentials in life - like energy, water and housing - are affordable again."

Promises including cutting VAT from household electricity bills and reducing business rates for some firms is "just the start", they added.

Earlier this month, Burnham promised to revitalise Britain's "hollowed out" high streets by helping councils block new vaping and betting shops.

He also brought forward a plan to end subscription traps and ban shops using misleading recommended retail prices, which can make it seem like discounts are larger than they really are.

In Ashley's letter, seen by the BBC and first reported by the Financial Times,, external he hit out at announcements made since Burnham succeeded Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister.

The businessman called on Burnham to use his first Budget, scheduled for 27 October, to lower costs for employers and change the government's position on business rates.

Pubs, social clubs and live music venues will get a 20% business rates cut from April, while a review has been launched into how the tax, which high street firms have long called for reform to, is calculated.

"Shortsighted or populist reactions to underlying business challenges are not the answer," Ashley said in the letter.

Ashley has repeatedly called for a fundamental overhaul of the tax, including levelling the playing field between High Street retailers and online rivals.

"If your answer is to tax larger retailers even more, through hiking business rates on retailer owned or third-party warehouses whilst reducing rates for pubs and clubs, then that is simply delusional," he wrote.

Burnham previously said before he was prime minister that cuts for pubs, clubs and music venues could be paid for by higher levies on warehouses operated by online firms such as Amazon, and targeting the owners of empty high street properties.

Ashley built Frasers Group from a single Sports Direct store in Maidenhead in 1982 to a sprawling empire of dozens of brands employing 30,000 people.

The billionaire has frequently attracted controversy from investors and the media, with accusations over the years of building success by exploiting workers.

In 2016, Ashley admitted to MPs that workers at his Derbyshire warehouse had been paid below the minimum wage and a policy of fining staff for being late was unacceptable.

The business, still owned by Ashley but run by his son-in-law Michael Murray, this month bought luxury department store Harvey Nichols and promised a "significant restructuring" of the business.

Ashley also used his letter to ask Burnham how the prime minister intends to revive Harvey Nichols, which has faced financial challenges in recent years.

Referencing comments by Tory peer and former Marks & Spencer boss Lord Rose, who called the announcements "hot air", Ashley said "I agree with him".

"It is the disastrous business rates position (which I have raised many times over the years) and the dramatically increasing cost of employing people that are really causing business to struggle," Ashley said.

"You have the chance to make a difference or get it horribly wrong," he added.

Ashley said the High Street will be "further devastated" without major reforms, and warned Burnham's suggestion he will consider further business rates changes in the coming Budget are "too little, too late".

He also used the letter to attack Burnham's plans to clamp down on the use of recommended retail prices, saying instead the real issue is "price fixing in sporting goods and other markets" - where he cited the rising cost of official football merchandise.

News.title: Number of asylum seekers in hotels halves in a year
News.content:
There was also a fall in the number of family members coming to the UK to join someone already legally in the country, while asylum claims were also down by a fifth.

Some 38,000 illegal arrivals were detected in the year to June - 33,000 of them on small boats across the sea from France.

More up to date figures show the trend in small boat arrivals has continued to be lower than last year. Correspondingly, claims for asylum have also fallen.

Some 86,000 people sought asylum - down a fifth on the previous year. About half of those applications for help came from people who were already legally in the UK, rather than having arrived on a small boat.

The rise in the use of hotels coincided with an increase in arrivals across the English Channel from 2019 and a slowing down of Home Office decisions as to how many of these claimants had a genuine right to stay in the UK or should be told to leave.

One of the first decisions of the new Starmer government in July 2024 was to order officials to work faster in deciding these claims, with a target of ending the use of hotels within five years.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said: "A little over two years into office and the asylum backlog is down, the number of asylum seekers in hotels is falling, illegal working arrests are at record levels, and deportations and returns are up markedly.

"Small boats numbers are also now falling, but we are not complacent and there is more we must do."

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said Labour was "moving illegal immigrants out of hotels and into flats in your building."

He said a Conservative government would deport every illegal immigrant and leave the European Court of Human Rights.

"The surest way to empty the accommodation is to make plain that nobody who crosses the Channel gets to stay," he added.

In response to the new figures, Reform UK said Britain was at "breaking point".

Zia Yusuf, its home affairs spokesman, said "Under Reform, illegal boats in the Channel will be stopped by our Navy, and all those here illegally will be detained and deported."

The number of people in houses around the country paid for by the Home Office has gone up from 65,000 at the end of 2024 to 69,000 in June this year - arrangements that are part of a decade-long standing contract with private providers.

The number of asylum claimants waiting for an initial ruling on their case - meaning they are told whether they have a genuine case for protection or should leave the UK - was 40,000. That is down from the peak of 175,000 in June 2023.

Meanwhile some 40,000 found not to have a reason to be in the UK - either foreign offenders, visa overstayers or failed asylum applicants - were removed from the country in the year to June 2026, an 8% increase on the year before.

Officials say about a third were failed asylum seekers - the highest number for 16 years and double the rate of removals that occurred in 2021.

News.title: One in eight young people still out of work or education ahead of major review
News.content:
Just under one million young people in the UK are not in education, employment or training - or "Neet" - according to data published ahead of a major report about a "lost generation".

The latest data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) suggests 981,000 people aged 16 to 24 were Neet between April and June. That is about one in eight people in that age group.

The final instalment of a major report by former minister Alan Milburn is expected to set out recommendations for tackling the problem in the coming weeks.

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden told the BBC ministers would "take those [recommendations] forward".

News.title: Teacher guilty of indecent assaults against two pupils
News.content:
A chemistry teacher has been found guilty of indecently assaulting two teenage pupils at an all-boys school in the late 1980s.

Sally-Anne Bowen, who taught at Christ's College in Finchley, north London, assaulted the boys when they were aged around 14 to 15 and she was in her mid-20s.

On Thursday, a jury at Harrow Crown Court found the 65-year-old guilty of seven counts of indecent assault after deliberating for six hours and 29 minutes.

One complainant told the court he had sex with the teacher "about 20 or 30 times" over several months. He said he visited her at home, considered her his girlfriend and had fallen in love with her.

The man, who cannot be named for legal reasons, told the court she had "drummed it" into him that he must not tell anyone about them and to keep it a secret.

A second complainant told jurors he had kissed Bowen in a cafÃ© after being "goaded" into it by other boys.

A former pupil at the school, Tobias Oliver, said during the trial that she acted like she was in "a Sabrina Carpenter video" while in the classroom and "dressed and behaved more like my teenage female friends than the other teachers".

"The topics of conversation in class often strayed away from chemistry and became quite sexual," said Oliver, who did not know the complainants.

He recalled incidents where Bowen flashed her underwear to a class while sitting on a table and went through and discussed a "sex manual" a student had brought in, which Oliver believed to be the Kama Sutra, with the class.

Richard Luker, who was head of science at the school in the late 1980s, told the court he remembered receiving a complaint from the first alleged victim's mother after she was worried that her son was planning to travel abroad with Bowen at the end of term.

During the trial, Bowen claimed the allegations were a "total fabrication" and that she had a medical condition which had not been diagnosed in the late 1980s and made sexual intercourse difficult and painful for her.

Bowen, of Hemel Hempstead, Hertfordshire, was granted bail.

She will be sentenced on 20 November.

News.title: BBC director-general says he was not aware of 'severity' of cuts needed
News.content:
During the conversation with Kirsty Wark, his first major industry appearance, Brittin also said he had been "impressed" by the "creativity and talent" at the BBC, but added "every media organisation is struggling with rapidly changing consumer behaviour and the power of the AI revolution".

Describing the corporation as "inward looking", he also criticised the organisation for this leading to "an aversion to risk".

"You've got very loud critics, many of whom are the commercial rivals of the corporation and you've got political pressure on everything that you do journalistically," he said.

Brittin, who previously worked at Google, took over from Tim Davie earlier this year.

He is the first director-general since Greg Dyke in 2000 to take on the role having not been a former BBC employee.

The former regional policy manager for the tech giant said he wanted to use those skills to "move faster through experimenting and learning" at the organisation and work with colleagues to "find a way to the future together".

Brittin also spoke about the BBC's need to "defend its integrity" as it challenges Donald Trump's defamation case.

The US president is seeking $10bn (Â£7.4bn) in damages in a Florida court over the editing of a Panorama documentary from 2024 about the US Capitol riots.

Legal representatives for the BBC are looking to have the case thrown out, and the corporation has previously apologised for an "error of judgement" in the editing of the programme.

"We moved to dismiss the case on the grounds of jurisdiction in that nobody in the US actually saw the show with the bad edits, and it was a bad edit, and he won the election, and he's got richer," Brittin said during the conversation.

President Trump has shared a chart ranking the best U.S. presidents, and the Republican predictably put himself in the top spot, above such heavyweights as George Washington and Abraham Lincoln.

The president’s Thursday post was in response to a clip from CNN, whose recent poll found that 53 percent of GOPers named Trump as the Republican president they admire the most, beating out Lincoln and Ronald Reagan.

Commentators noted a variety of oddities with Trump’s self-created ranking, such as leaving out his recent Republican predecessors entirely.

“Trump apparently has no opinion on where Ronald Reagan and George W. Bush rank as presidents,” historian Christopher W. Jones wrote on X.

“Trump's stupid chart of ‘greatest’ presidents is a chart from Life Magazine in 1948, with his name added at the top and the Democrats he doesn't like at the bottom,” conspiracy theory expert Mike Rothschild wrote on X. “Exactly the kind of thing a healthy, high-functioning person shares.”

open image in gallery President Trump shared a chart listing the best presidents on Thursday and put himself in the top spot, while leaving out popular Republicans such as Ronald Reagan ( Donald Trump )

The president may rank himself highly, but historians and experts tend not to agree.

Michael Bailey, a political scientist at Georgetown, recently told The New York Times that Trump is “easily the worst president in U.S. history.”

“The corruption and damage to long-term U.S. institutions and reputation are far beyond anything we’ve seen before,” Bailey said.

In 2024, a survey of historians and political scientists also put Trump at the bottom spot, while listing Joe Biden at number 14.

The American public also has a dim view of Trump at the moment, with the Republican’s approval rating hitting rock bottom last week with the support of just one-third of Americans.

President Trump has long taken an interest in history, albeit a highly partisan one.

open image in gallery President Trump previously redecorated the White House with a presidential ‘Walk of Fame’ ( AFP/Getty )

During his second term, he installed a presidential “Walk of Fame” at the White House featuring portraits of his predecessors and descriptions of their achievements.

Historians say the information on the plaques was highly partisan and often inaccurate.

One historian said that the level of scholarship that went into the plaques, which the White House claims Trump partially wrote himself, is about as high as “drawing mustaches on other people's portraits.”

In addition to spreading historical materials, President Trump has also taken a keen interest in removing materials he finds offensive.

Plaques and other materials detailing sensitive subjects — often involving America’s history of racism — have been removed at national historical sites, and the president ordered a wide-ranging audit against the Smithsonian aimed at eliminating information that didn’t fit with his conception of history.

As rescue teams searched for missing people following catastrophic flooding along the Nepal-China border, Earth scientists reviewed satellite imagery for clues to the cause and assessed the devastation.

The flooding Wednesday killed hundreds of people in Nepal and Tibet, and hundreds more are missing, including foreigners and pilgrims.

Geomorphologists Kristen Cook and Dan Shugar said initial images from Nepal were obscured by clouds and dust from the debris, so they could only see that part of a glacier had broken off from Langtang Lirung peak, near the border with Tibet. In clearer images from Thursday, they said they could see that the bedrock underneath the glacier had collapsed, taking the massive chunk of ice down with it and sending boulders and ice into the valley.

“It shows the whole area without anything hidden, and we could see that, yes, it looked like there was not only this glacier that had failed, but a much larger chunk of the bedrock of the mountainside itself that had given way,” said Shugar, associate professor at the University of Calgary. “You have this big bedrock failure that took part of the glacier with it.”

Shugar said it’s heart-wrenching to look downstream from there on the images, to where people were living, and see how the debris has buried villages.

After slamming to the valley floor, the debris maintained its momentum through the steep, narrow valley as ice melted, said Cook, at the Université Grenoble Alpes in France. Water and mud several stories high swept through communities.

The Trishuli River surged during the flooding. Before and after satellite images of the Kolpurtar, Betrawati and Syapru Besi areas of Nepal show that the river is now much wider, and brown and black, because it overtopped its banks in some areas and filled with debris in others. The change in the color of the water shows how much sediment the flow was carrying, turning from greenish to very brown because it's full of mud, Cook said.

Towns and villages that were devastated along the river banks are submerged in debris and mud. They appear as areas of brown. Some houses are still poking through in an image of the Betrawati area.

The flooding toppled and swept away buildings in Syapru Besi, a popular tourist spot where a famous trek to Langtang begins. In before and after images, a side river is now wider too, because the flow was so powerful it pushed upstream.

The flooding “left a wasteland in its wake” that will take many years to recover from, said Alton Byers, a mountain geographer at the University of Colorado at Boulder. Byers lived in Nepal and now returns there yearly to study glacial hazards and work with communities to prepare. This is the largest glacier flood he has seen, by far.

Byers, faculty research scientist at the university's Institute of Arctic and Alpine Research, said he thinks Wednesday's flooding is related to climate change. The Earth's warming is melting glaciers and permafrost, causing instability and the breakage of massive amounts of snow and ice at high altitudes. That can be a catalyst for a series of cascading events, he said.

“All the indicators, to me, point to the impacts of warming trends,” he said. “In this case, the permafrost that for millennia has helped to hold together high-altitude rock and ice and soil and glaciers is now weakening and becoming unstable."

Cook and Shugar said that at this point, they can't say for sure there's a direct link to climate change. Slopes fail and landslides happen, Cook said, though permafrost is melting and that is destabilizing mountainsides.

“While we cannot at this point directly link this collapse to climate change, it is not unexpected to see more events of this type with a warming climate,” Cook said. “Not this big, hopefully not this big.”

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has agreed to a $16.7 million deal for 6,000 pairs of gloves capable of delivering painful electric shocks, stating that officers will use them to subdue uncooperative detainees and protesters.

The purchase went ahead despite pushback from civil rights advocates and Democratic members of Congress, who warned that ICE officers cannot be trusted to deploy the equipment appropriately.

A notice on a federal database published Thursday revealed ICE signed a no-bid contract with Kentucky-based firm Compliant Technologies LLC, which produces the items. The transaction covers securing 6,000 devices, as well as support equipment and services, over the next six months.

open image in gallery The transaction covers securing 6,000 devices, as well as support equipment and services, over the next six months ( AP Photo/Dylan Lovan )

Civil rights advocates have said ICE officers already face criticism for their use of force with little oversight or accountability while enforcing President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown.

ICE published the notice hours after a group of U.S. senators, led by Democrat Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada, urged the agency to cancel its plan to buy the gloves. In a letter to ICE's acting director Thursday, Cortez Masto and 15 of her colleagues in the Democratic caucus questioned ICE's need for the devices.

“The blatant and tragic misuse of force in Los Angeles, Chicago, Minneapolis, Houston, Maine, and other locations around the country raises significant skepticism about the agency’s professional capability to safely deploy a new tool that could be used to harm Americans without cause,” the letter said.

The senators were the latest to express opposition to the plan, which became public this month when ICE published a notice outlining its intent to purchase thousands of “conductive distraction and de-escalation devices” for officers and investigators.

The devices are normal patrol gloves until an officer presses a button to activate the electrical mode. They must be applied directly to someone’s skin to produce a shock that causes pain, which is promoted as a way to gain compliance from people who are resisting. They have been used by some local jails and police departments in recent years.

ICE's notice said officers would use them in “high-tension environments,” including while making arrests, transporting combative detainees and responding to civil disturbances outside detention facilities.

open image in gallery ICE's notice said officers would use them in ‘high-tension environments’ ( AP Photo/Ryan Murphy )

“It will be used when a subject is actively or passively resisting and an officer needs to gain control quickly to prevent injuries to both parties,” the document said.

It said that the shocks would help “maintain control over inmates and prevent aggression or escape attempts,” allow officers to handcuff people hiding their hands, and assist in crowd control. The goal would be to avoid using “more severe force,” including firearms. The notice said the gloves would be used with “approved policy, training, and accountability standards,” but it did not elaborate.

Cortez Masto and the other senators said in their letter that the device “presents substantial risks if deployed during civil arrests — even more so if it is deployed without clear limits, appropriate training, and comprehensive oversight.” They said ICE must make public details about how officers will be trained and how use of the gloves will be documented and reviewed internally to avoid misuse.

ICE's parent agency, the Department of Homeland Security, reacted defiantly to critics of the purchase.

“Sanctuary politicians attempting to ban our federal law enforcement from any safety equipment is despicable and a deliberate attempt to undermine and endanger our officers,” the agency said in a statement.

News.title: ‘Most’ of Trump’s staff wants to leave the White House, reporter claims
News.content:

The mood inside the White House has reportedly taken a dive and numerous staffers could be heading towards the exit sometime soon, following Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt’s impending departure.

“He is not in a great place with his staff, according to everyone we talked to,” New York Times correspondent Maggie Haberman, co-author of a recent book on Trump, told MS Now on Thursday. “He is lashing out a lot, which tends to happen when things are not going well.”

“Most people have decided that they want to go do something else,” she added.

“Maggie Haberman of the Failing New York Times constantly speaks like she’s a Trump psychologist when in reality she just has a creepy obsession with the President and clings onto him for relevance,” White House spokesman Davis Ingle told The Independent in a statement. “It’s been very sad to watch for years.”

Reports have trickled out about tension inside the administration.

open image in gallery Numerous Trump staff members are considering leaving the administration this midterm season, according to Trump whisperer Maggie Haberman ( Reuters )

There has reportedly been grumbling inside the White House about Natalie Harp, an aide known for her intense devotion to the president.

“She is not beloved by a lot of her colleagues,” Haberman told CNN last week.

The president allegedly recently confronted Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at Camp David about how the Iran war is causing a shortage of U.S. munitions that could limit American options to end the conflict.

Trump allegedly expressed that he felt misled about the dwindling weapons stockpile, saying that he thought the issue “had been fixed,” two people familiar with the matter told The Washington Post.

The report prompted the president to lash out on social media against “treasonous” leakers.

“Defense companies are building the largest number of plants and factories in our country’s history,” the president wrote on Truth Social earlier this month about the “100 percent fake” news story. “The ‘leakers’ of these treasonous statements are being hunted down. Long term jail sentences will be sought!”

The White House was also reportedly unhappy that FBI Director Kash Patel was seen partying with members of the victorious U.S. Olympic hockey team earlier this year and openly discussed firing him.

The White House and Patel have denied such accounts, and the FBI director launched a defamation suit against The Atlantic over its reporting about Patel’s alleged troubles in office.

open image in gallery Multiple high-profile officials have left the Cabinet this year, including Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem ( PA )

Before Leavitt’s exit, expected at the end of this month, there were a few high-profile staff changes.

In March, Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem was ousted, in the wake of scrutiny into department spending and mass outrage after immigration agents fatally shot two protesters in Minnesota.

The following month, Attorney General Pam Bondi was fired, following chaos surrounding the DOJ’s handling of the Epstein files.

Over the fall, Trump had publicly called on Bondi to be more aggressive about prosecuting his enemies.

The U.S. is reportedly close to cementing a “massive” deal for access to Venezuelan oil fields.

"Calling this deal huge would be an understatement," a U.S. official familiar with negotiations told Axios. "It is massive."

The deal would reportedly see the U.S. gain an ownership stake or long-term access for oil fields with proven reserves of 90 billion barrels, officials told the outlet.

The State Department was in Venezuela last month to discuss the deal, according to Axios.

"This is real and being discussed at the highest levels of the U.S. ​and Venezuelan governments," an inside source told Reuters.

open image in gallery The Trump administration is reportedly close to striking a deal for U.S. ownership or long-term access to Venezuelan oil fields ( AFP/Getty )

The deal could take the form of a lease, with further auctions or tenders allocating oil fields to U.S. producers, according to the outlet.

The Independent has contacted the White House, State Department and Venezuelan government for comment.

The U.S. has been managing Venezuelan oil sales since American troops captured Venezuelan strongman Nicolás Maduro in a commando raid in January and brought him back to the U.S. to face criminal charges.

Shortly after the operation, the U.S. said major companies would be investing at least $100 billion in Venezuelan oil fields, which were degraded and plagued with corruption under Maduro and his predecessor, despite Venezuela possessing the world’s largest share of proven oil reserves.

President Trump said in July that the U.S. has collected more than $13 billion from the sale of Venezuelan oil.

″$13 billion from Venezuela? I think even more than that,” he told reporters. “We’ve paid for that war many times over.”

open image in gallery The U.S. has been controlling Venezuelan oil sales since capturing and deposing Nicolás Maduro in January ( @realDonaldTrump/Truth Social )

There have been few details released publicly about how the U.S. is facilitating the sales and how much oil revenue is being returned to the Venezuelan state.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said oil sales are being audited by the firm KPMG and money from the sales is being held in a Citibank account.

The Trump administration has issued temporary sanctions relief authorizing U.S. companies and individuals to do business with the Venezuelan oil sector.

An infusion of Venezuelan oil into U.S. markets could be a boon ahead of the midterms for the Trump administration, which has struggled with high fuel prices caused by the Iran war and its strangling of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital oil shipping route.

The Trump administration has a habit of teasing grand international deals, only for them to fall short.

The White House has repeatedly announced the end of the Iran war is near at hand, only for the conflict to continue. It has also watched as trade negotiations with Canada have fallen apart and Israel has rejected parts of its Gaza peace plan.

News.content:

The Trump administration has begun work on a project to build a stretch of border wall in southern Arizona along part of a Native American tribe’s reservation, pushing ahead with one of its signature projects despite protests from the tribe.

U.S. Customs and Border Protection says the area is a dangerous smuggling route and that building the wall will close a longstanding security gap. But members of the Tohono O'odham Nation, whose membership spans both sides of the U.S.-Mexico border, have accused the administration of trespassing and say the construction will damage land sacred to the tribe.

The wall segment is part of a $46 billion dollar effort by the Trump administration to fill the border with 30-foot (9-meter) steel bollard walls, vehicle barriers, and technology designed to stop undocumented immigration and smuggling.

But as building efforts have ramped up, the administration has run into opposition from landowners, environmental groups, and Native American tribes who say construction is violating property rights and desecrating sacred indigenous sites.

The Tohono O'odham Nation said in a statement Tuesday that about 20 Customs and Border Protection officers, working with contractors, went onto the tribe's land early that morning to begin construction.

Drone videos published by nation officials show roughly 14 vehicles and an industrial drill at one of the sites.

A federal judge permitted the government to move forward with construction earlier this month, but the tribe says the contractors are violating tribal codes and trespassing to access the border wall site.

The Tohono O’odham Nation, which has 37,000 members including thousands who live in Mexico, sued the federal government in June in an attempt to block construction of the border wall. The tribe argued that the wall would cause “significant devastation” on the reservation, including the destruction of mountain peaks sacred to the tribe, and would alter boundaries of their nation.

US District Judge Richard Leon in Washington, D.C., an appointee of former President George W. Bush, ruled in favor of the government, noting that the border wall wpi;d be built on a 60-foot (18-meter) wide buffer zone of federally owned land called the Roosevelt Reservation.

“Defendants have not yet articulated plans to construct outside the Roosevelt Reservation,” the judge wrote in his opinion.

The Tohono O'odham Nation said that even if construction were contained to the Roosevelt Reservation, driving onto tribal land to access the area still constitutes trespassing.

“The contractors, who are on the Nation illegally, were accompanied by agents as they worked on three separate locations near the border with drill trucks to conduct soil sampling and other activities,” tribal officials said in a statement.

The CBP agents were masked, armed, and set up a vehicle blockade to stop tribal police from removing the contractors, according to Tohono O’odham officials. The nation had set up “No Trespassing” signs before Tuesday.

So far, no physical confrontations between police or members of the Tohono O’odham nation have been reported.

CBP defended the need for the wall in a statement Tuesday, saying the desert spanning the Tohono O’odham Nation is a corridor for drug smuggling.

“The project will close one of the most dangerous smuggling and trafficking corridors on the Southwest border: remote desert that has facilitated decades of drug loads, migrant deaths, and cartel activity,” said CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott.

Tribal officials said they’re exploring further legal actions in an effort to remove contractors.

SLSCO Ltd., the Texas-based construction company building the section in Arizona, has secured over $390 million in funding from the Department of Homeland Security to build the border wall since 2023.

City officials on Thursday approved a $2.3 billion deal for a new Tampa Bay Rays ballpark funded by public and private money.

The 4-3 vote by the Tampa City Council came three months after a tentative agreement was reached for a stadium, which would include $967 million in tax money.

Rays Chief Executive Officer Ken Babby said in a statement that the stadium project will “deliver lasting benefits” for the region.

“The Tampa Bay Rays are grateful for the leadership and support of the City Council members to approve an investment that, when accompanied by the private funding guaranteed by the Rays, will secure the future of Major League Baseball in Tampa Bay while creating a landmark destination neighborhood that will serve our region for generations,” Babby said Thursday.

Hillsborough County Commissioners will vote on the project Friday morning.

The Rays ownership reached an agreement earlier this year with Hillsborough College to build the stadium and mixed-use entertainment district on the campus and to renovate some of the school's buildings. The property is located next to the New York Yankees’ spring training facility and across a highway from Raymond James Stadium, home of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

The Rays have said they hope to have the new stadium built within three years.

Since the team took the field in 1998, the Rays have played at Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, except for moving home games to the Yankees' George M. Steinbrenner Field in 2025 following hurricane damage at the Trop. The Rays' lease runs through at least the 2028 season. The team returned to the Trop last month for the start of this season.

A proposed $1.3 billion redevelopment deal for a new ballpark adjacent to the Trop fell through last year, raising new questions about the future of the team, which was bought last September by Patrick Zalupski’s ownership group.

News.title: Champions League draw: Arsenal to renew Mourinho rivalry with Real Madrid tie
News.content:
Hello and welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of the Champions League draw in Monaco, with the 36 teams in this season’s competition finding out their eight league phase fixtures.

The teams will be split into four pots of nine, based on “club coefficient rankings”, with defending champions Paris St-Germain automatically named as the top seed.

Liverpool, Manchester City and Arsenal will be among the teams joining the Parisians in pot one, while the two remaining English teams, Manchester United and Aston Villa, will be in pot two.

Proceedings will begin with a team from pot one being drawn at random, and they will be allocated eight fixtures – four at home and four away – by an automated software. They will face two teams from each pot, with one home game and one away game per pot, while they cannot play a team from their country.

This will be done for all nine teams from pot one, before the same process takes place for pot two teams, though they will already know their pot one opponents. Pot three teams will then find out their pot three and four opponents, before the pot four sides are allocated their fixtures against each other.

This season is the third under the new format, with a league phase instead of a group stage, and Uefa has confirmed that fixtures that have taken place in the league phase of the two previous seasons cannot be repeated this time around.

For example, Liverpool cannot host Real Madrid in the league phase this term after welcoming the 15-time European champions to Anfield at this stage of the previous two campaigns. Andoni Iraola’s side could, however, travel to the Bernabeu for an away meeting with Madrid.

The league phase will kick off on 8 September and will be wrapped up after all teams play at the same time on 27 January. The top eight teams of the league phase progress to the last 16 automatically, while teams that finish between ninth and 24th will be forced to navigate a play-off tie to reach the knockout stages.

The draw is expected to get underway at 5pm.

News.title: England return to proper Test cricket with gritty batting performance
News.content:
Cox unfurled some fine drives and assessed conditions like a veteran, scoring quickly to a run-a-ball 38 but only six more from his next 48 as Pakistan knocked over partners at the other end. It was vital Cox stayed in to stabilise the innings. It is the job of a No 3 to attack or defend; calibrate their game to what is required at the time. Cox, when he played briefly for England in New Zealand two winters ago and before injury cut short his tour, looked to be a player drunk on the Bazball fumes. He was out in a warm-up match against a New Zealand XI in Queenstown hooking and flailing at the ball. This was his second mature performance in a row, an innings of 55 to follow his 73 at Leeds and this was made in much harder circumstances.

Pakistan were better after their Headingley horror show. Mohammad Abbas must feel more at home on a dank London day than he does in Sialkot, and can earn a place on the honours board if he nicks the last England wicket after taking four for 56. Mohammad Ali bowled some jaffas, and some rubbish, for three for 67 and spinner Usman Ali kept it tight and found some turn before losing control as Smith went after him. England still scored at 4.4 an over a reflection of some of the wasted deliveries by Pakistan and 10 no-balls.

Inevitably they were a mixed bag in the field. Three dropped catches were redeemed by a run out and a world-class grab at slip by Salman Ali Agha – captain last week, left out here – to dismiss Cox when he lost his shape trying to hit the ball too hard.

News.title: Ebola response shifts to Congo’s river network
News.content:
Stacked with logs and crammed with hundreds of passengers, the giant barges are nudged day after day along one of Africa’s greatest waterways.

The weeks-long voyage looks sedate, but the tugs are pushing their heavily-laden charges along an unstoppable aquatic superhighway.

Sharing the Congo river with these trade behemoths are canoes, fishing boats and smaller wooden cargo ships.

The river connects the wild east of Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) to the capital Kinshasa, in a vital economic artery and transport corridor nearly 1,100 miles long.

The waterway is a lifeline for passengers, timber, produce and goods. Roads are rare and unreliable, and airfares are far too expensive for most.

Now there are concerns the river risks becoming a conduit for something else heading to the capital of nearly 18 million people: the deadly Ebola virus.

News.title: Great British fry-up implicated in Salmonella outbreak
News.content:
The outbreak, which involved packets of chicken-flavoured instant dried noodles, was traced back to a manufacturing plant near Kyiv by the European Centre for Disease Control (ECDC) in June.

“Epidemiological investigations have found that cases in Denmark, Estonia, Germany, Latvia and Lithuania had consumed flavoured noodle products from the same brand. Investigations have linked the products, which were distributed in several countries, to the same producer in Ukraine,” the ECDC said in a statement at the time.

Another outbreak, which lasted from 2021 to 2024, sickened 174 people in the UK and killed one. It was linked to frozen, steam-cooked chicken breast fillets produced in Ukraine.

Although it is not known if the latest outbreak is linked to Ukraine (the UK also imports eggs from countries including Poland, Spain, and Belgium ), Ukraine sits outside of the EU and Salmonella contamination is common in many of the country’s poultry farms.

A senior figure investigating a connected outbreak of Salmonella in the Netherlands told The Telegraph that the “working hypothesis” among British health officials is that the contaminated products have come from Ukraine.

“In Ukraine, thousands of salmonellosis cases are reported each year. The highest incidence is observed among children,” said a study published in the academic journal Advances in Animal and Veterinary Sciences earlier this year.

“The main sources of the pathogen are eggs, chicken meat, and meat and dairy products. Analysis shows that frequent outbreaks are associated with poor food storage conditions [...] predominantly in the southeastern regions of Ukraine,” added the authors from the Institute of Laboratory Diagnostics and Veterinary-Sanitary Expertise in Kyiv.

Britain’s egg consumption has boomed over the last two decades, with 209 eaten per person on average every year compared to roughly 163 per person in 2000.

The rise is thought to have been driven by a spike in baking during the pandemic, the rise of brunch culture and the rise of a focus on diets rich in protein among the young, according to experts.

News.title: Heading to a festival this weekend? Here’s how to fold down a pop-up tent in 60 seconds
News.content:
A pop-up tent can be pitched in seconds and, theoretically, taken down in less, making them perfect for music festivals, casual camping or even waiting in the queue at Wimbledon overnight.

Their problem is that they’re not actually as easy to put away as they should be. Angle it right, and the tent folds away as easily as it popped up. Approach without a plan, and you’ll find yourself wrangling with a seemingly live tent that refuses to fold back into its circular bag.

Here’s my step-by-step guide on how to put away a pop-up tent in less than 60 seconds, to help you avoid that problem. Watch the video to see exactly how I do it.

1. Unzip the doors

This is to let any air escape. Otherwise, you’ll find it balloons out as you try to fold it.

2. Gather the poles

Find the highest arch on both sides, then pull them together into the middle.

News.title: Savio scores on debut as Spurs cruise past Charlton in Carabao Cup
News.content:
It looked like this was going to be a night for “one of their own”, but Tottenham Hotspur’s latest big-money arrival, Sávio, stole the headlines to crank up the excitement at his new club.

Mikey Moore had set Spurs on their way to what proved a comfortable Carabao Cup success over Championship club Charlton Athletic and heard his name sung by the home fans.

But Sávio stepped off the substitutes’ bench to take the limelight with a late goal just a few days after completing his expensive switch from Manchester City, and head coach Roberto De Zerbi is demanding many more to come.

“A perfect day for him,” said De Zerbi. “His biggest improvement is to increase the number of goals. He is one of the best wingers, but the best wingers score many goals and I spoke with him two days ago, and we put the goal at 10-12 goals.

“We need 10-12 goals from the wingers. Last season, we suffered too much because the number of goals were not enough.”

News.title: German airport worker dies of malaria after mosquito imported on plane
News.content:
Five airport workers in Frankfurt have been infected with malaria and one has died after being bitten by a stowaway mosquito, health officials have said.

The employees are thought to have been infected in early July, but their diagnosis was delayed due to a lack of travel history to malaria-endemic regions, according to the Robert Koch Institute, Germany’s federal agency responsible for disease control.

It is believed that they were bitten by mosquitoes which arrived at the airport on a plane, most likely from Africa, where 95 per cent of global malaria cases are found.

The five surviving airport workers – who are all male and are said to work in different parts of the facility and in different jobs – are undergoing medical care.

Traps have now been installed across the airport in an attempt to catch any remaining mosquitoes and analyse their origin, according to an airport spokesperson.

It is not the first time that Frankfurt Airport, Germany’s busiest travel hub, has recorded a case of malaria, according to the Robert Koch Institute, which added that there was another incidence in 2023.

More than 610,000 people die of malaria every year, the overwhelming majority children under five in Africa who are unable to quickly access treatment.

The disease, which is caused by a parasite carried by infected mosquitoes, is largely curable if treated early with antimalarials.

In Britain and Europe, there are thousands of imported cases of malaria every year reported in returning travellers from Africa and Asia – but local transmission is exceedingly rare.

Of the 5,000 or so cases recorded in Europe every year, typically just five are caught locally – either from an airport or from a non-infected European mosquito picking up the disease from a sickened person and spreading it to others.

Early symptoms include fever, headaches, and chills, which can quickly develop into multi-organ failure.

Vaccines were made available for the first time in 2024 and are licenced for use in young children in Africa, although they are thought to be only between 30 and 50 per cent effective at preventing the disease.

News.title: Livestock bacterial disease spreading among humans in Europe
News.content:
In Barcelona, researchers found further evidence that the bacterium was spreading between people.

Nine cases identified between December 2025 and March 2026 were caused by strains that differed by just zero to four genetic mutations, suggesting the infections were part of a recent transmission chain rather than separate cases acquired from animals.

The bacterium can survive in crusted areas on the skin for up to 42 months, according to Dr McHale, raising questions about the role of contaminated surfaces, equipment and shared spaces.

People should not be alarmed by the infection, which is treatable with a course of antibiotics, he added.

This could make hygiene particularly important in places such as saunas, where people may have prolonged skin contact with others and with shared surfaces.

Saunas have historically been a destination for gay and bisexual men seeking social and sexual contact.

Dating apps such as Grindr have since made casual encounters in these environments far easier to arrange, experts say.

“What we’re seeing is the kind of in-person venues like saunas being combined with apps,” said Rusi Jaspal, a Professor of Psychology at the University of Brighton and expert on wellbeing among gay men.

“Someone might, for example, be in a sauna but also have their app on, and that might be a way of getting people to come to the sauna. So they’re not only attracting people who are already in the sauna, but who might be outside of that environment and coming in.”

Progress and complacency

Professor Jaspal believes the success of Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP), which protects against HIV, has also played a role.

“I think that is a really big contributor,” he said. “On the one hand, obviously it’s fantastic that PrEP is there. It prevents HIV; it’s extremely effective against HIV. But it’s not effective against other infections.”

He argued that because PrEP has removed the fear of HIV that shaped gay men’s sexual behaviour for decades, some men are now having condomless sex with more partners, in the belief that other infections are treatable in a way HIV once was not.

“Because they think, well, everything else is treatable – gonorrhoea, syphilis, it’s all treatable – they’re going to just not use condoms,” he said. “That is not only creating more of a risk of infection, but I think people are having more partners as well.”

Sexual contact is not the only route by which the bacterium appears to be spreading.

In Norway, ten cases have been linked to martial arts, with some infections occurring during training in Norway and others during trips to Thailand.

One case report described a 34-year-old Muay Thai fighter who developed recurrent pustular lesions after returning from a training trip, later confirmed as D. congolensis through whole-genome sequencing.

Dr McHale said the bacterium tends to take hold where the skin has already been compromised in some way.

“Predisposing factors for infection include cutaneous microtrauma, for example, from ultraviolet radiation, tick exposure and insect bites, and maceration of the skin,” he said.

Dermatophilus congolensis is notoriously difficult to grow in culture, meaning infections can easily go undiagnosed or be mistaken for more common skin conditions.

Researchers in Barcelona have warned that cases could be going unrecognised because sexual health clinics do not routinely test for the bacterium.

But Professor Jaspal believes the legacy of the HIV/Aids epidemic explains why this cluster was identified so quickly.

He said the crisis of the 1980s, when confusion and stigma allowed the virus to spread largely undetected, forced public health bodies to build far stronger surveillance and communication systems for outbreaks among gay and bisexual men.

That same infrastructure, he argued, has since been used to manage subsequent threats such as mpox – and now this obscure bacterium – far more effectively.

“I think we are quite rightly identifying cases early on, so that we can then communicate that risk to people and encourage precautions to protect themselves,” Professor Jaspal said. “That is really, really important.”
