Developed in collaboration with the Energy Ministry and relevant authorities, La Esperanza Solar aims to shore up the National Electricity System through long-term strategic energy infrastructure investment, as part of the government’s renewable energy plan.

Four days after financial close, the Federal Electricity Commission (CFE) agreed to purchase energy from La Esperanza Solar via a long-term power purchase agreement with CFE Calificados.

CFE Calificados is a CFE subsidiary specializing in providing Qualified Supply of electrical energy to large consumers and industries in Mexico. Qualified Supply refers to vendors whose services have been verified and approved.

“A contract of this nature provides certainty regarding demand, and certainty is crucial for investments of this magnitude to be able to secure financing and construction,” CFE said in a statement.

The combination of PV solar generation and energy storage is particularly relevant, since electricity production depends on the availability of solar resources.

This capacity allows for more flexible management of the energy produced by the plant and contributes to the electricity supply in the Yucatán Peninsula, a region plagued by blackouts in recent years while energy demand continues to rise.

The La Esperanza Solar project also reflects the role of CFE Calificados within the national electricity system. It acts as a marketer that, with the support of the Federal Electricity Commission, contributes to strengthening the transition and national energy sovereignty, explained the state-owned company.

This agreement is part of CFE Calificados’ strategy to strengthen and diversify its portfolio with different generation technologies and to support its customers in the transition to cleaner energy sources.

As part of its adherence to President Claudia Sheinbaum’s clean energy directive, CFE Calificados has signed hedging contracts for renewable energy projects. With these options, large consumers can support their operations with renewable energy and have greater certainty of supply.

Shortly after taking office in October 2024, Sheinbaum declared her government would pursue a target of 38%-45% clean energy by 2030.

With reports from El Economista, Power Gen Advancement and Energy Storage News

World.title: Mexico posts best jobs growth of 2026, but informal sector drives the gain
World.content:
Listen to this article

Mexico added almost 1.1 million informal sector jobs in July but lost more than 400,000 formal sector positions, according to data published by the national statistics agency INEGI on Thursday.

Mexico’s informality rate — the percentage of the total Mexican workforce employed in the informal sector — thus rose from 55% in June to 56.2% in July, the highest level since December 2021.

INEGI’s data shows that the number of people in informal sector jobs rose by just over 1.08 million in July to reach 34.1 million.

Meanwhile, the number of people in formal sector jobs — i.e. workers with employment benefits such as paid vacations and IMSS health insurance — declined 412,889 in July. Around 26.6 million workers, or 43.8% of the Mexican workforce, are employed in the formal sector.

The increase in informal sector jobs in July and the decline in formal ones left Mexico with a net gain of 670,991 positions last month, the best result this year. The net gain in jobs came after two months of declines, but the fact that the growth was due to a surge in informal employment is cause for concern.

The high level of informality in Mexico has “a direct cost on potential economic growth,” Gabriela Siller, director of economic analysis at Banco Base, wrote on X on Thursday. She noted that 2024 data from INEGI showed that Mexico’s vast informal sector generated just 25.38% of Mexico’s GDP even though it employed — and continues to employ — more than half of all workers.

La tasa de informalidad en México se ubicó en 56.20% en julio y promedia 55.16% en lo que va de 2026, por arriba

del 54.87% de 2025 y del 54.27% de 2024. Esta precarización tiene un costo directo sobre el crecimiento económico potencial. De acuerdo con la Medición de la… — Gabriela Siller Pagaza (@GabySillerP) August 27, 2026

Mexico has lost more than 775,000 formal sector jobs this year

INEGI data shows that Mexico added a total of 377,764 jobs in the first seven months of 2026.

The overall job growth is the product of the addition of 1.15 million informal sector jobs and the loss of 776,501 formal sector positions.

Siller said that the INEGI data is indicative of an ongoing deterioration of Mexico’s formal sector labor market. That deterioration is “one of the factors keeping the country in an economic stagnation trap,” she wrote in a Banco Base analysis.

Mexico’s economy has struggled to grow in recent times, although it did expand 1.4% on a quarter-over-quarter basis between April and June, the best second-quarter result since 2021.

INEGI’s employment data in detail

INEGI reported on Thursday that a total of 60.75 million people were employed in Mexico in July, while 1.81 million people were classified as unemployed. Mexico’s unemployment rate in July was 2.9%, an increase of 0.1 points compared to the same month of 2025. The unemployment rate was 3.1% for women and 2.9% for men.

Of the 60.75 million people in jobs in July, around 63% were employed in the tertiary or services sector while about 25% worked in the secondary sector, which includes the manufacturing, construction, mining and electricity industries. Most of the remaining workers — about 10.6% — were employed in Mexico’s primary sector, which includes agriculture and fishing, among other activities.

The secondary sector added 504,390 jobs in the 12 months to the end of July, while the primary and tertiary sectors lost 279,339 jobs and 208,494 jobs, respectively. The net result was a loss of 45,352 jobs in Mexico in the 12 months to July 31.

The growth of the secondary sector workforce was primarily due to the addition of more than 522,000 construction jobs in the 12 months to the end of July. The manufacturing industry lost just over 61,000 jobs in the period, while the mining and electricity sectors added almost 43,000 positions.

INEGI also reported that 6.7% of Mexico’s 60.75 million workers were underemployed in July, meaning they weren’t working as many hours as they wanted. That figure was down 0.6 points compared to July 2025.

Most workers in Mexico earn between one and two times the minimum wage, meaning they take home 315-630 pesos (US $18.50-$37) per day.

INEGI reported that 27.88 million workers —45.9% of the workforce — earned “up to a minimum wage” in July. Just over 19.4 million workers earned more than one but no more than two minimum wages. That number equates to 32% of the Mexican workforce.

Less than 1% of Mexican workers earned more than 5 minimum wages (1,575 pesos or US $93 per day) in July, according to INEGI, while 5.7% made 2-3 minimum wages and 2.4% earned 3-5 minimum wages.

With reports from El Economista

World.title: US pressures Mexico to stop its own citizens from crossing the border, sources say
World.content:
Foreign Affairs Minister Roberto Velasco and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio held their first face-to-face meeting in Washington, D.C., on Thursday, amid tensions in Mexico-U.S. relations.

Both officials commented on the meeting in social media posts, though a Bloomberg report citing sources familiar with the matter revealed a tougher private ask.

Velasco, who succeeded Juan Ramón de la Fuente as foreign minister in April, wrote on X that he and Rubio “reviewed security progress” and Mexico and the United States’ “joint work against drugs and arms trafficking and against transnational organized crime.”

He asserted that the bilateral “security cooperation scheme” has “yielded the best results in the region.”

Homicides in Mexico have declined significantly during the term of the current government, firearm seizures have increased and U.S. intelligence has helped Mexican authorities capture high-profile criminals, including former Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) leader Nemesio Rubén “El Mencho” Oseguera Cervantes, who was fatally wounded during a military operation in Jalisco in February. In addition, irregular migration to the United States via Mexico has declined sharply during the second Trump administration, although U.S. Border Patrol’s encounters with migrants at the United States’ southern border doubled in annual terms to more than 9,200 in July.

Velasco said that he and Rubio also spoke about “respect for the human rights of Mexican migrants in the United States.”

Me reuní hoy en Washington, D. C., con el secretario de Estado @SecRubio. Revisamos los avances en materia de seguridad: el trabajo conjunto contra el tráfico de drogas y armas y contra la delincuencia organizada transnacional. Es el esquema de cooperación en seguridad que ha… pic.twitter.com/6niYVJY0md — Roberto Velasco Álvarez (@r_velascoa) August 26, 2026

“I reiterated that our work with the United States is based on respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, shared responsibility, mutual trust and collaboration without subordination,” he wrote on X.

Mexico’s Ambassador to the United States Roberto Lazzeri and various other Mexican officials accompanied Velasco during his meeting with the U.S. secretary of state.

Rubio offered a briefer summary of Wednesday’s meeting, writing on X that he met with Velasco to “discuss decisive actions to end illegal immigration, halt fentanyl trafficking, and dismantle Foreign Terrorist Organizations and cartels.”

Eight Mexican cartels, including the CJNG and the Sinaloa Cartel, have been designated as foreign terrorist organizations by the U.S. government.

Bloomberg News spoke with anonymous sources who offered additional insight into the meeting between Velasco and Rubio.

Citing “people familiar with the matter,” the news agency reported on Thursday that the U.S. secretary of state told his Mexican counterpart that the Trump administration wants the Mexican government “to do more to stop undocumented migrants from crossing the U.S. border” given the recent spike in migrant apprehensions.

“… The push is led by Homeland Security Adviser Stephen Miller, a top Trump adviser, and the main U.S. demand is that Mexico stop its own citizens from crossing the border,” Bloomberg reported, once again citing its anonymous sources.

“That presents a constitutional and legal complication for [President] Sheinbaum’s government because Mexican nationals are free to travel within their own country, including from the poorer southern states where many migrants originate to northern Mexico and the U.S. border region,” Bloomberg wrote.

Meeting takes place against a backdrop of bilateral tension

The meeting between Velasco and Rubio took place at a time when Mexico-U.S. relations are strained for a variety of reasons.

Among the reasons for the bilateral tension are:

In a major speech on May 31, Sheinbaum railed against what she framed as U.S. interference in Mexican affairs, but nevertheless vowed to continue security collaboration with the Trump administration.

She has maintained a respectful relationship with Trump, even though the U.S. president has claimed she is “scared” of Mexican cartels and publicly mocked and mimicked her way of speaking.

With reports from La Jornada and Reforma

World.title: Thursday night’s ‘blood moon’ eclipse over Mexico: How and when to watch it
World.content:
Mexico’s moon will lose much of its glimmer Thursday night as Earth’s shadow covers nearly all of it in a deep partial lunar eclipse.

The eclipse — which will darken 96.3% of the moon’s disk at its maximum — will be visible across much of Mexico, with clear skies being the deciding factor.

Its partial phase will begin tonight (Thursday) at 8:33 p.m. Mexico City time, reaching its maximum at 10:13 p.m. and ending at 11:52 p.m., according to NASA. The subtler penumbral phase will begin at 7:23 p.m. and continue until after midnight.

At maximum, only a thin, bright edge of the moon should remain outside the umbra, Earth’s darkest shadow.

A lunar eclipse occurs when Earth passes between the sun and moon, with sunlight filtered and bent through Earth’s atmosphere reaching the moon. Blue wavelengths scatter more readily, while red and orange tones reach and reflect from the moon, giving it a dim, coppery or reddish appearance.

Because tonight’s event is extremely close to being a total eclipse, Mexican news outlets are calling it a “luna de sangre,” or “blood moon.” The popular term describes the red appearance of a fully eclipsed moon, although it is often used loosely for deep partial eclipses.

While tonight’s spectacle is notable, it is not exceptionally rare.

Eclipses covering at least 85% of the moon’s diameter — which includes total eclipses as well as deep partial eclipses — occur somewhere in the world every two-and-a-half to three years.

In recent years, Mexico has seen total lunar eclipses in January 2019. March 2025 and March 2026 — and ordinary partial eclipses are even more frequent.

Mexico’s last major solar eclipse occurred in April 2024 and drew many international visitors, especially in the eclipse’s arc across parts of Sinaloa, Durango and Coahuila. With the moon positioned directly in front of the sun, there was nearly total darkness in those areas before the eclipse continued through the United States and Canada.

Unlike a solar eclipse, a lunar eclipse can be viewed safely with the naked eye; no special glasses are needed. Binoculars or a telescope can sharpen the view of Earth’s shadow crossing lunar craters and other features.

Expert eclipse-watching guidance in Mexico City

Mexico City residents can attend a free pre-eclipse program at the capital’s 300 PILARES community centers, where science educators will offer guidance to people who bring their own telescopes, plus other eclipse activities.

A la Luz de la Luna (By the Light of the Moon) will run from 5 to 8 p.m., ending about half an hour before the partial phase begins and more than two hours before the greatest eclipse.

Advance registration is requested via the PILARES page, where you can also locate the community center near you. PILARES says telescopes will be available for people who don’t bring their own.

With reports from El Financiero, Radio Fórmula, Wired en Español and Infobae

World.title: Tamaulipas fuel-theft bust uncovers ranch hiding 135 exotic animals, from tigers to spider monkeys
World.content:
Raids on five properties in the northeastern border state of Tamaulipas resulted in the seizure of 68,000 liters of diesel fuel, several firearms, tactical communications equipment and 135 exotic animals.

The operation — carried out by the Navy, with assistance from the Federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR), the Security Ministry and state authorities — was a follow-up to ongoing investigations related to huachicoleo (the illegal practice of stealing, smuggling and selling fuel).

“Our investigations continue to dismantle this network and affect its logistical and financial capabilities,” Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said.

In an official statement released on Thursday, the Navy Ministry said that in addition to securing five properties, including a storage center, an illegal gas station, a house, a workshop and a ranch, one individual was arrested. The officials also seized an undisclosed number of tanker trucks and “fuel-handling equipment.”

Among the exotic animals impounded by the authorities — all at a single ranch — were at least 35 listed as endangered under Mexican law (21 spider monkeys, three jaguars, an ocelot, a green macaw, an American bison, bighorn sheep, a green iguana and an Aztec parrot).

Also found were Bengal tigers, a mandrill, a lemur, African lions, hyenas and sulcata tortoises, all of which are subject to special protection under international animal trade laws.

All the animals were placed at the disposal of the Federal Attorney for Environmental Protection for evaluation, safekeeping and specialized handling.

In addition to the diesel fuel, the raid netted a tractor-trailer, tanker trucks and other equipment.

The properties — located in the municipalities of Altamira and Tampico — have been sealed and were placed under the custody of the proper authorities. The suspect was turned over to the FGR for processing.

The Security Ministry said the investigation will seek to determine the origin of the fuel and the animals, as well as to establish potential liability and locate other members of the network under investigation.

It also emphasized that the operation aims to contribute to the protection and preservation of wildlife in Mexico.

With reports from Infobae, El Financiero, El Economista, Reforma and La Jornada

World.title: Mexico in Numbers: Mexico City rental prices
World.content:
Gentrification is a thorny issue in Mexico City, triggering protests last year in various parts of the capital, including in neighborhoods where many foreign residents live and many foreign tourists stay, such as Condesa and Roma.

A large part of protesters’ anger over gentrification was — and is — due to recent increases in rents for residential properties in certain parts of Mexico City.

With that in mind, this “Mexico in Numbers” article looks at how much it costs, on average, to rent a two-bedroom apartment in different parts of the capital, and how much rents increased in the 12 months to the end of June.

* The average monthly rents referred to in this article were calculated in June 2026 by Inmuebles 24, a real estate listing website. The El Economista newspaper and the news outlet Expansíon recently published the results of the Inmuebles24 Mexico City Index. The US dollar prices included in this article were calculated using the Bank of Mexico’s closing USD:MXN rate on Wednesday, Aug. 26, which was 16.96.

What’s the average rent across CDMX?

The average rent for a two-bedroom apartment across Mexico City is 21,921 pesos (US $1,292) per month, an increase of 9.6% compared to a year earlier. Mexico’s annual inflation rate in June was 3.37%.

By law, annual rent increases for existing renters remaining in the same property cannot exceed the headline inflation rate at the end of the previous year. At the end of 2025, Mexico’s headline rate was 3.69%.

At the end of May, the average monthly salary of a formal sector worker in Mexico was 20,419 pesos, an amount 1,502 pesos less than the average rent in the capital.

CDMX rental prices, by borough

Below we detail the average rents for a two-bedroom apartment in 10 of Mexico City’s 16 boroughs, or alcaldías as they are known in Spanish.

Cuauhtémoc

This borough — which includes the historic center of Mexico City as well as neighborhoods such as Roma, Condesa, Juárez, San Rafael and Doctores — has the highest average rents in Mexico City.

Rent for a two-bedroom apartment in the borough is, on average, 29,149 pesos (US $1,719), an annual increase of 13.7%.

Miguel Hidalgo

This borough — which includes neighborhoods such as Polanco, Escandón, Lomas de Chapultepec, San Miguel Chapultepec and Tacubaya — has the second-highest average rents in Mexico City.

Rent for a two-bedroom apartment in the borough is, on average, 27,786 pesos (US $1,642), an annual increase of 10.1%.

Cuajimalpa

This borough in western Mexico City has the third-highest average rents in the capital.

Rent for a two-bedroom apartment in the borough — which includes part of the Santa Fe business and residential district — is, on average, 21,355 pesos (US $1,262), an annual increase of 9.9%.

Benito Juárez

This borough — which includes neighborhoods such as Del Valle, Narvarte, Nápoles and Portales — has the fourth-highest average rents in the capital.

Rent for a two-bedroom apartment in the borough is, on average, 20,486 pesos (US $1,208), an annual increase of 6.9%.



Álvaro Obregón

This borough — within whose boundaries lies another part of Santa Fe as well as the pretty San Ángel neighborhood — has the fifth-highest average rents in the capital.

Rent for a two-bedroom apartment in the borough is, on average, 20,016 pesos (US $1,180), an annual increase of 9.7%.

Coyoacán

This borough — which includes the picturesque Coyoacán historic center as well as the “University City” campus of the National Autonomous University of Mexico — has the sixth-highest average rents in Mexico City.

Rent for a two-bedroom apartment in the borough is, on average, 17,306 pesos (US $1,020), an annual increase of 15.5%.

Azcapotzalco

This northern borough — home to the concert venue Arena Ciudad de México — has the seventh-highest average rents in Mexico City.

Rent for a two-bedroom apartment in the borough is, on average, 17,306 pesos (US $1,020), an annual increase of 15.5%.

Tlalpan

This southern borough — home to the Cuicuilco archeological site and the Six Flags amusement park — has the eighth-highest average rents in Mexico City.

Rent for a two-bedroom apartment in the borough is, on average, 13,607 pesos (US $802), an annual increase of 15.5%.

Gustavo A. Madero

Mexico City’s northernmost borough — where the Basílica de Santa María de Guadalupe is located — has the ninth-highest average rents in Mexico City.

Rent for a two-bedroom apartment in the borough is, on average, 13,424 pesos (US $791), an annual increase of 8.3%.

Venustiano Carranza

This northeastern borough — home to the Mexico City International Airport — has the 10th-highest average rents in Mexico City. In other words, it has the lowest rents among the 10 Mexico City boroughs included in the Inmuebles24 Mexico City Index.

Rent for a two-bedroom apartment in Venustiano Carranza is, on average, 13,021 pesos (US $768), an annual increase of 5.3%.

* Inmuebles24 didn’t publish data on average rents in the six other Mexico City boroughs, namely La Magdalena Contreras, Milpa Alta, Xochimilco, Iztapalapa, Tláhuac and Iztacalco.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: MND Local: Discover a different side of September in Puerto Vallarta
World.content:
September can be a strange month in Puerto Vallarta. The summer crowds have thinned, the heat and humidity are still very much with us, school’s back in session so traffic picks up, and it can be tempting to spend the month hiding indoors with the air conditioning on.

But there’s still plenty happening around town, and some of it offers a chance to experience the city as something more than a tourist destination. September is a good time to slow down, explore local neighborhoods, support small businesses and take part in traditions that have little to do with beaches or resort pools.

Naturally Mazcal Weekend Market

If you’re looking for something a little more local and a little less polished, the Naturally Mazcal Weekend Market is a good place to start.

Held on Saturdays at the east end of Isla Cuale, the market brings together local makers, small producers, food vendors and wellness businesses. It runs from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. and offers the kind of relaxed, neighborhood atmosphere that makes it easy to browse, stop for something to eat and discover something you didn’t know existed.

You’ll find handmade products, locally produced food, natural body care items, clothing, art and other small-batch goods. The market is also a chance to meet the people behind many of the products being sold, which gives the experience a more personal feel than a typical shopping trip.

The September market is particularly appealing because it gives residents a reason to get out during what’s traditionally one of Vallarta’s quieter months. The pace is generally unhurried, and the setting near the river and Isla Cuale makes it easy to combine a visit with a walk through one of the city’s most distinctive areas.

Mexican Independence Day

There are plenty of ways to celebrate Mexican Independence Day in Puerto Vallarta, but if you want to experience the heart of it, head downtown.

On Sept. 15, Plaza de Armas comes alive with music, dancing, food and the anticipation of the traditional Grito de Independencia, when the mayor recalls the historic call for independence and leads the crowd in the familiar cry of “Viva México!”

The ceremony is followed by the kind of celebration that reminds you this isn’t simply another event on the calendar. It’s one of Mexico’s most important national celebrations, and the energy in the plaza reflects that. Families, residents and visitors gather together, often wearing green, white and red, while vendors fill the surrounding area with traditional food and refreshments.

The following morning, Sept. 16, brings the traditional Independence Day parade through the city. It’s crowded and noisy, and it’s gloriously Mexican. School groups, marching bands, dancers, military personnel and community organizations typically make their way through the streets as spectators line the route.

It’s the perfect way to catch a memorable glimpse into one of the country’s most important traditions.

‘Estampas de México’

On Sept. 18, the Camerata de Puerto Vallarta will present “Estampas de México,” an evening celebrating some of the country’s most recognizable musical traditions.

The concert brings together young musicians trained through the Orquesta Escuela de Puerto Vallarta, offering a program built around Mexican composers and the country’s rich musical identity.

The performance is expected to be more than a night of familiar songs and national pride. It also represents another step in the development of a local musical program that’s been working with young people in the region.

Through the Orquesta Escuela de Puerto Vallarta, young musicians are given the chance to study, rehearse and build the experience needed to continue growing as performers. “Estampas de México” reflects that effort while also placing Mexican musical traditions at the center of the program.

The concert’s setting is part of its appeal, too. Rather than taking place in a hotel or tourist venue, it will be held at the Colegio Niños Héroes auditorium in Las Gaviotas, creating a more intimate connection between the musicians and the community they represent.

It’s a reminder that Puerto Vallarta’s cultural life exists well beyond the Malecón and the city’s entertainment districts, so the program offers an opportunity to hear music associated with Mexican composers and traditions in a setting that feels both local and accessible.

Estampas de México begins at 8:30 p.m. on Sept. 18. The Colegio Niños Héroes auditorium is located at Avenida Paseo del Marlin No. 89 in Las Gaviotas. Seating is limited, and tickets are available through WhatsApp at +1 (322) 241-6360.

Cuisine Without Borders: Nogada Edition

And then there’s food. Honestly, no list of things to do in Vallarta would be complete without including at least one culinary event.

Cuisine Without Borders: Nogada Edition runs through Sept. 20, bringing together Velas Vallarta, Casa Velas and Táu Beach Club for a culinary celebration inspired by chile en nogada.

The dish is one of Mexico’s most recognizable seasonal specialties. Traditionally prepared with a poblano pepper filled with a mixture of meat, fruit and spices, it’s covered with a creamy walnut sauce and finished with pomegranate seeds and parsley. The colors represent the Mexican flag, making chile en nogada especially popular around Independence Day.

This event takes that classic dish and looks at it through an international lens, incorporating techniques and ingredients from the United States and Canada into the menus. The result is a celebration of Mexican cuisine that also reflects the international character of Puerto Vallarta.

There are special rates for locals and residents, making this worth considering even if you’re not here on vacation. It’s a chance to enjoy the city’s hospitality and dining scene from a resident’s perspective, without necessarily having to wait for visiting friends or family to arrive.

There you have it: four events, and four very different ways of experiencing Puerto Vallarta.

You can browse local products at Isla Cuale, join the crowds downtown for Mexican Independence Day, listen to young musicians perform the country’s musical traditions, or sit down to a creative interpretation of chile en nogada.

And perhaps the best thing about it all is that in September, you don’t have to be a tourist to enjoy the city. You just have to get out and be part of it.

Charlotte Smith is a writer and journalist based in Mexico. Her work focuses on travel, politics, and community. You can follow along with her travel stories at www.salsaandserendipity.com.

World.title: Brazil’s Caixa Profit Rises 5.9% to US$757.0 Million in Second Quarter
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

BRAZIL · ECONOMY

Key Facts —

What happened Caixa, Brazil’s big state bank, earned R$3.9 billion (US$757 million) in the second quarter, up 5.9 percent in a year.

—

What drove it Housing is 69 percent of Caixa’s R$1.45 trillion (US$281 billion) loan book, and mortgage lending is booming.

—

The catch First-half profit is still down 17.6 percent, and loan-loss provisions nearly doubled in a year.

—

The worry Delinquency over 90 days rose to 3.64 percent, and farm-loan arrears hit 20.74 percent.

—

Who banks there Caixa holds about 68 percent of Brazil’s housing-loan market and pays out the main social benefits.

—

What the bank says Caixa argues its housing focus keeps expected losses low despite the jump in provisions.

Caixa Econômica Federal, Brazil’s giant state-owned bank, reported a second-quarter recurring profit of R$3.9 billion (US$757 million) on Wednesday. The 5.9 percent annual rise hides a weaker first half and a sharp increase in money set aside for bad loans.

The Caixa profit numbers in detail

The Caixa profit for April to June came in at R$3.899 billion (US$757 million) on a recurring basis. That is 5.9 percent above the same quarter of 2025 and 12.4 percent above the first quarter of 2026.

The quarter looks better than the year. First-half recurring profit was R$7.4 billion (US$1.44 billion), a fall of 17.6 percent over twelve months.

The financial margin, the money a bank earns from interest, reached R$19.7 billion (US$3.8 billion). That is a rise of 20.2 percent in a year.

Service revenue grew 12.9 percent to R$7.54 billion (US$1.46 billion). Administrative expenses rose 5.9 percent to R$11.44 billion (US$2.22 billion).

Return on equity, a measure of how hard shareholders’ money works, slipped to 9.16 percent. That is 2.7 percentage points below the level of June 2025.

Mortgages carry the result

Caixa’s total loan book reached R$1.448 trillion (US$281 billion) in June, up 11.9 percent in a year. Housing finance is the core business, at 69.4 percent of the total.

The mortgage balance alone hit R$1.005 trillion (US$195 billion), a rise of 15 percent. New housing loans in the quarter totalled R$137.6 billion (US$26.7 billion), up 29.3 percent.

The bank kept roughly 68 percent of Brazil’s housing-loan market. Loans to individuals grew 8.7 percent to R$156.5 billion (US$30.4 billion), and loans to companies rose 6.5 percent to R$113.9 billion (US$22.1 billion).

For foreigners, the scale needs context. Caixa is the bank that pays Brazil’s main social benefits, runs the federal lotteries and finances most Brazilian home purchases.

The bill for faster lending

Credit growth is not free. Delinquency above 90 days reached 3.64 percent of the portfolio, against 2.66 percent a year earlier.

The worst corner is farm lending, where arrears hit 20.74 percent, up from 7.02 percent. Individuals stand at 6.29 percent and companies at 14.05 percent, while housing loans show just 1.45 percent.

The bank answered with a much bigger safety buffer. Provisions for loan losses cost R$6.97 billion (US$1.35 billion) in the quarter, nearly double the level of a year ago.

Caixa says the concentration in housing and collateral-backed loans keeps expected losses low. The mortgage book’s 1.45 percent delinquency is the number behind that argument.

Why the Caixa profit matters

Caixa is a policy bank as much as a commercial one. Its results say something about Brazilian households, the housing market and the cost of credit.

The backdrop is the central bank’s key rate, the Selic, currently at 14.00 percent. That makes Caixa’s mortgage expansion stand out, because high rates usually cool housing demand.

The second quarter suggests the bank is bending back towards growth after a weak start to the year. The first quarter had brought a recurring profit of R$3.5 billion (US$680 million), down 34.4 percent in a year.

The figures in this article come from the bank’s earnings release and Brazilian financial media. Dollar conversions use the rate of R$5.15 per US dollar on 27 August 2026.

What to watch in the second half

The first question is whether farm-loan arrears keep climbing. A 20.74 percent delinquency rate in agribusiness leaves little room for error in that book.

The second question is whether provisions can come down. Another quarter near R$7 billion (US$1.36 billion) would eat much of the benefit of a stronger interest margin.

The third is profitability itself. A 9.16 percent return on equity is modest for a bank of this size, and it is moving in the wrong direction.

Frequently Asked Questions

First-half profit of R$7.4 billion (US$1.44 billion) was still down 17.6 percent. What drove Caixa’s second-quarter result? Credit growth, above all mortgages. Housing loans are 69.4 percent of Caixa’s R$1.448 trillion (US$281 billion) portfolio, and new housing lending rose 29.3 percent in a year. What are the weak spots in Caixa’s numbers? Delinquency over 90 days rose to 3.64 percent, and farm-loan arrears reached 20.74 percent. Provisions for bad loans nearly doubled, to R$6.97 billion (US$1.35 billion) in the quarter.

Sources: Caixa Econômica Federal earnings release via Valor, G1, InfoMoney and CartaCapital, 26 August 2026.

World.title: Brazil Police Postpone Banco Master Founder’s Hearing on Alleged Central Bank ‘Spies’
World.content:

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

BRAZIL · ECONOMY

Key Facts —What happened: Federal Police planned to question Banco Master founder Daniel Vorcaro on 27 August over alleged paid informants inside the Central Bank. —The claim: Police say a “Master group” chat linked Vorcaro to two supervision employees who leaked privileged information for money. —The catch: The videoconference hearing never happened; a prison internet failure pushed it to Friday 28 August. —Why it matters: It would be Vorcaro’s first interrogation since his March arrest and since two plea-bargain proposals were rejected. —The bigger case: The bank was liquidated in November 2025, stranding more than one million deposit-certificate investors.

Brazil’s Federal Police were set to question Banco Master founder Daniel Vorcaro on Thursday over alleged “spies” inside the Central Bank. The hearing was postponed to Friday after the internet failed at the prison where he is held.

What the police wanted to ask

The Federal Police, Brazil’s national police force, had scheduled the hearing for 10 a.m. on Thursday 27 August. Vorcaro was to appear by videoconference from custody in Brasília.

The inquiry is narrow and specific. Investigators suspect Vorcaro kept “spies”, the word the police themselves use, inside the Central Bank’s banking supervision department.

According to CNN Brasil’s reporting, officers found a WhatsApp group called “grupo Master” on Vorcaro’s phone. It included two Central Bank servants, Belline Santana and Paulo Sérgio Neves de Souza, both from banking supervision.

The messages allegedly shared privileged information in exchange for financial advantages. These remain police allegations, not proven facts, and no conviction exists on this point.

A hearing that never happened

The session collapsed for a mundane reason. The internet connection at the Papuda prison complex in Brasília, where Vorcaro is detained, was too unstable to hold the videoconference.

Defense lawyer Daniel Bialski said his client waited for hours for the signal to return. The testimony was rescheduled for Friday 28 August, according to Poder360.

The delay matters because of what the hearing represents. It would be Vorcaro’s first interrogation since his preventive arrest in March.

It is also his first since the police and the Prosecutor-General’s Office formally rejected two plea-bargain proposals. His defense says he will answer every question, limited to the inquiry’s scope.

The bank that failed

Banco Master grew fast by selling high-yield deposit certificates to retail investors. More than one million people bought them, drawn by returns well above the market average.

The Central Bank ordered the bank’s extrajudicial liquidation in November 2025. A last attempt to sell the bank to BRB, the state-owned Bank of Brasília, had already collapsed under scrutiny.

The case now sits at the Supreme Court. Justice André Mendonça is the rapporteur, after Justice Dias Toffoli stepped aside in February.

Ten phases of Operation Compliance Zero

The investigation runs under the name Operation Compliance Zero. It began in November 2025, when Vorcaro was first arrested while trying to leave Brazil.

He was released weeks later, then arrested again in March 2026. Police said at the time that he ran a group that intimidated adversaries and paid bribes to two Central Bank employees.

The operation has since reached far beyond the bank itself. A January phase blocked or seized more than R$5.7 billion (US$1.1 billion) in assets.

Later phases targeted the former BRB president, two sitting senators, a former Rio de Janeiro governor and Vorcaro’s own father. A July phase looked at the alleged monitoring of journalists who contradicted the banker’s interests.

What to watch next

Friday’s rescheduled testimony stays limited to the two Central Bank servants. Other hearings are planned for the other strands of the investigation.

Investigators see the session as a chance for Vorcaro to explain his side. Without a plea deal, what he says on Friday carries unusual weight.

For the one million savers still waiting, the questioning is a sideshow to the real issue. The liquidation process will decide how much of their money ever comes back.

Frequently Asked Questions

Was Banco Master’s Vorcaro questioned on 27 August? No. The videoconference hearing was postponed to Friday 28 August after the internet connection failed at the Papuda prison complex in Brasília, according to his defense. What are the alleged “spies” inside Brazil’s Central Bank? Federal Police suspect Vorcaro paid two banking-supervision employees, Belline Santana and Paulo Sérgio Neves de Souza, for privileged information. The claims remain unproven allegations. What happened to Banco Master? The Central Bank ordered its extrajudicial liquidation in November 2025. More than one million investors had bought its deposit certificates, and the case is now before the Supreme Court.

Sources: CNN Brasil and Poder360 reporting on the Federal Police inquiry. Exchange rate: R$5.1503 per US dollar on 27 August 2026.

World.title: Brazil Election Security: Federal Forces Approved for Five States
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

BRAZIL · ELECTIONS

Key Facts — What happened: Brazil’s electoral court unanimously approved federal troops for over 100 municipalities in five states.

— Where: Tocantins, Piauí, Ceará, Acre and Rio de Janeiro, including the capitals Fortaleza, Teresina and Rio Branco.

— Why: Local police said they cannot guarantee voting amid faction wars, land conflicts and remote terrain.

— The catch: The soldiers come from the Armed Forces, and the Defense Ministry, not the court, runs the operation.

— Who it touches: Voters in indigenous villages, border areas and riverside towns reachable only by boat or plane.

— What comes next: Troops deploy for the first round on 4 October, under rules keeping them 100 metres from polling stations.

Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court voted unanimously on Thursday to send federal forces into more than 100 municipalities for the first round on 4 October. The requests came from the places themselves, and they describe a map of Brazil’s hardest ground.

What the court approved

The Superior Electoral Court, known in Brazil by its Portuguese initials TSE, voted unanimously on Thursday 27 August. It authorised federal troops in more than 100 municipalities across five states.

The states are Tocantins, Piauí, Ceará, Acre and Rio de Janeiro. The list includes four state capitals: Rio de Janeiro, Fortaleza, Teresina and Rio Branco.

Federal force is a last resort in Brazilian election law. It applies when a municipality reports that local police cannot guarantee a normal vote.

Requests travel from state governments to the regional electoral courts, and from there to the TSE. Once approved, the Defense Ministry plans and runs the deployments.

Why these places asked for help

The requests describe hard terrain and hard politics. Some towns report few four-wheel-drive police vehicles, agrarian conflicts, wars between criminal factions and a history of violence.

Other requests are mostly about distance. They cite indigenous villages, far-flung municipalities, border regions and riverside communities reachable only by boat or plane.

What the troops will actually do

The forces are drawn from the Army, the Navy and the Air Force. Their job is twofold: keep order and move the election itself.

Logistics is the quiet half of the mission. The military routinely flies or ships voting machines, staff and materials to places with no road access.

Standing rules limit how close soldiers may get to voters. Troops must stay at least 100 metres from polling stations and need authorisation to enter during voting hours.

The politics in the background

Brazil election security is a sensitive subject after years of tension. Supporters of former president Jair Bolsonaro long claimed the electronic voting system was fraudulent, a charge never proven.

This deployment is narrower than that debate. It answers specific municipal requests, most of them about crime and geography rather than the count itself.

The court has been building the machinery all month. On 20 August it created two coordination bodies uniting the Federal Police, the Abin intelligence agency and the Armed Forces.

What happens now

The Defense Ministry now draws up the operational plan for each approved municipality. The first round of voting is on Sunday 4 October.

A runoff, where needed, follows on 25 October. The court can widen the deployment if more requests arrive before then.

For voters abroad and expats in Brazil, the practical effect is limited. Polling in the big cities proceeds as usual, and election day itself is normally uneventful.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which Brazilian states will get federal forces for the 2026 election? The electoral court approved deployments in Tocantins, Piauí, Ceará, Acre and Rio de Janeiro. The measure covers more than 100 municipalities, including the capitals Rio de Janeiro, Fortaleza, Teresina and Rio Branco. Why did Brazil’s electoral court approve federal troops? Municipalities reported that local police cannot guarantee a normal vote. The cited problems include criminal faction disputes, agrarian conflicts, a history of violence and remote areas reachable only by boat or plane. Can soldiers enter polling stations in Brazil? Not freely. Standing rules keep troops at least 100 metres from polling stations, and they may enter during voting hours only with authorisation.

World.title: Brazil’s Petrobras Redeems US$1.08 Billion in Global Bonds Early
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

BRAZIL · ECONOMY

Key Facts —

What happened Petrobras will redeem US$1.08 billion of 5.999 percent global bonds due 2028 ahead of schedule.

—

Why now Brazil’s state oil company is cutting costlier debt early as part of its liability management.

—

The catch The bonds are redeemed by a Dutch subsidiary, and the final price is only set on 22 September.

—

Also this week Two giant production vessels for the Búzios field were christened at Seatrium’s Singapore yard.

—

And Braskem Petrobras raised Braskem’s trade credit line from R$350 million (US$68 million) to R$2.35 billion (US$456 million).

—

What comes next The redemption settles on 25 September, and the two platforms head to Brazil for 2027 start-ups.

Petrobras said on Thursday it will buy back about US$1 billion of its own global bonds ahead of schedule. The redemption of Petrobras global bonds headlines a busy week in which the company also christened two offshore production giants and widened its credit lifeline to Braskem.

The early redemption of Petrobras global bonds

The company said its wholly owned subsidiary, Petrobras Global Finance, has sent redemption notices to bondholders. The notes in question are the 5.999 percent Global Notes maturing in 2028.

The principal being repaid totals US$1,080,945,000. Petrobras puts the size of the operation at roughly US$1 billion, excluding capitalised and unpaid interest.

The redemption will be priced on 22 September 2026. Settlement is scheduled for 25 September 2026.

The company framed the move as liability management. Paying the notes off early removes a fixed coupon of nearly 6 percent from the balance sheet two years before maturity.

It is at least the third early redemption of Petrobras global bonds in under a year. The company redeemed 8.750 percent notes due 2026 last December and announced another Petrobras global bonds buyback in May.

Two new production giants for Búzios

The same week brought a milestone on the production side. Singapore’s Seatrium christened two floating production, storage and offloading vessels, the P-80 and the P-82, at its Tuas Boulevard yard.

Both ships will sail to the Búzios field in the pre-salt area of the Santos Basin, off Rio de Janeiro. They will be the ninth and tenth production platforms deployed there.

Each vessel is designed to produce 225,000 barrels of oil per day and process 12 million cubic metres of gas per day. Together they add 450,000 barrels per day of capacity, an increase of about 34 percent for the field.

Búzios is Brazil’s largest field by reserves and production, and it has already passed 1.2 million barrels per day. Production from the two new units is scheduled to begin next year.

Seatrium built more than 110,000 tonnes of topside modules for the two projects across yards in Singapore, China and Brazil. The vessels include carbon capture and reinjection systems and other emissions-reduction technology.

Petrobras chief executive Magda Chambriard called the P-80 a giant platform for a giant field. Seatrium’s chief executive, Chris Ong, said the yard is now focused on offshore commissioning.

The Exploration and Production segment explores, develops, and produces…

A bigger credit line for Braskem

The third move concerns Braskem, the petrochemical producer in which Petrobras holds a strategic stake. The two companies agreed on Monday to raise Braskem’s trade credit line with Petrobras from R$350 million (US$68 million) to R$2.35 billion (US$456 million).

The credit finances Braskem’s purchases of raw materials supplied by Petrobras. It keeps feedstock flowing while Braskem works through an out-of-court restructuring of roughly US$11 billion in debt.

The structure runs until December 2026 and carries several guarantees. They include an assignment of Braskem receivables, an escrow account of R$300 million (US$58 million) and rights tied to a tax lawsuit estimated at R$2.7 billion (US$524 million).

Investors welcomed the news. Braskem shares rose more than 14 percent on the São Paulo stock exchange after the announcement.

What it adds up to

Taken together, the three moves show a company using a strong cash position on several fronts. Debt is being cut early, production capacity is expanding, and a key industrial partner is being kept supplied.

For holders of Petrobras global bonds, the practical date is 22 September, when the redemption price is set. For Brazil’s oil output, the bigger date is 2027, when the P-80 and P-82 start producing.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which Petrobras global bonds are being redeemed early? They are the 5.999 percent Global Notes due 2028, issued by the subsidiary Petrobras Global Finance. The principal totals US$1,080,945,000, with pricing on 22 September 2026 and settlement on 25 September 2026. What are the P-80 and P-82 vessels? They are floating production, storage and offloading vessels built by Seatrium for the Búzios field off Rio de Janeiro. Each can produce 225,000 barrels of oil per day, and both are due to start operating in 2027. Why did Petrobras raise Braskem’s credit line? The line finances Braskem’s raw-material purchases from Petrobras while Braskem restructures its debts. It rose from R$350 million (US$68 million) to R$2.35 billion (US$456 million) and runs until December 2026.

World.title: Brazil’s Habib’s Files for Judicial Recovery as OSX Creditors Back US$1.5 Billion Plan
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

BRAZIL · MARKETS

Key Facts —What happened: The owner of Habib’s filed for judicial recovery in São Paulo on 24 August with R$265.2 million (US$51.5 million) of debt. —Same day: Creditors of OSX, the former Eike Batista shipbuilder, approved a plan covering R$7.5 billion (US$1.5 billion) of debt. —The catch: OSX filed nothing this week; it entered recovery in January 2024, and a judge must still confirm the plan. —Who it affects: Habib’s, Ragazzo and Tendall restaurants keep serving customers, while OSX’s labor creditors rejected the plan. —What comes next: A São Paulo judge supervises the Habib’s restructuring, and a Rio de Janeiro court decides on the OSX plan.

Brazil’s Habib’s fast-food chain filed for judicial recovery on Monday, declaring R$265.2 million (US$51.5 million) of debt. The same day, creditors of Eike Batista’s OSX approved a R$7.5 billion (US$1.5 billion) restructuring plan.

What Habib’s filed on Monday

Grupo Gennius, the company behind Habib’s, Ragazzo and Tendall, filed the request on Monday 24 August. It declared debts of R$265.2 million (US$51.5 million).

A São Paulo court accepted the filing. The group says all of its restaurants continue to operate normally.

It blamed the lasting effects of the Covid-19 pandemic for the squeeze. Habib’s built its name on inexpensive esfihas, the Middle Eastern-style flatbreads sold across the country.

The company had already looked for breathing room earlier this year. The Rio Times reported in August on a court shield that froze its payments for 60 days.

This is the heavier, formal version of that protection. The whole debt pile now sits under a judge’s supervision.

What judicial recovery means in Brazil

Judicial recovery, known in Portuguese as recuperação judicial, is Brazil’s court-supervised restructuring for companies. Once a judge accepts the filing, most debt collections are frozen.

The company and its creditors then negotiate a payment plan. Creditors vote on it in an assembly, divided into classes by claim type.

If creditors reject the plan, the court can declare bankruptcy. Liquidation usually leaves creditors with less than a negotiated deal.

OSX’s creditors said yes on the same day

OSX did not file for court protection this week, despite some headlines suggesting it did. The shipbuilding group controlled by Eike Batista filed its second judicial recovery back in January 2024.

What happened on Monday was the vote. A creditors’ assembly approved the group’s new restructuring plan, covering about R$7.5 billion (US$1.5 billion) of debt.

The support was broad among the big creditors. Of the unsecured creditors present, 82.61 percent voted in favor by headcount.

Measured by value, the yes votes held 95.44 percent of the claims. Micro and small companies approved the plan unanimously.

The labor class was the exception. Its single registered vote was cast against the plan.

The approval does not end the process. The plan still needs confirmation from the 3rd Business Court of Rio de Janeiro.

The assembly also closed just in time. A legal deadline for the vote expired on 27 August.

From shipyards to square metres

OSX was founded in 2007 to build ships and service platforms for the oil industry. It listed on the stock exchange in 2010 as a crown jewel of Eike Batista’s EBX empire.

The fall came fast. Its main client, the oil company OGX, collapsed.

OSX filed its first judicial recovery in November 2013. That process ended only in November 2020.

The company that returned to court in 2024 is a different business. Its strategy now rests on leasing about 3.2 million square metres of land at the Port of Açu.

The finances remain deep in the red. First-quarter 2025 accounts showed negative equity of R$8.64 billion (US$1.68 billion).

The consolidated loss for that quarter alone was R$238.5 million (US$46.3 million). Those figures explain why Monday’s vote mattered so much.

Why the two cases matter

Brazil’s benchmark interest rate, the Selic, stands at 14.00 percent. Companies carrying heavy debt feel that cost every single month.

The same week, a Rio de Janeiro court converted telecom company Oi’s long recovery process into outright bankruptcy. Court protection buys time; it is not a rescue.

For foreigners living in Brazil, little changes at the counter. The esfihas and the delivery scooters keep running.

For creditors and investors, the coming court decisions matter more. They will show how much of these debts can realistically be saved.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Habib’s closing its restaurants? No. Grupo Gennius says Habib’s, Ragazzo and Tendall outlets keep operating normally. The São Paulo court now supervises the restructuring of R$265.2 million (US$51.5 million) in debt. Did OSX file for judicial recovery this week? No. OSX filed its second petition in January 2024. This week creditors approved a plan covering R$7.5 billion (US$1.5 billion) of debt. A Rio de Janeiro court must still confirm it. What is judicial recovery in Brazil? It is a court-supervised restructuring that freezes debt collections during negotiations. If creditors reject the resulting plan, the court can declare bankruptcy.

World.title: US Southern Command Chief Lands in Bogotá on Drug Fight
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Colombia · DEFENCE

Key Facts — Visit The US Southern Command chief reached Bogotá on August 26, 2026.

— Host Colombia’s new armed forces command led the talks on the local side.

— Status Washington has listed Colombia as failing on drug control since September 2025.

— Money The State Department pledged one billion dollars in assistance on August 7, 2026.

— Coca A UN count found 261,000 hectares planted with coca during 2024.

The US Southern Command chief spent two days with Colombia’s new commanders after years of strained ties.

General Francis L. Donovan, who leads the US Southern Command, arrived in Bogotá on August 26, 2026. He came to meet the military high command installed days earlier by President Abelardo de la Espriella.

A four-star visit to Bogotá

General Francis Donovan landed in Bogotá on August 26, 2026, aboard a United States military aircraft. Colombian troops received him with an honor guard at the start of a two-day agenda.

He heads the US Southern Command, the Pentagon’s combatant command for Latin America and the Caribbean. Its remit covers 31 countries and the waters around them.

This was the first senior American visit since the change of government in Colombia. Todd Blanche had led the United States delegation to the inauguration in Cali on August 7.

The US Embassy in Bogotá said Donovan came to meet the country’s new military leaders. It framed the talks around joint work against narcoterrorists and a firmer security partnership.

Who sat across the table

President Abelardo de la Espriella swore in a new military and police high command that same week. Major General Erick Rodríguez Aparicio now commands the armed forces.

Major General Carlos Carrasquilla Gómez took over as chief of the joint staff. Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora López also took part in the meetings.

The agenda ran beyond the capital. Reported stops included Tumaco on the Pacific coast and the Tolemaida military base.

Tumaco sits in Nariño, one of the departments with the densest coca planting in the country. Tolemaida is the army’s main training and aviation hub.

What the US Southern Command asked for

The US Southern Command described the trip as a step toward a stronger alliance for a safer region. Donovan spoke of synchronizing capabilities and holding sustained pressure on trafficking networks.

Technical talks covered intelligence, reconnaissance and special operations. Colombian officers also briefed the visitors on semi-submersible vessels and fast boats leaving Pacific inlets.

No joint written declaration followed the meetings. Neither government released a signed agreement or a list of fresh commitments on the day.

That absence matters for anyone tracking the relationship in detail. Statements of intent are not the same as budget lines, treaties or signed instruments.

Colombia is still decertified in Washington

This is the decisive backdrop to the visit. Colombia remains on the American list of countries judged to have failed demonstrably on drug control.

The White House determination for fiscal year 2026 was released on September 15, 2025. It named Afghanistan, Bolivia, Burma, Colombia and Venezuela.

The same memorandum said assistance to those four countries stays vital to United States national interests. That clause kept security aid flowing despite the label.

The next annual determination falls due in the middle of September. Whether Colombia comes off the list is the first hard test of the new alignment.

The money and the paperwork behind it

The State Department announced a US$1 billion assistance package on August 7, the day of the inauguration. It covers security cooperation alongside infrastructure, energy and small business programs.

Officials said the money would be arranged in collaboration with the United States Congress. No disbursement schedule or annual breakdown has been published so far.

A separate presidential determination signed on August 3, 2026, reached the Federal Register on August 10. It renews American support for intercepting aircraft suspected of drug trafficking in Colombian airspace.

That instrument is routine and renewed every year under a 1995 defense law. Its quiet signature shows the operational machinery kept running through the political quarrel.

The coca numbers behind the talks

The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, known as UNODC, tracks Colombian coca with a survey system called SIMCI. The Spanish name translates as the Integrated Illicit Crops Monitoring System.

Its report covering 2024 was published on June 25, 2026, roughly a year later than usual. It counted 261,000 hectares planted with coca, a rise of 3.5 percent.

For the first time in two decades the report withheld an estimate of cocaine production potential. The previous edition had put the 2023 figure at 2,664 tonnes.

Bogotá and the agency agreed to rebuild the estimating method before publishing fresh output numbers. The report did add a measure of cocaine kept off the market, at 889 tonnes.

What changed after the Petro years

Relations were strained during Gustavo Petro’s term, which ran from 2022 until August 2026. Washington withdrew certification in September 2025 and criticized his approach to armed groups.

Colombia joined the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition, known as A3C, in mid-August 2026. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth announced the step after meeting Minister Mora in Panama City.

The coalition is also called the Shield of the Americas and was launched in March 2026. Colombia became its nineteenth member and offered Medellín as its national headquarters.

The government has opened the door to joint operations with American forces on Colombian soil. That is the clearest break with the previous administration’s security policy.

The objections raised at home

Senator Iván Cepeda of the Pacto Histórico called the arrangement a surrender of sovereignty. He argued that the constitution gives the Senate, not the president, the power to admit foreign troops.

Article 173 of the Colombian constitution requires Senate consent for the transit of foreign forces. Several members of Congress have asked the government to explain what exactly was authorized.

InSight Crime, a research group that covers organized crime in the Americas, questioned the coalition’s strategy. Co-director Jeremy McDermott said security force pressure alone has not worked over the long term.

He pointed to Ecuador, where homicide rates climbed sharply despite a heavy military response. The group also noted that maritime strikes have not visibly slowed the flow of drugs.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who leads the US Southern Command? General Francis L. Donovan, a United States Marine Corps officer, took command on February 5, 2026. He succeeded acting commander Lieutenant General Evan L. Pettus of the Air Force. Is Colombia certified by Washington on counter-narcotics? No. The determination released on September 15, 2025 listed Colombia as having failed demonstrably. Assistance continued under a national interest clause in the same memorandum. What did the two sides agree in Bogotá? Neither government published a joint declaration or a signed accord. Officials described talks on intelligence, reconnaissance and special operations against trafficking networks.

World.title: Brazil Presidential Poll: Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro in Statistical Tie
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

BRAZIL · POLITICS

Key Facts — What happened: Lula leads Flávio Bolsonaro 38% to 35% in the first round, inside the margin of error.

— How close: A runoff would be tighter still, at 45% to 44% for the president.

— The real story: Lula has slipped from 41% in mid-August while Flávio Bolsonaro holds at 35%.

— The catch: Both men carry 49% rejection, and half of Brazil disapproves of Lula’s government.

— Where it tilts: Flávio Bolsonaro beats Lula 48% to 42% in Espírito Santo, while Minas Gerais is level.

— What comes next: Brazil votes on 4 October, with a runoff on 25 October if no one wins outright.

Brazil’s presidential race is now a statistical tie. A PoderData/Aya poll released on Thursday puts President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva at 38% and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro at 35% in the first round, five weeks before the vote.

A lead that fits inside the margin of error

The PoderData/Aya survey, released on Thursday 27 August, interviewed 2,400 voters by telephone between 23 and 26 August. Its margin of error is two percentage points, either way.

That margin swallows Lula’s three-point advantage over Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round. Read strictly, the Brazil presidential poll is a tie.

Behind the two leaders, the field is thin. Ronaldo Caiado, Renan Santos and Augusto Cury each take 4%, and Pablo Marçal takes 3%.

Two weeks ago the same institute had Lula at 41% and Flávio Bolsonaro at 35%. That survey left out Marçal, so the drop is partly a change of menu rather than a collapse.

The runoff projection is tighter still

In a head-to-head second round, Lula takes 45% and Flávio Bolsonaro 44%. Nine percent say they would spoil their ballot, and 2% are undecided.

The institute tested three other runoffs. Lula beats Renan Santos 44% to 37% and Romeu Zema 44% to 43%, while Caiado edges Lula 44% to 43%.

All four scenarios sit within or near the margin of error. On this evidence the October race has no clear favourite.

Half the country disapproves of Lula

Both front-runners are rejected by 49% of voters, who say they would never vote for them. That shared ceiling is what keeps the smaller candidates dreaming of an opening.

Lula’s government is disapproved of by 50% and approved by 42%. A rival BTG Pactual/Nexus survey released on Monday found nearly the same split: 49% against, 48% in favour.

Two states, two different warnings

The Real Time Big Data institute published state-level surveys on the same day. In Espírito Santo, Flávio Bolsonaro ties Lula 35% to 34% in the first round and wins the runoff 48% to 42%.

Lula is also the most rejected name in Espírito Santo, at 53%. The state is small, but its result flatters the senator’s claim that he can compete beyond the conservative south.

Minas Gerais, the second-largest electorate, points the other way. There Lula leads the first round 39% to 34%, and the runoff is a statistical tie at 46% to 44%.

The state’s own senator, Cleitinho Azevedo, leads every recent poll for governor of Minas Gerais. His strength makes Minas the most crowded battleground of the October vote.

What to watch before the first round

The broader polling picture agrees with Thursday’s tie. Datafolha found Lula ahead 39% to 33% on 21 August, and BTG/Nexus found a 46% to 45% runoff on 24 August.

Both point the same way as this Brazil presidential poll: Lula ahead on points, but not beyond doubt. The next round of surveys will show whether his slide has stopped.

Brazil votes on Sunday 4 October. If no candidate takes more than half of the valid votes, the top two meet again on 25 October.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is leading Brazil’s 2026 presidential election? No one clearly. The PoderData/Aya poll released on 27 August 2026 puts Lula at 38% and Flávio Bolsonaro at 35% in the first round, and 45% to 44% in a runoff, both inside the two-point margin of error. What is the rejection rate of Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro? Both are rejected by 49% of voters in the PoderData/Aya survey. That means nearly half of Brazilians say they would never vote for either man. When does Brazil vote in 2026? The first round is on Sunday 4 October 2026. A runoff, if needed, follows on 25 October 2026.

World.title: Brazil Industry Warns End of Blusinhas Tax Threatens 109,000 Jobs
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

BRAZIL · ECONOMY

Key Facts —

What happened Brazil’s industry confederation says ending the blusinhas tax puts 109,000 jobs at risk in 2026.

—

How big The same study puts R$21.8 billion (US$4.2 billion) of Brazilian production on the line.

—

The real story Zero duty on parcels under US$50 makes imported clothes and electronics cheaper than Brazilian-made ones.

—

The catch The figures come from the industry lobby fighting the change, not from the government.

—

What comes next The committee votes Tuesday 1 September, and both congressional floors vote on Wednesday.

—

The deadline If Congress does not act by 8 September, the 20 percent import duty returns on its own.

Brazil’s industry lobby says ending the blusinhas tax on small imported parcels could cost 109,000 jobs this year. Congress has moved up the vote, with final decisions now due days before the tax could return.

What the industry warning says

The Confederação Nacional da Indústria, Brazil’s National Confederation of Industry, published its technical note on Wednesday 26 August. It says ending the blusinhas tax threatens 109,000 jobs and R$21.8 billion (US$4.2 billion) of domestic production in 2026.

The estimate comes from Marcio Guerra, the confederation’s economics superintendent. He argues the tax narrowed the tax gap between Brazilian producers and foreign platforms.

The confederation projects low-value imports will grow by R$7 billion (US$1.4 billion) if the rate stays at zero. That is a 42.3 percent rise over a scenario where the 20 percent duty still applied.

It expects 249.5 million small parcels to enter Brazil in 2026 under the zero rate. With the duty in force, it says the figure would be 194.9 million.

In money terms, imports through the compliance programme would reach R$23.6 billion (US$4.6 billion). With the tax, the projection falls to R$16.6 billion (US$3.2 billion).

The jobs figure rests on a multiplier. For each real imported, the confederation says R$3.11 (US$0.60) is no longer generated along Brazilian supply chains.

Two-thirds of the impact would fall on manufacturing. Clothing, electronics and consumer goods compete most directly with cheap parcels.

How the blusinhas tax ended, and why it could return

The blusinhas tax is a 20 percent federal import duty on online purchases of up to US$50 by individuals. Congress created it in 2024 to shield local retail from foreign e-commerce.

The nickname comes from the blusinhas, or little blouses, that Brazilians order from sites like Shein and AliExpress. The duty is collected at checkout through a compliance programme called Remessa Conforme.

President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva signed a provisional measure on Tuesday 12 May 2026 that cut the rate to zero. A provisional measure is a presidential decree with immediate force of law in Brazil.

That measure expires on 8 September unless both houses of Congress convert it into law. If it lapses, the 20 percent duty returns automatically the next day.

A vote moved up as the deadline closes in

A joint committee of deputies and senators was due to start work only on 1 September. After Lula met congressional leaders on Wednesday, the installation was moved up to Friday 28 August.

Chamber of Deputies Speaker Hugo Motta named deputy Reginaldo Lopes to chair the committee. Senate President Davi Alcolumbre must still name the rapporteur, who will be a senator.

The committee is now expected to vote the rapporteur’s opinion on Tuesday 1 September. Floor votes in the Chamber and the Senate are scheduled for Wednesday 2 September.

Alcolumbre promised the measure will not expire. “This provisional measure will not die,” he told reporters after the meeting at the presidential palace.

The hurry is easy to explain. Congress has one working week left before the deadline, in the middle of an election campaign.

Who wants the tax back, and who does not

Industry and retail groups want the duty restored. The National Confederation of Commerce and the São Paulo industry federation had asked Alcolumbre to keep the debate off the election calendar.

Business groups have also taken the issue to the Supreme Federal Court, Brazil’s top court. They argue that zero duty creates unfair competition for Brazilian firms.

The government sees it the other way. Motta says ending the charge is a popular demand that eases the budgets of millions of online shoppers.

Supporters of the cut note that many Brazilian companies also sell through the same platforms. Consumers, not factories, paid the 20 percent charge.

The confederation’s numbers are estimates from an interested party. The government has not published a jobs forecast of its own.

What it means for shoppers in Brazil

Nothing changes at checkout for now. Parcels worth up to US$50 bought on compliant platforms enter Brazil without the federal import duty.

State sales tax still applies to those purchases. Only the federal import duty is at stake in next week’s votes.

If Congress approves the measure, the zero rate becomes permanent law. If it fails, the 20 percent charge returns on 9 September.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Brazil’s blusinhas tax? It is a 20 percent federal import duty created in 2024 on international online purchases of up to US$50 by individuals. A provisional measure cut the rate to zero in May 2026, and Congress must vote by 8 September to keep it that way. Why does industry say 109,000 jobs are at risk? The National Confederation of Industry says cheap imports would undercut Brazilian-made goods without the duty. It estimates 109,000 jobs and R$21.8 billion (US$4.2 billion) of production at risk in 2026. When will Congress vote on the blusinhas tax? The joint committee votes on Tuesday 1 September. Floor votes in the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate are scheduled for Wednesday 2 September.

Sources: Poder360 (CNI technical note, 26 August 2026), Agência Câmara, G1, Gazeta do Povo, Senado Federal.
