World.title: Partial Lunar Eclipse Will Be Visible Across Costa Rica Tonight
World.content:
Anyone in Costa Rica will have the chance to watch a dramatic lunar spectacle tonight, as a deep partial lunar eclipse will be visible across from start to finish. At its peak, 93 percent of the Moon will be swallowed by Earth’s shadow, leaving only a thin sliver of light along one edge.

According to the National Science and Technology Center foundation (Cientec), the eclipse begins at 7:23 p.m. and runs for five hours and 38 minutes in total. The early stage, when the Moon passes through Earth’s outer shadow called the penumbra, is subtle and difficult to notice with the naked eye. The more dramatic change arrives at 8:33 p.m., when the partial eclipse begins and the Moon starts moving into the umbra, the darker inner shadow.

Maximum coverage hits at 10:12 p.m., when 93 percent of the lunar surface will sit inside Earth’s shadow. Cientec described this as a particularly deep eclipse, noting that only a small edge of the Moon will remain outside the darkest part of the shadow at that moment. From there, the process reverses, with the partial phase ending at 11:51 p.m. and the final penumbral stage wrapping up at 1:01 a.m. Friday.

No special equipment is required to watch since unlike a solar eclipse, a lunar eclipse is completely safe to view directly, so no filters, telescopes or binoculars are needed. Anyone hoping for a good view should simply look for a spot with a clear sky, away from artificial lights, and wait for the show. Binoculars can help viewers pick out craters and surface features as they slip in and out of shadow, and the eclipse is easy to photograph with a phone camera, especially one with zoom.

As the Moon nears its deepest point in Earth’s shadow, it can take on reddish, copper or orange tones. This happens because sunlight bending through Earth’s atmosphere still reaches the lunar surface even when direct sunlight is blocked, casting the characteristic colors associated with a blood moon. Tonight’s event will remain a partial eclipse rather than a total one because the Moon will not fully enter the umbra, though at 93 percent coverage the difference will be barely noticeable to the eye.

For anyone wanting a more guided experience, the University of Costa Rica’s Planetarium in San Pedro is hosting a free public viewing with telescopes from 6 to 9 p.m., no reservation required. Because the event ends before the eclipse reaches its deepest point, visitors will be able to see the start of the partial phase but will miss the 10:12 p.m. peak. The planetarium is located in the Ciudad de la Investigación on UCR’s Rodrigo Facio campus.

Cientec noted that this is the second lunar eclipse of 2026, and that stargazers who miss tonight’s show will have a long wait for the next one, since the following partial lunar eclipse visible from Costa Rica will not occur until January 2028.

World.title: Costa Rica Moves Toward Satellite Cell Coverage With Starlink
World.content:
Costa Rica is getting its first taste of satellite connected cell phones, and both of the biggest telecom operators are behind it. Liberty and Kolbi, the state linked carrier formerly known as ICE, separately signed agreements with Elon Musk’s Starlink on the same day in April, setting up a race to bring satellite to cell technology where mountains, dense jungle and remote coastline leave plenty of gaps in mobile coverage.

The idea is simple even if the engineering behind it is not. When a compatible phone loses its terrestrial signal, it automatically searches for and connects to one of Starlink’s low orbit satellites instead, using the same network as any other phone call or text, just routed through space rather than a cell tower. No antenna, no separate satellite phone and no extra equipment is required. The only real conditions are a clear, unobstructed view of the sky and a phone running updated software.

Liberty is positioning its version, called Liberty Starlink, as a consumer product aimed at hikers, campers, anglers and anyone spending time outside cell coverage, along with a genuine safety net during emergencies. Kolbi’s approach so far looks different. Its satellite tie up is being introduced first for corporate, institutional and government clients rather than everyday consumers, framed more around expanding broadband access for business than as a hiking or fishing companion.

Neither service is live yet. Both companies have targeted the second half of 2026 for commercial launch, and Liberty’s own website describes the current period as one of preparation, with details on pricing, compatible phone models and exact features still to come.

What the first phase will actually deliver is more limited than it might sound. According to Liberty, initial functionality will cover text messages, Google Maps location lookups and specific WhatsApp features including text messages, voice notes and location sharing. Phone calls, video calls and anything requiring a steady, continuous connection will likely be limited or unavailable at launch. Voice and richer data access are expected to arrive gradually as the technology matures, though no firm date has been given.

The connection itself is not instant either. Establishing a satellite link can take a few minutes and may involve brief interruptions while the phone locks onto a passing satellite, with automatic reconnection attempts if the signal drops. Device compatibility is also still being finalized, and Liberty has said it will publish a list of supported phone models before the service goes live. Everything runs on standard 4G LTE handsets, so anyone hoping for satellite access on an older or unsupported model will need to wait for that list.

The technology has already proven useful elsewhere in the area. When Hurricane Melissa knocked out terrestrial networks across Jamaica, Liberty Latin America activated the same Starlink partnership to keep basic text and data communication running for affected customers, giving people a way to reach family and access emergency information even as cell towers went down.

Costa Rica’s rollout remains a preview rather than a working product. But with two major carriers pursuing satellite partnerships at once, it appears headed toward a future were losing signal on a remote beach or mountain trail no longer means losing the ability to send a text.

World.title: Another Tropical Wave Arrives as Costa Rica School Closures Rise Again
World.content:
When will it end? Costa Rica’s recovery from this month’s flooding suffered a setback today as the number of schools without in-person classes rose from 12 to 40. The increase comes as Tropical Wave 37 crosses, bringing yet another round of rain to northern and Caribbean communities where the ground remains soaked and some roads are still difficult to use.

Thirty-two of the affected schools and high schools are in the Northern Zone. Four are in Sarapiquí and another four are in the Guápiles education region. The schools will use Costa Rica’s hybrid education system while their buildings or access routes remain unsafe. In-person classes will resume once local conditions improve.

The increase does not mean Costa Rica has returned to the worst point of the flooding. On August 19, 473 schools remained closed and more than 1,300 people were staying in emergency shelters. By Wednesday, August 26, the number of school closures had fallen to 12. today’s rise to 40 shows how fragile that progress remains. Several days with less rain allowed rivers to fall and roads to reopen, but the ground has not had enough time to dry. A new downpour can quickly flood a low road, raise a stream or trigger another landslide.

If you didn’t know by now, tropical waves are long areas of unstable air that move west across the tropics. They are common during Costa Rica’s rainy season and do not automatically cause serious damage. The concern this time is that Wave 37 is arriving after weeks of repeated rain. Strong trade winds over the Caribbean Sea are also pushing more moisture toward Costa Rica. Rain was expected first near the Limón coast Thursday morning before spreading farther inland across the Caribbean and Northern Zone.

The strongest downpours are expected in the afternoon, particularly in mountainous areas. Rain could continue tonight over the Caribbean mountains and near the South Pacific coast. Anyone traveling through the Northern Zone, Sarapiquí or the Caribbean should check road conditions before leaving. Conditions can vary considerably between nearby communities, especially where the only access road crosses a river or passes below a steep slope.

Drivers should not try to cross flooded roads as water can hide damage to the pavement, and even a shallow-looking current may be strong enough to move a vehicle. The latest rain falls as nine flood-hit areas remain covered by a national emergency declaration: Guatuso, Turrialba, Sarapiquí, Talamanca, Matina, Limón, Guácimo, Pococí and Siquirres. The declaration is intended to speed up repairs to roads, bridges, water systems and other public infrastructure damaged by Tropical Waves 32 and 33 earlier this month.

Wave 37 should continue moving west after crossing Costa Rica and that may minimize its effects, but it will not immediately remove the danger left by saturated ground. Families in affected communities should continue checking school announcements because a school can reopen or close again as road and weather conditions change.

World.title: Panama and El Salvador Declare Alerts as El Niño Intensifies
World.content:
Panama and El Salvador declared states of alert on Tuesday over the El Niño climate phenomenon, which is expected to reach record levels and has already forced authorities to reduce traffic through the Panama Canal. El Niño is a natural climate phenomenon that occurs every two to seven years.

Surface waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean become warmer, bringing hotter and drier conditions to some areas and cooler and wetter weather to others, while increasing the risk of extreme weather events.It is occurring on top of human-caused global warming and, according to experts, could help make 2027 the hottest year ever recorded.

Against this backdrop, Panama’s Interior Minister Dinoska Montalvo announced Tuesday that a state of emergency had been declared so the country can “be prepared to face whatever may happen.” The measure is intended, among other things, to speed up administrative procedures in response to the climate phenomenon.

Last week, the Panama Canal Authority had already announced that because of water shortages, the interoceanic waterway would reduce traffic from 36 to 34 vessel transits per day starting September 3, and then to 32 per day beginning in mid-September. About 5% of global maritime trade passes through the 80-kilometer, or roughly 50-mile, canal.

Farther north, El Salvador also declared its highest alert level Tuesday because of El Niño, which is causing widespread drought. Environmental authorities said 14 temperature records were broken during August. “A red alert is declared due to meteorological and agricultural drought throughout the entire national territory,” the country’s Civil Protection agency wrote on X.

The measure includes monitoring water resources and crops, identifying communities facing emergency conditions and strengthening epidemiological surveillance, according to the agency. The lack of rainfall in El Salvador has lowered water levels at springs and caused crop losses. According to the Association of the Salvadoran Chamber of Small and Medium Agricultural Producers, the first harvest of basic grains is expected to suffer an overall production loss of about 20%.

The Ministry of Agriculture had previously announced food assistance for farming households affected by the drought. Part of El Salvador lies within Central America’s “Dry Corridor,” an arid region that is especially vulnerable to extreme weather. The corridor also includes part of Honduras, where southern and western areas have suffered losses of corn and bean crops. The government has placed nearly 80% of the country under alert.

The United Nations World Food Programme recently estimated that Central America will “probably be the region most affected in terms of the relative increase in food insecurity” caused by El Niño. From Mexico to northern Brazil, including areas along the Pacific coast and across the Guiana Shield, about 110 million people experienced the hottest July in the available record, according to calculations based on data from the European Union’s Copernicus climate program.

World.title: Sick Pelicans Keep Washing Up on Costa Rica’s Pacific Beaches and Nobody Knows Why
World.content:
If a pelican walks toward you on the beach, something is wrong with that bird. Don’t touch it. Sick, disoriented and dead pelicans have been turning up along Costa Rica’s Pacific coast since late June. Two months on, nobody has worked out what is killing them. Start with the question most people actually want answered.

It is not bird flu — at least not in anything tested so far. SENASA has processed 121 samples from 59 wild birds through August 10, covering pelicans, boobies, blue-footed boobies, hawks, owls and parakeets, and everyone came back negative for avian influenza. Tests for Newcastle disease came back negative as well, and the agency says nothing so far links the deaths to either virus. Negative results are not an answer, though.

They only rule things out. Randall Arguedas, who heads epidemiology at SENASA, points out that wild bird die-offs can come from a long list of causes — other infectious agents, poisoning, environmental conditions, nutritional problems — and that sorting between them takes more than viral screening.

The investigation has widened accordingly, into clinical assessments, tissue studies and necropsy findings, with SENASA, SINAC, the Health Ministry, Universidad Nacional and wildlife rescue centres all working the same problem.Arguedas is blunt that no single cause can be pinned down yet, and that whatever conclusion comes will have to rest on lab work rather than guesswork.

The pelicans are the bulk of what’s been examined. Nineteen of them account for 39 of the samples, alongside five blue-footed boobies and seven other boobies. There is one confirmed bird flu case in the country, and it is worth understanding because it is why this got attention in the first place.

In June a blue-footed booby found at Manuel Antonio tested positive for highly pathogenic avian influenza, type A, subtype H5 — Costa Rica’s first case since 2023. Sick pelicans started appearing shortly afterwards, and the timing alone was enough to make people assume the two were connected. So far the lab work says they aren’t.

What you would actually notice, if you came across one, is the behavior. Biologist Rodolfo Vargas, who founded Refugio Animal Costa Rica, has flagged pelicans approaching swimmers as abnormal for the species here, and counted 13 birds in that condition around Guanacaste over a matter of weeks. Reports have clustered in Guanacaste and around Jacó, with affected birds appearing weak, disoriented, or struggling to fly.

A healthy pelican wants nothing to do with you. One that lets you walk up to it is telling you it’s ill. So, leave it where it is and don’t handle sick or dead birds, and report what you’ve found so the people with protective equipment and a diagnostic protocol can deal with it. The nearest SINAC or SENASA office is the right call, and reporting promptly matters more than anything you could do yourself.

Resist the urge to move the bird somewhere shadier or carry it to a vet. You risk exposing yourself to something nobody has identified yet, and you remove the animal from the location where investigators need to find it. Keep your dog well away, and wash your hands if you’ve touched anything nearby.

None of this is a reason to change your beach plans. A handful of sick birds across a coastline this long is not an outbreak affecting people, and no health authority has restricted access to any beach. It is a reason to look, not touch, and to make one phone call if you see something wrong.

Two months of negative tests means the answer, when it arrives, is likely to be something less obvious than a virus.

World.title: BEL announces Tentative load shedding for tonight!
World.content:
BEL announces Tentative load shedding for tonight!

By Zoila Palma: Belize Electricity Limited (BEL) has announced a tentative load shedding schedule for tonight as the country’s power grid faces possible supply constraints due to high demand in Mexico.

BEL said Comisión Federal de Electricidad (CFE) has informed the company that it may need to curtail power because of high demand on its system. As a result, load shedding may become necessary in several sections of Belize to maintain stability of the national grid.

The tentative schedule indicates that power interruptions may occur between 8:00 p.m. and 11:00 p.m. in sections served by the San Pedro Feeder 2, Corozal Feeder 3, San Ignacio Feeder 1, Dangriga Feeder 1 and Ladyville Feeder 1 Zones 1 and 2.

In San Ignacio, affected areas include the downtown area, Kontiki, Swamyville, Mosquitoville, Boiton, Bradley’s Bank, Cahal Pech, Trapiche, Branch Mouth Road, New Area Santa Elena and portions of 2nd and 3rd Streets.

In San Pedro, areas include San Pedrito, the Airstrip area, San Pablo, San Marcos, DFC, Eiley Subdivision and surrounding communities.

BEL emphasized that the schedule is tentative and may change depending on energy demand and generation levels.

The company explained that load shedding involves deliberately disconnecting feeders or sections of feeders from the grid to match available generation and prevent a wider collapse of the electricity system.

World.title: NICH launches “Belize @45 Magical History Tour” with historian Assad Shoman
World.content:
NICH launches “Belize @45 Magical History Tour” with historian Assad Shoman

By Zoila Palma: The National Institute of Culture and History (NICH) is inviting Belizeans to explore the country’s history through the “Belize @45 Magical History Tour,” featuring historian Assad Shoman.

The initiative forms part of activities surrounding Belize’s 45th anniversary of independence and aims to encourage deeper reflection and discussion about the nation’s past.

The tour will include engagements with high school students, giving young Belizeans an opportunity to examine the country’s history critically and explore aspects that may not always be covered in traditional textbooks.

Public forums will also be held in the evenings, allowing community members to participate in discussions and ask questions about Belize’s historical development.

NICH said the tour will visit communities across the country, with activities scheduled at the Ignacia Cacho Public Library in Corozal on August 28.

In September, the tour will continue at the San Ignacio-Santa Elena House of Culture on September 3, Benque Viejo House of Culture on September 4, and the George Price Center for Peace and Development on September 7.

Additional sessions are scheduled for the Belize City House of Culture on September 11, Banquitas House of Culture in Orange Walk on September 15, and the Corozal House of Culture on September 16.

The tour encourages participants to reflect on Belize’s journey to independence and consider whether independence fully ended the social, economic and historical influences inherited from the colonial era.

NICH is encouraging Belizeans, particularly students and community members, to participate in the tour and engage in what it describes as an opportunity to ask difficult questions about the country’s history.

World.title: Team Belize represent at Gran Premio Panamá
World.content:
Team Belize represent at Gran Premio Panamá

By Zoila Palma: Belizean cyclists proudly represented the country at the Gran Premio Panamá, earning recognition from the Belize Olympic and Commonwealth Games Association for their efforts on the international stage.

The association praised the riders for competing with determination and carrying the Belizean flag throughout the event. Their participation provided another opportunity to showcase Belizean cycling talent in the region.

The Belize Olympic and Commonwealth Games Association thanked the cyclists for their commitment and for representing Belize with pride, noting that their efforts continue to put the country on the map through sport.

World.title: Rare red northern lights could appear alongside Red moon during Lunar eclipse
World.content:
Rare red northern lights could appear alongside Red moon during Lunar eclipse

By Zoila Palma: Skygazers could be treated to a rare double spectacle tonight as a partial lunar eclipse is expected to turn much of the Moon a deep coppery red while a geomagnetic storm could produce vibrant northern lights across parts of North America.

The partial lunar eclipse will be visible in the Americas, Europe, Africa and Western Asia.

The Moon will pass into Earth’s shadow, with about 96 percent of its surface expected to be covered during the deepest stage of the eclipse.

At the same time, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has issued a moderate G2 geomagnetic storm warning, raising the possibility that auroras could be visible as far south as parts of the northern United States.

Astronomers say observers in Canada and Alaska may have the best chance of seeing the aurora and eclipsed Moon at the same time.

The two phenomena are unlikely to appear in exactly the same part of the sky, but viewing conditions could allow the glowing auroral bands to appear alongside the reddish Moon, particularly for observers farther west.

The potential aurora display follows a powerful M-class solar flare recorded on August 25, which was followed by a coronal mass ejection—a large cloud of charged solar material traveling toward Earth.

NOAA forecast G1 and G2 geomagnetic storm conditions between August 27 and 28, coinciding with the lunar eclipse, which is expected to begin at around 9:23 p.m. EDT, reach its peak shortly after midnight and end around 3 a.m. Friday.

The eclipse will not technically be a total lunar eclipse, since a small portion of the Moon will remain outside Earth’s darkest shadow.

However, it is expected to be the deepest lunar eclipse visible worldwide until December 2028.

The Moon’s red appearance occurs because Earth’s atmosphere filters and bends sunlight toward its surface, while auroral colors are produced when charged particles from the Sun interact with gases in Earth’s atmosphere.

World.title: 29-year-old man busted with amount of cocaine so small it didn’t move the scale; jailed for outstanding $105 fine
World.content:
29-year-old man busted with amount of cocaine so small it didn’t move the scale; jailed for outstanding $105 fine

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City man who pleaded guilty to possession of an undetermined amount of cocaine has been sent to prison after he was unable to pay an old outstanding court fine.

Jamal Alexander Jones Jr., 29, a Waste Control worker, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Thursday, where he pleaded guilty to possession of a controlled drug.

Jones was busted on Saturday, August 22, 2026, on Administration Drive in Belize City with an amount of cocaine reportedly so small that it could not register on the gram scale.

For the drug offence, Jones was fined $130 plus $5 cost of court and was given until October 30, 2026, to pay. In default, he faces one month imprisonment.

However, the court also discovered that Jones had an outstanding $105 fine stemming from a 2023 conviction. The Magistrate ordered that the outstanding amount be paid immediately before he could be released.

Jones was unable to pay the $105 and was subsequently escorted to the Belize Central Prison on a warrant to serve prison time in default of the outstanding fine.

World.title: International News: Trump orders Lake Ontario renamed ‘Lake America’ due to escalating U.S.-Canada Trade War
World.content:
International News: Trump orders Lake Ontario renamed ‘Lake America’ due to escalating U.S.-Canada Trade War

By Zoila Palma: U.S. President Donald Trump has signed an executive order directing his administration to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America,” escalating tensions with Canada as the two countries remain locked in a worsening trade dispute.

Trump signed the order in the Oval Office today, instructing the U.S. Department of the Interior and the U.S. Board on Geographic Names to formalize the name change within 30 days.

During the signing, Trump compared the move to his decision last year to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America,” joking that the next step could be renaming one of the Atlantic or Pacific oceans.

The name Lake Ontario dates back centuries and is derived from an Iroquois word meaning “lake of shining waters.” The lake forms part of the shoreline of Toronto, Canada, while most of its volume and its deepest areas are on the U.S. side.

White House staff secretary Ben Moss described it as an “American lake” as he presented the order to Trump for signing.

The renaming comes amid a sharp deterioration in U.S.-Canada trade relations.

Trump recently imposed tariffs of up to 50 percent on a range of Canadian goods after trade negotiations broke down, while Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney responded with tariffs on U.S. exports ranging from 15 to 50 percent. Trump has also threatened to increase tariffs on Canadian automobiles and auto parts from 25 to 50 percent.

Canada has rejected the proposed name change and indicated it will continue referring to the body of water as Lake Ontario.

World.title: Honduran construction worker jailed after failing to pay $1,000 fine for entering Belize illegally
World.content:
Honduran construction worker jailed after failing to pay $1,000 fine for entering Belize illegally

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 25-year-old Honduran national who told immigration authorities he had been living in Belize since 2023 has been sent to the Belize Central Prison after he was unable to pay a $1,000 fine for an immigration offence.

Franklin Estralin Guerra Jacinto, a construction worker of the Gungulung area, appeared unrepresented before the Chief Magistrate on Tuesday, where he pleaded guilty to failing to produce a valid permit upon demand by an Immigration Officer.

Jacinto was fined $1,000 plus $5 cost of court, which he was ordered to pay forthwith. In default of payment, he was ordered to serve six months in prison.

According to the facts presented in court, police at the Raccoon Street Police Station contacted the Immigration Department on Sunday, August 23, after Jacinto was detained.

Immigration officers interviewed Jacinto and requested identification. He reportedly produced a Honduran passport, but checks revealed that it contained no Belize entry stamp.

Jacinto allegedly told authorities that he entered Belize through the Mopan River area near Benque Viejo, Cayo District, in October 2023 and had remained in the country since then.

Immigration officials subsequently searched the Migration Information and Data Analysis System, or MIDAS, using Jacinto’s name, date of birth and passport number, but reportedly found no record of his entry into Belize.

He was informed of his irregular immigration status and later charged.

Jacinto was unable to pay the $1,000 fine and was escorted to the Belize Central Prison to begin serving the six-month default sentence.

World.title: Honduran man Efrain Palacio remanded to prison for allegedly raping child twice
World.content:
Honduran man Efrain Palacio remanded to prison for allegedly raping child twice

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 56-year-old man has been remanded to prison without bail after a Preliminary Inquiry (PI) concluded with his committal to the High Court on two counts of rape of a child.

Efrain Dionisio Palacio, a Honduran national residing in the Spanish Town area of Ladyville, appeared unrepresented before the Chief Magistrate on Tuesday afternoon. Following a brief inquiry, the court determined that a prima facie case had been established against him. Palacio is now set to stand trial during the High Court session commencing on October 7, 2026.

The charges stem from an investigation launched early this year. On January 8, 2026, a young student, accompanied by her mother, reported the alleged abuse at the Ladyville Police Station. According to the report, Palacio—who was staying at the household at the time—entered the victim’s bedroom on two separate occasions in February 2023, turned off the lights, and raped her.

Following police investigations and recorded statements, Palacio was arrested and charged. He has remained in custody since January and was remanded back to prison following Tuesday’s hearing.

World.title: Fire engulfs Superior Parts dealership on Hagley Park Road
World.content:
A fire has engulfed the Superior Parts dealership on Hagley Park Road in St Andrew. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Firefighters are now battling a blaze that has engulfed the Superior Parts dealership on Hagley Park Road in St Andrew.

The cause of the fire is not yet known but the incident happened around midday. At least two units from the Jamaica Fire Brigade are on location.

There have been no confirmed reports of casualties.

More to come.

World.title: Waiting for water
World.content:
SOME school leaders are cautiously optimistic as they welcome the Government’s promise to provide water to schools ahead of next month’s reopening, but two of them have made it clear that the assistance must be more than an announcement but a reliable flow of support.

“The principals across all levels of the system are elated that the move is being made to secure sanitation across the schools… If water is provided at no cost or very low cost to schools, this is a move that we not only welcome for our students and our staff but also I am sure the parents would be quite elated to know that their children will be placed in safe and secure school environments because we’ll have the water required for cooking, cleaning and general sanitation,” Anniona Jones, president of the Jamaica Association of Principals of Secondary Schools (JAPSS) told the Jamaica Observer Wednesday.

Her comments came after Water Minister Matthew Samuda assured that the Government will be taking action to ensure that schools, farmers and early-childhood institutions have adequate water supplies amid worsening drought conditions across the island.

The minister’s comments came during official commissioning of the Bunkers Hill Water Supply System in Clarendon on Tuesday. He announced that water trucks will be available to schools while a structured tank programme is being developed to assist early-childhood institutions and farmers with inadequate storage capacity.

Jones, who is also the principal of Haile Selassie High School, argued that while the initiative is welcomed, many institutions across Jamaica would require more than just water assistance. She pointed to the need to have adequate storage facilities.

“It’s one thing to be willing to provide the water, however some schools may need additional support in having tanks and the plumbing costs required for connection to ensure that they will have sufficient water,” she said.

Highlighting the issues faced by her school, Jones said the Government must be ready to commit to frequent water trips, the provision of water tanks to institutions beyond just early childhood education centres, and further assistance with piping systems to minimise water woes come September.

“My school is in a community that has frequent water loss, particularly during the day. We do have some storage facilities, however we are definitely in need of additional tanks. We emptied some of the tanks,” she said, adding that some of the tanks were damaged by both Hurricane Beryl in 2024 and last year’s Hurricane Melissa.

“We would definitely need additional support with additional tanks and, of course, the cost to get those tanks connected to our bathroom facility. We’ve made a move as school administrators generally to secure our canteen, to secure at least one of our bathrooms — and many schools have done that for their staff sanitary facilities. However, given the population, our concern is always the number of tanks available, the number of students, and the frequency of refilling, because that can be quite costly,” she outlined.

Despite these concerns Jones said she is pleased with steps being taken by the Government, and expressed hope that delivery of the initiative will be as convincing as the announcement.

“We welcome not just the statements, but we really are looking for the follow-through. Several comments have been made to reassure the public, however what we will find reassuring at this point is action. We want consistent, clear action that shows that we’re going beyond the sound bites and public relations, but we’re going towards consistent maintenance of high-quality standards for education,” she said.

Sharing similar sentiments was principal of deCarteret College Dr Prim Lewis, who is also fond of the water initiative, and hopeful that the Government actually delivers on its promise.

While acknowledging that her school, located in the parish of Manchester, was not currently experiencing drought conditions due to its climate-resilient infrastructure, she noted that many other institutions are not as fortunate.

Pointing to St Elizabeth, the parish in which she lives and which was severely affected by back-to-back hurricanes, Lewis stressed that the Government will have to make a significant effort to avoid school closures due to empty pipes.

“In St Elizabeth we have not had water in some areas since before [Hurricane] Melissa, and that was basically exasperated by Melissa. Personally, I live in Horizon Park, and at home I have not had water since post-Melissa. I know that sometimes when the NWC operations personnel say that they will bring water, what will happen is that the water may come later than anticipated, based on the number of schools that they have to supply [with] water,” Lewis said.

“The [National] Water Commission has always responded when called, where water is concerned to be delivered to schools. As I said before, it’s just that sometimes the response is not as timely as we expect. I have seen where schools are waiting on water and keeping the school open, expecting that water will arrive at ‘x’ time and the water did not arrive at ‘x’ time and therefore the school had to be closed for that day. [So], I am cautiously optimistic,” she added.

World.title: Sandals even sweeter
World.content:
Executive chairman of Sandals Resorts International, Adam Stewart addressing awardees during the Unique Vacations 2025 MVP Awards ceremony at the Montego Bay Convention Centre Tuesday night. (Photo: Philp Lemonte)

MONTEGO BAY, St James —Sandals Resorts International Executive Chairman Adam Stewart says the devastation caused by last October’s Hurricane Melissa has given the resort chain an opportunity to transform several of its Jamaican properties and once again “change the game” in the hospitality industry.

“It is almost serendipitous on multitude levels,” he said of the rebuilding programme which has seen major work undertaken at Sandals South Coast, Sandals Montego Bay, and the former Sandals Royal Caribbean, now Sandals Caribbean Cay.

Addressing the Unique Vacations Limited (UVL) 2025 MVP Awards at Montego Bay Convention Centre on Tuesday night, Stewart said Sandals had compressed what would normally have been years of redevelopment into less than a year.

“We have done three years of work in what will be about nine and a half months,” Stewart said, contrasting Sandals’ approach with competitors which, he noted, were largely focused on restoring their properties to their pre-hurricane state.

Sandals South Coast is scheduled to reopen on November 18, followed by the transformed Sandals Montego Bay and Sandals Caribbean Cay.

Stewart said the redevelopment of Sandals Montego Bay was particularly significant, as the property was the first in the Sandals chain, opening in 1981 with 99 rooms.

Stewart said the upgraded property will be “unbelievable”.

He made a similar promise for Sandals Caribbean Cay, saying guests would barely recognise the property when it reopens.

Stewart, who said the scale of investment would help create products capable of strengthening Jamaica’s position in the global tourism market, expressed confidence in the future.

“Demand for Jamaica is back; 2027 is going to be incredibly strong. Jamaica is a gift to the world,” said the hotel chain tycoon.

He also highlighted Sandals’ response to the hurricane beyond the physical reconstruction of its properties, saying the company provided each team member with $30,000 in cash, retained approximately 2,000 employees on its payroll while they were unable to work, and channelled about US$6 million in assistance to affected communities through Sandals Foundation.

Stewart stressed that the recovery was not merely about rebuilding resorts.

“It is the people. It is you,” he told the UVL team, pointing out that the warmth and hospitality of Caribbean people remain one of the region’s greatest competitive advantages.

That message of resilience was echoed by UVL Senior Director of Call Centre Operations Leezo Wallace, who told the awards gathering that the company’s team had faced uncertainty and major disruptions but continued to deliver. UVL Montego Bay was devastated by the Category 5 hurricane.

“Resilience is not simply about getting through difficult times; it is about how you respond when things get difficult,” Wallace said.

He praised the team for maintaining a strong performance despite the challenges of the year and singled out the company’s top revenue earners, Peter-Gay Rhodes and Tia Matthews, who generated approximately US$5.9 million and US$5.8 million, respectively, in 2025.

Wallace also celebrated Marva Nelson who, after years of telling him that she would become an MVP before leaving the company, finally received the award Tuesday night.

He said the achievements being celebrated extended beyond revenue figures, noting that every booking, guest interaction, difficult call, and effort to support colleagues contributed to the company’s performance.

Wallace also acknowledged the management team for supporting employees through the difficult period.

Among the top awardees on Tuesday night were: Richard Somerville, who walked away with the Senior Director Award; Manager of the Year went to Sharieka Vassel; while Kaydeen White copped the Supervisor of the Year Award.

UVL Chief Executive Officer Jeff Clarke, who was unable to attend because of a scheduling conflict, delivered a video message in which he praised the team for maintaining service levels despite the hurricane’s impact on their personal lives and the business.

Clarke noted that the company had lost its office in the disaster but said the team quickly secured a new location and resumed operations.

“The team stepped up, found a new location, got up and running in a very short period of time, and continued delivering excellent service,” he said.

He said the MVP Awards recognised employees who had consistently delivered strong business results, exceptional service and leadership, while noting that the 2025 awards recognised 26 team members across sales, customer service, administration and leadership.

Clarke also highlighted the performance of the company’s highest revenue contributors.

For Stewart, the resilience demonstrated by the UVL team and the wider Jamaican population underscored the importance of continuing to invest in people and the destination.

He urged Jamaicans to “hold each other up” and encourage one another, rather than simply go through the motions of everyday life.

“I believe by being born in this country we won the lottery from day one,” Stewart said.

World.title: From Chris Brown to Cardi B: BZR bets big on Kingston
World.content:
US star Cardi B will headline the BZR Weekend at the National Stadium on October 18, 2026 .

The message coming out of Wednesday’s official BZR Weekend media launch was as ambitious as the superstar preparing to headline it: Kingston is ready for the world.

Come October 18, organisers are hoping to prove it.

Global rap superstar Cardi B will make her highly anticipated Jamaican concert debut inside the National Stadium as the headline attraction for BZR WKND 2026, an entertainment experience organisers believe can further position Kingston among the world’s premier destinations for major live events.

The announcement was officially celebrated inside the Innovative Gallery at the AC Hotel Kingston, where media, government officials, and entertainment stakeholders gathered for a launch hosted by media personality Chiney K, with DJ Narity providing the entertainment.

But amid the excitement surrounding Cardi B’s impending arrival, an even bigger vision emerged — one in which Jamaica was showcased as a destination capable of bringing some of the world’s biggest entertainers to its shores.

“The world is watching Jamaica,” declared Gramps Morgan, one of the event’s organisers. “People like Live Nation are looking at Kingston and Montego Bay the same way they look at Miami, New York, Los Angeles, and that’s because our culture has impacted the world.”

That confidence will be put to the test when BZR WKND unfolds from October 16-19, bringing together music, culture, entertainment, and lifestyle experiences, culminating with Cardi B’s National Stadium appearance.

For Kaylia “Press Kay” Williams, founder and CEO of Konnect Media Inc, the weekend represents an opportunity to create something that extends beyond a single concert.

“Today is more than just a press launch, it’s the beginning of what we believe will be one of the most talked-about entertainment weekends on the entertainment calendar,” Williams said.

“It’s not a rumour, we are bringing Cardi B to Jamaica and she will be bringing along some friends.”

Cardi B needs little introduction to Jamaican audiences. One of the most recognisable personalities in contemporary entertainment, the Grammy-winning rapper has built a global following through her music and larger-than-life personality, while repeatedly showing her affection for Jamaica and its culture. Now, Jamaican fans will finally get to experience her on a local stage.

BZR’s ambitions are not entirely untested as the brand made an emphatic entrance onto Jamaica’s entertainment landscape in 2023 when it brought R&B superstar Chris Brown to the National Stadium. That concert attracted a massive audience and demonstrated Jamaica’s growing appetite for large-scale international concerts. Three years later, organisers are looking to go even bigger.

“BZR Weekend is not just about bringing international entertainers to our shores, it’s about curating unforgettable experiences, and you would have seen that when we brought Chris Brown in 2023,” Williams explained.

“It’s also about showcasing Jamaica as a premier entertainment destination and giving our visitors another reason to come to Jamaica while giving Jamaicans an experience that feels exciting, premium, and uniquely ours.”

State Minister in the Ministry of Industry, Investment and Commerce Delano Seiveright believes Cardi B’s arrival could provide another significant boost to that ambition.

“BZR Weekend got a tremendous response when Chris Brown came here in 2023, and we expect a bigger and even better show for 2026 with Cardi B,” he said. Pointing to the rapper’s enormous international reach, Seiveright said the event presents Jamaica with an opportunity to expose its entertainment product to a massive global audience.

“With her coming to Jamaica, like Gramps said, Jamaica will start getting to the level where, just like Miami, Los Angeles, etcetera, we can host big events,” he said.

And with thousands of visitors expected to descend on the capital, Seiveright had some straightforward advice for those planning to make the trip.

“I would advise anybody booking tickets to Jamaica to do so now. Don’t wait until last minute. We look forward to welcoming Cardi B and the thousands of visitors to our capital.”

For Minister of Culture, Gender, Entertainment and Sports Olivia “Babsy” Grange, the significance of the event is also tied to the resilience of Jamaica’s entertainment sector.

She noted that the upcoming concert follows a particularly difficult period for the industry after Hurricane Melissa devastated sections of the island last October.

“This event is happening against the backdrop of one of the most difficult years the entertainment sector has seen in recent years,” Grange said. “Last year, Hurricane Melissa, a Category 5 storm and the most powerful ever to make landfall in Jamaica, brought devastation to our shores.”

“And so we must understand how resilient we are, because that was last October, and this year, look at us.”

According to Grange, Cardi B’s October 18 appearance will mark the rapper’s first headlining stadium concert in the Caribbean, a milestone she said speaks to the magnitude of what organisers are attempting.

“I’m very impressed by the team that’s making this happen,” she said, outlining that the concert’s potential impact stretches well beyond what happens on stage. An influx of overseas patrons could generate business for hotels, restaurants, transportation providers, vendors, and nightlife establishments across Kingston, allowing the economic benefits of the weekend to ripple through the capital.

In 2023, Chris Brown helped BZR test the possibilities. On October 18, Cardi B could help push them even further. And when one of the world’s biggest rap stars finally touches down in the 876, organisers are hoping the thousands filling the National Stadium will be witnessing more than Cardi B’s Jamaican debut, they could also be witnessing Kingston’s continuing evolution as a world-class entertainment destination.

World.title: Costly drought
World.content:
Water Minister Matthew Samuda and stakeholders examine work being done to lay transmission mains as part of the massive Western Water Resilience Project that is expected to boost supplies in several parishes.

Warning that “Jamaica’s drought is becoming an economic risk”, Nigel Davy, chair of the Private Sector Organisation of Jamaica’s (PSOJ’s) Energy, Environment and Climate Change Committee, has called on business interests to view water conservation as “both a business necessity and a public interest obligation”.

“Water scarcity is no longer only an environmental or household concern [but] is becoming a business, productivity and national resilience issue,” he said in a recent message on the PSOJ’s social media platform.

His comments come even as Jamaica grapples with prolonged drought driven by the El Niño weather pattern which has suppressed local rainfall and caused temperatures to soar. Jamaica’s Met Service has warned that the country could continue experiencing drought conditions into the peak of what is traditionally the main rainy season in October which could strain water supplies, disrupt agricultural production, and increase heat stress on crops and livestock. The crisis — intensified by long-term damage from Hurricane Melissa in October last year — has severely depleted water supplies, decimated agricultural production, increased business’ operating costs, and triggered strict prohibition orders across multiple parishes. Minister of Water, Environment and Climate Change Matthew Samuda has warned that restrictions are likely to move further west as dry conditions persist and dam levels decline.

Davy has called on “every business” to follow a “simple water hierarchy” centred on conservation, improving efficiency, expanding supply, only seeking additional resources after conservation and efficiency measures have been maximised. He said entities should “avoid unnecessary use, reduce the amount of water required to operate, reuse, capture and reuse water wherever practical”.

He cautioned that, as businesses strengthen their own resilience, they must ensure that their “actions do not restrict nearby communities from accessing this shared national resource”.

The PSOJ committee chair cautioned that the country “cannot keep treating drought as a temporary emergency”.

“The current conditions are exposing long-standing weaknesses in our water infrastructure, particularly across the Corporate Area and vulnerable farming communities,” Davy pointed out.

He noted that while important water-supply investments have been made in communities across St Elizabeth, St Catherine and elsewhere, “the larger structural challenge remains”.

Davy stressed that, given the impact of climate change, Jamaica must move beyond water trucking as a response to drought.

“When drought becomes prolonged and recurrent, emergency responses are no longer enough. Jamaica needs a water system designed for the climate realities we now face. Water is an economic input; it keeps farms producing, factories operating, hotels functioning, restaurants serving, construction sites moving, communities working. When supply becomes unreliable, businesses must spend more on tanks, trucking, storage and alternative sources. For SMEs (small and medium enterprises) in particular, those additional costs can be difficult to absorb. Water scarcity quickly becomes a cost of doing business,” he stated.

He spoke of the importance of the country developing a “reliable and diversified national water system built around modernised water infrastructure, stronger watershed protection, more efficient water allocation, agricultural adaptation, clear drought contingency planning, new pipelines and water — transfer infrastructure, greater use of available river resources, desalination where viable supported by lower-cost renewable energy and battery storage”.

“Water security must become part of Jamaica’s long-term economic strategy,” the PSOJ’s Energy, Environment and Climate Change committee chair asserted.

The Government last month announced a $350-million drought mitigation fund aimed at alleviating the growing water crisis across the country. Of that amount, $150 million has been allocated for water trucking which will be distributed through Members of Parliament. An additional $50 million has been allotted to assist with further trucking support to the National Water Commission to service critical infrastructure while $50 million will go towards the purchase of additional water tanks. Farmers will also benefit from relief through a $100-million tranche which will be managed under the Ministry of Agriculture, Mining and Fisheries.

World.title: ‘I WANT TO INSPIRE’
World.content:
Reggae Girlz Captain Khadija “Bunny” Shaw trains at the National Stadium on Friday, April 17. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

AFTER winning a historic second Women’s PFA (Professional Football Association) Players’ Player of the Year award, Khadija “Bunny” Shaw says she wants to continue inspiring girls in Jamaica to help reach their full potential.

The Reggae Girlz captain was presented with the prestigious trophy on Tuesday at the PFA’s annual awards ceremony in Manchester, England.

Manchester City striker Shaw was the standout player in the Women’s Super League (WSL) last season, scoring 21 goals to claim her third-consecutive Golden Boot while helping the club secure its second-ever WSL title and their fourth FA Cup.

The 29-year-old, who first won the PFA players’ player of the year accolade in 2024, became only the third player in the award’s history to win it more than once, joining England legends Lucy Bronze and Fran Kirby.

The former St Jago High standout, who joined City in 2021, also made history as the first player from outside England to claim the prestigious award.

“[I’m] truly honoured and grateful for everyone who voted,” Shaw said. “Last season was a special year for me personally but also for the players and the club as well, creating history.

“I couldn’t have imagined it [after leaving Jamaica] but you know what? As I continue my journey and continue trying to be the best that I can be, the dream started to become a reality. Obviously, coming to England was the biggest one for me, and then arriving here was a bit more challenging than I thought, but once I got my foot to the ground, kept my head down, kept working, obviously trophies like this would come.”

Although proud of her accomplishments Shaw says it wouldn’t have been possible without her teammates at Man City.

“I just feel like chemistry is the biggest thing,” she said. “When I look back on the players and what we’ve done, I’ve built good relationships with the players around me, on and off the pitch, and I think that’s also important as well. I feel like it’s been happening, and may it continue.”

Shaw continues to establish herself as one of the world’s best, both at club level and internationally, having played a key role in the Reggae Girlz’s historic FIFA World Cup appearances in 2019 and 2023.

She wants her achievements to serve as a source of hope for girls in her home country.

“I want to inspire young girls that it’s definitely possible. Once you believe, and have faith, and keep working hard, I think it’s possible. Even when I go home, I still try to inspire them and motivate them that it’s definitely possible,” Shaw said.

With the new season set to kick off on September 4, Shaw says she has no intention of resting on her laurels.

“I think, for me, just keep driving my personal standards, because I think that over the years I’ve noticed that it rubs off on everyone else,” she said.

“Obviously, the girls sometimes say I’m a bit harder on myself but I think me being who I am and want to be better, want to score more goals, want to help the team to achieve the highest of the highs, I think that’s something that I can definitely improve on — and I think once I do that, anything’s possible.”

Shaw’s Man City begin their title defence on September 6 against Birmingham City. She’s also set to lead the line for Jamaica’s crucial World Cup-qualifying decider in November against Costa Rica.

World.title: Broccoli Balls: A Fun, Veggie-Packed Lunchbox Treat
World.content:
Shanice Gore gets assistance from her daughter Mila in preparing the potato wedges. (Photo: Alan Smith)

Back-to-school lunches don’t have to be complicated to be fun, colourful, and nutritious. For my daughter Mila’s lunchbox, I put together a playful little lunch featuring homemade broccoli balls, apple sticks with a peanut butter dip, and yellow kiwi cut into heart shapes. I even made the peanut butter dip into a little “scary” character by adding two googly eyes — because sometimes making food fun is the easiest way to get little ones excited about eating it.

The star of this lunchbox is definitely the broccoli balls. They’re soft on the inside, lightly golden on the outside, and made with simple ingredients you probably already have at home. They’re also a great way to sneak some vegetables into your child’s lunch without making it feel like they’re being served a plate of vegetables.

Ingredients

• 1 large Irish potato

• ½ head broccoli

• 1 egg

• 1 cup shredded mozzarella cheese

• Salt, to taste

Method

1. Peel and cut the Irish potato into small pieces.

2. Place the potato in a pot of salted water and boil until almost tender.

3. Cut the broccoli into small florets and add to the same pot. Continue boiling until both the potato and broccoli are completely tender.

4. Drain well and transfer to a bowl.

5. Mash the potato and broccoli together.

6. Add the egg and mozzarella cheese and mix until well combined.

7. Using your hands or a small scoop, shape the mixture into small balls.

8. Place the broccoli balls on a lined baking tray.

9. Bake at 375°F for about 30 minutes, or until lightly golden and firm.

Packing the Lunchbox

For Mila’s lunchbox, I paired the broccoli balls with apple sticks and peanut butter dip, along with yellow kiwi cut into little heart shapes. I also had fun with the presentation and turned the peanut butter dip into a little scary character with two googly eyes. It’s such a simple touch, but those little details can make lunch feel much more exciting for a child.

I personally like to keep the rest of the lunch simple when the broccoli balls are included. With the fruit, protein from the peanut butter and cheese, and the vegetables in the broccoli balls, it makes a balanced and satisfying lunch without overcrowding the lunchbox.

Back-to-School Tip

These broccoli balls are perfect for meal prep. Make a batch ahead of time, allow them to cool completely, and store them in an airtight container in the freezer. When you need a quick lunchbox option, take out what you need and reheat.

Because at the end of the day, back-to-school lunch doesn’t have to be fancy — it just has to be made with a little love and a little creativity!

World.title: ‘Blazing a trail to success’
World.content:
Minister of state in the Ministry of Education Rhoda Moy Crawford delivering greetings at the 26th annual Burger King National Scholarship Programme Awards Ceremony 2026, hosted at the AC Hotel Kingston on Tuesday. Naphtali Junior

THIRTY-FOUR of Jamaica’s top-performing students have received a total of more than $14 million in academic support through the 26th annual Burger King National Scholarship Programme.

The scholarships — granted by Restaurant Associates Limited, franchise holders of Burger King in Jamaica — provides funding to students who sat the Primary Exit Profile (PEP) exam this year and are entering secondary schools, as well as students heading into accredited local universities.

Beyond standard academic excellence, the initiative also champions holistic development, awarding student-athletes and creative minds pursuing the arts.

The categories include secondary school book grants, sports bursaries, tertiary scholarships and bursaries, and the Lois Lake Sherwood tertiary scholarship and bursary that covers the expenses of a student pursuing the arts.

Delivering greetings at the awards ceremony held at the AC Hotel Kingston on Tuesday, minister of state in the Ministry of Education Rhoda Moy Crawford highlighted that since 2001, Burger King has invested some $120 million in scholarships which have benefited more than 400 Jamaican youth.

She argued that this demonstrated the company’s deep commitment to corporate social responsibility and its focus on empowering young Jamaicans through education.

“This is a legacy of opportunity and compassion. By now, we should all realise that this is not ordinary sponsorship. This is care, this is belief, and this is foresight. And all of us here and those right across Jamaica — those who could have benefited and those yet to benefit — we all owe deep appreciation to the Burger King family and Restaurant Associates family,” said Crawford.

Shifting her attention to the awardees, Crawford commended their hard work and academic dedication. She noted that out of more than 3,000 applicants, only 34 were selected, proving that their success was no accident but rather the direct result of their labour.

“You are the special 34. This privilege reflects your hard work and an earned opportunity in a very competitive field. Please know that this moment is more than a certificate or a stipend, it is a confirmation that your future matters. You have earned your place in a competitive field. Do not misuse or take this opportunity for granted. Instead, take this opportunity seriously. Stay curious, work hard, and remain grounded,” added Crawford.

As she highlighted the ceremony’s theme ‘Blazing a trail to success’, Crawford encouraged the scholars to continue on their path of excellence and to rise again when faced with challenges.

“To blaze a trail is to create a path where there may have been none before. It means pursuing your goals, even when the road is unclear. It means being brave enough to explore your abilities, to challenge yourself, and sometimes to go further than where anyone else in your family has gone before. Use this opportunity to develop the knowledge, skills, character, and confidence to make the most of your journey.

“When your career becomes difficult, an exam may not go as planned, a course may challenge you more than expected, or you may face rejection; any difficult moments, do not accept them as failure. Ask for help, learn from the experience, adjust your approach, and keep moving forward,” said Crawford.

Keynote speaker Kaysia Johnson Vaughn, chief customer and brand officer at the Victoria Mutual Group, also had words of advice for the awardees.

Johnson Vaughn urged the students to have belief in themselves, learn holistically across both academics and skills, and to aim higher than expected. She encouraged them to “zag” and realign when life unexpectedly “zigs” on to uncharted routes.

“So you’re all here today. You worked very hard. You put in the effort, and now you’re seeing the results of your effort. You have been chosen to get a bursary or a scholarship to pursue, whether it’s high school or tertiary, or just about to achieve whatever dream that you want. I want you to recognise that this is a big deal,” said Johnson Vaughn.

World.title: Présidentielle : les 8 temps forts des candidats devant le Medef
World.content:
Alors que le doute planait encore avant le départ en vacances de la candidate du RN sur la réforme qu’elle défendrait — Jordan Bardella, lui, avait fait miroiter une proposition de réforme sans âge légal de départ, dans le cas où il aurait porté les couleurs du parti —, la quadruple candidate à l’élection suprême a répété qu’elle défendrait le principe d’un retour à un âge légal de 60 à 62 ans suivant l’âge de l’entrée sur le marché du travail. Elle a dit “assumer” le coût supposé d’une telle réforme — 9 milliards d’euros par an, selon elle —, qu’elle a qualifiée de “choix de société”.

Hasard de l’actualité (ou pas) : au moment même où Marine Le Pen s’exprimait, Le Figaro annonçait que François Durvye, ancien collaborateur de Pierre-Edouard Stérin devenu conseiller économique de Jordan Bardella, polytechnicien et libéral assumé, avait décidé de ne pas participer à la campagne présidentielle de la championne du RN, en raison de ses divergences avec la candidate sur sa ligne économique.

On savait que le parti à la flamme préparait un contre-budget pour 2027, on connaît désormais l’ampleur affichée de son volet économies : “125 milliards d’euros”. Cette trajectoire “de rétablissement des finances publiques” sera présentée “avant les débats budgétaires”, soit début octobre, a promis la candidate. Sans s’avancer sur des postes de dépenses particuliers, Marine Le Pen a cité pêle-mêle “l’Union européenne, l’immigration, de nombreux instituts obscurs”. Par ailleurs, elle s’est dite favorable à “l’inscription d’une règle d’or dans la Constitution”.

2. Jean-Luc Mélenchon persiste et signe sur l’annulation de la dette

Pour sa première venue à la rentrée du Medef, le leader de La France insoumise a choisi son registre : l’interpellation des patrons — et ses concurrents qualifiés “d’assemblée des magiciens” qui ne “[veulent] plus rien payer” et discréditent sa proposition d’annuler les 18% de la dette française détenue par la Banque centrale européenne. Lui a décidé d’enfoncer le clou : “C’est une dette à nous-mêmes [...]. Les Américains font ça, ils viennent de se racheter leur propre dette, et nous, on serait les seuls de l’univers à renoncer à cette possibilité ?”

Autre appel, cette fois, à destination de l’audience : “Je vous mets en alerte : le budget Lecornu, plus l’inflation alimentaire, si vous n’augmentez pas les salaires, la France va tomber en récession”, avant de défendre ensuite l’augmentation du Smic.

Le candidat Insoumis a fermé la porte à la TVA sociale défendue par Patrick Martin. Idem pour la retraite par capitalisation : il faudrait “cotiser deux fois plus”. Pour rétablir les comptes publics, Jean-Luc Mélenchon a titillé son auditoire en imaginant, de manière “très provocante”, la suppression de toutes les aides publiques aux entreprises.

World.title: 4 takeaways from France’s first presidential debate
World.content:
No shared vision for Europe

Fault lines on EU policy emerged hours after Commission President Ursula von der Leyen used her speech at the same event to defend her pitch for the bloc’s massive, €2 trillion spending plan.

Philippe — a center-right candidate who was President Emmanuel Macron’s prime minister from 2017 to 2020 — lambasted the EU leader’s decision to sign a “pitiful treaty in Scotland” with U.S. President Donald Trump, referring to the Turnberry trade deal, while lauding Mark Carney’s resolve in dealing with Trump. He also threw his support behind an EU-wide capital markets union.

“We must convince our European partners to speak the language of power to China and the United States,” Philippe said.

Glucksmann, a center-left MEP, said that France had failed to seize on the current geopolitical situation to take control of a more strategically autonomous Europe, a gospel long preached by Macron.

“France can be the driving force behind this autonomous European power that knows how to defend its interests. But to do that, it must stop being afraid — afraid to defend its interests,” Glucksmann said.

Mélenchon, who has long criticized the EU as a vehicle for unbridled German-style capitalism, countered that the EU would not be able to impose its strength vis-à-vis global powerhouses like the U.S. and China while remaining attached to “free and undistorted competition and free trade ideology.”

World.title: Poland rules out hosting nuclear weapons despite Russian threat
World.content:
Paweł Zalewski seen speaking to the media during press conference, visiting the Bundeswehr deployment at the Polish air force base on December 10, 2025 in Malbork. | Mateusz Slodkowski/Getty Images

BRUSSELS — Poland "does not want" allied nuclear weapons stationed on its territory, the country's Deputy Defense Minister Paweł Zalewski said Thursday, despite growing worries of a Russian incursion into NATO territory.

"I would like to say very clearly and openly: Poland does not want to have nuclear warheads on its territory," he told reporters at NATO headquarters in Brussels. "We want to participate in NATO nuclear deterrence, [which] does not mean to have a nuclear warhead on our territory."

Zalewski's statement is Warsaw's most categorical statement on the topic. While it has previously expressed skepticism toward hosting nuclear weapons, Poland has also said it was in early-stage talks with the U.S. around a potential expansion of Washington's nuclear deterrent in Europe, and had in parallel joined a French initiative aimed at extending Paris' own deterrent in Europe.

Separately, Polish President Karol Nawrocki has left the door open to Warsaw eventually building its own nuclear weapons program.

Western officials have warned Russia could attack NATO territory by the end of the decade, while recent U.S. intelligence suggests an attack could come even sooner.

World.title: L’art de la bouteille d’alcool design menacé par la loi européenne antidéchets, alertent les verriers
World.content:
L’entreprise française de verrerie Saverglass fabrique depuis vingt ans les bouteilles emblématiques de la vodka Grey Goose, au design épuré et au verre dépoli. “Tout le monde reconnaît la forme de l’oie, la fenêtre, la bouteille satinée, les décors”, énumère Emmanuel Ladent, le président de l’entreprise.

Or, ces designs emblématiques comme celui-ci se heurtent à la volonté de Bruxelles de réduire considérablement les déchets d’emballage qui envahissent les poubelles du Vieux Continent. A partir de 2030, la législation européenne obligera les entreprises à utiliser le moins de matériaux possible pour empaqueter leurs produits. L’UE insiste sur le fait que le marketing ne justifie à lui seul pas l’utilisation d’emballages superflus.

Les fabricants de verre avertissent que, si elles sont appliquées à la lettre, ces règles pourraient conduire l’Union à un niveau d’uniformité orwellien dans les secteurs du vin, des spiritueux et même des parfums, ce qui nuirait à la compétitivité. Ils déplorent qu’une réglementation excessive pèse sur une industrie qui tire sa force de la créativité de ses marques, et qui doit déjà faire face à des coûts de décarbonation considérables.

“Demain, si tout le monde a la même bouteille, l’histoire de la vodka Grey Goose, elle n’existe plus”, prévient Emmanuel Ladent.

Fabrication bretonne

Ce ne sont pas seulement les produits iconiques qui seront concernés.

L’écosystème de la distillerie artisanale bretonne est bien loin de la machine réglementaire bruxelloise, mais même les producteurs de spiritueux artisanaux devront se conformer aux restrictions européennes en matière d’emballage — ce qui menace l’utilisation des bouteilles en verre décorées.

World.title: Tripolis will die Energielücke in Europa füllen, sagt Libyens Ölminister
World.content:
Das nordafrikanische Land verfügt über die größten nachgewiesenen Ölreserven des Kontinents und die viertgrößten Gasreserven. Es hat in den letzten Monaten versucht, die Produktion hochzufahren und neue Verträge mit großen Ölkonzernen abzuschließen.

Zwar liefert das Land bereits den Großteil seines Öls und eine geringe Menge Gas nach Europa. Das Ziel besteht allerdings darin, die Rohölförderung wieder auf das hohe Niveau der 1970er Jahre zu bringen – mehr als das Doppelte des derzeitigen Niveaus – und die Gaslieferungen erheblich zu steigern.

Dies folgt auf einen Rückgang der ausländischen Energieinvestitionen. Verschärft wurde diese Entwicklung durch den Bürgerkrieg von 2011, der zum Sturz des Diktators Muammar Gaddafi führte und das Land in zwei verfeindete Regierungen im Osten und Westen spaltete.

„Wir sehen hier eine Chance (...), mit internationalen Unternehmen und der EU zusammenzuarbeiten und sicherzustellen, dass wir die richtige Zusammenarbeit und Koordination haben“, fügte Abdel Sadig hinzu. „Wir sind bereit zu handeln, und wir handeln auch (...) aber wir müssen noch mehr tun.“

Die Kriege in der Ukraine und im Iran haben die Energiekosten in der EU in die Höhe getrieben, wobei die Erdgaspreise diese Woche auf ein Dreijahreshoch gestiegen sind. Diese Umstände seien ein „Weckruf“ für europäische Politiker, die diesem potenziell bedeutenden neuen Lieferanten vor ihrer Haustür mehr Aufmerksamkeit schenken sollten, sagte Abdel Sadig. „Wir müssen so schnell wie möglich handeln, bevor es zu spät ist.“

Er schien die Äußerungen des Moderators zu bestätigen, dass Libyen das Potenzial habe, ein „Norwegen am Mittelmeer“ zu werden.

World.title: Ratko Mladić, ‘butcher of Bosnia’, dies at the Hague aged 84
World.content:
Ratko Mladić prior to the pronouncement of the Appeal Judgment at the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals in The Hague, The Netherlands, 08 June 2021. | Pool photo by Jerry Lampen/EPA

Thousands of Bosniaks and Bosnian Croats were murdered, tortured and displaced by armed forces under his command.

Ratko Mladić, the former Bosnian Serb military commander who was the architect of the 1995 Srebrenica massacre during the Bosnian War, has died aged 84, according to Serbian state media.

The war criminal was serving a life sentence at The Hague for crimes against humanity, war crimes and genocide.

“Ratko Mladić is dead, and there’s not much to say about it. The fact [that he’s dead] does not change much. It doesn’t bring back the dead. It doesn’t erase the mass graves. It doesn’t alter the verdicts. It doesn’t turn a criminal into a historical figure,” Emir Suljagić, the head of the Srebrenica Memorial Center, posted on X.

World.title: EU budget must bankroll Europe’s independence, von der Leyen says
World.content:
The Commission has proposed a budget of almost €2 trillion. Germany and five allies — Austria, Denmark, Finland, the Netherlands and Sweden — are calling for cuts of several hundred billion euros. Italy and Spain are leading a separate group seeking a larger budget.

The size of the budget will determine how much money the EU can put behind von der Leyen’s economic agenda, including investment in strategic industries, energy and artificial intelligence — sectors she says are essential to reducing Europe’s dependence.

“With over €450 billion from the European Competitiveness Fund and the Horizon Europe program, we will support the entire chain — from research to innovation, from laboratories to business, and from initial prototypes to industrial production,” von der Leyen said, referring to the EU’s proposed fund for strategic industries and its research-and-innovation program.

“Europe cannot set new ambitions without providing the means to finance them,” she added.

The spending proposal is facing sustained opposition from German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his allies, who argue that the increase is unaffordable while national governments are cutting back.

“The current proposals call for an increase of up to 60 percent,” Merz said in a joint statement with the five countries later on Thursday.

World.title: Lobbyists grumble over soaring conference prices — then pay up to court Britain’s new power players
World.content:
With opinion polls in flux, lobbyists now feel compelled to invest in attending more conferences, including standalone business events put on by parties like Nigel Farage’s Reform UK.

Multiple industry professionals — some of whom were granted anonymity to speak frankly about the impact on their business — told POLITICO that they had planned to cut back their presence at the ruling Labour Party conference if ex-Prime Minister Keir Starmer had still been in power. But Burnham’s elevation to Downing Street, and the need to get clarity on his agenda, meant scaling back was too big a risk.

One senior in-house public affairs leader said the leadership shuffle had seen two executives now opting to attend in addition to the original core team members they had planned to attend Labour’s business bash — adding a further £11,000 to the firm’s conference bill for those tickets alone.

Labour leader Sir Keir Starmer, speaks at a Labour Business Conference at the Oval on February 1, 2024 in London. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images

After the party’s 2024 event fell so flat that firms demanded refunds, it stepped up its game for last year’s gathering — often jokingly referred to by industry pros as the “CEO creche.”

But business leaders are now privately questioning whether inflation-busting cost hikes can remain defensible given the increasingly tight margins on which many firms are operating.

“Generally, I think conference is getting more overpriced and overhyped each year, and certain senior leaders are driven more by FOMO [fear of missing out] than anything strategic,” the same senior in-house pro said. “Yes, you can have great conversations, and occasionally a meaningful breakthrough, but a large part of any public affairs pro’s successes come at events away from conference,” they said.

World.title: Hundreds gather in Oslo to support Norway’s King Harald V
World.content:
Norway’s King Harald V, 89, is in an “extremely serious” condition after his health deteriorated while he was being treated at Oslo University Hospital. Europe’s oldest reigning monarch has been in hospital since 17 August with haemolytic anaemia, later complicated by a bacterial bloodstream infection.

 

The worsening condition prompted Queen Sonja and Crown Prince Haakon, who is serving as regent, to cancel their official engagements and go to the King’s bedside, alongside other members of the royal family.

The news also prompted an outpouring of public support in Oslo. Hundreds of people gathered outside the Royal Palace, where they laid flowers, lit candles and left handwritten messages and drawings for the King. Similar gatherings were reported in other Norwegian cities as people waited for further updates on his health.

The deterioration also prompted senior government figures to change their plans. Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre cancelled a planned trip to Germany, saying he stood with the country in sending his thoughts to the King and the royal family. Parliament Speaker Masud Gharahkhani also cut short a visit abroad to return to Norway.

Harald has been Norway’s king since 1991 and has faced a series of health problems in recent years, including surgery to fit a permanent pacemaker. He has reduced his official schedule but has repeatedly ruled out abdication, saying the oath he took before Norway’s parliament was a lifelong commitment.
