Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun has been charged with denying Nazi crimes, a criminal offence in Poland that carries a prison sentence of up to three years. The charges relate to statements last year in which Braun, who has a long history of promoting antisemitic conspiracy theories, suggested that the gas chambers at Auschwitz, which was the Nazis’ main killing centre during the Holocaust, are “fake”. Komunikat o przedstawieniu posłowi do Parlamentu Europejskiego zarzutów publicznego i wbrew faktom zaprzeczania zbrodniom ludobójstwa popełnionym w niemieckim nazistowskim obozie koncentracyjnym i zagłady KL Auschwitz-Birkenau w Oświęcimiu. https://t.co/nLq3XKnXCK — IPN Kraków (@ipn_krakow) August 25, 2026 On Tuesday morning, Braun was summoned to appear as a suspect at the Kraków branch of the Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), a state historical body that has the power to prosecute crimes relating to the periods when Poland was under Nazi and communist rule. A group of his followers gathered outside the building to express their support for Braun, who finished fourth in last year’s presidential elections. Since then, his Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) party has risen to around 9% in polls, making it a potential kingmaker after next year’s parliamentary elections. After meeting with Braun, IPN prosecutor Robert Janicki announced that they had presented him with charges for “publicly and contrary to the facts denying the crimes of genocide committed by officers of the Third Reich in the German concentration and extermination camp KL Auschwitz-Birkenau”. The charges relate to two interviews Braun gave in July last year. He declared that “Auschwitz with its gas chambers is unfortunately a fake” and said that claims about the use of gas chambers are part of a “propaganda narrative” supporting a “quasi-religious cult”. In fact, gas chambers were used at Auschwitz, which was located in German-occupied Poland, to kill around 900,000 people, the vast majority of them Jews. Janicki noted that Braun’s remarks “clearly contradict common historical knowledge based on documents, witness accounts, perpetrators’ statements and findings from past criminal proceedings”. Far-right leader Grzegorz Braun says the gas chambers at Auschwitz are “fake” and it is a “fact” that Jews have committed ritual murder. Prosecutors have launched an investigation into whether he violated Poland's law against denying Nazi crimes https://t.co/7UUKzH5ndG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 10, 2025 When Braun originally made his remarks, they were widely condemned in Poland, which suffered enormously under German occupation during World War Two. Justice minister Waldemar Żurek asked the European Parliament, where Braun sits as an MEP, to lift his legal immunity so he could be charged. “For me, it is a scandal that, in a country that suffered such enormous war losses, there is a politician who can deny historical facts that are so painful for Poles,” said Żurek at the time, quoted by the Onet news website. “I won’t let this go. We must bring such people to justice.” In March, the European Parliament approved Żurek’s request, allowing Braun to face charges in relation to his Auschwitz comments, as well as for other alleged crimes. The European Parliament has again voted to strip Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun of immunity to face further charges for Holocaust denial as well as various antisemitic, anti-Ukrainian and anti-LGBT incidents during last year's presidential campaign https://t.co/4EHVEuSDnM — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 26, 2026 On Friday last week, the district prosecutor’s office in Warsaw charged Braun with those other crimes, including the theft of Ukrainian and EU flags he tore down and vandalism of an LGBT+ exhibition being displayed in parliament. In a separate case, in February this year, Żurek also asked the European Parliament to strip Braun of immunity to face charges of denying Nazi crimes over another incident in which he called the gas chambers at both Auschwitz and Majdanek, another Nazi-German camp in occupied Poland, “fake”. Meanwhile, Braun is already on trial in Poland for four other alleged crimes, including using a fire extinguisher to attack a Jewish Hanukkah ceremony in the Polish parliament in December 2023. The trial of Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun for his attacks on a Hanukkah celebration in parliament and a Holocaust lecture has begun. Polish state defence firm Mesko has signed an 8 billion zloty (€1.9 billion) agreement to supply its Piorun man-portable air-defence systems to the armed forces of Poland, Norway, Lithuania and Latvia. The deal is being financed through the European Union’s SAFE mechanism. The agreement represents the largest-ever purchase of Pioruns, which have become an export hit for Mesko after proving their worth during Ukraine’s defence against Russian aggression. Previous buyers include Sweden, the United States, Belgium, Estonia and Norway itself. Nowy etap #PolskaSAFE. Rozpoczynamy wspólne zakupy i to znów w polskim przemyśle! Polska🇵🇱, Litwa🇱🇹, Łotwa 🇱🇻i Norwegia 🇳🇴 kupują wspólnie polskie pioruny. To 63 umowa w ramach polskiego SAFE. Dziś 8 mld zł. Mesko od maja zwiększyło zatrudnienie o 200 osób. To jak to było,… pic.twitter.com/YIDWBGBvpm — Magdalena Sobkowiak (@magdasobkowiak) August 24, 2026 The deal will see the firm provide “several hundred” launchers and “several thousand” missiles for its shoulder-fired Piorun systems, which target low-flying aircraft such as planes, helicopters and drones. Over 80% will be supplied to Poland’s armed forces, with the remainder going to its three NATO allies. The purchase is being funded through SAFE, which provides loans at preferential terms for defence spending. While SAFE can be used individually by countries to make purchases for their own armed forces, some funds are designated for joint procurement by groups of countries (including non-EU member Norway). “Our partners from Lithuania, Latvia and Norway have decided to purchase from Poland,” declared deputy defence minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, who oversees Poland’s participation in SAFE. “We are a leader in the SAFE mechanism and are the first to create such agreements. For the first time, the [Polish defence ministry’s] Armaments Agency is making purchases not only for the Polish armed forces, but also for those of our allies.” “This is a measure of the success of the Polish arms industry,” declared defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, as the deal was announced on Monday. “This is the moment when Poland can proudly say: we are a European leader.” He noted that Mesko’s production capacity is now 2.5 times larger than it was when the current government took power in December 2023. Since SAFE launched in May, the firm’s staffing, which stood at 3,200 by the end of last year, has increased by around 200, added the minister. Poland is by far the largest recipient of SAFE funds, with around €44 billion. The government says that SAFE will not only bolster Poland’s defence capabilities but also provide a boost to the domestic defence industry, where around 90% of the funds will be spent. However, the programme has been opposed by the right-wing opposition and opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, who argue that it will give Brussels too much influence over Polish defence spending and burden Poland with decades of debt on uncertain terms. Wiceminister @magdasobkowiak: Dzisiaj rozpoczynamy etap wspólnych zakupów. Wiele było pytań o to, czy to zrealizujemy, a może będziemy kupować w Niemczech. I widzicie, co się wydarzyło. Nie dosyć, że te umowy realizujemy w polskim przemyśle zbrojeniowym, to jeszcze nasi partnerzy… pic.twitter.com/hFL8M2Laah — Ministerstwo Obrony Narodowej 🇵🇱 (@MON_GOV_PL) August 24, 2026 In 2022, Pioruns were among the large quantities of military equipment Poland provided to Ukraine to help its eastern neighbour defend itself from Russia’s full-scale invasion. The systems were successfully used to take down a variety of Russian aircraft. In that same year, Mesko announced that the US government had ordered “several hundred” Piorun systems, while Norway also put in a similar order. Last year, Belgium and Sweden announced that they would purchase hundreds of Pioruns, while Ukraine itself also revealed that it had requested a €120 million loan from Poland to help fund the purchase of Polish-made weapons, including Pioruns. Earlier this year, Mesko, which belongs to the state defence holding group PGZ, announced the best financial results in its 100-year history. The firm’s revenues of 2.3 billion zloty in 2025 were up 33% year-on-year, driven by international demand for Pioruns. World.title: Regulation on recognising foreign same-sex marriages comes into force in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. All registry offices in Poland can now recognise same-sex marriages conducted in other European Union countries, after a government regulation issued in May went into force. The decision came in response to a ruling by the Court of Justice of the EU (CJEU) requiring Poland to recognise such unions. Deputy prime minister Krzysztof Gawkowski expressed his “great joy, because finally in Poland we have a law that gives the right to dignity”. The government’s plenipotentiary for equality, Katarzyna Kotula, warned local authorities that they will be breaking the law if they refuse to comply with the new rules. However, the mayor of one town in a conservative region has already declared that his administration will not recognise such marriages. He argues that doing so would violate Poland’s constitution, which mentions marriage as a union between a man and a woman. Od jutra polskie państwo będzie lepiej chronić godność i prawa swoich obywateli. Nowe wzory aktów małżeństwa umożliwią transkrypcję zagranicznych aktów małżeństw jednopłciowych z pełnym szacunkiem dla par. To koniec administracyjnej fikcji i niepewności, z którą przez lata… pic.twitter.com/mRZYkEg9W4 — Krzysztof Gawkowski (@KGawkowski) August 22, 2026 Polish domestic law still does not allow any form of same-sex unions to be formed. However, last year, the CJEU ordered that the country recognise same-sex marriages conducted in other EU member states. That was followed by a similar ruling from Poland’s own Supreme Administrative Court (NSA). One obstacle to implementing those decisions was that, previously, Poland’s civil registry only allowed male-female marriages to be entered. But, under a regulation issued by the government in May, the system now allows either mixed-sex or same-sex marriages. Even before that went into force on Sunday, some Polish cities, starting with Warsaw and Wrocław, had already begun transcribing same-sex marriages conducted abroad into their registries. They simply listed one spouse in the “man” section and the other as a “woman”, even though that was not accurate for one of them. But some local authorities have refused to do so, pointing to article 18 of Poland’s constitution, which states that: “Marriage, being a union of a man and a woman, as well as the family, motherhood and parenthood, shall be placed under the protection and care of the Republic of Poland.” Such doubts were cited by the mayor of Zakopane, a town in southern Poland, last week when he announced that his administration did not intend to begin recognising foreign same-sex marriages after the regulation came into force. “We will not be issuing such transcriptions in Zakopane,” said Łukasz Filipowski, quoted by local news service Nasze Miasto. He argued that doing so would “not be in accordance with the constitution”, adding that, while Zakopane is “tolerant”, it “promotes the traditional family model…[as] our foundation”. Filipowski pointed to a ruling in July by the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), which found that the government’s regulation conflicts with the constitution’s definition of marriage. However, the government considers the TK to be improperly constituted and therefore regards its rulings as invalid. Poland's Constitutional Tribunal has ruled that a new regulation allowing foreign same-sex marriage certificates to be registered in Poland is unconstitutional. The government says it will not implement the rulinghttps://t.co/xDAzLjcJQ4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 28, 2026 In response to Filipowski’s remarks, Kotula told broadcaster TVN that officials who refuse to recognise foreign same-sex marriages “will be breaking the law”. She said that the personal views of officials cannot “translate into what [legal] actions they take” and that the government would be monitoring the situation. Gawkowski – who, like Kotula, is a leading figure in The Left (Lewica), a junior member of Poland’s ruling coalition – also warned municipalities against issuing refusals. He noted that, as well as the CJEU ruling, Polish courts have also issued orders to recognise foreign same-sex marriages. “In the end, these local authorities will lose [a court battle], so why embarrass themselves? Let’s not look for legal tricks. Let’s just implement something that has been done in other, normal countries for years,” Gawkowski told Polsat News. However, even once same-sex marriages are transcribed into Polish civil registries, there remains uncertainty about what legal consequences that will have in practice, especially given that Poland’s domestic law does not allow for any legally recognised form of same-sex union. Legal experts say that it may take years – and potentially many more legal challenges by same-sex couples – for the situation to be clarified. Separately, parliament earlier this year approved a bill, proposed by the ruling coalition, that would have granted same-sex couples in Poland certain rights normally granted to married couples. However, the law was vetoed by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition. Poland has begun recognising foreign same-sex marriages. But the legal consequences for such couples remain unclear, especially as Polish law does not allow any form of same-sex union We asked five experts for their view on what this will mean in practice https://t.co/h2KHmW8sMI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Ukraine to establish new national pantheon as Poland warns against honouring massacre figures
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Volodymyr Zelensky has signed a law establishing a new national pantheon to commemorate Ukrainian historical heroes. While it is not yet known which figures will be honoured there, Poland has expressed concern that they will include nationalist leaders associated with massacres of Poles in World War Two. On Sunday, a Polish deputy foreign minister warned that Kyiv “will have a huge problem” integrating with the European Union if it celebrates such individuals. But Zelensky reiterated that “only Ukrainians will decide who is a hero to us”. The establishment of the pantheon has taken place against the backdrop of a diplomatic crisis triggered in May by Zelensky’s decision to name a military unit after the “heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA)”. Parts of the UPA were responsible for the so-called Volhynia massacres during World War Two, in which Ukrainian nationalists killed around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, as part of an ethnic cleansing operation. Poland regards the episode as a genocide, though Ukraine strongly rejects that label. Many Ukrainians hold the UPA in high regard for the role that it played in fighting for independence from Moscow-backed Soviet rule. Poland condemned Zelensky’s decision and stripped him of the country’s highest honour, the Order of the White Eagle. In response, the Ukrainian president announced in late June that he would seek to create a new national pantheon, because “no one will dictate which heroes we should honour”. A bill creating the pantheon was subsequently approved by the Ukrainian parliament in July, and, on Saturday, Zelensky signed it into law, just ahead of today’s celebrations of Ukrainian independence day. “A Ukrainian pantheon will definitely be established, and only Ukrainians will decide for themselves who our heroes are,” declared Zelensky at a meeting with military veterans on Saturday. “All our true heroes…who fought for Ukraine, for our independence…deserve due honour.” However, the introduction of the law only now begins the process of building the pantheon itself – where the remains of those chosen as national heroes will be reburied – and the establishment of an advisory body that will decide which figures should receive such an honour. It therefore remains unknown for now who will be included in the pantheon. However, on Sunday, Polish deputy foreign minister Marcin Bosacki warned against honouring figures associated with the Volhynia massacres. “Every nation and its government has the right to choose the heroes they deem appropriate,” emphasised Bosacki in an interview with broadcaster TVP. “However, if individuals responsible for mass crimes against civilians, such as [Stepan] Bandera or [Roman] Shukhevych, are included in Ukraine’s national pantheon, it would significantly worsen Ukraine’s relations not only with Poland but with Europe in general,” he added. Bandera was the leader of a faction of the Organisation of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN-B), which in turn founded the UPA. Shukhevych was a military leader of the UPA. Both figures continue to be honoured in Ukraine, often prompting protests from Poland. 🇵🇱 Polskie MSZ ostrzegło Ukrainę przed „ogromnymi problemami” z Europą z powodu Bandery i Szuchewycza „Ukraina wie, że z tymi, którzy zabijali nie tylko Polaków, ale także Ukraińców, Czechów, Żydów i Romów, na swoich sztandarach będzie miała ogromne problemy z integracją… pic.twitter.com/hyujMppbEw — NEXTA Polska (@nexta_polska) August 24, 2026 “Ukraine knows that, with those who murdered not only Poles, but also some Ukrainians, Czechs, Jews and Roma, on its banners, it will have a huge problem integrating with Europe,” added Bosacki. However, the deputy minister also emphasised that, “strategiaclly, the interests of Poland and Ukraine remain very close” and that Poland must continuing “supporting Ukraine in defeating the aggressive Russia”. “We do not differ much with the Ukrainians, only with certain parts of the Ukrainian authorities after their absolutely erroneious decision to name a unit after the ‘heroes of the UPA’.” The proportion of Poles who hold a negative view of relations with Ukraine has risen to the highest level ever recorded by state research agency CBOS Meanwhile, the proportion who believe reconciliation with Ukraine is possible is at its lowest ever level https://t.co/YYBCFkVxNr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2026 Polish government figures have previously made it clear that, if Ukraine honours figures associated with historical massacres, that will make it harder for the country to achieve its ambitions of joining the EU. In June, deputy prime minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz warned that “you can’t build a pantheon to those who destroy European cooperation”, and that countries seeking EU membership should “not build national identity…on events, people or systems that in some way raise objections or pain among EU partners”. Kosiniak-Kamysz declared that, just as Zelensky said no one will tell Ukraine who they can honour, “no one will tell us how to vote on the entry of any state into the European Union”. That was an allusion to the fact that Poland, like all other EU member states, can veto Ukraine’s accession to the bloc. Polish and Ukrainian media have widely quoted Poland's deputy PM as saying: “With Bandera, Ukraine will not enter the EU.” However, he did not actually speak those words. World.title: Historic Invalidovna Building in Prague Begins Major Reconstruction
World.content:
The long-awaited reconstruction of Prague’s Invalidovna has officially begun.

The Baroque complex in Karlín will undergo a major renovation costing CZK 2.15 billion, with work scheduled for completion in 2030.

The project is the largest investment in the history of the National Heritage Institute (NPÚ). Alongside the restoration of the historic building, two new extensions will be constructed on the southern side of the complex.



One will provide facilities for the Prague Philharmonic Choir, while the other will house technical infrastructure needed to operate the site.

Much of Invalidovna will remain open to the public

Once the reconstruction is complete, the NPÚ will use part of the complex for restoration workshops, laboratories, archives and study rooms.

An underground garage with space for 50 vehicles is also planned.

Around 80 percent of the complex is expected to remain accessible to the public. The restored site will include exhibition and conference spaces, visitor routes through the Baroque interiors, a café and facilities for children’s groups operated by Prague 8.

A new multi-purpose hall in one of the extensions will be suitable for concerts, conferences and other events. The modern section will also contain technical facilities that cannot be accommodated inside the protected historic building.

The courtyard and gardens will be opened through the original entrances.

A Baroque complex with a long military history

Invalidovna was built between 1731 and 1737 based on plans by Kilián Ignác Dientzenhofer, one of the leading architects of the Czech Baroque. The institution provided accommodation and care for war veterans and their families until 1935.

The original complex was designed at a time when European armies were beginning to develop more systematic forms of care for soldiers who had been wounded or disabled in war.

Military campaigns were often accompanied by outbreaks of diseases such as cholera and typhus, which could kill even soldiers whose battlefield injuries were not life-threatening. Separate psychiatric institutions were later established for veterans suffering severe mental trauma after their military service.

World.title: PIZZA! PIZZA! POP-UP Returns to Holešovice Market on September 3
World.content:
Prague’s Holešovice Market will turn into a one-day celebration of Italian food next Thursday, September 3, with the fourth edition of PIZZA! PIZZA! POP-UP.

The event will run from 11 a.m. to 10 p.m., with more than two dozen food and drink businesses serving pizza, pinsa, pasta, arancini, Italian desserts, coffee and drinks. Admission is free.



Among the returning participants will be Pizza Metro, Mate’s PIZZA TRUCK, PIZZA Therapy, Pinsa Al Forno, HOLY PASTA, La Mia Spitzeria, Spojka Karlín, ŝam.ŝam.Piaggio, PIZZAKOLEM, Picoška, Vege Stará Placka, Naše maso and Cukrárna U Moučků.

This year will also bring a new style of pizza to the event. Third Coast Pizza will serve Detroit-style pizza, alongside the wide selection of Neapolitan pizza available from other vendors.

Visitors looking for something beyond pizza can try fresh pasta, pinsa, arancini and Italian sweets.

Drinks will include prosecco, beer, cocktails and coffee, with Gin Twist, Aperol Ape, Milujemě Prosecco, Pivovar Chroust and Garage 22 running various bars and stands. Garage 22 will also operate a negroni bar.

Bovelii Caffé will arrive in its red Piaggio, serving coffee roasted in Parma, Italy.

The programme will include music and Italian lessons from Lingua Nostra. Beads & Lemons will also be at the market with jewellery inspired by life by the sea.

PIZZA! PIZZA! POP-UP has been held at Holešovice Market for four years, bringing together restaurants, food producers and other businesses focused on Italian cuisine. This year’s edition will feature more participants than last year, including both returning vendors and newcomers.

World.title: Manifesto Market’s Craft Beer Returns for Its Third Edition
World.content:
Prague’s beer lovers can look forward to one of the city’s biggest beer events of the year as Manifesto Market brings back its annual beer festival for a third edition.

The two-day event will bring together some of the Czech Republic’s best-known craft breweries, alongside a guest brewery from Berlin, with more than 40 beers available to taste throughout the weekend.

Zichovec, Sibeeria, Chroust, MadCat, Fracek, Pivovar VIK and Berlin-based BRLO will each have their own pop-up tent, giving visitors the chance to explore a wide range of beer styles directly from the breweries.



More breweries are expected to be announced ahead of the event.

One of the highlights will be the festival’s limited-edition glass. It serves as the ticket for accessing the festival specials and can also be taken home as a souvenir.

The beer will be accompanied by food from more than 10 international kitchens at Manifesto. Visitors can expect everything from juicy burgers and tacos to spicy ramen and authentic Chinese roast duck, making it possible to turn the beer tasting into a full weekend meal.

World.title: More Czechs Are Living Paycheck to Paycheck, New Survey Finds
World.content:
The number of Czechs who have nothing left from their paycheck at the end of the month is rising.

This year, 13 percent say they have no money left after covering their expenses, up from 9 percent last year. Meanwhile, 84 percent have at least a small amount left over, five percentage points less than in 2025.

The findings come from a May survey conducted by loan provider Provident Financial among 1,000 respondents.



According to the survey, Czechs’ ability to save is declining. Only 43 percent of respondents have at least 20 percent of their monthly income left after covering their expenses, down nine percentage points from last year. Almost half of Czechs nevertheless regularly set aside part of their paycheck each month.

At the same time, their overall financial resilience appears to be improving. More than a quarter of respondents have enough savings to cover their expenses for more than a year, compared with just 15 percent last year. The share of people with no financial reserve at all has also fallen, from 18 percent in 2025 to 13 percent this year.

The gap between men and women in the amount of money left at the end of the month has also narrowed. This year, 45 percent of men have at least 20 percent of their paycheck left after expenses, compared with 59 percent last year. Among women, the figure has fallen from 45 percent to 39 percent.

The share of Czechs with enough savings to cover 12 months without their main source of income has increased sharply this year, rising by 11 percentage points compared with 2025. At the same time, the proportion of respondents whose savings would last less than three months fell to 12 percent, down from 17 percent a year earlier.

Men are considerably more likely than women to report having enough savings to cover at least six months of expenses. The figure is 63 percent among men, compared with 39 percent among women.

Education also appears to play an important role in financial preparedness. Seven in ten respondents with a university degree say they have enough savings to cover at least six months, compared with 43 percent among people with lower levels of education.

World.title: Not Ready for Summer to End? 3 Places to Take the Kids Before August Ends
World.content:
The end of the summer holidays is in sight. While school supplies, pencil cases and sports shoes are already making their way onto shopping lists, there are still a few days of summer left to enjoy.

Before the September school routine kicks in, here are three ways to make the most of the final days of August with the family.



Letni Letna

When: 12–31 August

Where: Prague, Letenské sady

Letenské sady is taking on a new look until 31 August, transforming into a colourful festival village. The Letní Letná Festival isn’t just about evening acrobatics for adults. It also offers a programme for younger visitors called Letní Letná for Children.

From morning until late afternoon, the huge children’s tent comes alive with fairy-tale performances and other activities. Kids can take part in creative and juggling workshops, explore an interactive play area made from recycled materials or take a ride on the iconic hand-carved wooden carousel.

Most of the children’s activities take place under the festival tents, so an unexpected rain shower won’t disrupt the day.

The festival also offers a “Night Watch” childcare service for children aged four and up. Parents can enjoy the evening programme while experienced entertainers look after their children.

When: 24–29 August

Where: Liberec and the surrounding area

Fancy a trip beyond Prague at the end of August? Head north to Liberec from 24 to 29 August, when the city hosts Crystal Valley Week, a celebration of Czech glassmaking and jewellery.

This year’s theme focuses on the interconnection of cultures, with the Czech glass bead at the centre of the programme. Children can also enjoy a free ride aboard the special Crystal Tram, which has been decorated this year to resemble a long-distance train.

There are plenty of opportunities to make your own jewellery from glass beads, with workshops and craft sessions taking place throughout Liberec for both children and adults.

When: Sunday, 30 August, 11:00–19:00

Where: Prague, Ladronka Park

On the last Sunday of the summer holidays, skip cooking lunch and head to the F.O.O.D. Picnic in Prague’s Ladronka Park. The popular event returns for its 16th edition this year.

Entry to the festival grounds is free, with 120 food and farm stalls to explore, including food trucks. There is also a large children’s zone with games and creative workshops, as well as a raffle for younger visitors.

It’s a family-friendly way to spend the final Sunday of the holidays, combining food, activities and a relaxed atmosphere before the new school year begins.

World.title: Airbnb Accounts for 1 Percent of Prague’s Housing Stock, Analysis Finds
World.content:
Prague’s short-term rental market has grown into a professional business but Airbnb accounts for only a small share of the city’s housing stock, according to a new analysis.

In June 2026, around 7,878 entire apartments and houses in Prague were actively listed on Airbnb. With roughly 720,000 apartments across the capital, that represents about 1.1 percent of the total housing stock.

The situation is very different in individual parts of the city. In Prague 1, Airbnb-listed properties account for around one-fifth of all apartments, according to the Prague Institute of Planning and Development (IPR). In Prague 2, the share is around 7 percent, while in some outer districts it is below 0.5 percent.



The concentration of short-term rentals has also changed the nature of the market. IPR data show that hosts managed an average of two apartments in 2019. By 2024, that figure had risen to three, while more than half of Prague’s Airbnb listings were operated by hosts with at least five properties.

This means short-term accommodation is increasingly being run as a business rather than as occasional home-sharing.

Prague’s housing shortage is much larger

Despite the impact Airbnb can have in central neighborhoods, the analysis points to a much bigger problem behind Prague’s housing crisis — a long-term shortage of new construction.

Since 2006, Prague has accumulated a housing deficit of more than 91,000 apartments, according to the analysis. That shortfall is about 11.5 times larger than the number of apartments currently listed on Airbnb.

Even if every Airbnb property in the city were suddenly returned to the long-term rental market, Prague would still be short more than 83,000 homes.

The accumulated construction deficit reportedly became larger than the number of active Airbnb apartments around 2009 or 2010. Since then, the gap has continued to grow.

This suggests that Prague’s housing crisis began well before short-term rentals reached their current scale.

Tourism brings other concerns

Housing availability is also not the only issue surrounding short-term rentals.

Residents in central Prague have complained about noise, disruption and visitors staying in residential buildings.

The city also collects accommodation fees from short-term stays, although payment is not automatic because apartment owners must register and pay the fees themselves.

The debate over Airbnb in Prague therefore extends beyond housing. While short-term rentals can change the character of central neighborhoods and create problems for residents, the latest figures suggest that the city’s wider housing shortage is primarily the result of years of insufficient construction.

World.title: ASEAN Plus Three Film Festival Returns to Prague for Its Fifth Edition
World.content:
The ASEAN Committee in Prague (ACP), representing the embassies of ASEAN member states, together with the embassies of China, Japan and the Republic of Korea, will host the fifth edition of the ASEAN Plus Three Film Festival (APTFF).

The festival will begin on Monday, September 7, 2026, at the Municipal Library of Prague.

Organised in cooperation with the Municipal Library of Prague, the festival will run until September 14 and feature seven full-length films, alongside a curated selection of short films from across the ASEAN Plus Three region.



Since its launch in 2022, the APTFF has introduced Czech audiences to the diverse cultures and cinematic voices of ASEAN and its Plus Three partners.

Previous editions have featured acclaimed films including Escape from Mogadishu (Republic of Korea), Father and Son (Viet Nam) and Yuni (Indonesia).

This year’s programme includes Solata: Friends Are the Family We Choose (Indonesia), Babah (Malaysia), The Beginning (Myanmar), I’m Perfect (the Philippines), 4 Tigers (Thailand), Song of the South (Viet Nam) and One and Only (China).

A selection of short films will also be screened during the opening night on September 7.

The programme includes Mbiyodo/Communal Work (Indonesia), Ninavau (Malaysia), Myanmar Be Enchanted (Myanmar), Lola Loleng/Grandma Loleng (the Philippines), Give to Getters (Thailand), Welcome to Viet Nam (Viet Nam), My Chinese Ecological Notes (China), Pukkulapottas and Hours in the Forest (Japan), and Persona (Republic of Korea).

Beyond its cultural programme, the festival is part of a broader effort by ASEAN and its Plus Three partners to introduce Czech audiences to the region, its societies and creative industries, as well as its shared identity as a community of more than 690 million people.

All screenings are open to the public and free of charge. Films will be shown in their original languages with English and Czech subtitles.

The full programme and schedule are available on the Municipal Library of Prague website.

World.title: GALLERY: Light Installation “Synapse” Coming to Florenc Metro Station
World.content:
Jan Poš light installation Synapse will go on display in the Florenc Line C metro passage at the end of September.

The artwork will track passengers’ movements and complement the existing Battle of Sokolovo mosaic. Prague city councillors approved around CZK 1.38 million in funding to complete and install the artwork.

“Synapse” is a light-based installation by visual artist Jan Poš (1996) and the winning entry in the “Light for the Metro” competition held in 2023.



The aim was to create a light artwork for the passage connecting the north and south concourses of Florenc metro station. A total of 23 artists and teams submitted proposals, with four advancing to the final stage, which was conducted as a competitive dialogue.

The five-member jury considered the artwork’s long-term maintenance and its ability to withstand demanding operating conditions.

According to Poš, the artwork, installed on the wall opposite the underpass’s main staircase, comes into view as metro passengers ascend or descend the stairs.

It becomes part of their daily journey while remaining elegantly set apart, creating a space where it can stand on its own and offer a moment of respite from the hustle and bustle.

Poš says the work’s format and style enliven and build on the Battle of Sokolovo mosaic, creating a bridge between the past and present of the city.

The artwork was originally due to be installed alongside the completion of the reconstruction of the station’s ceiling slab. Prague’s public transport operator, DPP, has been repairing the structure since 2022 due to corrosion.

World.title: Russia threatens to cut oil and gas supplies to Hungary after Budapest labels Moscow a security threat
World.content:
A Russian State Duma member has warned that Moscow could suspend oil and gas supplies to Hungary after the country’s new government formally described Russia as a security threat. The warning comes as Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s administration pursues a major foreign policy shift away from the close Budapest-Moscow relationship maintained under former PM Viktor Orbán.

Russia threatens Hungary’s energy supplies

Andrey Kolesnik, a member of the Russian State Duma’s Defence Committee and a member of President Vladimir Putin’s United Russia party, said Russian energy deliveries to Hungary could now be called into question. Speaking to Russian outlet Gazeta.ru, Kolesnik suggested that Moscow could stop supplying Hungary with oil and gas following Budapest’s decision to classify Russia as a threat.

“I think that after such statements, oil supplies to Hungary and energy supplies from Russia to Hungary are in question,” he said.

Kolesnik also claimed that Hungary had adopted the new position under pressure from Brussels, arguing that the country could ultimately be the first to abandon Russian energy imports as it aligns itself more closely with EU policy towards Moscow. His comments do not amount to an official announcement from the Russian government that supplies will be halted.

Hungary formally labels Russia a security threat

The warning follows the publication of a document outlining Hungary’s position ahead of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly. In the document, the new Hungarian government condemns Russia’s military aggression and expresses full support for Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. At the same time, Budapest calls for negotiations aimed at achieving lasting peace and security guarantees.

Crucially, the document states that Russia’s behaviour represents a threat to Hungary, Europe and the global order, while also posing a threat to the Hungarian minority living in Transcarpathia. The statement represents a significant departure from the foreign-policy approach of the previous government.

Read more here: Fundamental changes in Hungary’s foreign policy reflected in new UN guidelines

Major foreign policy shift under Péter Magyar

Péter Magyar’s Tisza Party defeated Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz government in April’s parliamentary election. Since taking office, Magyar has pledged to strengthen Hungary’s ties with the European Union and NATO while moving away from the close relationship with the Kremlin that characterised much of the Orbán era.

Under Orbán, Hungary repeatedly opposed or blocked EU statements and sanctions targeting Russia. The former prime minister also argued that Moscow did not pose a direct threat to Hungary, pointing to NATO’s military strength and Hungary’s membership of the alliance.

Russia’s intelligence services previously criticised Magyar in an unusual written statement, portraying him as an instrument of the EU and echoing narratives promoted by Fidesz. Since the change of government in Budapest, however, Russia’s Foreign Ministry has said it remains prepared to maintain pragmatic relations with Hungary’s new leadership.

Hungary still heavily dependent on Russian energy

This warning is particularly significant because Hungary is one of the EU member states most dependent on Russian energy. Budapest continues to import substantial quantities of Russian crude oil and natural gas through pipeline infrastructure dating back to the Soviet era. Alongside Slovakia, Hungary received an exemption from EU and US restrictions on Russian pipeline oil imports introduced after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Any major disruption to these supplies could therefore have significant consequences for Hungary’s energy security.

World.title: Photos – Shocking rescue in Budapest: Child pulled from underneath tram after accident
World.content:
A child was seriously injured after being hit by a tram at Batthyány Square in Budapest on Wednesday afternoon. Firefighters used hydraulic lifting equipment and a spreader cutter to free the boy from underneath the vehicle before handing him over to paramedics. He was reportedly revived and taken to hospital in a life-threatening condition.

Child trapped underneath tram

The accident happened at Batthyány Square in Budapest on Wednesday afternoon, when a tram struck a young boy, leaving him trapped underneath the vehicle. The Budapest professional firefighters who arrived at the scene carried out a technical rescue operation to reach the child.

Using hydraulic lifting equipment and a spreader cutter, the firefighters raised the tram and freed the boy from underneath the carriage. Once he had been brought out, the child was placed on a stretcher and handed over to the ambulance crew.

If you missed it: Shocking tragedy: former Hungarian world and European champion kayaker dies aged just 42

Boy taken to hospital in life-threatening condition

According to Hungary’s National Ambulance Service, the child was successfully resuscitated following the accident. He was then transported to hospital in a life-threatening condition.

Photos published by the Zsaruhírek Facebook page show emergency crews working around the tram during the rescue operation. Following the rescue, firefighters also returned the tram to the tracks. The exact circumstances of the accident have not yet been disclosed.

World.title: Hungary sets 2030 euro target: Government reveals when budget deficit could fall below 3%
World.content:
Hungary’s new government has set its sights on adopting the euro by 2030, with Finance Minister András Kármán revealing how and when the country could bring its budget deficit below the EU’s key 3% threshold. The government says it will tackle the country’s huge fiscal gap without imposing austerity measures on households.

Hungary targets euro adoption by 2030

The new government plans to meet the Maastricht criteria required for euro adoption by the end of the current parliamentary term in 2030, Kármán said in an interview with Hungarian public broadcaster Kossuth Radio. One of the most important conditions is bringing the budget deficit below 3% of GDP. The target is particularly challenging given the fiscal situation inherited by the new administration following the spring 2026 election.

According to Portfolio, Kármán said the government would submit a new medium-term programme by the end of October, alongside next year’s budget. This will set out the path towards meeting the criteria for joining the euro area by 2030. The government argues that adopting the common currency would eliminate Hungary’s exchange-rate risk and contribute to permanently lower inflation and interest rates, providing greater stability and predictability for households and businesses.

Finance Minister András Kármán. Photo: Facebook/Kármán András

Deficit was much worse than expected

According to Kármán, the previous government’s 2026 budget had initially been based on a deficit target of just 3.7% of GDP. However, a review carried out after the change of government found that the deficit could have reached 8.3% without intervention. The finance minister said the previous budget had relied on unrealistic economic growth assumptions and that numerous unfunded spending commitments had been made before the election.

He also pointed to hidden financial obligations and projects whose actual costs under existing contracts were significantly higher than the amounts included in the official budget. The revised 2026 budget now targets a deficit of 7.5% of GDP.

If you missed it: Another severe food price surge is taking shape: prices could start rising in the autumn, with 2027 bringing the greatest pain

Government promises no household austerity

Rather than raising the burden on households, the government says it plans to close the fiscal gap by cutting wasteful state spending and renegotiating or cancelling overpriced contracts. Kármán said the government had already saved around HUF 400 billion (EUR 1.1 billion) this year by terminating or renegotiating unfavourable state contracts. A further HUF 300 billion in excessive spending is expected to be reversed by the end of the year.

Among the measures cited by the minister are the abolition of the Sovereignty Protection Office, cuts to MPs’ remuneration and the cancellation of an operating contract for part of the M6 motorway. The latter was reportedly reassigned to another operator at around one-third of the previous price, which the government estimates will save approximately HUF 100 billion over the next 11 years.

Targeted support instead of blanket benefits

Kármán said the government’s economic policy would also place greater emphasis on means-tested social support and transparent management of public funds. The new administration has introduced a HUF 100,000 school-starting allowance, removed VAT from prescription medicines and increased the social firewood allowance, he said.

A similar targeted approach is expected for pensions and potential additional benefits, such as a proposed pensioners’ SZÉP Card. According to Kármán, support should primarily reach those who genuinely need it. Following Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s subsequent announcement that the lowest old-age pensions would be raised to HUF 120,000, Kármán added that the lowest pensions would be increased further on a tiered basis.

Kármán’s interview can be listened to below (only in Hungarian):

New tax scheme could replace KATA

The Finance Ministry is also working on a new simplified tax regime with minimal administration, aimed at self-employed people and small businesses. The scheme is intended to provide an alternative to the former KATA small-business tax system, which was significantly restricted in 2022. For the government, the aim is to combine a simpler tax environment for small businesses with a more sustainable fiscal framework.

Can Hungary really join the euro by 2030?

The 2030 target represents a significant shift in Hungary’s economic policy. Meeting the Maastricht criteria would require a substantial improvement in public finances, particularly given the current 7.5% deficit target.

Kármán stressed that EU rules allow a new government following a change of government to present a fresh medium-term fiscal programme. The new administration now plans to use that opportunity to set out a path towards getting the deficit below 3% and fulfilling the conditions for euro adoption by 2030.

World.title: Former Hungary international footballer Buzsáky missing, concern grows in England
World.content:
The disappearance of former Hungary international footballer Ákos Buzsáky has sparked concern both in Hungary and England, where the midfielder spent much of his career. The 44-year-old has been reported missing by Hungarian authorities, while his former club Queens Park Rangers has said it is praying for his safe return.

Former QPR star reported missing

Buzsáky’s disappearance was first reported in Hungary on Tuesday by Blikk, when it emerged that police were searching for the former international as a missing person. His current whereabouts remain unknown, and reports suggest that even members of his family and people close to him have been unable to establish contact with him.

The news has now attracted attention in England, where Buzsáky is a familiar name to football supporters. The Sun and Daily Mail have both reported on the case, highlighting his time in English football and the concerns surrounding his disappearance.

Queens Park Rangers, one of Buzsáky’s former clubs, has also reacted to the news.

“The club are concerned to learn that R’s favourite Ákos Buzsáky has been reported missing. We’re all praying he’s found safe and well,” the club said.

From Porto success to English football

Buzsáky enjoyed an impressive playing career. After establishing himself at MTK and with Hungary’s Under-21 side, he moved abroad in 2002, joining Portuguese giants FC Porto. Although he struggled to establish himself in Porto’s first team, he was part of a hugely successful squad that won the Portuguese league and cup as well as the UEFA Cup.

He subsequently moved to England, initially joining Plymouth Argyle. Buzsáky quickly became a favourite with supporters, with then-manager Ian Holloway praising his creativity and ability to surprise opponents. In 2007, he moved to QPR, where he played in the Premier League as well as the Championship. He later represented Portsmouth and Barnsley before returning to Hungary and joining Ferencváros.

Persistent injuries eventually brought his playing career to an end in 2015.

If you missed it: The shocking truth about Hungarian football finances: clubs are funded not by the fans, but from the central budget

A difficult period after retirement

Buzsáky later moved into coaching, working as sporting director and manager at III. Kerületi TVE before subsequently taking charge of BVSC. However, his post-playing career was overshadowed by personal difficulties.

In previous interviews, the former footballer spoke openly about struggling to adjust to life after professional football and developing an addiction.

He explained that the end of his playing career had left him in a difficult psychological state and that he had eventually become dependent on one of the forms of addiction he had previously been able to keep away from.

Buzsáky also said that professional football had provided him with an extremely disciplined lifestyle and that, after leaving the game, he struggled to find the same sense of purpose and enjoyment.

Business interests in Greece add to the questions

Reports have also emerged that Buzsáky had become involved in construction businesses in Greece in recent years. However, there is currently no confirmed information explaining why police are searching for him or what may have happened.

Buzsáky earned 20 caps for Hungary during his international career. His former clubs and fans are now hoping for news that the popular midfielder has been found safe.

World.title: Would you work in Hungary for this median salary? Half of the Hungarians earn even less
World.content:
In June, the gross average earnings of full-time employees stood at 754,700 forints, while net average earnings reached 529,700 forints. Gross average earnings rose by 7.1 per cent, net average earnings by 9.4 per cent and real earnings by 7.6 per cent compared with the same month a year earlier, the Central Statistical Office (KSH) reported on Thursday. However, the median salary was much lower.

Median salary shows reality

Gross median earnings reached 617,900 forints, while net median earnings stood at 438,000 forints (EUR 1201) – increases of 8.8 per cent and 10.9 per cent respectively since June last year. Compared with May, gross earnings fell by 9,339 forints and net earnings by 6,137 forints.

The KSH noted that the rise in net average earnings outpaced the increase in gross average earnings partly because of the expansion of the family tax allowance and tax concessions available to mothers.

Regular gross average earnings, excluding bonuses, rewards and one-month special payments, stood at 708,600 forints, up 7.9 per cent on the same period a year earlier. Regular gross average earnings were 700,800 forints in the business sector, 717,600 forints in the public budget sector and 757,600 forints in the non-profit sector, representing annual increases of 7.5 per cent, 9.0 per cent and 8.3 per cent respectively.

Gross average may be tempting

In June, gross average earnings stood at 788,000 forints in manufacturing, 613,000 in construction and 589,000 in agriculture. Monthly gross earnings reached 1.204 million forints in telecommunications and information technology, and 1.181 million in the financial and insurance sector.

During the first half of the year, gross average earnings rose by 11.5 per cent year on year to 772,800 forints, while net average earnings increased by 13.7 per cent to 541,200 forints.

World.title: One of Hungary’s top five construction companies, Orbán-linked Bayer Construct, could go bankrupt
World.content:
Bayer Construct Ltd. has filed a request with the court to initiate insolvency proceedings, Attila Balázs, the owner of the Bayer Group, told employees yesterday. According to the company chief, developments over recent months have left the business facing serious financial exposure. He cited regulatory changes affecting projects under way, the Government’s decision concerning Zugló City Centre and adverse market conditions.

A minor technicality may have derailed a supposedly fixed mega-project

The most pressing problem is likely to be the Zugló City Centre development being built behind Bosnyák Square. The state bought the office complex in November 2023, but for the sale to be completed, entries relating to pre-emption rights had to be removed from certain title deeds. That did not happen, and the new Magyar Government announced on 3 August that it was withdrawing from the purchase of the office complex.

The new Zugló City Centre built by Bayer Construct: nobody wants it. Photo: Facebook/Velkey György László

The Zugló office complex had already attracted considerable controversy. Critics have argued that it is unnecessary, cannot be properly utilised and makes little sense from a public-transport perspective. They have also warned that the geothermal energy it consumes could deplete the wells supplying Budapest’s thermal baths.

Geothermal heating of Zugló city centre could deliver fatal blow to Budapest’s thermal baths

Bayer Construct disputed the Government’s decision and had previously threatened legal action, Telex reports. Meanwhile, the Zugló municipal council could also sue the company if the council approves a proposal to that effect on 3 September.

Bankruptcy on the horizon

It is important to note that insolvency proceedings do not automatically mean that a company is about to collapse. On the contrary, the purpose of the legal procedure is to give a business facing payment difficulties time to reach an agreement with its creditors and stabilise its operations. Bayer Construct says it will continue operating during the proceedings, complete its projects under way and settle claims made by its partners.

Bayer Construct did not become one of the construction industry’s leading players overnight. The group has more than two decades of history and operates not only in Hungary but also in Romania.

Its Hungarian portfolio includes the Hungaroring, the Zenit shopping centre, Waberer’s Ecser Logistics Centre, Kincsem Residential Park and the Láng Quarter. Alongside residential and office buildings, the group is involved in civil engineering and water-management projects, structural construction, steel fabrication, prefabrication and geothermal developments. The Zugló City Centre was the group’s largest project to date.

The company is also involved in the development of Epres Liget in Debrecen, while its Budapest portfolio includes the Szilas Liget residential project. In Romania, the Bayer Group is primarily engaged in construction work and the sale of products, particularly in Transylvania. Its Romanian subsidiary, Bayer Strada, builds residential and non-residential properties.

One of Orbán’s biggest business allies could be forced to shut up shop

In 2025, Bayer Construct recorded net sales of approximately HUF 217 billion and after-tax profit of HUF 13.2 billion, while employing 1,340 people. By revenue, the company ranks among the largest players in Hungary’s construction industry, placing around the top five in publicly available rankings for 2025.

In Hungarian public life, Bayer Construct is regularly described as a company close to the NER, chiefly because of the business links between Attila Balázs and István Tiborcz, Viktor Orbán’s son-in-law, as well as the group’s substantial volume of state contracts. According to an earlier summary by Telex, Attila Balázs is a business associate of István Tiborcz, while Bayer has signed state agreements and received public contracts worth several hundred billion forints in recent years. These deals effectively propelled it into the top five of Hungary’s construction market.

Attila Balázs was also the man who urged his employees on 12 April to vote for Fidesz. “Anyone who disagrees with this, please do not take part in our team,” he added. He later apologised for the letter.

World.title: Magyar government to raise minimum old-age pension, but it will still remain very low
World.content:
From 1 January, the minimum state pension will rise to HUF 120,000 (EUR 330), Péter Magyar, the Prime Minister, announced on Thursday, outlining the Government’s decision taken the previous day on his Facebook page.

In a video, Péter Magyar pointed out that the measure would bring a substantial increase for several hundred thousand elderly people, doubling the pensions of many recipients. He recalled that the minimum old-age pension had remained unchanged at HUF 28,500 (EUR 78) since 2008, MTI wrote.

Péter Magyar delivering his speech at Kossuth Square. Photo: MTI/Bruzák Noémi

“There are debts that cannot be repaid in forints. One such debt is owed by the nation to those who worked for decades, raised children, cared for their parents and helped Hungary through its most difficult periods,” the Prime Minister said. He added that the debt could never be repaid in full, but every government could demonstrate through its decisions how much it valued older people.

“During the Orbán government’s 15 years in office, we have reached the point where nearly one million of our elderly compatriots are living in severe deprivation,” Péter Magyar said. He recalled that, before the election, the Tisza Party had already pledged to raise the minimum pension to HUF 120,000 and to increase the lowest pensions in a targeted manner.

He added that exempting prescription medicines from VAT and cutting the VAT rate on firewood from 27 per cent to 5 per cent would also help hundreds of thousands of “our most forgotten elderly compatriots” to live a life of dignity. The Tisza Party made further pledges concerning older people and pensions, and preparations for fulfilling them have already begun, the Prime Minister said.

“The Orbán government left Hungary in a tragic economic and financial state. We inherited a huge deficit and a ruined, drained budget. In such circumstances, a humane country begins by offering help where it is most needed,” Péter Magyar said. He stressed that a pension was neither a gift nor a favour. “After a lifetime of work, our elderly compatriots are entitled to security, respect and dignity.”

World.title: Shocking tragedy: former Hungarian world and European champion kayaker dies aged just 42
World.content:
Gergely Boros, a former world and European champion kayaker and ex-professional director of the Hungarian Canoe Federation, has died in tragic circumstances at the age of 42. News of the sportsman’s death sent shockwaves through Hungary’s canoeing community.

Hungarian kayaker champion dies at a tragically young age

Boros’s death was announced by the Hungarian Canoe Federation, although its statement did not disclose what had led to the tragedy. It later emerged that the 42-year-old had been killed in an industrial accident in Paks. The incident took place near Vácika Street, close to the tennis courts of Paks SE, Blikk wrote.

Police were already at the scene on Wednesday evening after a local news agency reported that a 42-year-old man from Paks had died in what was believed to have been a workplace accident. The authorities said they would provide further details at a later stage.

Further information emerged on Thursday morning, when police confirmed that proceedings had been opened over the death at the construction site on Vácika Street. The investigation is examining suspicions of negligent endangerment in the course of an occupation resulting in death.

Gergely Boros more than 10 years ago in Moscow. Photo: Facebook/Magyar Kajak-Kenu Szövetség



He was building a padel court

The tragedy occurred during the construction of a padel court. According to information obtained by Index, a large glass wall fell on Boros.

Boros was born in Paks and began kayaking with ASE before going on to become one of the most influential figures in Hungarian canoeing. He served as the federation’s professional director from 2018 to 2024. His former club remembered him as a cheerful, energetic, dependable and highly motivated man.

World.title: iMapp Bucharest 2026 to feature seven digital art shows, Nadia Comăneci tribute
World.content:
The 11th edition of iMapp Bucharest will take place in Constituției Square on September 19 and 20 under the theme PAST. FORWARD. The free event will feature seven international video mapping competition winners and a special moment celebrating Romanian gymnastics legend Nadia Comăneci.

The façade of the Palace of Parliament, covering approximately 23,000 square meters, will once again be transformed through large-scale digital projections.

This year’s theme explores the relationship between past and future through memory, heritage, technology, and imagination, the organizers said. Each of the seven works in the competition will offer a different perspective on time and memory while incorporating the Palace of Parliament into its narrative.

“The fact that iMapp Bucharest has reached its 11th edition says something important about how the city’s public has come to view the event: not only as a large-scale show, but as a cultural landmark,” ARCUB director Mihaela Păun said. “Over 11 years, iMapp has managed to create a tradition around digital art and bring new perspectives and artists into dialogue with a very broad audience.”

The seven artists and studios competing in the Winners League were selected through partner festivals in Hungary, Japan, Germany, France, China, the United States, and Brazil.

An international jury will select the winner of the Jury Prize, while spectators can vote for their favorite work by sending a standard-rate text message to 1755. The entry receiving the most votes will win the Audience Award.

The 2026 edition will also include a special video mapping show marking 50 years since Nadia Comăneci’s historic performance at the 1976 Montreal Olympic Games and highlighting her impact on international sport.

The two-day program will also feature music, entertainment, and outdoor experiences, with the participating performers due to be announced later.

Organized by Bucharest City Hall through ARCUB as part of Bucharest Days, iMapp Bucharest is open to the public free of charge.

World.title: Cambridge School of Bucharest celebrates exceptional examination results across IBDP, IGCSE, AS and A Level
World.content:
News from Companies

Cambridge School of Bucharest is celebrating another outstanding year of academic achievement, with impressive results across its two internationally recognised pathways: Cambridge International Education (CIE) qualifications and the International Baccalaureate Diploma Programme (IBDP).

Founded in 1994, CSB has a long-established history in Romania and has helped generations of students graduate with internationally recognised CIE qualifications for more than two decades. This year's achievements continue that tradition while marking an exceptional beginning for the school's first IBDP cohort.



Students completing CIE qualifications achieved strong results across IGCSE, AS Level and A Level. At A Level, 15% of grades were awarded at A*, while 36% were between A* and A. At AS Level, 36% of grades were awarded at A, the highest possible grade at this stage.



IGCSE students achieved equally impressive outcomes, with 60% of grades awarded between A* and A and 96% between A* and C. These results provide a strong foundation as students progress into Sixth Form, where they can choose between A Levels and the IBDP.



CSB's first IBDP cohort also achieved exceptional results. The Class of 2026 attained an average score of 39 points out of 45, compared with the worldwide average of 30.88 points for the May 2026 examination cycle. The school's highest-performing student received the maximum score of 45 points, and the entire cohort achieved a 100% pass rate.



These results demonstrate what is possible when academic expertise, individual support, and student ambition come together. They celebrate the determination of the students, the dedication of their teachers, and the encouragement of the families who supported them throughout their educational journeys.



High-quality teaching sits at the heart of the CSB educational experience. Students are guided by teachers who bring specialist subject knowledge, strong academic backgrounds, and a genuine commitment to helping each learner fulfil their potential.



This academic ambition is accompanied by a strong emphasis on well-being and belonging. Students learn within a community where they are known and valued, and where success is understood as something broader than a final grade. Confidence, Success, and Belonging are central to school life, shaping how students learn, collaborate, and prepare for the future.



For many members of the graduating class, these results represent the culmination of an educational journey that began at CSB in Nursery, when they were just three years old. Their progress from the earliest years of education to internationally recognised qualifications demonstrates the value of a continuous learning experience that develops knowledge, character, independence, and personal responsibility.



As students progress through the school, the curriculum allows them to discover their strengths, develop their abilities, and choose the pathway best suited to their interests and ambitions. Critical thinking, independent enquiry, and meaningful discussion are embedded throughout the learning experience, helping students become confident and articulate learners.



Examination preparation is one part of this wider journey. Dedicated university and careers guidance helps students explore international study options, understand application processes and make informed decisions about their next steps.



An extensive supercurricular and extracurricular programme also allows students to take their learning further. These are classed as activities or academic pursuits that explore a specific subject beyond the standard school curriculum, such as competitions, societies, and further learning.



Through academic enrichment, leadership, sport, the creative arts, and community service, students deepen their interests, develop new skills and build the confidence to participate fully in university life and beyond. Supercurricular activities also strengthen applications to leading universities by demonstrating intellectual curiosity and engagement beyond the curriculum.



This approach has enabled CSB graduates to progress to highly regarded universities around the world. UK destinations have included the University of Cambridge, the University of St Andrews, the University of Warwick, and the London School of Economics and Political Science, alongside other leading Russell Group universities.



Across Europe, graduates have continued their studies at institutions including Bocconi University, IE University, LUISS University, Delft University of Technology, Eindhoven University of Technology, Ecole Polytechnique, and Erasmus University Rotterdam. Students have also secured places at respected universities in the United States, Canada, Hong Kong, Australia, and the United Arab Emirates, reflecting the international outlook of the school community.



The next chapter for CSB promises to be equally exciting. Two new buildings will open during the coming academic year, expanding the opportunities available to students. New spaces for science and technology, sport and the creative arts will encourage further experimentation, discovery, collaboration, and creativity.



These facilities will build upon the elements behind this year's achievements: inspiring teachers, ambitious students, a future-focused curriculum, and a community in which every learner can belong.



Families are invited to book a visit, experience the school community and discover the Cambridge School of Bucharest formula for success.



*This is a press release.

World.title: Interim PM Ilie Bolojan hails Romania-Moldova ties as Chisinau marks 35 years of independence
World.content:
Romanian interim prime minister Ilie Bolojan sent a message on Thursday, August 27, marking 35 years after the proclamation of the Republic of Moldova’s independence, saying that Romania has been and will remain “the closest partner.”

The prime minister recalled that Romania was the first state to recognize the independence of the Republic of Moldova, on August 27, 1991.

“Happy birthday, Moldova! Happy birthday, Bessarabian brothers!” Bolojan said in a Facebook post. The official emphasized that Romanians and Bessarabians are bound by “the same language, a shared history and a common destiny.”

Several festivities are taking place in Chisinau, including a military parade and a concert, to mark the Independence Day of the Republic of Moldova, celebrated on August 27.

Nicușor Dan on visit to Moldova

Romanian president Nicușor Dan is also currently in the Moldovan capital, where he will be received by President Maia Sandu and attend the military parade organized for the occasion. At the same time, Nicușor Dan will hold a trilateral meeting with Maia Sandu and the president of Ukraine, Volodymyr Zelensky, according to the president’s official agenda.

In the evening, Maia Sandu, Nicușor Dan and Volodymyr Zelensky will address citizens in Great National Assembly Square, where a concert dedicated to Independence Day will take place, featuring established artists and musical bands from the Republic of Moldova. The event is part of the national program “Independence that unites us. Moldova-35.”

The program includes a total of more than 20 cultural, educational, commemorative, and festive events taking place throughout the year.

Message from Marco Rubio

United States state secretary Marco Rubio also sent a message marking the 35th anniversary of Moldova’s independence. “On behalf of the United States of America, I congratulate the people of Moldova on the anniversary of their independence,” he said at the beginning of the message.

“The United States is proud to continue strengthening our partnership with Moldova. Over the past year, our two countries have deepened cooperation across a range of shared priorities. We have expanded economic ties, strengthened border security, and worked together to promote stability in the region,” the message continued.

In conclusion, the US official promised continued support for the “Moldovan people’s sovereignty and independence.”

World.title: Record 180 museums in Romania and Republic of Moldova to participate in Night of Museums in Villages
World.content:
Over 180 museums and rural heritage collections from Romania and the Republic of Moldova are set to participate in the fourth edition of the Night of Museums in Villages.

The sites, spread over a diverse area of rural heritage, will be open to the public with free admission on Saturday, August 29, 2026.

Unlike its sister event, the Night of Museums, the Night of Museums in Villages also features multiple types of sites. Visitors can explore wooden churches and fortified churches, fortified manor houses and mansions, traditional houses and peasant households, mills and ovens, workshops and collections of old objects, archaeological sites, memorial houses, traditional households, cultural centers, village schools, inns, parks, creative barns, narrow-gauge steam trains, contemporary art collections, orchards with sculptures, castles and palaces, gastronomic points, mausoleums, arboretums and fishing villages.

This year’s edition also brings a first: 14 sites from the Republic of Moldova are participating in Night of Museums in Villages for the first time. These include traditional houses, village museums, ethnographic collections, traditional gatherings and handicraft circles.

“180 participants means 180 reasons to hit the road on August 29. The fact that we have reached such a large number of participants and that, for the first time, we have such a strong presence from the Republic of Moldova shows us that Night of Museums in Villages has become more than just an event. It is a network that grows year after year and connects people, communities and places that need to be seen,” said Dragoș Neamu, initiator of Night of Museums in Villages and project manager.

World.title: Cordia analysis: Bucharest gaining attention of regional investors thanks to its affordability
World.content:
Bucharest is increasingly standing out on the residential investment map of Central and Eastern Europe as its new-build home prices remain more affordable than in Budapest, while rental yields are comparable to those seen on the Polish market, according to an analysis by Cordia, one of Europe’s largest residential developers and investors.

More homebuyers and investors are looking beyond the simple price per square meter. Total investment cost, rental potential, and long-term market prospects are becoming increasingly important considerations. From this perspective, Bucharest is emerging as one of the region’s most attractive residential markets. While the average price of new-build homes in Budapest has exceeded EUR 5,200 per square meter and prices in Warsaw are approaching EUR 4,700 per square metre for unfinished units, the average price of new homes in Bucharest has remained below EUR 3,600 per square meter, even after significant growth over the past year.

“These price differences, which can be substantial in some cases, may also attract the attention of Hungarian investors. For our cross-border projects, we naturally assist buyers wishing to purchase a new-build home either elsewhere in the region,” said Áron Görög, Head of Sales at Cordia.

At the same time, gross rental yields in Bucharest stand at approximately 5-6%, a level comparable to that seen across major residential markets in Poland.

The analysis also shows that residential markets across Central and Eastern Europe cannot be compared solely based on headline prices. For example, unlike in Romania and Hungary, developers in Warsaw traditionally sell homes in an unfinished condition, which means buyers face significant additional fit- out costs before moving in.

At the same time, construction costs for an average residential project in Bucharest or Warsaw are approximately 25-30% lower than in Budapest, while land prices per square meter in the Polish capital are more than twice as high as in either Bucharest or Budapest.

Differences between tax systems are also important. In Hungary, VAT on newly built homes is currently 5% and can be reclaimed for homes located in designated brownfield regeneration areas. In Poland, the VAT rate is 8% for residential properties up to 150 square meters, while any floor area above that threshold is taxed at 23%. In Romania, following a period of reduced taxation, VAT returned to 21% in August 2026.

“Prices are strongly influenced not only by differences in underlying costs, but also by the complexity of administrative processes, varying levels of demand and the range of government support schemes available to buyers,” added Áron Görög.

World.title: Fire breaks out in southeastern Romania after alleged drone explosion
World.content:
A fire broke out on Wednesday, August 26, and spread over 2,000 square meters in Tulcea County, southeastern Romania, after a drone allegedly exploded.

The fire was quickly extinguished by the local authorities, and investigations are ongoing to determine the exact cause.

“The most likely cause of the fire, according to the testimony of residents, appears to be the explosion of a drone,” said representatives of Romania’s forest authority Romsilva.

The drone was spotted by residents of the locality of Plauru, situated 2 kilometers from the forest.

The Tulcea Inspectorate for Emergency Situations is carrying out checks to determine the cause of the fire, and a team of EOD specialists from the Ministry of National Defence is heading to the area to conduct an on-site investigation.

“The area was secured, the vegetation fire was extinguished by the structures of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, together with the local authorities, and a Border Police crew secured the perimeter during the night,” MApN representatives said.

However, the Defense Ministry noted that no incursions into national airspace had been reported for the same day.

According to the same source, Romania has seen 63 attacks near its borders with Ukraine since the start of the year, and 25 unauthorized entries in its airspace. Four drones were also brought down by Romanian or allied fighter jets after infringing the national airspace.
