World.title: Romanian IT company Arctic Stream posts EUR 1.32 mln consolidated net profit in H1 2026
World.content:
Romanian IT infrastructure and cybersecurity integrator Arctic Stream recorded a consolidated net profit of RON 6.95 million (EUR 1.32 million) in the first half of 2026. The consolidated operating revenue more than tripled year-on-year to RON 96.3 million (EUR 18.3 million).

The consolidated operating expenses rose by 180% to RON 89.7 million.

The consolidated figures include the results of companies in the Arctic Stream ecosystem, namely Data Core Systems, Optimizor, and Cyber Arena. The company attributed the net profit mainly to the contribution of Data Core Systems, in which it holds a 23% stake.

On a standalone basis, Arctic Stream reported a net profit of RON 5.51 million (EUR 1.05 million) and an operating profit of RON 6.11 million (EUR 1.16 million).

Its standalone operating revenue increased by 202% to RON 91.7 million, compared with RON 30.4 million in the first half of 2025. The operating expenses rose at a slower rate of 172%, reaching RON 85.6 million.

“The results from the first half of this year confirm the positive dynamics of Arctic Stream’s business and our ability to turn market opportunities into successful projects and increasingly strong results,” CEO Florin Mărginean said.

He attributed the performance to efforts made during the previous year to expand the company’s customer base and secure major contracts.

Looking ahead, Mărginean said Arctic Stream expected to continue operating amid geopolitical and economic uncertainty and potential technological disruptions.

“I am convinced that the strategic partnerships within the Arctic Stream ecosystem - Data Core Systems, IT Prepared (Optimizor), Cyber Arena and Faur.ai - will continue to provide complementary expertise and differentiate us in the market,” he added.

Since its previous financial report, Arctic Stream has signed a RON 17.3 million contract to supply and commission communications systems, computing equipment, and other IT components. The project is scheduled for completion by December 2026.

The company also completed a share buyback program under which it purchased 82,645 AST shares at an average price of RON 21.8644 per share.

The Financial Supervisory Authority has approved another offer covering up to 50,000 shares, equivalent to 1.1553% of the company’s share capital. The offer will run from August 27 to September 9 at RON 23 per share.

Founded in 2017, Arctic Stream is listed on the Bucharest Stock Exchange under the AST ticker. Its activities include IT infrastructure, cybersecurity, managed IT services, and locally deployed artificial intelligence solutions.

World.title: New classical music festival brings 11 weekends of concerts to Constanța Casino
World.content:
The first edition of the Cazino Music Festival will take place at Constanța Casino this fall, between September 12 and November 22. The program will bring international musicians and ensembles to the Black Sea city for 11 consecutive weekends.

Held under the artistic direction of Ioan Holender, who led the Vienna State Opera for almost two decades, the festival will feature chamber music, vocal recitals, jazz, and crossover performances.

“The most important thing is for what happens inside the Casino to match what the building represents on the outside. Quality must remain the common thread,” Holender said.

“Music should not be approached with the preconception that you first need to understand it to enjoy it. You can come without knowing, but you must come with an open mind and be curious enough to stay,” he added.

The festival will open on September 12 and 13 with the Janoska Ensemble, comprising brothers Ondrej, Roman, and František Janoska and double bassist Julius Darvas. Their program will combine classical works by Johann Strauss, Brahms, Bizet, Bartók, and Vivaldi with music by the Beatles and Astor Piazzolla.

Then, Italian ensemble I Solisti Veneti will perform on September 19 and 20, presenting works by Albinoni, Händel, Vivaldi, and Tartini.

Austrian baritone Liviu Holender and soprano Adriana González will take the stage on September 26 and 27 with a program ranging from Mozart, Verdi, and Leoncavallo to Bernstein, Gershwin, and American musical theater.

The lineup for October and November also includes CrossNova, Romana Amerling & The Henry Love Group, Hugo Wolf Quartett, Eddie Luis 5, sisters Ania and Sophie Druml, and Romania’s Arcadia Quartet. Soprano Adela Zaharia and baritone Ionuț Pascu will join Ioan Holender for two special recital and discussion evenings.

The festival is organized by Constanța Casino in partnership with the Mamaia-Constanța Destination Management Organization. It is intended to attract visitors to the seaside outside the traditional summer season.

“Culture can build a tourist season that continues long after summer,” organization president George Măndilă said. “A concert featuring international-level artists in a Casino that many Romanians want to see after its restoration can become the starting point for an entire weekend by the sea.”

Tickets are available through the Casino’s official website, its ticket office, and ticket machines located on the seafront.

The restored Art Nouveau landmark has reopened to the public and is now also being used as a cultural venue.

World.title: War Criminal or ‘Serb Hero’: Reactions to Ratko Mladic’s Death Reflect Balkan Divisions
World.content:
In Serbia, this divide was further reinforced by the stance of pro-government media outlets, which glorified Mladic’s wartime role while emphasising efforts by the Serbian authorities to secure his release and bring him to Belgrade when he was seriously ill and about to die. In contrast, some opposition politicians have spoken of his death as the passing of a convicted war criminal.

When he died, 84-year-old Mladic was serving a life sentence for committing genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes during the 1992-95 war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. He has suffered severe health problems for several years and was being treated by medics at the UN Detention Unit.

Serbian pro-government media amplified claims by nationalist politicians that Mladic was “killed” by the UN court in The Hague because he was not brought to Belgrade for medical care, as his lawyers had repeatedly requested.

“From Gavrilo Princip to Ratko Mladic, the best Serbs are killed while bound,” declared Aleksandar Vulin, former Serbian Interior Minister and ex-head of the Security Intelligence Agency.

Vulin argued that “the Serbian state owes convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic a state and military funeral, as well as a day of mourning”, Bosnian news agency SRNA reported.

Vojislav Seselj, leader of the far-right Serbian Radical Party, also convicted of wartime crimes by the UN court, said that Mladic had long been battling a serious illness and the Hague “villains” had not provided him with proper medical treatment for several years.

Serbia’s public broadcaster RTS and pro-government media outlets highlighted how Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic had appealed to the court the previous week to release Mladic and allow him to come to Serbia.

“I do not understand why they would not allow someone to spend their final days outside a prison cell. But am I particularly surprised? No,” Vucic said at the time, as reported by Informer, one of Serbia’s main pro-government tabloids.

Informer’s high-profile editor-in-chief, Dragan Vucicevic, said that “the real news today should not be that Ratko Mladic has died, but that he was killed in The Hague Tribunal”.

“That is a terrorist organisation whose aim is to convict Serbs of genocide, and now it has killed a general,” Vucicevic said.

Milorad Dodik, leader of the Alliance of Independent Social Democrats, SNSD and former president of Bosnia’s Serb-dominated Republika Srpska entity, also described Mladic’s death as murder.

“This really is a killing, because everything pointed to his poor state of health, and this was an organised approach that was intended to lead to a fatal outcome,” Dodik said, according to Republika Srpska’s public broadcaster RTRS.

World.content:
The signing of the new gas interconnector agreement between North Macedonia and Serbia in Skopje. Photo: Government of the Republic of North Macedonia.

North Macedonia’s gas network could be connected with Serbia’s system as early as 2028, under an agreement signed by the two countries in Skopje on Thursday. The project involves the construction of a 67-kilometre pipeline, which should be completed by 2027.

It is part of a broader effort to knit together the gas networks of Southeast Europe and enable diversification for a region that has historically relied heavily on Russian supplies.

The new link will be developed alongside a separate North Macedonia-Greece interconnector, which is expected to be operational in 2027.

At the signing event, North Macedonia’s Prime Minister Hrisitijan Mickoski said that together, the two projects would grant his country “full vertical energy connectivity”.

The pipelines may also turn North Macedonia from a largely end-point market into a key part of a south-north transit route, allowing gas entering from Greece to move towards Serbia and potentially further into Central Europe.

The Alexandroupolis terminal is particularly important to this strategy. Its floating LNG facility can receive gas from global suppliers and feed it into Greece’s transmission system, giving countries in the region access to supplies beyond traditional pipeline sources.

The European Union and the countries involved have been promoting the new infrastructure as part of the wider Vertical Gas Corridor linking LNG infrastructure and gas networks across Southeast and Central Europe.

Mickoski has also framed the project in geopolitical terms, saying the planned route could carry US LNG from Alexandroupolis through North Macedonia and Serbia towards Hungary and Austria. He added that he hopes North Macedonia’s other Northern neighbor, Kosovo, would build a similar interconnector with his country.

LNG from other sources – such as Azerbaijan – could also use the route, creating more options for the region. Mickoski estimates the eventual capacity could be between three and six billion cubic metres annually, making it a potential competitor to Russian gas supplies in the region.

Serbia, in particular, remains strongly dependent on Russian gas. In 2025, Serbia imported around 2.76 billion cubic metres of gaseous natural gas. Of that, 2.45 billion cubic metres were imported from Russia, 232 million cubic metres from Azerbaijan, and 112.5 million cubic metres from the EU.

However, Belgrade has increasingly been seeking alternative sources and routes. It has already reserved 300 million cubic metres of capacity at the Alexandroupolis LNG terminal for the next 10 years.

The timing of this new infrastructure also reflects a fundamental shift in Europe’s energy map. The EU formally adopted legislation this year to phase out the use of Russian natural gas. LNG imports will be subject to a full ban from the start of 2027, with pipeline imports to follow in the autumn.

Serbia is making links with North Macedonia and Romania a priority for diversifying its supply routes. Meanwhile, the Energy Community – which includes all six Western Balkans countries as well as EU member states – says stronger cross-border infrastructure will improve the security of supply across Southeast and Eastern Europe.

World.title: Kosovo Judicial Council Rejects Serb Judges’ Reinstation
World.content:
Kosovo Judicial Council meeting on August 27, 2026. Photo: Kosovo Judicial Council.

The Kosovo Judicial Council, KJC, on Thursday denied the requests of several Serb judges and court administrative staff to return to their posts, nearly four years after Kosovo Serbs staged a mass resignation from Kosovo institutions in 2022.

The KJC will send the names of the judges to acting President Albulena Haxhiu, who will formally confirm the original resignations.

Haxhiu posted on Facebook that she “welcomes the proposal by the Kosovo Judicial Council to relieve the Serbian judges who resigned in 2022 of their duties”, confirming she would “take action to relieve them of their duties”.

The decision follows a similar ruling in July by the Kosovo Prosecutorial Council, KPC. It denied requests by several Serb prosecutors to return to the posts from which they had resigned in 2022. Media in Kosovo reported that five prosecutors and 15 administrative staff members had asked to return.

The Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe, OSCE, has warned that Pristina must ensure Serb participation in Kosovo’s juducial institutions. It said the KJC should “promptly fill the vacant positions through transparent, inclusive, and merit-based recruitment,” adding that “a judicial system that reflects the communities it serves is essential to ensuring equal and effective access to justice for all”.

Most Serbs in Kosovo’s four Serb-majority northern municipalities who were working in Kosovo state institutions resigned on November 5, 2022, in protest at Pristina’s failure to implement EU-mediated agreements between Serbia and Kosovo.

The Belgrade-backed Kosovo Serb party Srpska Lista coordinated the resignations. The party’s then leader, Goran Rakic, said the boycott would remain in force until Pristina fulfilled its commitment under the 2013 Brussels Agreement to establish an Association of Serb-Majority Municipalities.

Kosovo Serb voters also boycotted the extraordinary elections in April 2023, resulting in extremely low turnouts and the election of ethnic Albanian mayors in majority-Serb municipalities. Their installation triggered violence between protesters and members of NATO’s KFOR peacekeeping force who had formed cordons around the municipal buildings. Kosovo authorities also later shut down a number of institutions serving Kosovo Serbs, claiming they were illegal.

Brussels blamed Pristina for inflaming ethnic tensions and imposed sanctions in June 2023. Those measures were not lifted until March this year, following the return of Serb mayors in December 2025.

Ahead of that, Srpska Lista admitted that urging Serbs to abandon Kosovo institutions had been a mistake. It still maintained that the move had successfully attracted the international community’s attention.

World.title: Ratko Mladic: Genocide Convict Who Left Trail of Blood Across Bosnia
World.content:
Mladic was convicted of genocide of Bosniaks in the eastern town of Srebrenica in 1995, the persecution and extermination of Bosniaks and Croats across the country, terrorising the population of Sarajevo with a campaign of shelling and sniper attacks, and taking UN peacekeepers hostage.

But he was acquitted of committing genocide in six other Bosnian municipalities in 1992.

It is for Srebrenica – the systematic killings of Bosniak men and boys and the subsequent cover-up operation – that Mladic will be remembered by history. According to the ICTY’s indictment, “more than 7,000 prisoners captured in the area around Srebrenica were summarily executed from 13 July to 19 July 1995. The killings continued thereafter.”

The Bosnian Serb Army and Serb paramilitary formations tried to hide the extent of the crimes by burying victims in mass graves. A total of 95 mass graves have been discovered around the Srebrenica area; seven were primary mass graves, where bodies were initially buried. The rest of them were secondary or tertiary grave, to which bodies were moved in subsequent cover-up attempts.

The ICTY rejected Mladic’s appeal against his conviction in June 2021, finally bringing some kind of justice to thousands of families of people who were killed.

Refija Hadzibulic, one of the mothers of the victims of the Srebrenica genocide, said at the time that the final verdict was a recognition of their suffering.

“It means a lot to us to know that there was a genocide, that they committed genocide. Because they always deny it. And now they can’t deny it, the whole world sees what happened and what they did,” Hadzibulic said.

But Bosnian Serb political leaders still see Mladic as a hero who fought to defend Republika Srpska, the Serb-dominated entity of the country that was established, with Radovan Karadzic as its leader, just before the war erupted in 1992.

Milorad Dodik, who has long been the most powerful Bosnian Serb politician, said that the Mladic verdict had “nothing to do with law and justice”.

Dodik claimed that the trial was held in order to “Satanise” Serbs, and complained that “an attempt is being made to create a myth about the genocide in Srebrenica, which did not happen”.

A family legacy of war

World.title: US Army Selects Croatian Company Orqa to Supply FPV Drones
World.content:
Srdjan Kovacevic, one of the three founders of Orqa. Photo: Orqa.

The Croatian company Orqa, which produces first-person-view (FPV) drones, has been selected as a supplier for the US Army. The company, headquartered in Osijek in eastern Croatia, announced the news on its LinkedIn profile on Thursday.

The company confirmed that the US Army’s 2nd Infantry Division had selected Orqa following an assessment of several suppliers.

“Orqa is delighted to announce that the US Army’s 2nd Infantry Division has confirmed an agreement to procure our FPV drones after a focused evaluation of multiple suppliers,” the company said in a LinkedIn post.

“Orqa emerged as the chosen provider based on the proven performance of its systems in the field,” it company added.

However, details of the agreement have not been disclosed. It is not known how many drones are involved and what the value of the entire deal is.

The announcement comes as the US military continues to expand its use and evaluation of small FPV drone systems for tactical applications.

The 2nd Infantry Division has also been developing its drone capabilities on the Korean Peninsula, including through recent training involving FPV systems.

Founded in Osijek in 2018 by Srdjan Kovacevic, Ivan Jelusic and Vlatko Matijevic, Orqa develops FPV drones and advanced remote-reality technology.

The three founders started as enthusiasts involved in FPV drone racing and have since built a company that produces tens of thousands of technologically advanced products.

The latest development highlights the growing international role of Croatian-developed drone technology at a time when unmanned systems are becoming increasingly important to modern military operations.

In May, Orqa announced that, in cooperation with US cyber and defence solutions provider By Light Professional IT Services, it had established Orqa US, a company focused on drone production for the US market. The move was a strategic response to the requirements of new US Department of Defence programmes, including the Drone Dominance plan, Orqa said at the time.

Building on its capacity to produce up to 280,000 drones annually in Osijek, Orqa has been extending this model globally through an international manufacturing network. Orqa US is headquartered in Palo Alto, in Silicon Valley, and has a 17,000-square-metre production facility in Florida.

The company has already established manufacturing partnerships in North America, Europe, the Middle East and the Indo-Pacific.

World.title: Ratko Mladic, Convicted Bosnian Serb War Criminal, Has Died
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp

Ratko Mladic waiting for his appeal judgment in The Hague, June 2021. Photo: EPA-EFE/Jerry Lampen/Pool.

Ratko Mladic, wartime commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, died on Thursday at the age of 84 at the UN Detention Centre in The Hague.

Mladic was was serving a life sentence for committing genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes during the 1992-95 war in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Demo Berisa, Serbia’s Minister for Human and Minority Rights, confirmed to BIRN that “it is true that Ratko Mladic has died”.

Serbian Justice Minister Nenad Vujic told Srna news agency that his ministry will handle the transfer of the body to Serbia, saying that Mladic’s family and the ministry are now “waiting for instructions” from the UN court.

A statement later on Thursday from the UN’s International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals officially confirmed that Mladic “passed away today while hospitalised in The Hague” and that the Dutch authorities have “commenced the standard procedures and investigations required under Dutch national law”.

As head of the Bosnian Serb Army, Mladic oversaw the mass executions of over 8,000 mainly Bosniak men and boys around Srebrenica in 1995 after his forces overran the town – a crime classified by international courts as genocide.

The UN court in The Hague confirmed his conviction and life sentence after an appeal in 2021.

Emir Suljagic, director of the Srebrenica Memorial Centre, where thousands of victims are buried, saying that the fact of Mladic’s death does not change the historical evidence or erase the consequences of the genocide of Bosniaks by Bosnian Serb forces in July 1995.

“The people he sent to their deaths did not get the chance to grow old. That is the only fact about his death that matters to me,” Suljagic said.

Mladic, who had been in custody in The Hague since his arrest in 2011, had suffered serious health problems in recent years. The UN court stated last week that he was approaching the end of his life.

Read BIRN’s profile of Mladic, his life and crimes here.

World.title: Serbia’s Competition Commission Approves Acquisition of Critical Media Outlets
World.content:
Amid a process that has raised questions about media pluralism and independence, Serbia’s competition regulator told BIRN on Thursday that it had given the green light to the sale of the country’s most prominent government-critical media outlets.

As a result, the N1 and Nova S television stations, Danas newspaper and Radar magazine will come under the same ownership umbrella as Euronews, whose majority owner is Alpac Capital, a Portuguese investment firm.

“The concentration involving European Future Media Investments S.C.S. and Adra News S.a r.l. was notified to the Commission for Protection of Competition on 8 June 2026. Following the conducted proceedings, the notified concentration was approved,” it is said.

The decision has yet to be published on the Commission’s website.

United Group told BIRN late on Wednesday that it had transferred its news businesses in Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia and Slovenia to European Future Media, a Luxembourg-based fund backed by Alpac Capital.

“The remaining steps, including the transfer of the Luxembourg licences for the N1 and Nova S channels and the transfer of certain United Group interests in Montenegro, will follow in line with the terms of the agreement conditional upon the receipt of requisite regulatory approvals,” United Group said.

Montenegro’s Commercial Court in mid-August temporarily blocked planned changes to the ownership and management structure of TV Vijesti.

On Tuesday, Alpac Capital’s CEO Pedro Vargas David said that his company had received all the required permits from the Bosnian authorities for the acquisition of the N1 and Nova outlets there.

Serbian website Raskrikavanje reported on Wednesday that United Group stated in an internal memo to management that the sale of several media outlets was “substantially implemented” on August 24.

On August 18, before the ownership was transferred, Pedro Vargas Santos David was registered as director of four companies – Adria News, United Media Digital, Adria News Nova S, and Dan Graf, the companies that run N1 and other media outlets in Serbia. The sitting directors were dismissed.

The European Federation of Journalists and Serbian civil society organisations have all voiced concerns about the sale of the media outlets, with the EFJ warning of a potential impact on “media pluralism, editorial independence [and] public opinion”.

The timing of the sale, with the parliamentary elections in Serbia likely before the end of the year, has also triggered alarms. United Group’s outlets had been among the few which published critical opinions of President Aleksandar Vucic and his governing Serbian Progressive Party, SNS.

Alpac Capital acquired a majority stake in the pan-European news channel Euronews in 2022. French newspaper Le Monde reported in 2024 that this takeover was partly financed by funds linked to the then Hungarian leader Viktor Orban.

Alpac CEO Vargas David’s comments on Wednesday will not have reassured those who would like the former United Group outlets to continue their robust, government-critical editorial line. In an open letter to Serbia’s Information and Telecommunications Minister Boris Bratina, Vargas David wrote that he wanted a return to “non-activist” journalism.

“When news organisations believe that they are the news, and their mission is not to report on the news but to be the news, they enter the arena; they become part of the game. With this come the attacks from politicians, the boycotts, the aggressiveness. When journalists use their platform to share an agenda, they change the nature of their profession,” Vargas David wrote.

Vargas David’s letter followed a call by Serbian minister Bratina for Alpac Capital to register its new acquisitions with Serbia’s media regulator, REM.

World.title: Albanian Businessman Arrested in Information Agency Tenders Corruption Case
World.content:
Albanian businessman Ergys Agasi in front of the SPAK organised crime and corruption prosecution office in Tirana. Photo: LSA.

Albanian businessman Ergys Agasi, arrested on Wednesday in Durres, is suspected of being part of a scheme that utilised organised crime to manipulate and extort public procurement procedures valued at approximately 59 million euros.

Albania’s organised crime and corruption prosecution SPAK confirmed the arrest in a statement saying saying that “at the time of the arrest, this individual (Ergys Agasi) was accompanied by U. Sh., a former police officer, who was arrested immediately for the criminal offence of ‘aiding the perpetrator of a crime’.”

Agasi is accused of forming a structured criminal group with another businessman, Ermal Beqiraj, to rig and extort tenders from the National Agency for Information Society, AKSHI, including through the use of violence and hostage-taking.

Agasi denies the allegations. His lawyer Maksim Haxhia told media on Thursday that “it is a fact that he has not touched public funds, as he has never held a position of authority involving the management of public finances, nor has he participated in any tenders.”

His alleged partner in the scheme, Beqiraj, was arrested in France on July 24 while flying a light aircraft through restricted airspace over the Penly nuclear power plant. He was escorted by air force units until he landed at the Albert airfield in the Somme region of northern France.

According to SPAK, further investigations by French authorities identified assets belonging to Beqiraj in France that are suspected to be of criminal origin. SPAK alleges that Beqiraj transferred a portion of his illicit proceeds to France, using the funds to purchase a château, two apartments, and motor vehicles, while also depositing over 2 million euros into bank accounts.

Beqiraj has not commented publicly on the allegations so far.

SPAK initially charged Agasi and Beqiraj with “illegal competition through violence”, “illegal deprivation of liberty”, “violation of equality in tenders”, involvement in a “structured criminal group” and “laundering of the proceeds of a criminal offence”, in December last year.

AKSHI coordinates the development of state information systems and digitalisation procedures, and administers the state public services portal, e-Albania. For over a decade, the agency managed a massive budget; in just 19 procedures investigated by SPAK, the estimated total value (limit fund) amounted to 5.9 billion lek (approximately 59 million euros).

The SPAK investigation alleges that AKSHI director Mirlinda Karcanaj and her deputy, Hava Delibashi, placed these funds in the hands of a group linked to organised crime, pre-selecting winners and ensuring the diversion of tens of millions of euros into the accounts of IT businessman Beqiraj and Agasi.

Karcanaj and Delibashi have both denied the allegations.

World.title: Croatian Pensions to Increase Following Latest Adjustments
World.content:
August the 28th, 2026 – Croatian pensions are set to increase once again following the latest adjustments, with differences set to be paid for July 2026.

The Croatian Pension Insurance Institute (HZMO) has announced that at the recently held 26th session of the Management Board a Decision was adopted on the current value of the pension (AVM) from the 1st of July 2026, which amounts to 15.64 euros. Poslovni reports that it was calculated on the basis of the published official data of the Croatian Bureau of Statistics. “Since the AVM from the 1st of January 2026 amounted to 14.84 euros, and the rate of increase of the AVM from the 1st of July 2026 is 5.40%, the new AVM amounts to 15.64 euros,” HZMO states.

They explain that the rate of adjustment of the current value of the pension, which is applied on the 1st of January and the 1st of July of every calendar year, is determined by adding the rate of change of the average consumer price index in the previous half-year relative to the half-year preceding it and the rate of change of the average gross wage of all employees in the Republic of Croatia in the previous half-year relative to the half-year preceding it.

If the share of the rate of change of the average consumer price index in the sum of the rates is less than or equal to 50 percent, the pension adjustment rate is determined by adding 15% of the rate of change of the average consumer price index and 85% of the rate of change of the average gross wage. If the share of the rate of change of the average consumer price index in the sum of the rates is greater than 50%, the pension adjustment rate is determined by adding 85% of the rate of change of the average consumer price index and 15% of the rate of change of the average gross wage.

The share of the rate of change of the consumer price index in the sum of the rates of change is less than 50 percent, which means that the annual pension growth rate is determined by adding 15% of the rate of change of the average consumer price index and 85% of the rate of change of the average gross wage, so that the adjustment rate from the 1st of July 2026 amounts to 5.40%. “Pensions increased according to the new current value will be paid in September (with the pension for August), together with the difference for July 2026,” they emphasised.

At the session, a Decision was also adopted on the lowest pension for one year of pensionable service from the 1st of July 2026, according to which the lowest pension for one year of pensionable service from the 1st of July 2026 amounts to 16.58 euros, as well as a Decision on the base for determining compensation due to physical impairment and on the adjustment of cash benefits due to physical impairment from the 1st of July 2026, according to which the base for determining compensation due to physical impairment arising from a work injury or occupational disease amounts to 358.48 euros.

World.title: August 1995: The Croatian Freedom Train Sets off From Zagreb to Split
World.content:
August the 28th, 2026 – Turning the clock back to August 1995, and the Croatian Freedom Train which finally set off from Zagreb to Split, making a journey that was inconceivable just weeks before.

Just after the end of Operation Storm (Oluja), more specifically on the 26th of August 1995, a train departed from Zagreb’s Main Station the likes of which had not been able to run through Croatia for years. Index reports that the final destination was Split, and the route led via Knin and parts of the country where railway traffic had been interrupted since the beginning of the war.

It was named the Croatian Freedom Train, and its journey was not conceived merely as the reopening of a railway connection. In a political and symbolic sense, it represented a demonstration that Croatia’s north and south were once again linked by land after Operation Storm. The train left Zagreb at 08:07. It carried around 700 passengers, including President Franjo Tuđman, members of the state leadership, politicians, military officials, cultural and public figures, singers, actors, refugees and numerous other guests. The 21-carriage composition was pulled by two diesel locomotives.

this train line had been out of function for over 4 years

Special importance was given to the entire event by the Lika railway line. The railway connection between Zagreb and Split via Knin had been interrupted for more than four years because of the war and the occupation of part of Croatian territory. After Operation Storm, railway workers and the army were given the demanding task of restoring the line in a very short time. In some sections the area was mined, signalling and safety systems had been destroyed, and stations and other infrastructure had been damaged.

Despite this, the line was made ready for the special train only a few weeks after the end of the operation. Because of the state of the infrastructure, preparing the journey was demanding, especially since the train was carrying almost the entire state leadership of the time. The journey lasted nearly the whole day. The train stopped in Karlovac, Gospić and Knin, and along the route it was welcomed by everyone it passed.

knin – the most important and poignant stop of all

The central moment of the journey was of course, the train’s arrival in Knin. The town had been placed back under Croatian control only three weeks earlier, on the 5th of August during Operation Storm, after having been the political centre of the self-proclaimed Republic of Serbian Krajina since back in 1991. At Knin station Tuđman delivered a speech in which he gave the train’s arrival a far broader meaning than simply the restoration of railway traffic. He spoke of Knin as a key symbol of Croatian statehood and claimed that by liberating the town the future of independent Croatia had been secured.

The entire event took place in an atmosphere of strong victorious sentiment after Operation Storm. Thus, the Croatian Freedom Train symbolised for the Croatian authorities and a large part of the public the end of years of occupation and the re-connection of the country.

at 18:11, the croatian freedom train finally arrived in split

After Knin, the train continued towards coastal Dalmatia. It arrived at Split station at 18:11, a little more than ten hours after leaving Zagreb. A large welcome was organised there, after which President Franjo Tuđman delivered another speech. He recalled that he had earlier promised he would come to Split by train from Zagreb. At one point the crowd began chanting “Vukovar”, which at that time was still not under Croatian control. Tuđman replied that Croatia still had to regain Vukovar, eastern Slavonia and Baranja, and expressed the hope that this would be achieved by peaceful means. That is exactly what eventually happened. The Erdut Agreement was signed a few months later, in November 1995, and the Croatian Danube region was gradually returned to Croatia’s constitutional and legal order through the process of peaceful reintegration, completed at the beginning of 1998.

a symbolic journey of a reconnected croatia

The Freedom Train has remained one of the more striking images of Croatia from the summer of 1995. Its practical significance was obvious: the railway link between Zagreb and Split via Knin was operating again after more than four years. It was precisely the symbolism that is the reason the journey is remembered three decades later. The train that left Zagreb that morning passed through an area where fierce fighting had been taking place only a few weeks earlier. Ten hours later it arrived in Split. Croatia thereby wished to send a very simple message: the territory that for years had cut the country in two no longer divided it.

World.title: Fire Burns for 10 Days in Konavle Hills
World.content:
August the 28th, 2026 – A fire has been burning for 10 days straight in the Konavle hills in the extreme south of Croatia, having spread from neighbouring Bosnia and Herzegovina.

In the very far south of Croatia, right next to the border with Montenegro, fires that spread from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina have remained active for the tenth day already. Index reports that Canadair aircraft are also participating in the firefighting in Konavle, and around 50 firefighters are on the ground every day. Difficult terrain, months-long drought and wind are making extinguishing harder, while residents have been waking up to the stench of smoke for days now.

Inaccessible terrain is complicating the work of the present firefighters, whose top priority is to keep the fire away from any houses. “We successfully defended the houses and pushed the fire back up into the hills. Now we’re monitoring it and hope we can catch up with it. Two days ago we followed it for 10 kilometres, and the Canadairs helped us. We go to every open flame and every place that is still smoking, because if a firefighter hasn’t passed through, it isn’t classed as extinguished. The Canadair helps significantly and reduces the flames, but if the firefighter’s boot and water don’t arrive, the fire will continue to burn and spread,” said Nikša Miletić, commander of the Dubrovnik Intervention Fire Unit.

on duty 24 hours per day

In the small villages of Stravča and Njivice, residents continue to watch the flames with uncertainty and hope for rain, which has not fallen at all for three months now. “It’s extremely hard to breathe, there’s a lot of smoke. It’s uncertain whether it will become dangerous for houses, people and livestock,” said a resident of Stravča. “In the morning it’s terrible, you can’t breathe because of the smoke. Luckily the firefighters are extinguishing the flames, but the hill has been completely burned. Those who have livestock now have no pasture to put them in,” added a fellow villager. Canadairs have been flying over this whole area for days, and a large number of firefighters have been on the ground almost without a break ever since the fire on Pelješac broke out.

“On such a large area, 50 people have to be engaged every day. We’re on duty 24 hours a day because that is the only way to try to deal with this. This is a very serious fire, and the area from Molunat to Cavtat is covered in smoke every single morning. Today, even the area around the airport was unrecognisable,” said county fire commander Stjepan Simović.

bosnia and herzegovina didn’t request the help of croatian canadairs

The fires in the Konavle hills and the general area of Župa dubrovačka spread from neighbouring Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is located within a mere few miles. “The first fire on Ivanica started on the 18th of August and lasted until the 24th of August. There was only one day when we weren’t up there. That one is now under control, and colleagues from Ravno have remained on duty. We do hope it stays that way,” said Štefi Bogdan, commander of the Župa Dubrovačka volunteer fire department. Simović explained that at no point did a request for the assistance of Croatian Canadairs arrive from Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is why the spread of the fire was inevitable. “According to my information, they didn’t submit a request from either side in Bosnia and Herzegovina, so our Canadairs were unable to operate. That isn’t usual, especially with fires like these. It should have been reacted to earlier,” Simović explained.

The biggest problem now can be created by the problematic Dalmatian winds, primarily the bura. Firefighters hope to bring the fire under control soon, but there is still a lot of work to be done on the ground.

World.title: Hajduk Reach Group Stage of European Competition for First Time in 16 Years!
World.content:
Hajduk secured European football this autumn for the first time in 16 years, coming through against Poland’s Raków in the final round of Conference League qualifying!

After both legs finished 2:2, the tie was decided in extra time in the away leg in Poland, with Rokas Pukštas netting the winner in the 94th minute.

With their win in Poland, Hajduk have booked their place in a European group stage for the first time since 2010. The last time Hajduk bypassed qualifying was in 2010, when they got past Romanian sides Dinamo Bucharest and Unirea Urziceni to reach the Europa League group stage.

Gonzalo Garcia made just one enforced change, with Pajaziti suspended after his red card in the first leg, replaced by Acapandie. On the home side, coach Dawid Kroczek opted for two changes: Struski came in for Kocherin, while Kwiatkowski also dropped out of the strongest XI, with Makuch taking his place.

In the first leg at Poljud, Hajduk let a win slip while down to ten men in the final minute of stoppage time. In the return leg, they made a flying start, going ahead after just 54 seconds. Dalisson whipped in a corner, and Ron Raci headed home to make it 1-0.

The referee had initially flagged an offense in the build-up but pointed to the center circle after a VAR check. Raków hit back in the 12th minute with their first real chance. Diaby found Makuch with a low ball into the box, and Makuch finished into the net, but VAR ruled the Raków forward marginally offside.

In the 27th minute Hajduk had a chance to extend their lead: Pukštas slipped the ball through to Šego, who shook off his marker and struck from the edge of the box, but the shot went just wide of the left post.

In the 34th minute the home side appealed for a penalty, claiming Marešić had handled the ball, but the referee waved play on. Three minutes later Makuch threatened again, but his effort was saved by Silić.

Just four minutes into the second half, there was a brief flare-up on the pitch, with the referee calming things down by showing yellow cards to Ameyaw and Sigur. The hosts had a big chance in the 54th minute, but Emreli failed to find the target — the former Dinamo forward headed wide from Ameyaw’s cross from the right. In the 58th minute, Silić bailed Hajduk out, saving Ameyaw’s effort.

Unfortunately, a minute later Raków won a penalty. Marešić brought down Racovitan, and Lamine Diaby-Fadiga made no mistake from the spot to make it 1-1. The Polish fans’ joy was short-lived, though — Hajduk restored their lead in the 66th minute through Michele Šego.

It was a brilliant Hajduk counter-attack: Šotiček broke clear of the home defence after a pass from Pukštas, then squared it low for Šego, who put Hajduk back in front.

In the 71st minute Garcia made a triple substitution, bringing on Šutalo, Melnjak and Del Moral for Dalisson, Acapandie and Bamba. A few minutes later Šotiček also made way, replaced by Huram.

In the closing stages, the hosts threw everything forward, and once again Hajduk couldn’t hold on late on, as has happened so often recently. Raków equalized in the 88th minute through Emreli, who had also scored in the first leg. Diaby-Fadiga won a header from a cross into Hajduk’s box and nodded it across to the far post, where a completely unmarked Emreli finished from five meters to make it 2-2.

In the second minute of stoppage time, Hajduk appealed for a penalty after a Šego jump in the box, but the referee waved it away, and the match went to extra time. Hajduk weren’t deterred, and in the 94th minute the visitors found a third lead. After a short corner routine, the ball reached the far post and Darija Marešić, whose cutback found Pukštas, who slotted home to make it 2-3.

Marešić was injured in the buildup to the goal and had to be substituted, with Van Hoorenbeeck coming on. In the 105th minute the Polish side almost equalized, but Silić produced a brilliant save to deny Kochergin.

In the 108th minute the game could have been put to bed: Marko Livaja, who had come on for Šego at the start of the first period of extra time, broke through one-on-one with the Raków keeper but shot wide. Even without that chance, though, Hajduk held on — and ended their long European drought!

World.title: The Secret Real Estate and Maritime Rights Only Croatian Citizenship Unlocks
World.content:
August the 27th, 2026 – There’s a hack to the complicated and bureaucratic minefield of Croatian real estate and maritime rights, and that is possessing Croatian citizenship. It might sound obvious, but there’s far more to it than you might imagine.

Croatia’s administration is full of red tape. Anyone who has had any experience with it will know that bureaucracy is rife and one area in which this is particularly true is when it comes to real estate laws and maritime rights. In this sense, your passport matters more than you might think it would, and the key to bypassing a lot of the drama is holding Croatian citizenship. That trusty little blue passport allows you to purchase any type of real estate or land you like, without needing to make additional applications, seek extra permissions or adhere to zoning.

If you are an American of Croatian descent, you’ll likely have already read about our extensive coverage of the lifestyle perks of reclaiming your heritage. It spans from making entering and travelling around the EU more easily, to reconnecting with your roots in a concrete way, to providing your children and even grandchildren with an open door to not only Croatian but EU education and career opportunities. The list of benefits to turning the hands of the clock backwards through time to allow you to be granted Croatian citizenship is not only extensive but surprising, and extends far beyond the obvious. Even if you’re not considering doing anything like moving to Croatia or setting up a business there, long, hot summers on the Adriatic, the slower pace of life, and the security of a EU passport is often enough of a reason to explore the route in and of itself.

if you’re looking to purchase property, land, or spend a significant amount of time on the adriatic sea, there are barriers for non-citizens…

If you are looking to buy land, property, invest in a piece of land, or spend significant time sailing on the Adriatic Sea, there is an enormous legal barrier that an American passport simply cannot (and likely will never) be able to cross. To truly unlock the Croatian coastline and islands in a totally unbridled way, you’ll need to move past the tourist visa and the constantly ticking Schengen clock. Here’s exactly how obtaining your Croatian citizenship (more specifically your Domovnica) fundamentally alters and upgrades your legal rights when it comes to real estate and maritime ownership.

Many in the Croatian diaspora dream of buying that classic, traditional old stone house with an attached olive grove, a little vineyard, or a piece of forested land handed down through generations. Dreaming about it is often where it ends for those who don’t seek citizenship. Here is the cold, bureaucratic reality: Third-country nationals (which US citizens are) are extremely heavily restricted from buying agricultural land (known legally as poljoprivredno zemljište) or what is listed as a protected nature zone anywhere in Croatia.

While the EU moratorium on foreign ownership of agricultural land has officially expired, strict reciprocity laws and complex local bureaucracy mean that as a US citizen, your purchase is tied up (or rather tangled up) in ministry approvals for months on end, or outright denied from the get-go, as the case often is.

if you’re a croatian national, the bureaucratic headache vanishes

The second you hold a Croatian passport, you have the absolute, unrestricted right to buy any piece of agricultural land, OPG (family farm), or forestry anywhere in the country. You completely bypass the Ministry of Justice approvals, allowing you to secure that dream vineyard or piece of agricultural land with the exact same ease as a local.

What makes this so monumental is that an absolutely massive percentage of the Croatian diaspora technically owns land right now, they just don’t legally have their name on it. Millions of parcels of land dotted up and down the coast and in the hinterlands are tied up in multi-generational legal limbo, still registered to great-grandparents who emigrated to the US a century ago and have long since passed away. In fact, this is a bit of a Croatian right of way. Arguing with family members over ancient, falling apart houses for decades is a joke many Croats will smirk at, as they’ve likely been involved with it. Trying to clean up a messy land title (which is aptly named gruntovnica) or claim your rightful inheritance as a foreign national is an extremely expensive, bureaucratic nightmare. There are also unscrupulous lawyers who will look at a naive person entering into this proverbial ring with dollar signs flashing in their eyes, knowing from the start that there’s no way around this without a passport.

the citizenship application gives you an official way in

When you apply for Croatian citizenship, you officially enter the system. You get a Croatian personal identification number (OIB) and the ball gets rolling. As a citizen, you have the legal standing to easily interact with all of the municipal courts, hire local representation to clear up multi-generational titles, and officially claim ancestral property without facing the discriminatory tax rates or legal hurdles aimed at foreign buyers. You also bypass the aforementioned lawyers who will be more than happy to “help” a US citizen without a Croatian passport just to get absolutely nowhere.

croatian maritime laws and the citizenship golden egg

For many, the ultimate goal of spending time in Croatia is spending long, lazy periods of time sailing the Adriatic and exploring the 1,000 islands. However, all that comes grinding to a violent halt when Croatia’s ultra-complicated maritime laws are delved into. Croatia is very fiercely protective of its waters, and navigating them as an American boat owner is both highly restricted and incredibly expensive.

As a Croatian citizen, however, you can legally register a vessel under the Croatian flag (and by extension, the flag of the European Union). This allows for much, much lower mooring and marina fees reserved for local residents and EU citizens, and the legal right to apply for highly coveted communal berths (known as a komunalni vez), which is a privilege protected and reserved just for citizens. It also unlocks the ability to legally charter or monetise your vessel on the wider EU market without facing third-country commercial bans.

there’s no need for reciprocal agreements

When an American buys a standard residential property in Croatia, the sale cannot legally close straight away. The purchase is subjected to a “reciprocity check” by the Ministry of Justice to ensure a Croatian citizen could buy the equivalent property in the buyer’s home US state. This process can take anywhere from six months to a year, leaving your deposit in limbo and sellers (rightfully) frustrated. Knowing this, many Croatian sellers simply avoid American passport holders like the plague, which greatly limits your ability to do anything at all.

As touched on previously, Croatian citizenship totally eliminates any need for any kind of Ministry of Justice review. Your property transaction can close in mere days rather than months and months, making you a far more attractive buyer to local sellers who don’t want to wait on government paperwork.

that window might not be open forever…

Croatia’s current citizenship laws (specifically Article 11 for Croatian citizenship by ethnicity) are among the most generous in not only the EU but in Europe as a whole. Currently, diaspora applicants do not have to pass a Croatian language test or a culture exam to reclaim their citizenship and lock in all of these benefits. However, it does need to be stated that the Croatian property market has faced a massive boom and EU immigration policies are forever tightening up, meaning that these legal windows very rarely stay open forever. You only have to look at how neighbouring Italy suddenly opted to make it extremely difficult for Italian-Americans to get their foot in the door administratively in Italy. Croatia isn’t immune to making such a move. Therefore, if your long-term plan involves owning a piece of the Adriatic coast or captaining a boat in Croatian waters without the need to worry about limits, fines and bans, getting your Domovnica and your Croatian passport isn’t just a sentimental nod to your heritage or a way to bypass long airport queues, it’s a critical financial and legal tool.

here’s how croatianbydescent can help you get the ball rolling

Croatian by Descent is a service aimed at US citizens who have Croatian roots and are on the hunt for Croatian citizenship. The administrative pathway to being granted citizenship in Croatia, while arguably easier than in many other countries, is still burdened with administrative pitfalls, delays, paperwork upon paperwork and very little help (if any at all) from the Interior Ministry (MUP), which handles applications.

Acting as your guide, a free consultation with them will allow you to see the situation in a more structured and less overwhelming way. Founded by members of the Croatian diaspora, they know the situation you’re facing better than anyone else, and have navigated this process personally in their own lives and with their own loved ones. With fair pricing and genuine guidance, applying for Croatian citizenship as an ethnic Croat is made easier and clearer, without the worry of the infamous fali ti još jedan papir (you’re missing another paper) that so many who have opted to try to go it alone have heard repeatedly.

World.title: Croatian Firefighters Receive New vehicles for Extinguishing Forest Fires
World.content:
August the 27th, 2026 – Croatian firefighters have received six new, highly specialised modern vehicles for extinguishing forest fires.

A ceremony for the handover of new vehicles for extinguishing forest fires was held yesterday at the State Firefighting School in Zagreb. Index reports that the attendees included Chief Fire Commander Slavko Tucaković, county fire commanders and presidents of the firefighting associations of the counties receiving the vehicles, Buzet Mayor Damir Kajin, and representatives of the firefighting units to which the vehicles were allocated.

The six new specialised firefighting vehicles for extinguishing forest fires were financed from funds for the general-purpose functions of forests (OKFŠ). Those funds are distributed through the competent ministry in cooperation with the Croatian Firefighting Association.

a total of 78 new vehicles have been ordered

Chief Fire Commander Slavko Tucaković said that continuous investment in firefighting equipment further strengthens the operational capabilities of Croatian firefighters.

“By distributing these brand new vehicles, we’re raising the operational readiness of units not only for extinguishing outdoor fires, but also for a range of other sorts of interventions. These vehicles will immediately be put into operational use. Previously allocated vehicles have already been used on major fires on Korčula and near Lokva Rogoznica,” said Chief Fire Commander Tucaković, emphasising that the vehicles were built according to the requirements of fire commanders in the field.

where in croatia will they be put into function?

These vehicles are modernly equipped firefighting vehicles designed entirely for extinguishing forest fires and interventions in very demanding terrain. They have 4×4 drives, large water tanks, a fire pump and additional equipment for work in the most difficult conditions. A total of 40 vehicles with 2,500-litre water tanks and 38 vehicles with 5,000-litre tanks have been ordered. Today, five larger-capacity vehicles and one smaller-capacity vehicle were handed over.

The new vehicles were received by the Public Fire Brigade of Petrinja, the Public Fire Brigade of Buzet, the Public Fire Brigade of Imotski, the Public Fire Brigade of Županja, the Senj Volunteer Fire Department and the Brestovac Volunteer Fire Department.

World.title: Croatian Fires Often Occur on Overgrown, Neglected Private Land
World.content:
August the 27th, 2026 – Croatian fires often occur on overgrown and neglected private land where it’s difficult or impossible for Croatian Forests (Hrvatske šume) to enter and deal with the situation.

Large fires have become a European reality and no longer pose a threat only to the extreme south of Europe. As never before, fires have also hit the United Kingdom, the continental part of France and Germany. Marija Brnic reports for Poslovni that there have been fires up in Scandinavia as well, and in conditions of increasingly frequent extreme heatwaves they represent a greater threat than before for a far larger number of countries. The authorities have duly recognised this, as a joint defence has already been established, so that unlike earlier times, member states help one another by sending firefighting teams and firefighting fleets.

According to the European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS), forest fires already reached a historic record last year – more than one million hectares of forest burned within the EU back in 2025. This year, according to data from the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre, as of the first week of August, 506 thousand hectares of forest area had burned, which is a third more than in the same period of the most devastating 2025.

Since the recovery of a destroyed forest ecosystem is measured in decades compared with agricultural crops or buildings, the question arises of what to do with these areas, and how this changes the picture on the timber raw material market. As of the first week of August, 506 thousand hectares of forest area had burned – a third more than in the same period of the most devastating 2025.

it’s still too early to make educated estimates

These questions are also relevant at the Croatian level, although, fortunately and thanks to a well-organised fire defence, the areas burned so far are still below the record levels of 2017 and the devastating 2022. By mid-August, 9.6 thousand hectares had been affected by fire.

Croatian Forests were asked for their estimates of damage to forested areas under their management that were affected by fires, and what the ratio of affected areas is compared with the previous year. They revealed that it is too early for any estimates; more concrete information will only be possible after the end of the fire season. However, they significantly emphasised that in the largest fire this year, the one in the wider Omiš area, only about ten percent of the total burned area was under the management of Croatian Forests.

As for the rehabilitation of the fire-affected areas, they explain that the law provides that it must be carried out no later than two growing seasons after the fire occurred. They are responsible for rehabilitating areas owned by the state, and they carry it out mainly independently or by engaging external subcontractors. The first step, if it concerns so-called high forest, is the extraction of timber mass, followed by preparation for the replanting of trees, which is done purposefully, in accordance with the adaptation of the tree species to the particular terrain.

However, some forest areas also regenerate on their own, especially those under pine trees, because during a fire the cones practically explode and disperse seed up to about ten metres. This brings us to the increasingly frequent and louder public questioning of replacing the flammable Aleppo pine with another tree species. Europe, precisely because of fires and climate change, is intensively considering abandoning conifers and switching to mixed and more resistant deciduous forests.

changes are unfortunately not likely

As for changes along Croatia’s long, heavily irregular coastal area, this is not currently likely. Experts have long pointed out that on karst and rock, where there is no fertile soil, deciduous trees cannot survive, and that the Aleppo pine is precisely suitable because it has extremely modest requirements. Moreover, it is the best at creating conditions for the start of humus production. That is also the reason why on the areas affected by fires that are under Croatian Forests, a rapid change of tree species is not likely.

“Given the conditions we constantly encounter, the pioneer species, in this case the Aleppo pine, simply does not manage to perform its primary function because of fires – creating conditions for the successful growth of other species. Unfortunately, we find it increasingly difficult to wait the sufficient number of years that are approximately needed for that process of conversion into mixed forests, because fires due to the climate and human behaviour have become ever more frequent and destructive,” they emphasise from Croatian Forests, reminding that 90 percent of them are caused by human negligence and carelessness or malicious intent.

Among other things, they note that fires often start from neglected and overgrown agricultural areas in private ownership, for which they are not responsible and which they are not allowed to enter, and which are very often overgrown precisely with Aleppo pine that has not been maintained there and has no firebreaks.

World.title: How do Croatian Fuel Prices Compare to the Rest of the EU?
World.content:
August the 27th, 2026 – Croatian fuel prices have been up and down like a yo-yo, but just how do they compare to those across the rest of the EU?

Energy expert Jasminko Umićević assessed that Croatia is not facing a fuel shortage, but warns that high prices could persist. Drivers in Croatia are once again paying more for fuel as of Tuesday. However, Eurostat data show that the rise in fuel prices over the past year was still milder than the European Union average. Diesel in Croatia rose by 14 percent, and petrol by eight percent.

Poslovni reports that according to data issued for July 2026, the average diesel price in the European Union was 20 percent higher than a year earlier. The largest increases were recorded in Romania and the Netherlands, both at 31 percent, followed by Germany at 27 percent, France at 24 percent and Greece at 22 percent.

croatia remains below the eu average

With a 14 percent increase, Croatia remained six percent below the EU average. A slightly milder increase was recorded in Slovenia at 13 percent, while Hungary, with a rise of only one percent, is clearly at the bottom of the observed group of countries.The difference is even more pronounced for petrol specifically. Its price across the rest of the European Union rose by an average of 15 percent over the year, almost twice as much as in Croatia.

The largest increase was recorded in Lithuania at 25 percent, followed by Romania at 23 percent, Germany at 22 percent and the Netherlands at 21 percent. In France and Poland, petrol rose by 16 percent, and in Austria by 15 percent. Croatia and neighbouring Italy, both with an eight percent increase, are at the bottom of the presented ranking. In Slovenia, petrol rose by nine percent, and in Greece by 13 percent.

The annual growth data comes at a time when Croatian drivers are being hit by yet another new price increase. The government adopted decrees at a telephone session under which a litre of petrol costs 1.66 euros as of Tuesday, three cents more than before. Diesel rose by six cents to 1.86 euros per litre, and blue diesel by five cents to 1.32 euros. Liquefied petroleum gas also rose in price. LPG for tanks now costs 1.27 euros per kilogram, three cents more, while the price of gas in bottles rose by four cents to 1.85 euros per kilogram.

The government has retained reduced excise duties and limited traders’ margins. According to its calculation, without these measures petrol would cost 1.81 euros and diesel 2.07 euros per litre. The new prices are valid for seven days.

there will be no shortages, but prices will go up

Energy expert Jasminko Umićević assessed that Croatia is not facing a fuel shortage, but warns that high prices could persist. The problem is particularly pronounced on the diesel market, whose price has remained high even after the fall in the price of crude oil. Over the past twenty years or so, Europe has reduced its refining capacity by approximately 30 percent, even though it consumes more diesel than across the pond in America. After the interruption of imports from Russia, it has relied more on Arab countries, and disruptions related to the Strait of Hormuz have further reduced supply.

Croatia is in a more favourable position thanks to the Rijeka refinery. Although it isn’t yet operating at full capacity because testing is ongoing, domestic production reduces dependence on imports and the risk of shortages.

World.title: A look back at Estonia's presidential elections | Episode 3: Arnold Rüütel, 2001
World.content:
As one person can serve a maximum of two consecutive terms as president, it was certain in 2001 that Estonia would have a new president after Lennart Meri's two terms in office.

To understand the broader context, it is important to note that Mart Laar's second government was in power at the time, comprising the Isamaa Union, the Reform Party and the Moderates (later the Social Democratic Party, or SDE). The coalition was popularly known as the Triple Alliance. Together, the parties held 53 seats in parliament, meaning there was essentially no prospect of electing a president in the Riigikogu.

The 2001 presidential election began with rounds of voting in the Riigikogu. In the first round, the opposition nominated Peeter Kreitzberg, while the coalition nominated Andres Tarand. Kreitzberg received 40 votes and Tarand 38, meaning neither secured enough votes.

In Tarand's case, it is worth recalling that polls conducted two years before the presidential election showed him to be the most popular presidential candidate, with 17 percent support, ahead of both Edgar Savisaar at 15 percent and Toomas Savi at 11 percent. Unlike the Center Party and the Reform Party, however, the Moderates decided to use Tarand's personal popularity to raise the party's profile in the 1999 local elections as well. City residents were left with a memorable reminder of the campaign: images of the presidential candidate's face on trash cans.

The campaign did not bring the Moderates success in the local elections. The party was completely routed in Tallinn and Tartu, while its results across Estonia were also fairly poor. This left the Moderates with little reason for optimism in the Electoral College either. The media at the time speculated that, had the Moderates not presented Tarand as a presidential hopeful in the 1999 local elections, he might have entered the presidential election as the overwhelming favorite.

Mart Laar gave Rüütel red carnations after his election as president, widely seen as a perceived jab at Rüütel's Soviet past. Source: SCANPIX/DELFI MEEDIA/PRIIT SIMSON

In the Riigikogu's second round, Kreitzberg faced Peeter Tulviste of the Isamaa Union. By then, Tulviste had risen to become the most popular candidate among the public in opinion polls. Kreitzberg received 36 votes and Tulviste 35. The same two candidates faced each other again in the third round, when both received just 33 votes.

The presidential election once again went to the Electoral College where Peeter Kreitzberg, Arnold Rüütel, Toomas Savi and Peeter Tulviste were nominated for the first round on September 21.

Rüütel received the most votes in the first round, with 114, but not enough to win. He advanced to the second round alongside Savi who received 90 votes and edged out Tulviste by the narrowest possible margin — a single vote. There has been speculation that had Tulviste finished ahead of Savi, he would have had a better chance against Rüütel in the second round.

A second round of voting between the two leading candidates was held the same day. A total of 366 Electoral College members took part. Rüütel received 186 votes and Savi 155. There were 23 invalid ballots, which were thought to possibly have come from the Isamaa Union. Even if all of them had gone to Savi, however, it would not have been enough. Rüütel received the votes of more than half of the Electoral College members who participated in the ballot and was elected president of Estonia.

Mart Laar, Toomas Hendrik Ilves and Siim Kallas congratulate Arnold Rüütel after his election as president. Source: ERR archival footage

Sharp political competition

Rain Rosimannus recalled that neither Arnold Rüütel nor Toomas Savi was able to have his candidacy put forward in the Riigikogu because they did not have the required 21 votes. "Because competition between the parties was fierce at the time, there was no way to borrow the votes from other parties either. As a result, both candidates immediately began preparing for the Electoral College and arguing that the Electoral College had broader legitimacy and that it was therefore more appropriate for the president to be elected there," Rosimannus said.

He added that taking the election to the Electoral College gave parties an excellent opportunity to keep themselves and their candidates in the public eye and campaign extensively over a prolonged period.

Rosimannus said Rüütel's success was helped by an agreement between People's Union leader Villu Reiljan and Edgar Savisaar, which secured additional Center Party votes for Rüütel.

"Savisaar had never been interested in anyone from his own party other than himself becoming president. With every candidate, he made sure they never got anywhere near the presidency," he said.

"No one at the top of the Reform Party made a similar effort and it appears that not all the votes from our competitor, the Isamaa Union, went to Savi in the second round either, as there were spoiled ballots," Rosimannus said.

"The calculation in some circles, including Mart Laar's, was that it might actually be a good thing if Rüütel won because then the so-called 'second Estonia' would have its own political outlet and the political system would be better balanced. As Toomas Savi's campaign manager, I certainly did not share that view," Rosimannus said.

Agreements fail to hold

Tõnis Arro, who managed Isamaa Union candidate Peeter Tulviste's campaign at the time, recalled that Tulviste's narrow loss to Toomas Savi in the Electoral College probably meant that someone had failed to keep their promises.

"We regularly consulted with the Reform Party and the Moderates and certain agreements were reached. We were fairly confident that Tulviste would win and then face Rüütel. But why it turned out the way it did, I don't know. I think more was promised than was delivered," Arro said.

Although Savi and Tulviste were in a tight race, Arro said Rüütel was still the main opponent.

"Naturally, the main opponent was Rüütel. The question was who would have a chance against Rüütel. In their discussions with one another, all three parties in the coalition expressed the view that we needed one of our candidates to win, rather than Rüütel. That cooperation wasn't good enough and the agreements didn't hold up well enough for that to happen. I and everyone else thought Tulviste would have had a better chance against Rüütel than Savi did," Arro said.

Peeter Tulviste lost to Toomas Savi by just one vote in the first round of the Electoral College and did not advance to the second round. Source: SCANPIX/DELFI MEEDIA/PRIIT SIMSON

On October 8, 2001, President-elect Arnold Rüütel took the oath of office before the Riigikogu. Rüütel was 73 when he became president.

In his address to the Riigikogu, he said Estonia needed to restore broad-based social dialogue as a prerequisite for understanding different interests and, in turn, identifying common interests amid those differences.

"Our fundamental problem is a lack of trust and responsibility. All of us need to think about this, at both the local and national levels of government. The president's first task should therefore be to consult not only with the prime minister but with the heads of all constitutional institutions," Rüütel said.

He added that representatives of local governments at all levels needed to be brought together to strengthen regional policy.

Arnold Rüütel taking the presidential oath of office. Source: ERR archival footage screenshot

World.title: Work ability appeals fall as success rate climbs, data shows
World.content:
The number of appeals against work ability assessment decisions has steadily declined over the years, Minister of Economic Affairs Erkki Keldo (Reform) wrote in a letter to an MP.

Keldo was responding to Center Party MP Aleksandr Tšaplõgin and noted while the number of successful appeals has remained more or less unchanged, the share of successful appeals has gone up at the same time the total number of appeals has declined.

In 2023, 17.5 percent of appeals were upheld, compared with 23.1 percent in 2025. Last year, 2,564 work ability assessment decisions — or 5.8 percent of all work ability decisions — were challenged, while 577 of those appeals were upheld.

In the bulk (89 percent) of successful appeals, the reason was new information about the individual's health that had been submitted or emerged during the appeal process. In the remaining 11 percent of cases, the existing data was assessed on a different basis.

The number of court disputes has remained stable, with 51 work ability assessment decisions reaching the courts in 2023, and 48 in 2025.

According to the ministry, the decline in challenged decisions has been aided by continuous quality control of work ability assessments, improvements to guidelines and better-quality health data. A change in the outcome of a work ability assessment does not necessarily mean there is an error in the system, as a person's health may improve or deteriorate over time.

Last year, the work ability assessment remained unchanged in about 72 percent of reassessments. In 17 percent of cases, work ability was assessed as lower than previously, meaning the person's health had deteriorated. In 12 percent of cases, work ability was assessed as having improved.

There were 1,234 cases in which a person previously assessed as having no work ability was assessed as in fact having partial work ability upon reassessment. In 140 cases, people previously assessed as having no work ability were found upon reassessment not to have a reduced work ability.

The number of people with reduced work ability may be partly affected by hazards arising from the working environment, which in turn can reduce life expectancy and can reduced the number of years being employed while in good health. A safe and health-preserving working environment must support the maintenance of work ability and help prevent its decline, it was found.

World.title: Isamaa MP confirms deliberately not backing Ülle Madise nomination
World.content:
Isamaa MP Helir-Valdor Seeder said he deliberately withheld his signature supporting Ülle Madise's recent presidential nomination, rejecting claims it was a technical error.

Speaking on Vikerraadio's "Reporteritund" Thursday, Seeder said he had no technical trouble using the system.

"It's downright defamation to suggest I'm so incompetent that I couldn't find the right button," he continued. "Pass that message along to the prime minister so he doesn't spread rumors at his press conference."

Seeder was one of three MPs from parties backing Madise that did not sign Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise's nomination for president.

"Presidential candidates can't be nominated by parties, parliamentary groups or committees either," he added. "Only by individual MPs."

He also declined to say how he will vote in the presidential election in the Riigikogu, citing the Constitution's requirement that MPs vote individually and secretly.

Seeder also noted that he was following the same principles of independence and impartiality that Madise herself has emphasized.

MP Peeter Ernits (Center). Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

"It's a secret ballot, so I won't disclose how I'll be voting," he emphasized. "You won't find out afterward either."

'I'll be there'

Conservative People's Party of Estonia (EKRE) MP Rain Epler argued that Estonia should consider direct presidential elections, saying a president elected by a large popular mandate would likely receive greater political attention.

"Of course, then people would say, as [Madise] also said yesterday, that the president's powers would need to be changed then," Epler noted.

"I wouldn't say that's imperative," he continued. "If a president is elected by the people with significant support, politicians across the board would pay closer attention to what the president does."

Center MP Peeter Ernits, meanwhile, said he plans to attend the presidential election next Wednesday, despite signals that some Center lawmakers may stay away.

"I'll be there," Ernits confirmed. "Of course we'll be there. Just because someone says something, doesn't mean everyone should take it at face value. No one can stop me [from voting]."

World.title: Gallery: Estonia's timber Nature House taking shape on Tallinn waterfront
World.content:
The glass and timber Nature House complex is nearing completion in Põhja-Tallinn, the future home of the Estonian Museum of Natural History and state environmental agencies.

Called Taru, short for tark ruum, or "smart space," the 24,600-square-meter complex located next door to the Seaplane Harbor includes an office building and a party underground museum space, anchored by a main building with arched glass facades and a roof of shipbuilding-inspired criss-crossing glued laminated timber beams.

Once completed, it will become Estonia's largest wooden building, with extensive timber used in its structures, facades and interiors.

The main building will also house a waterfront cafe and event spaces, while its lobby, unlike the complex office building, will remain open to the public.

TaRu, Estonia's timber Nature House complex, is taking shape in Põhja-Tallinn. August 2026. Source: Mait Ots/ERR

Although construction is due to finish in November, installing museum exhibits will take at least another year, pushing the Museum of Natural History's expected opening at its new location to late next year.

The Nature House site will also incorporate landscaped plots representing Estonia's various natural environments, with further greenery to be incorporated into the main building's lobby and museum exterior.

The design is based on Estonian architecture firm Kavakava's winning entry in a 2019 international design competition. Nordecon is building the complex under a €54.4 million contract, excluding VAT.
