World.title: Kazakhstan Seeks to Expand Non-Commodity Exports to South Korea Through Direct Business Ties
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan is seeking to turn growing trade with South Korea into broader opportunities for domestic producers, with more than 200 representatives of businesses and government agencies from the two countries gathering in Almaty on Aug. 27 for a Kazakhstan-Korea Business Forum and business mission organized with the Korea Importers Association (KOIMA).

The forum focuses on a practical question facing Kazakhstan’s export strategy: how to move beyond traditional commodity exports and secure a larger share of the Korean market for agricultural, food, industrial and other higher-value products.

The event brought together nearly 100 representatives from the Korean side, including importers and business leaders, alongside Kazakh producers and government and industry representatives. The program included presentations of Kazakhstan’s export potential and one-on-one B2B meetings between pre-selected Kazakh exporters and Korean importers.

From trade growth to export diversification

According to the Ministry of Trade and Integration, Kazakhstan and South Korea have maintained expanding economic ties, with bilateral trade reaching $3.17 billion in 2025, up 1.4% from the previous year. In January-June 2026, trade reached $1.3 billion, while Kazakhstan’s exports to South Korea increased 17.2% to $510 million, according to Vice Minister of Trade and Integration Aidar Abildabekov.

While Kazakhstan’s exports remain concentrated in commodities such as oil, ferroalloys and titanium, the government is seeking to expand the range of products reaching the Korean market.

“We are interested in further expanding and diversifying mutual trade, and also in ensuring that business interaction between our countries increasingly results in concrete commercial agreements, sustainable supplies and long-term partnerships,” Abildabekov said.

Kazakhstan’s participation in the Korea Import Expo in Seoul in June provided an initial platform for presenting domestic products. Fifteen Kazakh food and agricultural companies participated, showcasing beef, flour, pasta, confectionery, dairy products, camel milk powder, flaxseed oil, snacks and beverages.

The latest forum brings that effort closer to the commercial stage by putting producers directly in front of potential buyers.

Why the Korean market matters

For Kazakhstan, South Korea represents not only a large consumer market but also an opportunity to diversify the geographic and product structure of its exports in East Asia. KOIMA Chairwoman Yoon Young Mi said Korean importers are actively looking for new and reliable suppliers, creating opportunities for Kazakhstan to expand exports beyond raw materials.

“Kazakhstan has not only abundant natural resources, but is also an important economic and logistics hub connecting Europe and Asia,” Yoon said.

She highlighted Kazakhstan’s energy, industrial and critical-mineral resources, as well as its agricultural and food industries, as areas that could help South Korea diversify and strengthen its supply chains.

“We see significant potential for expanding imports from Kazakhstan. This is not limited to raw materials and natural resources, but also includes agricultural and food products and other competitive goods,” she said.

The statement points to a potentially broader role for Kazakhstan in South Korean supply chains, provided domestic companies can meet the market’s technical, certification and quality requirements.

Direct negotiations aim to close the gap

The forum’s B2B meetings were structured around specific matches between Kazakh exporters and Korean importers, allowing participants to discuss product ranges, potential volumes, commercial terms, certification and the steps required to enter the Korean market.

This approach is intended to address one of the persistent challenges of export promotion: generating not only interest in Kazakh products, but actual commercial transactions.

Abildabekov emphasized that understanding technical requirements before products are shipped is essential to reducing additional costs and barriers for exporters.

“Our task is for the Kazakh producer to understand these requirements even before production and shipment of the export batch, which will help minimize technical barriers and additional costs for businesses,” he said.

He said cooperation among QazTrade, KOIMA and KazStandard could help create detailed “maps” of technical requirements for priority products, covering standards, testing, certification, labeling, packaging and documentation.

The Aug. 27 forum is part of a broader sequence of trade-promotion activities. QazTrade and KOIMA have already established contacts through the Korea Import Expo, while a Kazakhstan trade and economic mission to South Korea is planned for Sept. 14-16.

World.title: Samruk Kazyna Posts Strong Financial Results, Increases Support for Domestic Producers
World.content:
ASTANA – Samruk Kazyna Sovereign Wealth Fund reported financial results above its targets for the first seven months of 2026, while increasing procurement from domestic producers as the fund seeks to strengthen the role of local companies in its supply chains.

Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov chaired a meeting of the Samruk Kazyna Board of Directors on Aug. 27, where members reviewed the fund’s operational and financial performance, support for domestic manufacturers and the implementation of investment and innovation projects.

Financial performance exceeds targets

Samruk Kazyna generated 12.5 trillion tenge (US$27.24 billion) in revenue in January-July, 5% above its target, according to its Chairman Nurlan Zhakupov.

EBITDA exceeded 3.4 trillion tenge (US$7.41 billion), coming in 7% above plan, while net profit surpassed 1.2 trillion tenge (US$2.62 billion), 4% higher than the target.

The results indicate that the fund’s major portfolio companies have maintained stronger-than-expected financial performance despite differences across sectors.

For Samruk Kazyna, however, financial returns represent only part of its role in the economy. As the holding company overseeing major state-linked enterprises, its procurement and investment decisions can also influence the development of domestic production and industrial capacity.

Domestic procurement rises

One of the key areas discussed at the meeting was support for Kazakh producers through procurement by companies within the Samruk Kazyna Group. Since the beginning of the year, contracts worth 694 billion tenge (US$1.51 billion) have been signed with domestic producers, a 32% increase compared with the same period of 2025.

The procurement system currently includes more than 16 measures designed to support local manufacturers. These include preferential treatment for Kazakh-made goods, long-term contracts, mandatory 30% advance payments and accelerated payment mechanisms.

The fund also signed 52.8 billion tenge (US$115.1 million) in offtake contracts during January-July.

Science and innovation remain part of the strategy

The fund’s research and development portfolio currently includes 55 research and development projects worth 13.9 billion tenge (US$30.3 million), seven of which have already been completed.

Following the meeting, Bektenov instructed the relevant bodies to ensure the timely implementation of investment projects and further improve procurement processes across the Samruk Kazyna Group.

World.title: Key Appointments, New Government: What Comes After Kazakhstan’s Kurultai Vote
World.content:
ASTANA – With Kazakhstan’s first Kurultai election concluded and the new unicameral Parliament set to convene for its inaugural session tomorrow, attention now turns to the institutional changes and key appointments that will shape the next phase of the country’s political transition.

The Kurultai, named after gatherings when Turkic and Mongol tribes used to make major decisions, will have its first session on Aug. 28. As in every other year, the first session is opened and chaired by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev.

“The political and institutional steps are clearly set out in law. The next stage will begin with the opening of Kurultai’s inaugural session, where the newly elected deputies will take the oath of office,” Zhandos Aktayev, chairman of the Esti Bol Qory public foundation and doctor in law, told The Astana Times.

The inaugural session will formally activate the political system established under the country’s new Constitution that took effect July 1. The Central Election Commission registered the 145 members of Kurultai on Aug. 27.

Deputies will take their oaths, elect Kurultai’s leadership and begin a process that will include the formation of a new government, the appointment of a vice president and the establishment of the People’s Council.

Under the new Constitution, the 145-seat Kurultai serves as Kazakhstan’s sole legislative chamber, where members serve a five year term. It passes laws, approves the president’s nominees for vice president and prime minister, oversees the government and national budget, authorizes certain senior judicial and state appointments, and decides on matters including war, peace, referendums and presidential elections. It may also hold government members to account and pass a vote of no confidence in the government.

“The election of the new Kurultai marks a continuation of Kazakhstan’s political reforms, meaning its decisions and use of its newly defined powers will face close scrutiny. The members of this first convocation will be remembered for their role in shaping a new political culture and advancing public policymaking in Kazakhstan,” Aktayev said.

Under the Constitution, Kurultai’s first order of business will be to elect its chair from among the 145 deputies. The President nominates a candidate, who must be fluent in Kazakh and secure an absolute majority in a secret ballot. Once elected, the chair will nominate three deputy chairs, who must also be approved by a majority of all Kurultai members.

Aktayev said the first session of Kurultai will be followed by the formation of the Kazakhstan People’s Council, a new supreme constitutional advisory body that replaced the Assembly of the People of Kazakhstan.

“The council will have the authority to submit legislation to the Kurultai, initiate national referendums and serve as a platform for dialogue between the state and civil society,” he added.

The opening of the first session will also set the government formation process in motion. The government has to resign its powers before the new chamber. The President will submit a nominee for prime minister following consultations with the political party factions represented in the Kurultai.

The legislature will also participate in the selection of members of the government, although its role in that process is consultative. The prime minister presents prospective ministers to the relevant permanent committees before submitting their names to the President. Each committee will issue a conclusion on the nominee, but its recommendation will not be legally binding.

Despite being a new institution, experts say the Kurultai will not begin with a blank legislative agenda.

“Although the Kurultai is a new institution, it will inherit legislation left unfinished by the previous Parliament, giving deputies an immediate and substantial workload,” said Aktayev.

“I expect its initial focus to be on lawmaking and improving the regulatory framework rather than public-facing activities. The country has shifted to a unicameral legislature and a proportional electoral system based on a single nationwide constituency, and the new chamber will still need to establish an effective working rhythm within this redesigned institutional framework,” he said.

“It would also be reasonable to expect elections to local representative bodies, known as maslikhats, to complete the transition to the new system and renew elected representation at every level. Such elections, however, can take place only if the President dissolves the current maslikhats after consulting the prime minister and the chair of the Kurultai,” Aktayev said.

The composition of the government will offer another measure of the transition’s scope. It will show whether the constitutional changes bring significant personnel and policy renewal or largely preserve the existing governing structure. Early appointments point to continuity in several key state institutions. On Aug. 24, Tokayev reappointed Timur Suleimenov as National Bank governor, Yermek Sagimbayev as National Security Committee chairman, Dmitry Malakhov as head of the Supreme Judicial Council and Artur Lastayev as commissioner for human rights. All four already held those positions.

The reappointments suggest that the constitutional transition will not necessarily produce a broad turnover across the state apparatus. Tokayev, however, has said changes are expected but described reshuffles as a way to give the cabinet fresh momentum rather than an exercise in dismissals.

The President also nominates the vice president, which is subject to Kurultai’s approval. The appointment must be made within two months of the inaugural session. The choice of vice president, a new office established under the Constitution, carries longer-term significance because the office is situated immediately below the presidency in the revised hierarchy. It does not necessarily mean a successor, but under the law the officeholder immediately takes on presidential powers in case the President dies, leaves office or is unable to exercise duties.

Experts will also be watching how the seats are allocated given the scale of Adilet’s victory. According to the CEC, Adilet will have 110 seats in Kurultai followed by Auyl with 10. Respublica will have nine seats, while the National Social Democratic Party and Aq Jol each will have eight.

“The President has repeatedly stressed that the public expects to see a new generation of younger professionals in Kurultai. I do not think the parties will disregard that message,” he added.

Adilet, a pro-presidential party, secured 71.17% of the vote, according to final results, giving it an overwhelming majority in the new legislature. The outcome has also raised questions about political competition. Although Adilet is a newly established party, its platform closely reflects Tokayev’s political agenda. Party chairman Aibek Dadebai, a former head of the presidential administration, has described Adilet as a “political pillar” of Tokayev’s strategic course.

A large majority could allow Adilet to advance legislation quickly and provide the political stability needed to implement the new constitutional framework. At the same time, the scale of its victory increases the party’s responsibility to demonstrate that the Kurultai can scrutinize government policy rather than merely ratify executive decisions.

The inaugural session will put Kazakhstan’s new constitutional model into practice, but institutional redesign alone does not guarantee political change. Whether it can exercise meaningful oversight and permit genuine debate or whether it becomes a more efficient vehicle for implementing decisions made by the executive remains to be seen.

World.title: Kazakhstan Expands Air Connectivity as New Routes, Digital Border Controls Reshape Travel
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is expanding its international air connectivity while investing in digital technologies designed to make border and aviation services faster, signaling a broader effort to strengthen the country’s position as a regional transport and travel hub.

The latest measures range from a significant increase in permitted flights between Kazakhstan and Saudi Arabia to the expansion of biometric border-control systems and the use of data analytics to assess the commercial potential of new air routes.

Kazakhstan and Saudi Arabia expand flight opportunities

Kazakhstan and Saudi Arabia signed an air services agreement on Aug. 26 in Riyadh, creating additional opportunities for regular air connectivity between the two countries. The agreement was signed by Deputy Minister of Transport Talgat Lastayev and Acting President of the General Authority of Civil Aviation of Saudi Arabia Suleiman bin Ahmed Al-Bassam.

Under the new arrangements, the number of permitted regular flights between the countries will increase from 28 to 70 per week. The expansion is expected to support trade and business ties, investment and tourism, while providing airlines with greater flexibility to develop new routes.

Air carriers are planning to launch direct regular flights between Astana and Riyadh and increase the number of connections with other Saudi Arabian cities.

Data-driven approach to developing routes

The expansion of air connectivity is also being supported by new analytical tools developed in Kazakhstan. Echelon Alpha, in cooperation with the Ministry of Transport, has developed a digital platform designed to optimize civil aviation route networks and assess the commercial viability of flights.

The system analyzes demand on different routes, forecasts transit potential and models possible future route networks. According to Echelon Alpha founder Rakhman Asambayev, the system was built using around 170 reports from airlines and data covering 200 million flights over the past five years.

“For building the analytical model of air connectivity, around 170 airline reports and a dataset covering 200 million flights over the past five years were processed,” Asambayev said.

The platform also takes into account regional macroeconomic indicators, population, consumer preferences, business activity and major events.

“It operates exclusively on the basis of open and commercial sources, as well as geomarketing data, ensuring forecasting accuracy of up to 90%,” he said.

The technology could help airlines and authorities make route-development decisions based not only on existing passenger flows but also on projected demand and the potential of cities to serve as transit points.

Digital border controls expand

Around 200 additional Q-Gate biometric terminals are also planned to be installed at Kazakhstan’s border checkpoints by 2028, expanding the use of a domestically developed automated passport-control system. The terminals, developed by Kazdream Special Systems, are already operating at 11 checkpoints, including the international airports of Astana and Almaty. A total of 54 terminals have been installed so far.

The system verifies a passenger using facial biometrics and passport data, with the process taking between 15 and 50 seconds.

According to Kazdream Special Systems CEO Duman Sembayev, the technology can significantly increase passenger-processing capacity without requiring an expansion of physical infrastructure.

“The terminal enables citizens aged 16 and over to cross the state border without contact and without having to approach a border service officer. Passport and facial biometric verification takes 15 seconds, increasing checkpoint capacity sixfold without expanding its physical infrastructure,” Sembayev said.

The company estimates that processing a flight carrying 200 passengers manually takes around 30 minutes, while Q-Gate can process the same aircraft in approximately seven minutes.

Another 198 terminals are expected to be installed by 2028. Work is also underway on algorithms for automated contactless processing of foreign citizens. A pilot project is additionally testing the possibility of crossing the border using a QR code generated through eGov instead of presenting a physical passport.

World.title: Adventure Tourism and Global Events Can Put Kazakhstan at Central Asia’s Tourism Center
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan is positioning tourism as more than a source of visitor spending, seeking to build a regional hub that connects adventure travel, international events and global tourism markets. Recent cooperation with international tourism organizations and the growing number of major events hosted by Astana and Almaty point to an emerging strategy: turn Kazakhstan’s geography, infrastructure and natural landscapes into a competitive tourism ecosystem for Central Asia.

The latest developments come as Kazakhstan seeks to attract international expertise, strengthen tourism products and establish direct links with foreign travel businesses. The country’s efforts range from cooperation with the Adventure Travel Trade Association (ATTA) to hosting major international sporting events and bringing German tourism industry representatives to Kazakhstan and more.

From natural potential to international tourism product

Kazakhstan has many of the ingredients required for adventure tourism: large mountain areas, the Caspian coastline, steppe landscapes, canyons and diverse cultural heritage. But natural attractions alone do not make a country a successful international destination. The challenge is turning these assets into products that international travelers and tour operators can easily access, book and trust.

This is where the partnership with ATTA could become significant. During an Aug. 26 meeting in Astana, Vice Minister of Tourism and Sports Miras Tulebayev and ATTA CEO Shannon Stowell discussed international assessment of Kazakhstan’s tourism potential, guide training, safety standards and sustainable tourism.

“Today, tourists are increasingly looking for unique experiences: nature, culture and active routes. Kazakhstan has enormous potential for this. Cooperation with ATTA will allow us to build this work systematically – from training guides to cooperation with foreign partners,” Tulebayev said.

A memorandum signed between Kazakh Tourism and ATTA provides for expert assessments of regional tourism potential, professional training and familiarization tours for foreign partners. The sides will also explore the possibility of holding major ATTA events in Kazakhstan.

ATTA estimates that the global outbound adventure travel market reached $1.16 trillion in 2024, while 67% of international travelers are considered open to adventures – potentially interested in travel combining nature, culture and active experiences.

For Kazakhstan, capturing even a small share of this market could create demand in regions beyond the traditional tourism centers. But doing so will require reliable transport, accommodation, trained guides, safety standards and products that can be integrated into international travel itineraries.

International events can create another gateway

Tourism development is also linked to Kazakhstan’s ambitions to host major international events. Astana and Almaty are scheduled to host a series of international sporting and industry events this autumn, including world championships, international competitions and meetings of the World Anti-Doping Agency’s governing bodies.

“Autumn will see Kazakhstan host competitions in a wide range of sports – from the President’s Cup and world championships to finals of major international series,” Minister of Tourism and Sports Yerbol Myrzabossynov said.

He stressed that the value of such events should extend beyond the competitions themselves.

“For us, it is important that each such event leaves a practical legacy: gives Kazakh athletes the opportunity to compete at home against the strongest opponents, improves the qualifications of specialists, contributes to infrastructure development and promotes event tourism,” he said.

The country plans to host around 20 major international competitions at world and continental level in 2026. Astana is expected to host six world championships and the 51st UEFA Congress in 2027.

The economic significance goes beyond ticket sales. International events bring athletes, officials, fans and media, generating demand for hotels, restaurants, transportation and other services. They can also provide international exposure for a destination that might otherwise struggle to reach foreign audiences.

Germany offers a test of Kazakhstan’s tourism ambitions

Astana hosted the DRV Destination Forum 2026 on Aug. 26, bringing nearly 130 participants to Kazakhstan, including 69 representatives of German tour operators, travel agencies, industry associations and specialized media.

“Germany is one of Kazakhstan’s strategically important tourism markets. We are seeing sustained growth in tourist flows and are interested in further expanding practical cooperation with the German tourism business,” Tulebayev said.

“Our task is to move from general promotion of Kazakhstan to the joint development and promotion of specific tourism products, the development of B2B ties and the formation of long-term partnerships between companies from the two countries,” he added.

DRV represents more than 3,000 German tourism companies, accounting for about 90% of organized tourist trips in Germany. According to DRV estimates, such initiatives could increase German tourist arrivals to Kazakhstan by 25% next year, followed by further annual growth.

Adventure tourism requires internationally recognized safety practices and qualified guides. Remote destinations need roads, accommodation and emergency services. International events require hotels, transportation capacity and venues. And foreign tour operators need predictable logistics and commercially viable tourism packages.

The recent agreements suggest that Kazakhstan is beginning to address these elements simultaneously rather than treating tourism promotion as a standalone task.

World.title: Experts: Political Trust Sets Stage for Next Phase of Kazakhstan-Singapore Partnership
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Singapore need to translate strong political ties and mutual trust into tangible economic outcomes, including more investment, joint projects and technology exchange, as cooperation expands into transport, artificial intelligence, digitalization and other strategic sectors, according to experts.

“The key now is to translate the excellent political relationship and mutual trust between our countries into tangible economic outcomes – more Singaporean investment and companies in Kazakhstan, more joint projects, greater technology and knowledge exchange, and stronger connections between our business communities and people,” Honorary Consul of Singapore in Kazakhstan Talgat Chinikeyev told The Astana Times.

Singapore Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong’s Aug. 26 visit to Kazakhstan highlighted the growing scope of bilateral cooperation, with discussions covering investment, transport and logistics, aviation, smart city development, agriculture, critical minerals, tourism, water management, AI and digitalization.

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev highlighted Singapore’s transformation into a global center of finance, trade, innovation and technology.

“Your country’s experience serves as an inspiring example for the international community,” Tokayev told Lee.

Tokayev noted that bilateral relations are developing dynamically, supported by regular political dialogue, growing trade and an accelerated inflow of Singaporean capital.

“In fact, Kazakhstan and Singapore remain each other’s largest trading partners in their respective regions – Central Asia and Southeast Asia. The number of companies with Singaporean capital operating in our country has reached nearly 500 and continues to grow,” he said.

Bilateral trade approached $1 billion last year, while trade reached $777 million in January-June, up 2.5 times from the same period last year. Singapore’s gross foreign direct investment inflows into Kazakhstan doubled in 2025 to approximately $1.5 billion.

Lee said the relationship had reached “a qualitatively new level,” noting growing interest among Kazakh companies in entering the Singapore market. He welcomed the ratification of the Agreement on the Reciprocal Promotion and Protection of Investments and the Agreement on Trade in Services and Investment.

“Our relationship has significant potential to move forward,” Lee said.

Investment and regional connectivity

For Aidar Kurmashev, head of the Asian Studies Department at the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies under the President of Kazakhstan (KazISS), Singapore’s strategic value lies in combining investment and technology with access to Southeast Asia.

“I would not separate Singapore’s role as a source of investment and technology from its role as a ‘bridge’ to Southeast Asia. Its strategic value for Kazakhstan lies precisely in combining these functions,” he told The Astana Times.

Kurmashev said Singapore’s strengths in finance, logistics, technology and corporate governance could help Kazakh projects gain access to capital, modern standards and regional business networks.

He identified the Middle Corridor as one of the most substantive areas of cooperation. A joint venture between PSA International and Kazakhstan Temir Zholy has already moved cooperation to practical route management. During the visit, the two countries also signed an agreement to develop the Middle Corridor.

The next stage, Kurmashev said, should focus on predictable delivery times, digital documentation, cargo tracking, integrated logistics solutions and links with port networks in Asia and Europe.

Aviation and digitalization

Aviation is another area where Kazakhstan plans to draw on Singaporean expertise.

Tokayev said Kazakhstan intends to build a new modern airport in Astana and highlighted Singapore’s Changi Airport as the “gold standard” of global aviation.

“We intend to draw on this experience in implementing the new project and take bilateral cooperation in the aviation sector to a new level,” Tokayev said.

Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov earlier met with Changi Airport Group CEO Yam Kum Weng to discuss Astana’s airport infrastructure, including plans to build a second airport. Yam confirmed the group’s readiness to provide expertise and experience.

AI and digitalization also featured prominently in the visit. Tokayev proposed expanding cooperation in these areas, noting Kazakhstan’s establishment of the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development and its declaration of 2026 as the Year of Digitalization and Artificial Intelligence.

Lee visited Alem.ai, which Chinikeyev described as a promising new dimension of practical cooperation.

“Singapore has extensive experience in digitalization, innovation and technology, while Kazakhstan has made AI and digital development important national priorities,” he said.

Potential areas include cooperation among technology companies, start-ups, universities and specialists, as well as AI, GovTech and cybersecurity.

Expanding practical cooperation

The two countries are also exploring smart city development, water management, agriculture, critical minerals and tourism.

Kurmashev identified Alatau City as a potential project for Singaporean expertise in urban planning, digital city management, utilities, private investment and international business infrastructure.

An agreement on water management provides for experience exchange, professional development of Kazakh specialists and modern approaches to managing water resources.

Both experts emphasized that the next stage should focus on practical results rather than simply exchanging experience.

For Chinikeyev, Kazakhstan and Singapore can also serve as gateways to their respective regions: Singapore for Kazakh companies seeking Southeast Asian and ASEAN markets, and Kazakhstan for Singaporean businesses entering Central Asia.

The visit therefore underscored a partnership with significant potential in investment, connectivity, technology and human capital. The challenge now is to turn the strong political relationship into concrete projects and deeper economic links between the two countries.

World.title: Kazakhstan Makes 50 Government Services Available Through eGov GPT
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has made 50 government services available through eGov GPT, allowing citizens to access them through a chat-based interface without visiting a Public Service Center (PSC), First Vice Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Rostislav Konyashkin said on Aug. 26.

The service was presented during the unveiling of the Action Plan to implement Kazakhstan’s Digital Qazaqstan strategy at the Alem.ai International Center for Artificial Intelligence, Kazinform reported.

“Recently, we launched eGov GPT, through which 50 government services can already be obtained simply in a chat format,” Konyashkin said.

Government services move to chat format

The new service lets users request government services through a conversational interface. Citizens can describe the service they need and continue the process through a chat, similar to interacting with AI assistants.

“If you use ChatGPT or other agents, you can simply communicate with it in the same way and receive government services,” Konyashkin said.

The development is part of a broader effort to shift government services away from traditional in-person interactions and toward digital and proactive delivery. This shift is already reflected in the declining number of visits to PSCs. In the first half of 2026, citizen visits to PSCs fell by 30% compared with the same period in 2025.

“We have been actively working on the top 10 government services, which account for 79–80% of all traffic from our citizens,” Konyashkin said.

The ministry plans to expand the range of services available digitally. At least another 150 government services are expected to be launched through eGov GPT by the end of 2026. More than 20,000 services had already been delivered through the new format at the time of the earlier announcement.

AI increasingly used inside government

AI use is also expanding within government agencies, where it is being applied to process documents and large volumes of information. Konyashkin said government employees cannot use AI models that process data on servers located outside Kazakhstan. To support secure processing of government information, Kazakhstan has launched a supercomputer that allows AI tools to work with official data within the country.

“Now we can safely process official correspondence and documents. Already, artificial intelligence helps create summaries of letters, analyse large volumes of requests, prepare reports and presentations, and provide translation,” Konyashkin said.

Konyashkin compared the current transition to AI with the earlier adoption of digital documents and services, which initially faced uncertainty among citizens but eventually became part of everyday digital life.

“When we first launched this, people also had doubts and wondered how to use it,” he said, referring to digital services. The government subsequently integrated some services into banking and mobile applications because citizens already use those platforms regularly.

“We are looking for the simplest way to reach our citizens and show them new opportunities through the ecosystems and mechanisms that are already available to them,” Konyashkin said.

World.title: Resources Are Not Enough: How Energy Routes Are Becoming Geopolitical Battleground in Eurasia
World.content:
ASTANA — For decades, the geopolitics of energy was largely understood through a familiar map of resource abundance: the Persian Gulf held vast oil and gas reserves, Russia was a major supplier to Europe, and countries such as Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan were important producers whose influence depended largely on how much they could extract and sell. But as wars, sanctions and geopolitical competition increasingly disrupt established trade routes, that logic is changing.

The strategic value of an energy resource is no longer determined only by what lies beneath the ground, but increasingly by whether it can reach international markets, through which route and with how many alternatives if that route is disrupted.

For oil and gas producers in Central Asia, the answer has become increasingly consequential. Kazakhstan remains heavily dependent on routes that cross Russian territory, Turkmenistan has enormous gas reserves but limited export options, and Uzbekistan is looking increasingly southward toward Afghanistan as it seeks additional connections to international markets. At the same time, China is building multiple routes into Eurasia as it seeks to reduce its exposure to maritime chokepoints and dependence on any single corridor.

When energy routes become strategic assets

Abzal Narymbetov, an oil and gas industry expert, framed the broader issue through the structure of global energy markets. While the United States and China dominate many categories of energy production, countries with large exportable surpluses are more narrowly concentrated, particularly in the Middle East, where reserves are vast relative to population and domestic consumption.

“The Middle East is the only region that can actually supply oil and gas to growing China and India’s needs,” Narymbetov said, noting that the central vulnerability lies in the routes through which those supplies move. For him, the Strait of Hormuz is the clearest example of how geography can turn an energy question into a strategic one.

“When you have a bottleneck like the Hormuz, then you will have the next road is only the inland,” he added.

The point is not that continental routes can replace maritime energy flows. They cannot, at least not on the same scale. Rather, the geopolitical value of inland routes rises when maritime routes become vulnerable, and that is precisely why China’s expanding network of pipelines and rail connections across the Eurasian landmass matters. Narymbetov said that China has little choice but to develop those alternatives because its energy needs cannot simply be reduced by changing transport patterns.

“China needs to develop inland routes, because there is no way that you will replace the oil and gas consumption that China now needs,” he said.

That logic places Central Asia in a strategically different position from the one it occupied when energy was discussed primarily in terms of exports and revenues. Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan are no longer simply producers supplying global demand; their infrastructure and geographic location are becoming part of a wider effort to make energy systems less vulnerable to geopolitical disruption.

Why Turkmenistan is suddenly at the center of the map

This is particularly evident in the case of Turkmenistan, which was repeatedly described during the discussion as an underappreciated energy power. The country possesses one of the world’s largest gas reserves, but its strategic significance comes from more than the size of its resource base. Turkmenistan sits between China, Iran, the Caspian Sea and the broader South Asian space, making it a potential junction for several competing east-west and north-south routes.

Ken Moriyasu, senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, referred to a discussion with a former U.S. administration official where he illustrated the point with a simple “tic-tac-toe” diagram, placing Turkmenistan in the middle of the map to show how several potential routes from China to the Caspian Sea converge around the country.

“So Turkmenistan is the key,” he said, recounting the logic behind the map.

The claim is deliberately stark, but it captures a broader shift in the way the country is viewed. But the question surrounding Turkmenistan is not simply how much gas it has, but how many viable ways it eventually has to move that gas. That question also explains why Uzbekistan’s interest in Afghanistan has become increasingly important. Moriyasu said one of the biggest takeaways from his meetings in the region was “how much the Uzbekistan leaders were talking about the importance about Afghanistan.” For Central Asian states, he said, Iran has historically offered one of the shortest routes to international waters, but political uncertainty and sanctions have made long-term infrastructure planning through Iran more difficult.

“I think there’s a collective souring of sentiment towards Iran because of the situation now,” Moriyasu said, noting that Central Asian governments may be increasingly unwilling to wait for a stable and business-friendly environment in Tehran before developing their external connectivity. His assessment of the emerging hierarchy of routes was blunt. “Right now I think Middle Corridor, then Afghanistan, and then the China Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), and then Iran is plan four.”

Read that as Moriyasu’s interpretation rather than a formal regional strategy, but it captures an important trend: Central Asian governments are seeking redundancy. Uzbekistan in particular has promoted the idea of Afghanistan as a potential connector between Central Asia and Pakistani ports, even while facing serious security, political and water-management concerns related to its southern neighbor.

The contradiction is striking. Afghanistan could provide Uzbekistan and other Central Asian states with a route to the Indian Ocean that bypasses some existing constraints, while developments such as the Qosh Tepa Canal simultaneously create new concerns for downstream countries dependent on the Amu Darya. Yet the prospect of Afghanistan becoming part of a broader regional transport architecture appears increasingly difficult for Central Asian governments to ignore.

From new corridors to new vulnerabilities

For China, these developments matter for a related reason: diversification. Moriyasu said Beijing does not want to become overly dependent on Kazakhstan because existing overland routes are concentrated there.

“China doesn’t want to be too dependent on Kazakhstan because, as I said, everything goes through Kazakhstan right now,” he said.

The China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway is therefore significant not simply as another transport project, but as part of a broader effort to create additional options. One possible route would connect onward towards Turkmenistan and Iran; another, under much more demanding political and security conditions, could eventually connect China through Central Asia and Afghanistan to Pakistan. The strategic logic is not necessarily to replace Kazakhstan, Iran or maritime trade, but to ensure that no single route becomes indispensable.

That same logic is increasingly visible in Kazakhstan’s own energy vulnerabilities. For Kazakhstan, the CPC is the clearest example of how a commercial asset can become a geopolitical fault line. The CPC is critical to Kazakhstan’s oil exports, yet the infrastructure runs through Russian territory before reaching global markets, meaning disruptions caused by the war in Ukraine can affect Kazakhstan even though it is not a party to the conflict. Moriyasu said repeated Ukrainian attacks on CPC-related infrastructure reflect what he sees as a broader shift in Kyiv’s strategy.

“The whole purpose of the strikes on the CPC facilities is to internationalize the competition,” he said, noting that the objective is to make other stakeholders, including Kazakhstan, Japan and buyers of Kazakh oil, feel pressure to intervene and, from the Ukrainian perspective, increase pressure on Russia to move toward a ceasefire.

That interpretation is Moriyasu’s assessment rather than an established explanation of Ukrainian policy, and it is precisely because of that distinction that the CPC issue deserves attention. Whatever the stated rationale behind individual strikes, once infrastructure carrying Kazakh oil becomes entangled with another country’s military calculations, the consequences extend well beyond the battlefield.

Kazakhstan’s strategic problem is therefore not simply that its oil exports depend on a particular pipeline. It is that the pipeline connects multiple political and commercial interests, including Kazakhstan, Russia, international oil companies and foreign buyers, meaning that an attack on infrastructure can produce economic and diplomatic consequences across a much wider geography.

Moriyasu interpreted President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s engagement with Putin in Omsk through that lens, saying that Kazakhstan increasingly understands the changing character of the risk.

“The real threat he feels is the Ukrainian strategy,” he said.

That conclusion should again be treated as an expert assessment rather than a definitive explanation of Kazakhstan’s policy. Astana has its own reasons for maintaining high-level dialogue with Moscow, just as it has reasons to preserve relations with Ukraine, China, Europe and the U.S. But the CPC shows why the space to separate economics from geopolitics is becoming increasingly narrow. Kazakhstan’s oil exports remain economically essential, but the infrastructure connecting them to world markets can become exposed to a war in which the country has no direct military role. The larger lesson is that Eurasia’s energy map is being redrawn not necessarily because the location of resources has changed, but because the political meaning of the routes around them has.

For decades, energy security was largely discussed in terms of reserves, production and price. Increasingly, it is also about redundancy, chokepoints and political risk. In that sense, Central Asia’s strategic importance is growing for reasons that go beyond the size of its reserves. And resources are no longer enough. The decisive question is increasingly who can move them, through which route, under whose protection and with what alternatives when those routes are disrupted. Across Eurasia, pipelines and ports are no longer merely infrastructure. They are becoming bargaining chips, strategic assets and, in some cases, potential targets, making the geography of energy inseparable from the region’s geopolitics.

World.title: Why is Russian tourist boom in Abkhazia giving way to falling demand? Video from Pitsunda
World.content:
Russian tourists in Abkhazia

Pitsunda is perhaps the most popular tourist destination in Abkhazia. The town receives around 20–25% of all incoming tourist traffic, thanks to the high-rise Pitsunda Resort complex and its private accommodation sector.

The overwhelming majority of tourists visiting Abkhazia come from Russia, meaning the success or failure of the tourist season largely depends on the situation there.

Even before international sanctions were imposed on Russia following the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, Abkhazia received around 1.2–1.5 million tourists per season, with Pitsunda already operating at the limits of its ageing accommodation capacity.

At the time, Abkhazia was marketed as a budget alternative to neighbouring Russia’s Sochi. Infrastructure problems — including water and electricity shortages and ageing utility networks — existed even then, but were viewed more tolerantly because of the low cost of holidays.

After the start of the war in Ukraine, Abkhazia saw an unprecedented influx of Russian tourists. A record 1.88 million people visited in 2025.

Demand increased as many countries introduced restrictions affecting Russian citizens.

But since the start of the 2026 season, demand for holidays in Abkhazia has fallen noticeably, by 15–20%.

Experts cite several main reasons:

Increased competition. Inflation has pushed prices in Abkhazia to levels comparable with holidays in Turkey, Egypt and cheaper European destinations.

Legal and logistical barriers. In particular, border-crossing rules for children under 14 are creating significant difficulties.

● Infrastructure problems, including electricity and water outages at the height of the tourist season.

● Price dumping by major Russian tour operators, which is driving small local businesses out of the market.

● The threat to Pitsunda’s relict pine grove from uncontrolled construction.

● A general mismatch between the quality of service provided and the prices being charged.

What Abkhazia’s tourism market looks like

The private sector and guest houses account for 65–70% of the market, including small hotels, flats in apartment blocks and private homes in the villages of Ldzaa and Alahadzy. Most tourists choose these types of accommodation.

Large hotels, boarding houses and Soviet-era resorts, including the high-rise buildings of the Pitsunda Resort complex, as well as sanatoriums and newer mid-sized hotels, account for 30–35% of the market. However, they attract the lion’s share of the most lucrative tourists — those who book organised tours and package holidays.

Positive developments over the past couple of years include the partial modernisation of old Soviet-era resort buildings, the opening of modern boutique hotels in Ldzaa and the digitalisation of services, with a shift towards online booking and cashless payments.

Private accommodation sector reluctant to pay taxes

The main economic problem is that an estimated 60–70% of private accommodation providers have operated in the shadow economy for years, without paying full taxes into the local budget.

In recent years, the authorities have sought to tighten oversight by introducing a patent-based tax system for the self-employed and mandatory classification of accommodation providers. However, these measures have been slow to take hold.
