World.title: Australians endure anxious wait for news on loved ones after Nepal floods
World.content:
The family of a Newcastle woman have made an impassioned plea for information, after losing contact with her on the border of Nepal and Tibet prior to deadly floods.

The family of Reshma Patel boarded a plane on Friday morning headed to Nepal intent on joining the search effort to find her.

Nepal flash floods updates: Follow this story as it unfolds with our live blog.

Family friend Chin Valsan said in a Facebook post the 46-year-old from Rankin Park near Newcastle was last seen at border immigration building about 10 minutes before the flood.

"Since then, family and friends have been unable to reach her and are deeply concerned for her safety and wellbeing," Mr Valsan said.

"If anyone has seen Reshma, has travelled with her, has information about her whereabouts, or has any contacts with local authorities, hospitals, rescue teams, tour operators, or pilgrimage groups in the region, please contact the family immediately or notify the nearest police authority."

Ms Patel is one of 39 Australians confirmed missing following deadly floods in Nepal and Tibet which have killed at least 392 people.

Like many of the missing Australians Ms Patel was on a pilgrimage, taking the trip of a lifetime to one of the world's most sacred regions: the Langtang Valley.

Each year, the valley sees thousands of visitors arrive to take part in a sacred Hindu pilgrimage, with the region also sacred to Buddhists and Jains.

Reshma Patel was in one of three pilgrimage groups linked to the spiritual organisation Isha Foundation that are now missing, with the flood hitting as they participated in the Kailash Sojourn pilgrimage.

Overcome with emotion following the tragedy, the founder of the spiritual group Sadhguru reported 80 people were missing, 11 of them Australian.

Spiritual leader Sadhguru says several groups on a pilgrimage remain missing following the accident. (YouTube: Sadhguru)

'Entire group' in building destroyed by flood

Ms Patel's family said her last known contact was at an immigration checkpoint on Nepal-Tibet border, which Sadhguru said had been totally destroyed by flood.

"At 9.05am [a guide] sent a message that they have arrived at the immigration, so after that, this happened at 9.14am," he said, fighting back tears.

" Literally the entire group was there in the building. "

Queensland woman Kanagamah Sundrasan is one of the Australian pilgrims now missing, with the flood hitting during her planned trip to Mount Kailash.

Her daughter Swaatika Kanniah said her mother was due to arrive the day after the flood hit.

"According to her itinerary, [Thursday] was supposed to be the day she was getting there, basically," Ms Kanniah said.

"It's a very sacred spot, so it was one of her dreams to fulfil."

Queensland woman Kanagamah Sundrasan was on a pilgrimage in the region when the flood hit. (Supplied)

The mother of two owns a business with her husband in Queensland and last spoke to her family on Tuesday.

"It's been a bit worrying because we haven't been able to contact her yet. It's been really hard to grab a hold of anyone who has any information," Ms Kanniah said.

"We really want her to come back home and we miss her a lot."

Ms Kanniah said her mum was "very giving" and "the kindest woman ever".

"She doesn't really go on trips like this. That's why it was very exciting for her to travel and do this thing that she always wanted to do," she said.

Himalayan tour group still not accounted for

Search-and-rescue efforts are continuing in the region, with tour group operators still waiting on fresh information about tour groups they have lost contact with.

US-based tour group operator Himalayan Glacier said the company has lost contact with a missing group in the region that includes 15 Australians.

"We had a group of 47 including our guides who went missing around 8.30am local time in Nepal," Himalayan Glacier managing director Sanket Pandey told ABC News Breakfast.

" Currently, we are waiting on any news from the new round of search-and-rescues. "

He said new lists of those found are expected to be released by Nepali authorities later on Friday morning.

A family of four from Cherrybrook in Sydney’s north-west has also been identified as being among the missing Australians in the Himalayan Glacier tour group.

Sreedharan and Lakshmi Iyer and their sons Rishab, 23 and Rudhra, 20, were travelling in the region when the flood hit.

The Iyer family were on a Himalaya Glacier tour. (Supplied)

Family friends have told the ABC both sons are currently studying medicine, with Rishab in his last year at the University of Newcastle and Rudhra studying at the University of Western Sydney. Sreedharan Iyer works in finance and co-owns a childcare centre in Riverstone in Sydney's north-west with his wife Lakshmi, who is known to some friends as Roopa.

Venkatraman Balakrishnan, 52, and his wife Chitra Venkatraman, 46, from Western Sydney, were also taking part in a Himalayan Glacier tour when the natural disaster struck.

The couple's son told the ABC he last spoke to his parents when they were approximately 15 kilometres from the Tibet border.

He said he had not heard from them since, but he held out hope the entire tour group would be found safe.

"I'd like to see my parents and everyone who went with them back in one piece, and that everyone else there is as safe as possible," he said.

Chitra Venkatraman and Venkatraman Balakrishnan are still missing after floods in Nepal. (ABC News/Supplied)

Australian-Nepali communities feel absence of family members

The absence of the 39 people still missing has been deeply felt in Australia's Nepali diaspora, with communities in capital cities gathering together at vigils as they await further news.

Floodwaters ravaged the countryside near Nepal's Langtang Valley on Wednesday, taking with it much of the crucial infrastructure of the region including roads, internet and telecommunications access.

It has created a void of information for families back in Australia, who say they have been left following the sparse updates posted from the country on social media.

Keshav Kandel, vice president of Melbourne's Australian Nepalese Multicultural Centre, said the traumatic images being shared online were only compounding the anxiety for the community.

"The posts of the video on the social media, the photos and videos that have been circulating, they're quite devastating and they makes us really, really not well," he said.

A community in Diggers Rest in Melbourne's north-west gathered for a vigil on Thursday, praying together for victims of deadly floods in Nepal. (ABC News)

Mr Kandel spoke at a vigil held on Thursday night, with dozens of community members attending the multicultural centre in Melbourne's north-west to pray.

"We are praying for the people who are still looking for help and praying for those families who are suffering," he said.

"Today's session is mainly for us to get together as a community together and show the solidarity for the people of Nepal."

If you want to help support the thousands affected by the crisis, the ABC is supporting the Emergency Action Alliance member charities and their local partners. You can find more information here.

World.title: Breaking: 'Psychological risk': Australian scientists to abandon remote island over bird flu fears
World.content:
The Australian Antarctic Division will launch a mission to extract personnel from Macquarie Island in the Southern Ocean due to the psychological risk posed by a potential outbreak of bird flu.

The sub-Antarctic island, 1,500 kilometres south-east of Hobart, is a World Heritage-listed wildlife sanctuary with up to 4 million seabirds and 100,000 seals.

The island is currently free of the deadly H5 strain of bird flu.

But once it arrives, up to 90 per cent of baby elephant seals could perish, as happened on Heard Island over summer, when 13,000 pups died from bird flu.

The Australian government says exposing expeditioners to such harrowing scenes is untenable.

The station is right in the middle of a population of southern elephant seals. (Supplied: AAD)

"We've come to this really difficult decision of withdrawing staff," federal environment department deputy secretary Sean Sullivan told the ABC.

"And that's being done primarily for the psychological risks that will be facing staff if they are there for extended periods of time inside a mass mortality event."

Australia's research station on Macquarie Island is located within metres of a 2,500-strong colony of elephant seals.

There is a colony of about 2,500 seals on the island. (Supplied: AAD/Jarrod Hodgson)

Mr Sullivan said it would be highly distressing for expeditioners to endure a prolonged wildlife mass mortality event on their doorstep in the event of an outbreak.

"There would be thousands of deaths," he said.

"You can imagine the impacts that would have in terms of being restricted to base.

"Obviously the distress of being around a mass mortality event, as well as impacts with respect to air quality, as you can imagine, that would have long-term impacts on staff."

Expeditioners work and live next to seals and other wildlife on the island. (Supplied: AAD/Kerry Steinberner)

Icebreaker to be deployed for retrieval mission

The station is currently home to 24 expeditioners, who began what was expected to be a year-long deployment in May.

Instead, they will now be extracted in just over a month, shortly before the peak of the seal breeding season, when experts warn a major mortality event is most likely to occur.

The Nuyina will visit Macquarie Island in October to extract the expeditioners. (Supplied: AAD Simon Payne)

"I'm sure [staff] will be disappointed," Mr Sullivan said.

"It's a special place and … people are coming into summer where a lot more work can be done and so there will be great disappointment from staff."

Australia's icebreaker RSV Nuyina, which is currently in Singapore for routine maintenance, is expected to arrive at the island in early October to retrieve the team.

"It is unprecedented and we are in unprecedented times," Mr Sullivan said.

"We're making this decision primarily because staff are our number one priority."

Extracting staff from the island in October will also remove the risk of having to mount an evacuation during the busy summer season, when the Nuyina is scheduled to resupply bases in Antarctica.

"We have a window of opportunity where we'll minimise the impacts on our broader season plan," Mr Sullivan said.

There is a limited window for the Nuyina to conduct the mission without impacting other Antarctic work. (AAD)

Australia's Antarctic stations not affected

It remains unclear when expeditioners will be able to return to Macquarie Island.

But over the next month, plans will be developed to set up live camera feeds and drones to allow staff in Australia to monitor for any signs of bird flu once personnel leave.

"The Australian Antarctic Division is exploring options for monitoring the situation on Macquarie Island, with a view to returning expeditioners to the station in coming seasons," Mr Sullivan said.

" We remain committed to maintaining a long-term presence on Macquarie Island. "

The island is also home to gentoo penguins. (Supplied: Jason Munday/AAD)

Mr Sullivan said Australia's three stations on the Antarctic continent did not pose the same level of risk, and there were no plans to extract personnel from those bases.

"Macquarie Island is unique," Mr Sullivan said.

"The station is inside a seal colony, and so the implications are direct — they're on the front door.

"That's not the case with the other Antarctic stations."

Withdrawal to delay $370m station rebuild

Australia has had a permanent, year-round presence on Macquarie Island since 1948.

Multiple agencies utilise facilities at the research station, including the Bureau of Meteorology, Geoscience Australia and the Tasmania Parks and Wildlife Service.

The deaths of seals and other wildlife on the doorsteps of expeditioners would be harrowing and cause hazards, Mr Sullivan said. (Supplied: AAD)

The Australian Radiation Protection and Nuclear Safety Agency (ARPANSA) also conducts monitoring in support of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty.

"The Australian Antarctic Division is currently working through steps to mitigate impacts for our international monitoring obligations, wildlife monitoring and infrastructure, and to best prepare the station for temporary closure," the AAD said in a statement.

The Australian government is currently in the process of modernising the outdated facilities on the island.

About $370 million has been allocated over nine years for a new station that won't be subject to the risks of ocean inundation or landslips caused by earthquakes.

"The government's made a significant decision to rebuild Macquarie Island," Mr Sullivan said.

"This will have implications for that in terms of slowing that down, but this hasn't changed the government's decision to rebuild Macquarie Island."

World.title: Iran becomes 'war of attrition' where peace prospects are 'bleak'
World.content:
Shortly after declaring war on Iran six months ago, US President Donald Trump said the operation would take four weeks or less.

"We took a little excursion … to get rid of some evil. I think you'll see it's going to be a short-term excursion," he said in an interview days after launching Operation Epic Fury.

Half a year and a failed ceasefire later, experts and former US government officials say both sides are locked in a stalemate, with prospects for peace "bleak".

The US announced a shift in strategy this week, from a military onslaught to an economic one. Rather than bombing Iran, the White House announced an "economic D-Day" where it would sanction countries that do business with Iran instead.

What is the new US plan for Iran? The US threatens to target the economies of countries that cooperate with Iran in what it calls an "economic onslaught" against the Iranian regime.

Meanwhile, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian this week declared "the entire world approved our victory and the [US] is hated".

Experts say there is a way out of the war, but it will not be easy. Both sides will need to make concessions they do not want to make, yet neither side believes the cost for peace is currently worth paying.

"The conflict is settling into a war of attrition and prospects for a negotiated settlement are bleak," Allison Minor, who served as the director for Arabian Peninsula affairs on the National Security Council during Mr Trump's first administration, told the ABC over email.

"Both sides seem to think that time is on their side and that they will be able to secure better terms as the other side is worn down by economic and political pressure."

Lessons from a failed ceasefire

On June 18, the US and Iran sparked hope when they announced they had signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU). The deal, in short, was to stop fighting for 60 days while they hashed out a permanent peace plan.

But optimism about the war ending quickly dissipated.

Days later, Mr Trump threatened to "blow the shit" out of Iran if it did not keep the Strait of Hormuz open. Iran, after signing the MOU, struck ships that did not follow its approved route through the waterway.

By July 8, Mr Trump had declared the ceasefire "over".

Loading...

The failed deal holds lessons for future peace talks, experts say, including that Iran should not be underestimated.

"The Iranians are infamous for being really, really good negotiators and for understanding that, most of the time, they can outlast their opponent," Emily Harding, who served as the Iran director on the National Security Council during the last Bush administration, told the ABC.

" I'm not sure the Trump administration took that warning seriously enough. "

Another lesson is that any future peace deal needs clear terms and mechanisms for enforcing it.

Experts said the MOU was too vague, giving Iran the belief it could control the strait while Washington argued it must reopen to unhindered shipping.

"Both sides demonstrated that they were willing to enforce those positions," said Ms Minor, who is now director of the Atlantic Council's Project for Middle East Integration.

The viral moment Iran left the room In June, high-level peace talks hit an early snag when one of the Iranian representatives abruptly left the room while the Americans were taking their seats.

The ambiguity meant the agreement was doomed to fail. Since then, mediators have continued trying to push talks forward, but experts said securing a deal could be challenging.

Both sides believe, rightly or wrongly, they have the upper hand, meaning mediators have a difficult task ahead, says Naysan Rafati, the senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group.

"The Americans feel that the economic sanctions will continue to bite, that they have a military option if need be. The Iranians are thinking that the Trump administration faces midterms and wants an exit sooner rather than later," he told the ABC.

"I think that when you have two sides that both think they have the upper hand … it really is an uphill battle to get kind of diplomacy at the forefront, even though the attempts continue."

Carrots, sticks and difficult negotiations

Merely getting back to the negotiating table would require both sides to make concessions, said Elizabeth Dent, a US foreign and defence policy expert at the Washington Institute who previously served in several roles at the Pentagon.

"I don't expect that to happen until Trump's new economic strategy has had some time to play out or both sides conclude that continued escalation is less helpful than compliance," she told the ABC over email.

And then, if the US and Iran do get back to direct talks, there are more difficult decisions to be made.

Iranian authorities have erected giant anti-US billboards across Tehran. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

Ms Harding, now an intelligence expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said one option still available to the US involved "classic diplomacy: carrots and sticks". But, she warned, it is a difficult needle to thread.

The "sticks" must be credible enough that Iran would fear them. The US has been sanctioning Iran for decades, so "it's a hard sell" to convince the regime more sanctions would hurt, Ms Harding said.

"I think you make some very explicit threats about what your next military targets are if you're going back to fighting," she added.

The other difficulty is the "carrots" Iran would want from the US — such as the unfreezing of assets and help building critical infrastructure — are things the Trump administration does not want to give.

Ms Minor, who has helped negotiate peace agreements in her career, said successful negotiations depended on two things: one is that "both sides must believe that they will be better off under a negotiated settlement" and the other is that "for an agreement to hold, it must be constructed and implemented in a manner that holds both sides accountable to their commitments".

"Neither of these conditions appears to have been met in the Iran context," she added.

Could the 'economic squeeze' work?

There have been fears the Iran war could become another "forever war".

But experts said the fact the US had ruled out putting troops on the ground, as well as Mr Trump's unwillingness to get involved in other countries' affairs long-term, meant it was unlikely.

"Would it be a forever war like Afghanistan or Iraq where we have US troops on the ground for decades? No, I can't see that happening," Ms Harding said.

"Could it be a forever war when you see occasional exchanges of fire, especially between Israel and Iran? I could see that."

A billboard in Iran depicts Donald Trump lying in a coffin. (Reuters: Majid Asgaripour/WANA)

The Trump administration has many reasons to try to end the war, chief among them the upcoming midterm elections. The Iran war is, as Ms Harding puts it, a "loser of an issue for them politically".

But the US also feels pressure not to walk away until it has either inflicted more damage on Tehran or sorted the Strait of Hormuz issue.

Iran, however, in many experts' view, currently has the upper hand. It has demonstrated it can use the strait to wreak havoc on both the US and the world — a trump card it will not want to give up — and is not facing enough pressure to make concessions in peace negotiations. Yet.

Despite Trump's threats, Iran is 'at war with its own people' Three Iranians have shared their insights on life under the regime, as the war passes its fifth month.

While Iran has shown it can deal with hardship, several experts said Mr Trump's "economic onslaught" could apply the pressure that was needed.

"The economic squeeze is one that I think is quite real on the Iranian system," Mr Rafati said.

"The question is whether it's matched towards some kind of diplomatic offering that they would be willing to accept, or whether the US conditions of collapse or capitulation are something that just makes them double down on their attempt at perseverance."

Its effectiveness could also depend on whether Iran's government, and not just its people, feels the pain.

As Ms Dent said: "Iran values survival of the regime above all and will likely accept severe hardship if its leadership, fractured as they may be, believe surrender would threaten that."

Additional reporting by Brad Ryan

World.title: The secret of Wests Tigers remarkable NRLW rebirth
World.content:
Traditionally, Wests Tigers have found wins hard to come by in the NRLW.

The joint venture has endured difficult times since it entered the competition three years ago.

Before this season they'd won just five of their 29 matches and never more than two in a single campaign.

They entered 2026 on the back of consecutive wooden spoons and most pundits predicted more of the same.

But Craig Sandercock's side has emerged as the success story of the season, winning six of eight matches thus far — more than they've won in the rest of their existence combined — to sit third on the ladder with three rounds remaining.

Only Brisbane and the Sydney Roosters, the two premiership favourites, have managed to lower their colours, and their most recent win, a one-point triumph over Newcastle courtesy of a last-minute field goal in an instant classic, showed just how far they've come.

According to backrower Shaylee Bent, who joined the club this season from Gold Coast, losing such games used to be a Tigers trademark.

"I'll be honest, they'd finished bottom of the table two years in a row and from playing them they could be in the fight but they'd always lose late," she said.

"They never had the experience to win the moments that really count.

"The girls who have been here in the past, they have all the potential in the world but now they have those experienced players around them they can do what they're best at.

"That clarity lets them be good at what they're good at."

Bent is playing some of the best football of her career at the Tigers. (Getty Images: Ian Hitchcock)

Bent is one of those experienced players, having played in three grand finals and for New South Wales and Australia during her career.

Along with fellow recruits such as halfback Raecene McGregor and lock forward Holli Wheeler, she's helped spearhead a turnaround that has the Tigers on the brink of their first ever NRLW finals series.

In doing so, Bent is playing the best football of her life — better than anything she produced on the more star-studded rosters she enjoyed at St George Illawarra and Gold Coast when she was a New South Wales and Jillaroos regular.

She's scored as many tries this season as in her last four years combined and is putting up career highs for run metres per game, tackles per game, line breaks and tackle busts.

Bent says she's taken it on herself to be a leader for the young Tigers side and the responsibility clearly agrees with her.

"I'm proud of myself for getting involved more. When I've been on good teams with good players around me I've let them take the hard runs, take the runs to win the game and things like that," she said.

"But I've found what works for me here.

"I'm in a team where I don't have all those names around me. I have to be a leader and I'm loving it. I love being that energy bunny and hopefully there's a ripple effect."

The addition of Bent and Wheeler, who Bent cites as one of the greatest influences on the team's all-effort mentality, has rounded out a strong pack that includes wrecking machine Sarah Togatuki and ageless wonder Kezie Apps.

Apart from former Dally M winner and three-time NRLW champion McGregor, the rest of the roster is filled mainly with up-and-comers who went through those hard times and are now daring to dream of something greater.

"They might not have the experience of players like Kezie, but they aspire to be like her and we're still growing together," Bent said.

"We have so much young depth and in the years to come they're going to be where we are.

"Sandy isn't just prepping them to play for one week. He's developing them."

The Tigers are fixing to be a club that relies on local juniors, but that development isn't restricted to youngsters.

Caitlin Turnbull is one of Wests Tigers biggest success stories. (Getty Images: Brett Hemmings )

Caitlin Turnbull, who made her NRLW debut last year at 25, has experienced another strong season at fullback, and rugby union convert Faythe Manera is enjoying success as a backline utility in her first season in league as the club's equal-top scorer.

But the greatest challenges, for them and the rest of the side, are still to come.

A win over Canterbury this weekend will lock up a finals berth, but they'll face Gold Coast — who seem the team most likely to break the Roosters and Broncos hegemony — and fellow finals aspirants Canberra to round out the regular season.

Bent's top-level experience will prove vital for a club who is experiencing the heady glories of premiership contention for the first time.

"Some of these girls haven't had a taste of that before. I might have taken it for granted in the past but for these girls it's so massive," Bent said.

"I'm so grateful to be here at the Tigers, because we can be a part of history."

World.title: Before and after: Nepal-Tibet's flood destruction
World.content:
High-resolution satellite imagery has confirmed structures and settlements that had been in the destructive path of a mass of glacial water during the Nepal-Tibet floods have been wiped off the map.

The flash flooding has killed at least 392 people, and hundreds are still missing, including at least 39 Australians.

Nepal flash floods updates: Follow this story as it unfolds with our live blog.

River levels rose by up to nine metres in just 30 minutes, catching people by surprise and causing widespread destruction.

This high-quality satellite imagery has been captured by commercial satellite provider Vantor.

It shows the Rasuwagadhi border point between Nepal and Tibet. The large multi-storey building and surrounding infrastructure have been completely destroyed.

Before: Between Nepal and Tibet on April 19, 2024. . . After: August 27, 2026. (Vantor) . . Instructions: Use left and right arrow keys to control image transition Before and after images SLIDE Between Nepal and Tibet on April 19, 2024. / August 27, 2026. (Vantor)

In imagery captured in April 2024, the border point can be seen, along with several large buildings, a basketball court, and other structures.

The image from after the flash flood shows almost all of the structures are gone. It appears the area has been reduced to bedrock.

Loading...

Giant glacial avalanche buries Nepal villages Climate scientists have been warning that the Himalayas are warming faster than the rest of the world, increasing the chances of a disaster of this scale.

This is the same part of the Himalayan mountain range that was captured in horrific CCTV footage showing the moment the wall of water hit.

Simon Gascoin, a researcher from the Center for Spatial Studies of the Biosphere, noted in a post online that Sentinel-2 satellite imagery showed the flood had impacted the area with such force that it surged up the sloping terrain for at least 2.5 kilometres.

The disaster is believed to have been triggered when part of a Himalayan glacier broke off and crashed into the river below.

Further downstream, the low-lying areas of the village of Syapru Besi have been swept away, leaving mud and debris.

Before: Syapri Besi on October 18, 2023. . . After: August 27, 2026. (Vantor) . . Instructions: Use left and right arrow keys to control image transition Before and after images SLIDE Syapri Besi on October 18, 2023. / August 27, 2026. (Vantor)

The first image was captured in October 2023, and the second in the aftermath of this natural disaster.

Some homes on the road down to the valley have not been impacted. Those closer to the water did not stand a chance against its force.

Accessing this area to look for survivors is difficult because so much of the infrastructure has now been destroyed.

Near Syapru Besi, a bridge that crossed the Trishuli River was visible in satellite imagery from 2023.

Before: The Trishuli Bridge on October 18, 2023. . . After: August 27, 2026. (Vantor) . . Instructions: Use left and right arrow keys to control image transition Before and after images SLIDE The Trishuli Bridge on October 18, 2023. / August 27, 2026. (Vantor)

It is now gone, along with all the structures and some vegetation around it.

The same happened to many other bridges in the area, with video capturing this bridge further down the valley in the town of Trishuli being swept away by a torrent of water.

World.title: Labor, Coalition and One Nation fight among themselves on migration
World.content:
The Coalition has joined Labor and One Nation to wrestle with itself over migration policy, as the three parties grapple with the realities of determining which communities and industries will lose out from attempts to cut immigration.

After tripping up Labor and One Nation earlier this week, division has now also emerged inside Angus Taylor's Coalition leadership team on whether to reduce the number of refugees granted humanitarian visas if the party was to win government.

Mr Taylor this morning opened the door to cuts to the refugee intake, just a day after a senior member of his party said it would not be touched.

"When we see what housing construction looks like, we will announce the [net overseas migration] number and the visa classes will align with that. What is clear though is we are a very generous country, but charity starts at home, and we have got to do the right thing by Australians first," Mr Taylor told News24.

That contrasts with comments yesterday by Shadow Housing Minister Andrew Bragg that "refugees will not be the target of [the Coalition's] migration policy".

"The migration policy that we will resolve in due course will be focused on the other cohorts … We have been a proud nation that has housed millions of refugees since the Second World War, and I think it's important we maintain that status, and I just don't think it's refugees that are the problem here," Senator Bragg said.

Andrew Bragg said humanitarian visas would not be the target of the Coalition's migration cuts. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Shadow Foreign Minister Ted O'Brien told ABC Radio National "nobody is actually a target" of the Coalition's migration policy.

"When it comes to the numbers of different categories, they will be announced closer to the next election," Mr O'Brien said.

Refugee visa reduction killed off

The debate follows Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's decision to kill off a plan to reduce the humanitarian visa intake from 20,000 places a year to 13,750 by allowing a temporary four-year increase to expire at the next federal budget.

Yesterday morning, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke's office confirmed a decision had been taken to reduce the humanitarian visa program, angering left-faction Labor members who felt too much ground had been ceded on asylum seekers and refugees.

By the afternoon, Mr Albanese had intervened to say the humanitarian visa would be kept at 20,000 places.

Mr O'Brien said Mr Burke had been overruled twice in recent weeks on immigration by the prime minister, and said Mr Albanese's intervention was contrary to forecasts in May's budget.

"That will be up for the prime minister, the treasurer and the home affairs minister to explain why they seem to be at odds," Mr O'Brien told ABC Radio National.

Anthony Albanese confirmed the government would not reduce humanitarian visa places. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Frontbencher Mark Butler denied the decision was a backflip.

"It has to go through the usual process of budget renewal, but there's been no change for a number of years in the Australian Labor Party position on the humanitarian intake," he told Channel Seven.

Greens senator David Shoebridge said the government had clearly reversed course.

"Minister Burke wouldn't have presented those savage cuts unless he'd been through a process. And then it's turned on its head by the prime minister in less than 24 hours," Senator Shoebridge told ABC Radio National.

What is NOM? What exactly is Net overseas migration, what kind of factors cause it to fluctuate, and where do the political parties stand?

Meanwhile, Pauline Hanson is still cleaning up comments made by junior MP David Farley suggesting One Nation's migration plans would bring about as many immigrants to Australia as Labor, and its actual annual intake would be well above 130,000, and "at minimum" 230,000.

Senator Hanson said yesterday the party's net migration target was 130,000, but she also conceded the actual rate was above that because it did not account for some Pacific worker visas, which One Nation would keep.

The One Nation leader defended the party's position to keep the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) visa places, about half of which are not officially counted in the net migration target.

"As I have always said, PALM workers are the visa holders that can come into the country," Senator Hanson said.

"Rural and regional Australia would die if they didn't have the workers coming in, especially the abattoirs and farmers, so that's a different program. These people are given accommodation by the farming sector."

She said Mr Farley "didn't understand" and had "got confused" about Pacific worker visas.

David Farley told ABC Insiders the party's policy position would set net migration "at minimum" above 230,000, but was later corrected. (ABC News: Tobias Hunt)

Mr Taylor seized on her remarks, saying Senator Hanson had "three policies in three minutes".

Migration debate makes mess for Hanson, Albanese and Taylor alike

The federal government, opposition and One Nation have all snagged on the reality of where to find cuts to Australia's migration program, with reductions to any visa class deeply unpopular among at least one community or industry.

Business groups have warned changes to skilled migration could exacerbate worker shortages, and farmers have warned not to slash their workforce by cutting working holiday-maker visas or PALM visas.

Universities say cutting international student visas would devastate the sector and dry up a pipeline of skilled workers. And there are few gains to be made by cutting family visas, where there is already a massive backlog of demand.

One Nation has said it intends to cut student and temporary graduate visas, though it has not specified by what amount, while the Coalition says it will tie its migration targets to housing completions, though it has not explained which visa classes would be cut to reach those targets.

The home affairs minister had planned to detail the government's migration changes at a National Press Club address several weeks ago, but it was postponed, and a final position has been settled.

Alongside the decision to retain 20,000 humanitarian visa places, Mr Albanese also closed the door this week on a proposal to require British backpackers to work on farms, which would have reduced demand for the working holiday-maker program.

With migration a driving concern of voters, and a major force behind One Nation's rise in popularity, all three parties have confirmed they are determined to slash the migration program, even if none can spell out exactly how they will get there.

World.title: Police say woman assaulted in days before death as man charged with murder
World.content:
A 38-year-old man has been charged with the murder of a 28-year-old woman in Perth's south-eastern suburbs.

St John WA paramedics found the woman unresponsive at a home on Taree Street in the suburb of St James on Wednesday night.

Police were called to the scene and the woman was taken to Royal Perth Hospital but was declared dead.

Police have alleged the incident is a case of family and domestic violence. (ABC News: Lauren Smith)

Police have alleged the woman was assaulted by the man in the days prior to her death and had suffered extensive injuries.

They have also alleged it is a case of family and domestic violence.

Homicide Squad detectives spent yesterday investigating what happened at the house and questioning the man in custody.

The St James man is due to appear in the Perth Magistrates Court today.

World.title: 'Life gets dark': Mother running in Sydney Marathon in memory of dad
World.content:
Despite Natasha Littler having run six marathons in Australia, the race this weekend means the most.

She is set to run the 42.2-kilometre Sydney Marathon in memory of her father, Garry Rae, who died by suicide when she was seven.

"It's very hard to remember, but I remember that he was a smart man. He loved playing the good old Minesweeper [video game]. He worked in tech and IT," the 36-year-old said.

Ms Littler's parents divorced when she was three.

"He remarried, but I don't think it was ever the same and then it was just too much, I think. Life just gets dark," she said.

Before that, her father served in the Royal Australian Air Force, which also took its toll on his mental health.

Now, almost 30 years later, the Adelaide-based nurse who has worked with mentally unwell patients, is running to raise funds for Beyond Blue and awareness of mental health.

"I've always known I wanted to be a nurse and I feel like it's because I can help people, which is also going hand-in-hand with running for the charity," she said.

Ms Littler's dad died when she was seven years old. (Supplied)

Ms Littler said more advertising of mental health supports available to men was needed, as well as encouragement for them to speak out.

"Back in those days, people were just staying silent, encouraged to stay silent," she said.

"Whereas now, I feel like people are talking a bit more.

" It's still changing, but hopefully it keeps changing for the better. "

Ms Littler is running to raise funds for Beyond Blue. (Supplied)

According to Beyond Blue, nearly 5 million Australians live with anxiety or depression, and last year more than 300,000 people reached out to the Beyond Blue Support Service.

Ms Littler has so far raised almost $2,500 for her chosen charity.

As per the Sydney Marathon's Grassrootz fundraising page, more than 9,200 fundraisers have contributed over $12.7 million so far of the event's $13 million goal.

Role modelling for the next generation

Ms Littler and her husband caught a flight to Sydney on Thursday and will be sweating alongside their friends during the marathon on Sunday, which starts from 6:15am.

It will be the second year Sydney has been a part of the Abbott World Marathon Majors series, which also hosts events in seven other locations including Tokyo and London.

The Sydney Marathon begins on Sunday from 6:15am. (Supplied: Sydney Running Festival)

More than 40,000 runners and elite wheelchair athletes from across 140 countries will begin the course north of the Sydney Harbour Bridge, make their way through Centennial Park and finish at the Sydney Opera House.

The event is expected to draw 125,000 spectators to the city to watch the charity groups and general runners.

Ms Littler hoped her three kids — 11-year-old Ryan, 10-year-old Caleb and seven-year-old Spencer — would watch the livestream of the marathon with their grandmother back at home.

"They love watching us and getting inspired," she said.

Ms Littler and her husband often go running together with their children. (Supplied)

Ms Littler said she wished to be a role model for her children.

They often participate in 10km races, attend their local Parkrun each week and embark on holidays based around running.

"We've got three boys and in this day and age, well, especially having lost my own dad, we just want to try and promote to them to be healthy and active," she said.

"They see how happy we are running and how we feel fulfilled afterwards, so we hope to pass that on to them rather than the mental health stigma."

Running has become a passion for Ms Littler. (Supplied)

'Testing the limits'

Ms Littler began running shortly after the birth of her second child 10 years ago, before lacing up her shoes for a midnight marathon in 2018.

"It's interesting to see what we're capable of, pushing your body, testing the limits," she said.

" If I'm not having a great day, I'll go for a run and I'll feel better usually afterwards. "

The link between exercise and mental health Experts say there should be more focus on using physical activity, by itself or in combination with other treatments, to treat and prevent depression and anxiety.

She has been busy training for this weekend's event.

"I've been running about five days a week, so a mix of some intervals, some easy runs and then the long run, so I've done a couple of over 30 kilometres," she said.

Ms Littler said she was hoping for a finishing time of less than 4 hours and 30 minutes, well under the 7-hour time limit, while still "remembering that we're doing this for all these people that can't do it".

Transport for NSW said there would be city-wide road closures between 2am and 4.30pm in North Sydney, the Sydney CBD, Pyrmont, Darlinghurst, Moore Park and Kingsford.

Special event clearway parking restrictions will also be in effect, with people encouraged to use public transport.

World.title: Demon’s tough draw and Tiley’s $150 million US Open splash
World.content:
SportTennisUS Open Demon’s tough draw and Tiley’s $150 million US Open splash Marc McGowan August 28, 2026 — 11:40am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Alex de Minaur faces a potentially career-defining fortnight in New York as younger rivals emerge to threaten his top-10 position amid a prolonged form dip. The year’s fourth and final grand slam, the US Open, begins on Sunday night (AEST), with de Minaur again headlining the Australian assault as the No.6 seed in a men’s singles draw so far featuring seven compatriots, while Daria Kasatkina leads the country’s five players in the women’s event. Alex de Minaur has not played at his usual lofty standard in recent months as new rivals emerge. Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press via AP De Minaur starts against a qualifier, but has difficult projected rivals beyond that, including Botic van de Zandschulp (second round), 31st seed Zizou Bergs (third round), No.12 seed Rafael Jodar (fourth round) and top seed Alexander Zverev (quarter-finals). The 27-year-old has advanced to the US Open quarter-finals the past two years – and three times overall – but lost in the third and fourth rounds, respectively, at Roland-Garros and Wimbledon.



Related Article Wimbledon ‘It breaks me inside’: Devastated Demon offers frank admission after Wimbledon exit De Minaur, who married British player Katie Boulter on Wimbledon men’s finals day in July, has also won no more than two matches at any of his three tournaments since leaving London, and his ranking has slipped from a career-best No.5 to 7. That downturn from de Minaur’s typically lofty standards has coincided with hot streaks from rising stars Arthur Fils and Jodar, who are on the verge of making their top-10 debuts. Fils, 22, beat Australia’s seven-time major quarter-finalist in straight sets last week en route to the Cincinnati Masters title, while 20-year-olds Learner Tien and Jakub Mensik are also inside the top 20 and increasingly looming. Jodar, 19, amassed a 10-3 record in the lead-in American hardcourt events, including making the Canadian Masters semi-finals and the Washington Open final. The Spaniard drew Australia’s Thanasi Kokkinakis in the first round.



Related Video Video icon 1:15 Kyrgios tests positive for cocaine The US Open men’s championship race appears to be as open as it has been in years, with Jannik Sinner (knee) withdrawing and defending champion Carlos Alcaraz (wrist) returning for his first event since April. The likes of Roland-Garros titlist Zverev, 24-time grand slam-winning legend Novak Djokovic, Fils, Ben Shelton, Taylor Fritz, Felix Auger-Aliassime, Flavio Cobolli and even Jodar would fancy their chances of lifting the trophy. James Duckworth, Rinky Hijikata, Adam Walton, Aleks Vukic, Alexei Popyrin and wildcard Dane Sweeny are Australia’s other men’s representatives. Hijikata and Duckworth drew seeded rivals Auger-Aliassime and Matteo Arnaldi, respectively. Popyrin reached the last 16 in New York two years ago, but has not won a grand slam match in 2026 and his ranking has plummeted to No.130. He, too, has a qualifier as his first-round opponent.



Joining Kasatkina, who also married her long-time partner Natalia Zabiiako post-Wimbledon, in contesting the women’s singles are Kim Birrell, Talia Gibson, Maya Joint and wildcard Taylah Preston. Kasatkina starts with former top-tenner Paula Badosa, while Gibson drew Olympic silver medallist Donna Vekic and Joint faces Russia’s Liudmila Samsonova, who was ranked in the top 20 as recently as May. Samsonova defeated Joint in three sets in Toronto a fortnight ago. Aryna Sabalenka is clinging to the world No.1 ranking. Getty Images The women’s draw is similarly wide open, particularly with world No.1 Aryna Sabalenka enduring a form slump and Australian Open champion Elena Rybakina dealing with an ankle injury. Resurgent Pole Iga Swiatek, 2023 winner Coco Gauff and 2024 runner-up Jessica Pegula are serious contenders, as are the past two grand slam champions, Mirra Andreeva and Linda Noskova.



Australia’s Chris O’Connell, Tristan Schoolkate and Storm Hunter have advanced to final-round qualifying. Australians’ US Open first-round opponents Men: Alexei Popyrin v Qualifier; WC-Dane Sweeny v Corentin Moutet (France); Thanasi Kokkinakis v 12-Rafael Jodar (Spain); 6-Alex de Minaur v Qualifier; Rinky Hijikata v 3-Felix Auger-Aliassime (Canada); Aleks Vukic v Qualifier; James Duckworth v 30-Matteo Arnaldi (Italy); Adam Walton v Wu Yibing (China). Women: WC-Taylah Preston v Alycia Parks (United States); Kim Birrell v Petra Marcinko (Croatia); Talia Gibson v Donna Vekic (Croatia); Maya Joint v Liudmila Samsonova (Russia); Daria Kasatkina v Paula Badosa (Spain). Another top-100 Aussie Preston has more than halved her ranking this year on the way to becoming the third Australian woman in the past 18 months to make her top-100 debut. The 20-year-old West Australian edged her way to exactly No.100 on Monday, three weeks after capturing the biggest singles title of her life at the Vancouver WTA 125 event.



Preston follows countrywomen Joint, 20, and Gibson, 22, in achieving the ranking milestone, which will guarantee her entry into all four grand slams if she can maintain it. Her rise came narrowly too late for direct US Open entry, but she scored Tennis Australia’s reciprocal wildcard. Taylah Preston made her top-100 debut in the past week. PENNY STEPHENS “It’s an amazing feeling [to be in the top 100],” Preston said. “It’s taken a lot of hard work, a lot of years. But it’s definitely been a goal for a long time now … I’m extremely grateful to be given a chance to compete in the main draw in New York. It means a lot to me.” Tiley makes an instant splash



Former Tennis Australia and Australian Open supremo Craig Tiley is not mucking around in his new role as the United States Tennis Association’s chief executive officer. The US Open will hand over the most prizemoney in tennis history this year, a 20 per cent increase on 12 months ago to a record $US108 million ($150.4 million). For comparison’s sake, the Australian Open’s 2026 prizemoney was $111.5 million. Craig Tiley, third from left, oversaw a huge prizemoney increase for this year’s US Open. Bloomberg Tiley said: “This is a significant first step in a multi-year investment in athletes as the US Open continues to be the best economic opportunity for players and the most valuable platform in tennis for players, fans and partners.” Less popular was the USTA’s decision to initially overlook retiring Swiss great Stan Wawrinka for a wildcard, but he ended up scoring one when American Patrick Kypson withdrew injured.

World.title: These 223 schools harnessed talent for the NRLW. One became a juggernaut
World.content:
SportNRLNRLW 2026 These 223 schools harnessed talent for the NRLW. One became a juggernaut Nick Wright August 28, 2026 — 11:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Nestled in the heart of the Gold Coast, one school has become a powerhouse of women’s rugby league talent production – a juggernaut boasting more NRLW graduates than any other institution in the country. Before the female game received its first national competition in 2018, Keebra Park had built a girls’ sporting excellence academy. Just last year, on the back of the surging popularity of the code, they forged a separate rugby league excellence program, featuring three weekly on-field or gym training sessions, and a classroom session geared towards developing skills for budding athletes to handle the rigours of professional sport. Queensland’s Tiana Raftstrand-Smith is one of the many Keebra Park graduates to go on to play NRLW. Getty Among the mentors for the near 200-strong academy are former rugby sevens and NRLW star Niall Williams Guthrie, brother to cross-code athlete Sonny Bill Williams.



“It’s very much an aspirational sporting pathway, and we’re trying to make sure they’re prepared for that – making sure they’re resilient and have all their life skills outside of footy,” program head James Chapman says. “We want to develop them for the rigours of professional sporting life, but I think the overall lessons of the program are we want to make sure they have a positive experience with rugby league, and want to be a steward of the game and play footy beyond just high school.” Of the 355 players currently named on each NRLW squad’s roster, 19 hail from Keebra Park. Only two other schools – Marsden State High School (12) in Logan and The Hills Sports High School (12) in Seven Hills, Sydney – enter the double digits for NRLW graduates, with academy pathways still developing as the code continues to grow. When asked what had made the program so successful, Chapman says: “It all comes back to the coaching staff. We have an awesome coaching team, collectively, who give up so much time and genuinely do care about the girls.



“Yes, winning is great, and it’d be great to bring back some trophies every year, but I think the level of care they have for the girls and the drive they have to see them improve every day is probably unmatched anywhere in Australia, I’d reckon.” Related Article AFL 2026 ‘Mum lost her soulmate’: The tragic death driving premiership hero’s new mission Several former students have become future leaders of the competition, including Raftstrand-Smith sisters Tiana and Ebony of the North Queensland Cowboys – the former representing the Maroons twice. “Because rugby league was still so new at the time, the girls who separated themselves from the others really liked the contact element – that was Tiana. If you’ve seen any of her games, particularly early on, she loved the physical element,” Chapman says. “A lot of the girls early on were transferring from touch football – highly transferable skills – but just developing confidence in contact has been an evolution in itself. We’re at the point now you could ask a 12-year-old girl ‘how long have you been playing footy?’ and she could say five or six years.



“The game has really changed in such a short space of time.” There are 223 schools represented in the NRLW this season, including 172 with one representative. Teagan Levi celebrates her brilliant try. Matt Roberts/Getty Images. Among those is Miami State High School, where rugby sevens star Teagan Levi was educated. On secondment from Rugby Australia, Levi has gone on to ignite the Titans’ premiership prospects. Once the NRLW season ends, Levi will return to rugby and in preparation for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics, alongside sister Maddison, who in Australia’s 100th rugby union Test made her Wallaroos debut in the 15-a-side code against the Black Ferns.



“I think that [Wallaroos] could have been an opportunity that opened up for me, but I wanted to come home to the Gold Coast Titans,” Teagan says. “[Being a dual-code international] is something we’ve both wanted for quite a while.” Such has been the way she has taken to rugby league, champion NRL halfbacks Andrew Johns and Johnathan Thurston have been awed by her exploits – after she twice showcased a grubber kick ahead for herself to score. Loading “I’m loving the opportunity to learn a different game, each week is a new challenge in itself – learning the different opposition, knowing what’s best to stick away from, so I’m really enjoying the process,” Teagan says. She had no desire to ease into rugby league. When she arrived at the Titans, she had her eyes on the Gold Coast’s five-eighth duties, and consulted former duel-code international Mat Rogers – of whose management agency she is a client – for insight.



“He just said to back yourself and do what you do best, that’s what got you selected to come over to the Titans. The game’s different, so I have to learn the different rules and structures, but [he said] to back your instincts and have a go.” Teagan has scored seven tries, while coming up with five try assists and linebreak assists and averaging 104 running metres a game from eight appearances – which has included the club’s seven-straight wins to surge to second on the ladder, trailing only their round-one conquerors, the Roosters. Loading “I wanted to go in the halves. I thought my skills from sevens would help quite a lot, and I loved the challenge. I wanted to put myself in that position – if I didn’t think I was ready I wouldn’t have put myself forward,” she says. “I did all the hard work before I even came across to league; I was doing Zoom calls, making sure I was catching up, coming home back to the Gold Coast whenever I could to make sure I was putting my best foot forward to make sure the team had trust in me.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: This entire novel is one sentence. Somehow, it works
World.content:
CultureBooksReview This entire novel is one sentence. Somehow, it works Jack Cameron Stanton August 28, 2026 — 11:11am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If awards ceremonies are anything to go by, the one-sentence novel is having a moment. The Norwegian Jon Fosse and Hungarian Laszlo Krasznahorkai, winners of the Nobel Prize for Literature in 2023 and 2025 respectively, see the humble full stop as a needless barrier to be banished from their richly textured and deeply introspective novels. Lucy Ellmann’s Ducks, Newburyport, a Goldsmiths winner and Booker shortlistee, is composed of a single sentence detailing the protagonist’s far-reaching anxieties that persist over a thousand pages, held together with the refrain “the fact that”. These writers are rule breakers. They dispense with full stops, scene breaks, and chapters by using an array of conjunctions and punctuation, both workmanlike and exotic, to keep the damn thing rolling. Each page is a formidable, handsome wall of text. They write the literary equivalents of a horror vacui, a painting afraid of emptiness, a canvas completely covered. At his best trawling through the history books: Adam Ouston.



Despite these books being a single, unbroken sentence, I doubt anyone reads them in one sitting, nor that the authors indeed intend for us to do so. You would need a preternatural concentration or heroic dose of stimulants. Likely both. They offer no restorative pit stops, no spaces to breathe, nowhere obvious to rest a bookmark and take stock of everything that has come before. You must rip yourself away from the currents, forever amid a gathering thought. Editor's pick Literature Sydney Writers’ Festival names new artistic director Once the books get going, however, the effect is a degree of immersion beyond that of conventionally stylised fictions. Sure, they make demands on us, but difficulty (more than idle, easily absorbed fiction) rewards. I find myself switching between two mental states: one of hypervigilance, following every thread, and another that lets the stream of words wash over me. I’m no proselytiser for the one-sentence novel. I trudged through Mathias Enard’s Zone like an explorer with a machete chopping through an overgrown path. I never finished Ducks, Newburyport. And yet, the new novel from Tasmanian writer Adam Ouston has me, if not converted, at least showing up for Sunday service. Ouston’s debut, Waypoints, took as its subject the lesser-known history of Harry Houdini’s first controlled flight, which happened in 1910 in Diggers Rest, Victoria. His latest novel, Mine, also embraces smoke and mirrors, but this time on the level of the sentence.



Mine by Adam Ouston. It begins after a poet falls into an abandoned mineshaft. Injured and trapped in that elemental darkness, the ageing poet reminisces about his campaigns as an ecoactivist while other memories and voices start to intrude, hinting at “something bigger than him, a secret story beneath the apparent one”. Appraising Ouston’s novel by what happens is about as illuminating as recounting Waiting for Godot. Ouston’s single sentence is not the poet’s life flashing before his eyes. It is a broad narrative frame to capture a deeper history. In this sense, the set-up shares more DNA with a poem than a plot-driven novel. We learn that the poet has been exploring the West Coast of Tasmania to research his magnum opus, a collection inspired by hauntology, an attempt to capture the “island’s soul”. A hauntology: the past is a revenant in the present and therefore has not passed at all. At first Ouston allows the hauntology to drift ill-defined, more spirit than flesh, until other stories rise in the poet’s mind. These include most notably the true histories of settler-colonial explorers and mining magnates laying claim to the land, alongside other accounts of exploration paired with environmental extremes, such as the Mawson and Mertz Antarctic expedition in the early 1900s. Dispersed among these are the poet’s own memories of his youthful days of climate action and a tender reflection upon the death and funeral of a dissident journalist friend.



The most vital of these non-fictional strains is Ouston’s lively reconstruction of the ascent and rivalry of two enterprising capitalists, Bowes Kelly and James Crotty, whose legacies culminated in the Mount Lyell Mining and Railway Company. We begin to suspect these historical anecdotes are not arbitrary and may, taken together, begin converging upon this “secret story beneath the apparent one”. Ouston is at his best trawling through the history books. At times Ouston’s descriptions of the Tasmanian landscape reach for the grandeur “of desolation, ferocity, madness, and hopelessness, but also beauty, wisdom, protection and valour, and inspiration”. It’s classic romanticism: grandeur evoked abstractedly. But when he finds an original image – “whenever he heard of the plight of the South Pole he would picture a black rubber mask melting in the middle of an interminable stretch of outback highway, eye sockets collapsing, mouth hole shrivelling as though releasing an unending scream” – it’s magic. Late in Mine, Ouston’s poet arrives at the conclusion that the battle for Tasmania’s environment has been lost. I realised that Ouston has written a dire allegory: an eco-poet howls at the bottom of a mineshaft, where no one can hear him. Mine by Adam Ouston is published by Transit Lounge ($35). World.title: ASX edges higher as tech stocks jump; Virgin surges
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX edges higher as tech stocks jump; Virgin surges Staff writers Updated August 28, 2026 — 11:06am ,first published August 28, 2026 — 5:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket has advanced at the open after a solid night on Wall Street, with stocks jumping as Nvidia, Salesforce and others reported fatter profits than expected. The S&P/ASX 200 was up 19.5 points or 0.2 per cent to 9057.7 in early trade. The ASX lost 1 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was stronger at US71.95¢. Positive results from Nvidia and Salesforce helped allay concerns over AI stocks and drove Wall Street higher. Bloomberg Reporting season is drawing to a close and Virgin Australia surged by 9.5 per cent in early trade as it reported robust results, with underlying pre-tax earnings surging by more than 13 per cent to $753 million. Virgin will pay a dividend of 7.6¢ a share. Retail giant Harvey Norman slid 0.2 per cent as it reported that net profit increased 2 per cent to $528.5 million in the financial year.



Nvidia’s strong results pushed Wall Street’s Nasdaq higher overnight, and the positive sentiment flowed through to local technology stocks, with Xero jumping 5.9 per cent, WiseTech and Technology One each up 3.5 per cent and NEXTDC 3 per cent higher. Mining stocks are mixed with Fortescue up 0.4 per cent, BHP flat and Rio Tinto shedding 1 per cent in early trade. Gold stocks advanced with the price of the precious metal steady near $US4600 an ounce as investors weighed the outlook for US interest rates ahead of a key speech by Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh. Financial stocks are steady with National Australia Bank up 0.1 per cent, Westpac and Commonwealth Bank down 0.1 per cent and ANZ Bank 0.3 per cent lower. Energy stocks are higher with oil prices advancing overnight before steadying in early Asian trade. Woodside and Santos added 1.1 per cent each while refiner Ampol rose 0.9 per cent. Overnight, the S&P 500 rose 0.7 per cent and pulled closer to its all-time high set earlier this month. The Dow Jones added 105 points, or 0.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 1.6 per cent.



On Wall Street, Nvidia was the strongest force pulling the market higher, and the chip giant rallied 8.7 per cent after once again delivering stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. More importantly for Wall Street, it also gave forecasts for coming revenue growth that topped analysts’ estimates, suggesting demand remains strong for chips to power artificial-intelligence projects. “AI has reached its inflection point,” Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang said. “It’s doing useful work. Its tokens are productive and profitable.” Related Article Updated

Earnings season Qantas boss says air traffic delays at Sydney Airport ‘not OK’ That helped calm some of the worries that have built around AI stocks generally, which have been under pressure recently. After rocketing higher for years because of the frenzy around AI, stocks in the industry are confronting scepticism that they shot too high and that booming demand for AI chips may fade if the AI revolution does not produce as much profit as promised. Another big tech company, Salesforce, jumped 22.6 per cent after it said that AI helped it deliver one of its best quarters in history. It reported stronger profit than analysts expected, and chief executive Marc Benioff said it’s “seeing incredible demand for our AI and data products” and that it’s “turning AI into customer success at unprecedented scale”.



Salesforce, which helps companies to manage their customers’ data, also raised its forecast for revenue over the full year and announced an expanded partnership to pair Anthropic’s Claude chatbot with its platform. It’s notable because Salesforce’s stock struggled earlier on worries that competitors powered by AI could ultimately steal away customers from Salesforce and other software companies. Salesforce’s stock had its best day in six years. Elsewhere, though, trends were more mixed across big US companies, and the majority of stocks within the S&P 500 fell. HP sank 2.9 per cent even though it topped analysts’ expectations for profit and revenue in the latest quarter. Analysts pointed to worries about its sales of personal computers, as well as how higher prices for computer memory and other commodities are pressuring its profit margins. Best Buy and some other retailers sank amid continued worries that US shoppers could be stretched because of high inflation and discouragement about the economy. Best Buy fell 4.4 per cent even though it topped analysts’ expectations for both profit and revenue in the latest quarter. One potential winner from high inflation could be dollar stores, which could see higher-income households become new customers as they look for less expensive places to shop.



Dollar General rose 2.5 per cent after reporting a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. But rival Dollar Tree sank 3.9 per cent despite blowing past profit expectations. More attention may have been on its forecasted range for an important underlying measure of revenue, whose midpoint fell short of analysts’ expectations. In the bond market, Treasury yields ticked higher following a report suggesting that the US job market remains solid. Fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, an indication that layoffs could be remaining low. The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.67 per cent from 4.66 per cent late on Wednesday. Yields have been largely climbing through the summer on worries about high inflation, the US government’s gargantuan and growing debt and other factors. They got so high that the US Treasury Department made a surprise announcement last week to intervene in the bond market, though analysts say its effect could be limited. The next big event for the bond market will be a speech coming on Friday from Warsh. He has been adamant about giving financial markets fewer clues about what the Fed will do in future with interest rates to control inflation. But the pressure is on him to give clearer guidance.

The ICAC has heard that despite Wednesday’s evidence that Anita Perrottet had only heard of Jean Nassif through media reports, she appeared to send a detailed email advocating for his developments to a lobbying firm.

The email shown to the commission from Perrottet’s Macquarie Consulting company contained details about Nassif’s development issues, and used technical language about planning matters.

Anita Perrottet gives evidence before the ICAC on Friday. ICAC

Peggy Dwyer, SC: “Mrs Perrottet your evidence was that you knew nothing about Nassif apart from the media reports. I want you to think really carefully … in that email, Toplace was mentioned eight times. Nassif was mentioned multiple times. That’s an email sent by somebody with a detailed knowledge of what Jean Nassif wanted for Toplace and the projects.

“I don’t mean to embarrass you by that email. I’m suggesting you’ve been put in an impossible situation. Do you want to take some time to think about it before you answer the question: that was not the email that you sent on behalf of Macquarie Consulting? Was it?”

World.title: Guns, drugs and romance: GTA 6 explodes onto Netflix with a 27-minute trailer
World.content:
Updated TechnologyVideo games Guns, drugs and romance: GTA 6 explodes onto Netflix with a 27-minute trailer Tim Biggs Updated August 28, 2026 — 11:00am ,first published August 28, 2026 — 8:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

With a detonation of drugs, chaos, killings and hand-holding, Rockstar Games has given its first in-depth look at upcoming blockbuster Grand Theft Auto VI, releasing a 27-minute trailer composed entirely of in-game footage on Netflix. And while some elements are proving divisive, fans have been largely positive on the direction of what is expected to be the largest launch of an entertainment product in history. Set to launch on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S on November 19, the game, which has been estimated to have cost about $US2 billion ($2.8 billion) to develop, follows Lucia and Jason, a fugitive criminal couple getting into scrapes across Vice City and its surrounds. The trailer begins with the pair tensely navigating their way into a drug den to pick up for a client, only for a police raid to throw them into a bloody firefight. The GTA VI trailer has arrived. The protagonists and their romantic relationship features heavily in the footage, with some hints as to how their love affair will play out. It appears that while in the open world players can choose which character to control, can instantly switch to the other, or use their phones to call them in for back-up, to pull off a robbery or to hang out at the zoo. When they’re together, the player can have them hold hands, or quickly switch between who is driving a vehicle and who is passenger, whether they’re relaxing or shooting a shotgun out a window. In an interview with IGN, Rockstar North head of development Rob Nelson said the romance was optional, and players had the choice to play the characters as platonic partners. There’s no gameplay benefit to exploring the relationship, though the story will change. The trailer showed other ways of influencing the protagonists’ lives, similar to fan-favourite GTA entry San Andreas, including working out, eating and grooming.



Players will be able to customise Lucia and Jason and influence their relationship. Early looks at the game gave an ambiguous impression of the couple’s relationship, indicating that they could potentially turn against each other early on. But this trailer makes it clear they will be a unit for the large bulk of the game, and that whatever trouble they’re in (it sounds as though they could be working with police, or have some complicated secret agenda), they’re in it together. On online forums discussing the trailer, fans enthused about the look of the game and seemed excited by the prospect of managing a criminal couple’s relationship. Many expressed disappointment about Jason’s characterisation, however, specifically, his deep voice and monotone delivery. It will be interesting to see how he’s received once players can appreciate his arc through the whole game. As always, the massive game world is explorable in cars and other ground transport, or in planes, boats and helicopters. It has been 13 years since Grand Theft Auto V, a massive hit that topped bestseller charts for more than 10 years and made more than $14 billion in revenue, and US culture and politics has changed enormously in that time. So many commentators have wondered whether Rockstar could keep its satire sharp and relevant, or if the company may come off as out of touch given the protracted development cycle.



But the video may indicate that the funny stuff is taking a back seat. The opening scene’s drug raid is surprisingly grim, with police indiscriminately executing surrendering gang members and unarmed workers in their underwear. Later, while working as security for a coked-up VIP, Lucia is choked by a violent gatecrasher until she manages to embed a stiletto in his eye. The state of Leonida, a fictionalised Florida, goes far beyond city limits. If there are specific satirical jabs at the current state of affairs in the US, they’re not really hinted at in the trailer. There is a quick funny scene where a boy livestreaming on his phone animatedly asks his chat what he should do now that he’s been kidnapped, but in general, it appears to be familiar targets like America’s predatory commercialisation of food, guns and drugs that will get the gags. From a gameplay point of view, shooting, driving and interacting with the world appears to be a lot more fluid and seamless than before, which you’d expect given the previous game was two console generations ago. But most noticeable was how Rockstar’s characteristic focus on minuscule details has expanded along with the complexity and graphical fidelity of the scenes. The density of the areas and the level of animation is truly impressive; it’s a very expensive-looking game. Lucia and Jason are in some sort of bind together, but their relationship is sure to be tested at some point in the story.



We also saw a significant influence on the game from Red Dead Redemption 2 – the development team’s most recent game, released in 2018 – including dynamic safehouses, expanded conversation options and the ability to study and document wildlife. That game featured a much more grounded and emotional story than previous GTA editions, and was much slower with players able to take in the world and its many optional activities at their own pace. It’s unclear what the pace will be like here, but we did see many such activities, including scuba diving, parachuting, boat racing and visiting strip clubs. Editor's pick Video games Red Dead Redemption 2 review: a Wild West work of art Demand for Rockstar’s new game has been immense, with parent Take-Two already raking in more than $1 billion in pre-orders despite some players grumbling about the $130 price, some game features being locked behind the $160 Ultimate Edition, and the lack of an option to buy it on disc. Similarly, although some people were upset that the new video was exclusive to Netflix (it will be posted on YouTube on Friday at 11am), interest was high enough that the streaming service briefly crashed at 5am when the footage made its debut. World.title: Unemployed and unpaid: what the fate of sacked Qantas workers tells us
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAviation Opinion Unemployed and unpaid: what the fate of sacked Qantas workers tells us Chris Zappone Senior reporter, aviation August 28, 2026 — 11:00am

August 28, 2026 — 11:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

What do Qantas, labour law firm Maurice Blackburn or the Transport Workers’ Union have in common? None would tolerate a lengthy delay, with little explanation given, if they were in line to get a significant sum of compensation for an egregious, life-altering breach of their rights. Justice Michael Lee demanded an explanation from Maurice Blackburn when it asked for more time to distribute funds. Dominic Lorrimer But this isn’t the case for the 1822 illegally sacked Qantas workers who were turfed out of their jobs during the COVID-19 pandemic. They have been promised $35 million in penalty payments and $120 million from a compensation fund - both amounts paid up by Qantas in 2025. Six years after wrongly being forced out of work by the airline, five years after the move was ruled illegal, and almost two years after a major chunk of the compensation was first agreed, they still haven’t been paid.



And the wait goes on. Related Article Aviation ‘Chapter of Genesis’: Judge gets biblical over sacked Qantas workers It’s hard to imagine the other protagonists in this saga being forced to accept their fate as blindly as these workers. It took intervention from Justice Michael Lee of the Federal Court earlier this month to ensure the workers’ $35 million in penalty payments were decoupled from the $120 million compensation fund that has become mired in technicalities, allowing the smaller chunk of money to be paid out quickly. Maurice Blackburn had represented the TWU and its members in its case against Qantas, and then oversaw the administration of the employees’ compensation. After nailing the case, the firm has fumbled the administration.



When Maurice Blackburn informed Lee of a delay in the weeks preceding the July 31 deadline, he immediately ordered a hearing to ask why the firm hadn’t advised the court of the hitches as soon as possible? Why, in other words, did there appear to be so little urgency from the class action giant that brands itself as “fighting for fair”? Maurice Blackburn’s lawyers explained that the process got hung up both by a string of legally insufficient independent medical assessments of the fired workers and questions about how to repay Services Australia for treatment the employees had already accessed. There is a tension between the lawful requirement for accurate compensation based on a worker’s history, and a more timely resolution, but why not tell the judge about the issue and sort it out? As Lee said on August 6: “One can’t let the perfect be the enemy of the good.” Many of the 1800 sacked Qantas workers have taken a financial punch from their dismissal and not really recovered. A large proportion of them are doing so late in their careers when their options are constrained. Getting compensation isn’t just about the elegance of justice; the money is needed to inject some financial breathing space into their lives. On August 6, Lee told the sacked workers, “Your payment will be made within the next few business days into the bank account you previously provided to Maurice Blackburn.”



Related Article Aviation Alan Joyce has been writing his book. Here’s how five people illegally sacked by his airline have fared He appointed another firm, William Roberts Lawyers, in August to oversee the fine component of the case, such was Lee’s apparent level of faith in the larger firm. But even that has led to a further delay, albeit for a good cause. On Thursday, William Roberts Lawyers asked for another delay to the payments so that it could include more ex-workers, or their heirs. One ex-employee, Ryan Perrett, told the hearing that the money should be split equally among all affected workers, noting (in a very AI-era sentiment) that younger workers would get a bigger share, but they anyway will have “missed out on a larger opportunity to work further into the future”.



Payments now appear to be on track to come after September 1. The payout scheme’s long tail is emblematic of a broader reality. If people at the more modest end of the economy don’t see civil society working for them, politicians and business leaders can’t expect those same workers to uphold the status quo. That disjunct might be the bitter aftertaste of the largest corporate fine in Australia’s history. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion.
