World.title: Brilliant or boring? The verdict on Rachel Cusk’s new novel
World.content:
CultureBooksReview Brilliant or boring? The verdict on Rachel Cusk’s new novel Miranda Darling August 28, 2026 — 11:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Reading Rachel Cusk’s Life of M is a destabilising experience. The pages shadow you; the strange discomfort of their atmosphere lingers – as intended, surely, as most specifically intended. This is Cusk, after all, and her writing is no one’s comfort zone. Life of M has provoked much debate “in real life”, fed by the supposedly furious reactions of the famous actress whom “M” is allegedly based on, with entertainment channels thrilling about a feud between the writer and the Hollywood superstar. Outrage is performed, and it’s VERY EXCITING; more stories probe the line (maybe it’s more of a demilitarised zone) between what’s acceptable and what’s not when turning a famous life into fiction. The actress’ friends are said to be incandescent; others call out Cusk’s novel as a “cheap publicity stunt”, as if this were a brand-new form of intrusion, an unprecedented liberty taken. In other words, it’s difficult to read Life of M on the page alone, to experience it without the subsonic thrumming of this parallel storyline creating and/or revealing a whole other dimension to the novel. Rachel Cusk’s new novel has attracted attention well beyond the page. It took me a while to finish. After an enthusiastic dive into the familiar spartan beauty of Cusk’s sentences I found myself reacting with a mix of frustration, incredulity, boredom and confusion. I resisted reading for a few days while I unravelled my reluctance. Then I realised that the interesting dance was taking place off the page, that the novel was a commentary and a mirror, a performance, a provocation and a participation, all at once. We are warned in the very first paragraph: “Would you just make it up? she said.” Many scenes do feel “made up” in the sense that they feel clichéd, like the work of a lazy writer skimming the well-worn surface of things – the fashion model in the bookstore stood out as a clanger. Other scenes have descriptions of tables and glass tumblers and flowers that have a flatness to them, a banality, almost a Dick-and-Jane quality: “They are filled with books but also with other things, perhaps put there in haste to clear the room: [a list follows].”



The reminder that Cusk’s writing can be electrifying bursts in occasionally. Describing an art exhibition that M attends, there is a sudden rush of blood and life in the writing. The warning is there: Cusk is a fantastic, whip-smart writer who doesn’t ask to be liked, and we underestimate her at our peril. It remains, though, that Life of M presents more surface: the occasional descriptions of ugliness as some form of antidote fail to fragment the power of “seems”. The theatre director who chooses to pay no attention to his appearance as a statement of his power opens a small and interesting thematic door that the narrator fails to walk through. Indeed, in their brittle self-regard, the narrator resembles M to the point that we almost have a conflation. (This resonates if the narrator is indeed “making it all up”.) I found myself reacting with a mix of frustration, incredulity, boredom and confusion. I resisted reading for a few days while I unravelled my reluctance. Complicity runs through the work. The novel begins with first-person narration, and the ground seems solid. Early references to “we” appear initially to refer to the narrator and a partner; the use of the first-person plural then becomes increasingly claustrophobic until it becomes clear we are now dealing with a single entity of sorts that could very well include us, the “we” retaining the intimacy afforded by “I” yet adding a layer of reader inclusion. “We” unfixes the point of view. It can be read as a self-aggrandising royal “we” as a pretentious affectation, or a distancing from the earlier authorial “I”; “we” might be a comment on how completely we give over our identities to a partner that even childhoods blur into a shared space; it could suggest a mild psychosis, or offer a comment on the ubiquitous reach of non-binary pronouns. Very possibly and likely, all of the above and more are in play. Related Article Opinion

Literature Is Rachel Cusk’s new novel a ruthless betrayal of Natalie Portman? Jane Sullivan Books columnist and reviewer The novel provokes and performs a destabilisation of “truth” that goes beyond an unreliable narrator. It pulls us as readers into a co-creation that is fed by our own half-knowledge and dark assumptions. It’s all through the book: “People begin to see her, as though she were an image developing out of their own knowledge. She sometimes wonders whether it is she who needs this process to occur.”





Life of M by Rachel Cusk is published by Faber ($33) on September 1. The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: Demon’s tough draw and Tiley’s $150 million US Open splash
World.content:
SportTennisUS Open Demon’s tough draw and Tiley’s $150 million US Open splash Marc McGowan August 28, 2026 — 11:40am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Alex de Minaur faces a potentially career-defining fortnight in New York as younger rivals emerge to threaten his top-10 position amid a prolonged form dip. The year’s fourth and final grand slam, the US Open, begins on Sunday night (AEST), with de Minaur again headlining the Australian assault as the No.6 seed in a men’s singles draw so far featuring seven compatriots, while Daria Kasatkina leads the country’s five players in the women’s event. Alex de Minaur has not played at his usual lofty standard in recent months as new rivals emerge. Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press via AP De Minaur starts against a qualifier, but has difficult projected rivals beyond that, including Botic van de Zandschulp (second round), 31st seed Zizou Bergs (third round), No.12 seed Rafael Jodar (fourth round) and top seed Alexander Zverev (quarter-finals). The 27-year-old has advanced to the US Open quarter-finals the past two years – and three times overall – but lost in the third and fourth rounds, respectively, at Roland-Garros and Wimbledon.



Related Article Wimbledon ‘It breaks me inside’: Devastated Demon offers frank admission after Wimbledon exit De Minaur, who married British player Katie Boulter on Wimbledon men’s finals day in July, has also won no more than two matches at any of his three tournaments since leaving London, and his ranking has slipped from a career-best No.5 to 7. That downturn from de Minaur’s typically lofty standards has coincided with hot streaks from rising stars Arthur Fils and Jodar, who are on the verge of making their top-10 debuts. Fils, 22, beat Australia’s seven-time major quarter-finalist in straight sets last week en route to the Cincinnati Masters title, while 20-year-olds Learner Tien and Jakub Mensik are also inside the top 20 and increasingly looming. Jodar, 19, amassed a 10-3 record in the lead-in American hardcourt events, including making the Canadian Masters semi-finals and the Washington Open final. The Spaniard drew Australia’s Thanasi Kokkinakis in the first round.



Related Video Video icon 1:15 Kyrgios tests positive for cocaine The US Open men’s championship race appears to be as open as it has been in years, with Jannik Sinner (knee) withdrawing and defending champion Carlos Alcaraz (wrist) returning for his first event since April. The likes of Roland-Garros titlist Zverev, 24-time grand slam-winning legend Novak Djokovic, Fils, Ben Shelton, Taylor Fritz, Felix Auger-Aliassime, Flavio Cobolli and even Jodar would fancy their chances of lifting the trophy. James Duckworth, Rinky Hijikata, Adam Walton, Aleks Vukic, Alexei Popyrin and wildcard Dane Sweeny are Australia’s other men’s representatives. Hijikata and Duckworth drew seeded rivals Auger-Aliassime and Matteo Arnaldi, respectively. Popyrin reached the last 16 in New York two years ago, but has not won a grand slam match in 2026 and his ranking has plummeted to No.130. He, too, has a qualifier as his first-round opponent.



Joining Kasatkina, who also married her long-time partner Natalia Zabiiako post-Wimbledon, in contesting the women’s singles are Kim Birrell, Talia Gibson, Maya Joint and wildcard Taylah Preston. Kasatkina starts with former top-tenner Paula Badosa, while Gibson drew Olympic silver medallist Donna Vekic and Joint faces Russia’s Liudmila Samsonova, who was ranked in the top 20 as recently as May. Samsonova defeated Joint in three sets in Toronto a fortnight ago. Aryna Sabalenka is clinging to the world No.1 ranking. Getty Images The women’s draw is similarly wide open, particularly with world No.1 Aryna Sabalenka enduring a form slump and Australian Open champion Elena Rybakina dealing with an ankle injury. Resurgent Pole Iga Swiatek, 2023 winner Coco Gauff and 2024 runner-up Jessica Pegula are serious contenders, as are the past two grand slam champions, Mirra Andreeva and Linda Noskova.



Australia’s Chris O’Connell, Tristan Schoolkate and Storm Hunter have advanced to final-round qualifying. Australians’ US Open first-round opponents Men: Alexei Popyrin v Qualifier; WC-Dane Sweeny v Corentin Moutet (France); Thanasi Kokkinakis v 12-Rafael Jodar (Spain); 6-Alex de Minaur v Qualifier; Rinky Hijikata v 3-Felix Auger-Aliassime (Canada); Aleks Vukic v Qualifier; James Duckworth v 30-Matteo Arnaldi (Italy); Adam Walton v Wu Yibing (China). Women: WC-Taylah Preston v Alycia Parks (United States); Kim Birrell v Petra Marcinko (Croatia); Talia Gibson v Donna Vekic (Croatia); Maya Joint v Liudmila Samsonova (Russia); Daria Kasatkina v Paula Badosa (Spain). Another top-100 Aussie Preston has more than halved her ranking this year on the way to becoming the third Australian woman in the past 18 months to make her top-100 debut. The 20-year-old West Australian edged her way to exactly No.100 on Monday, three weeks after capturing the biggest singles title of her life at the Vancouver WTA 125 event.



Preston follows countrywomen Joint, 20, and Gibson, 22, in achieving the ranking milestone, which will guarantee her entry into all four grand slams if she can maintain it. Her rise came narrowly too late for direct US Open entry, but she scored Tennis Australia’s reciprocal wildcard. Taylah Preston made her top-100 debut in the past week. PENNY STEPHENS “It’s an amazing feeling [to be in the top 100],” Preston said. “It’s taken a lot of hard work, a lot of years. But it’s definitely been a goal for a long time now … I’m extremely grateful to be given a chance to compete in the main draw in New York. It means a lot to me.” Tiley makes an instant splash



Former Tennis Australia and Australian Open supremo Craig Tiley is not mucking around in his new role as the United States Tennis Association’s chief executive officer. The US Open will hand over the most prizemoney in tennis history this year, a 20 per cent increase on 12 months ago to a record $US108 million ($150.4 million). For comparison’s sake, the Australian Open’s 2026 prizemoney was $111.5 million. Craig Tiley, third from left, oversaw a huge prizemoney increase for this year’s US Open. Bloomberg Tiley said: “This is a significant first step in a multi-year investment in athletes as the US Open continues to be the best economic opportunity for players and the most valuable platform in tennis for players, fans and partners.” Less popular was the USTA’s decision to initially overlook retiring Swiss great Stan Wawrinka for a wildcard, but he ended up scoring one when American Patrick Kypson withdrew injured.



Watch the US Open live on 9GO!, 9NOW and Stan Sport from 1am AEST Tuesday. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: These 223 schools harnessed talent for the NRLW. One became a juggernaut
World.content:
SportNRLNRLW 2026 These 223 schools harnessed talent for the NRLW. One became a juggernaut Nick Wright August 28, 2026 — 11:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Nestled in the heart of the Gold Coast, one school has become a powerhouse of women’s rugby league talent production – a juggernaut boasting more NRLW graduates than any other institution in the country. Before the female game received its first national competition in 2018, Keebra Park had built a girls’ sporting excellence academy. Just last year, on the back of the surging popularity of the code, they forged a separate rugby league excellence program, featuring three weekly on-field or gym training sessions, and a classroom session geared towards developing skills for budding athletes to handle the rigours of professional sport. Queensland’s Tiana Raftstrand-Smith is one of the many Keebra Park graduates to go on to play NRLW. Getty Among the mentors for the near 200-strong academy are former rugby sevens and NRLW star Niall Williams Guthrie, brother to cross-code athlete Sonny Bill Williams.



“It’s very much an aspirational sporting pathway, and we’re trying to make sure they’re prepared for that – making sure they’re resilient and have all their life skills outside of footy,” program head James Chapman says. “We want to develop them for the rigours of professional sporting life, but I think the overall lessons of the program are we want to make sure they have a positive experience with rugby league, and want to be a steward of the game and play footy beyond just high school.” Of the 355 players currently named on each NRLW squad’s roster, 19 hail from Keebra Park. Only two other schools – Marsden State High School (12) in Logan and The Hills Sports High School (12) in Seven Hills, Sydney – enter the double digits for NRLW graduates, with academy pathways still developing as the code continues to grow. When asked what had made the program so successful, Chapman says: “It all comes back to the coaching staff. We have an awesome coaching team, collectively, who give up so much time and genuinely do care about the girls.



“Yes, winning is great, and it’d be great to bring back some trophies every year, but I think the level of care they have for the girls and the drive they have to see them improve every day is probably unmatched anywhere in Australia, I’d reckon.” Related Article AFL 2026 ‘Mum lost her soulmate’: The tragic death driving premiership hero’s new mission Several former students have become future leaders of the competition, including Raftstrand-Smith sisters Tiana and Ebony of the North Queensland Cowboys – the former representing the Maroons twice. “Because rugby league was still so new at the time, the girls who separated themselves from the others really liked the contact element – that was Tiana. If you’ve seen any of her games, particularly early on, she loved the physical element,” Chapman says. “A lot of the girls early on were transferring from touch football – highly transferable skills – but just developing confidence in contact has been an evolution in itself. We’re at the point now you could ask a 12-year-old girl ‘how long have you been playing footy?’ and she could say five or six years.



“The game has really changed in such a short space of time.” There are 223 schools represented in the NRLW this season, including 172 with one representative. Teagan Levi celebrates her brilliant try. Matt Roberts/Getty Images. Among those is Miami State High School, where rugby sevens star Teagan Levi was educated. On secondment from Rugby Australia, Levi has gone on to ignite the Titans’ premiership prospects. Once the NRLW season ends, Levi will return to rugby and in preparation for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics, alongside sister Maddison, who in Australia’s 100th rugby union Test made her Wallaroos debut in the 15-a-side code against the Black Ferns.



“I think that [Wallaroos] could have been an opportunity that opened up for me, but I wanted to come home to the Gold Coast Titans,” Teagan says. “[Being a dual-code international] is something we’ve both wanted for quite a while.” Such has been the way she has taken to rugby league, champion NRL halfbacks Andrew Johns and Johnathan Thurston have been awed by her exploits – after she twice showcased a grubber kick ahead for herself to score. Loading “I’m loving the opportunity to learn a different game, each week is a new challenge in itself – learning the different opposition, knowing what’s best to stick away from, so I’m really enjoying the process,” Teagan says. She had no desire to ease into rugby league. When she arrived at the Titans, she had her eyes on the Gold Coast’s five-eighth duties, and consulted former duel-code international Mat Rogers – of whose management agency she is a client – for insight.



“He just said to back yourself and do what you do best, that’s what got you selected to come over to the Titans. The game’s different, so I have to learn the different rules and structures, but [he said] to back your instincts and have a go.” Teagan has scored seven tries, while coming up with five try assists and linebreak assists and averaging 104 running metres a game from eight appearances – which has included the club’s seven-straight wins to surge to second on the ladder, trailing only their round-one conquerors, the Roosters. Loading “I wanted to go in the halves. I thought my skills from sevens would help quite a lot, and I loved the challenge. I wanted to put myself in that position – if I didn’t think I was ready I wouldn’t have put myself forward,” she says. “I did all the hard work before I even came across to league; I was doing Zoom calls, making sure I was catching up, coming home back to the Gold Coast whenever I could to make sure I was putting my best foot forward to make sure the team had trust in me.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: This entire novel is one sentence. Somehow, it works
World.content:
CultureBooksReview This entire novel is one sentence. Somehow, it works Jack Cameron Stanton August 28, 2026 — 11:11am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If awards ceremonies are anything to go by, the one-sentence novel is having a moment. The Norwegian Jon Fosse and Hungarian Laszlo Krasznahorkai, winners of the Nobel Prize for Literature in 2023 and 2025 respectively, see the humble full stop as a needless barrier to be banished from their richly textured and deeply introspective novels. Lucy Ellmann’s Ducks, Newburyport, a Goldsmiths winner and Booker shortlistee, is composed of a single sentence detailing the protagonist’s far-reaching anxieties that persist over a thousand pages, held together with the refrain “the fact that”. These writers are rule breakers. They dispense with full stops, scene breaks, and chapters by using an array of conjunctions and punctuation, both workmanlike and exotic, to keep the damn thing rolling. Each page is a formidable, handsome wall of text. They write the literary equivalents of a horror vacui, a painting afraid of emptiness, a canvas completely covered. At his best trawling through the history books: Adam Ouston.



Despite these books being a single, unbroken sentence, I doubt anyone reads them in one sitting, nor that the authors indeed intend for us to do so. You would need a preternatural concentration or heroic dose of stimulants. Likely both. They offer no restorative pit stops, no spaces to breathe, nowhere obvious to rest a bookmark and take stock of everything that has come before. You must rip yourself away from the currents, forever amid a gathering thought. Editor's pick Literature Sydney Writers’ Festival names new artistic director Once the books get going, however, the effect is a degree of immersion beyond that of conventionally stylised fictions. Sure, they make demands on us, but difficulty (more than idle, easily absorbed fiction) rewards. I find myself switching between two mental states: one of hypervigilance, following every thread, and another that lets the stream of words wash over me. I’m no proselytiser for the one-sentence novel. I trudged through Mathias Enard’s Zone like an explorer with a machete chopping through an overgrown path. I never finished Ducks, Newburyport. And yet, the new novel from Tasmanian writer Adam Ouston has me, if not converted, at least showing up for Sunday service. Ouston’s debut, Waypoints, took as its subject the lesser-known history of Harry Houdini’s first controlled flight, which happened in 1910 in Diggers Rest, Victoria. His latest novel, Mine, also embraces smoke and mirrors, but this time on the level of the sentence.



Mine by Adam Ouston. It begins after a poet falls into an abandoned mineshaft. Injured and trapped in that elemental darkness, the ageing poet reminisces about his campaigns as an ecoactivist while other memories and voices start to intrude, hinting at “something bigger than him, a secret story beneath the apparent one”. Appraising Ouston’s novel by what happens is about as illuminating as recounting Waiting for Godot. Ouston’s single sentence is not the poet’s life flashing before his eyes. It is a broad narrative frame to capture a deeper history. In this sense, the set-up shares more DNA with a poem than a plot-driven novel. We learn that the poet has been exploring the West Coast of Tasmania to research his magnum opus, a collection inspired by hauntology, an attempt to capture the “island’s soul”. A hauntology: the past is a revenant in the present and therefore has not passed at all. At first Ouston allows the hauntology to drift ill-defined, more spirit than flesh, until other stories rise in the poet’s mind. These include most notably the true histories of settler-colonial explorers and mining magnates laying claim to the land, alongside other accounts of exploration paired with environmental extremes, such as the Mawson and Mertz Antarctic expedition in the early 1900s. Dispersed among these are the poet’s own memories of his youthful days of climate action and a tender reflection upon the death and funeral of a dissident journalist friend.



The most vital of these non-fictional strains is Ouston’s lively reconstruction of the ascent and rivalry of two enterprising capitalists, Bowes Kelly and James Crotty, whose legacies culminated in the Mount Lyell Mining and Railway Company. We begin to suspect these historical anecdotes are not arbitrary and may, taken together, begin converging upon this “secret story beneath the apparent one”. Ouston is at his best trawling through the history books. At times Ouston’s descriptions of the Tasmanian landscape reach for the grandeur “of desolation, ferocity, madness, and hopelessness, but also beauty, wisdom, protection and valour, and inspiration”. It’s classic romanticism: grandeur evoked abstractedly. But when he finds an original image – “whenever he heard of the plight of the South Pole he would picture a black rubber mask melting in the middle of an interminable stretch of outback highway, eye sockets collapsing, mouth hole shrivelling as though releasing an unending scream” – it’s magic. Late in Mine, Ouston’s poet arrives at the conclusion that the battle for Tasmania’s environment has been lost. I realised that Ouston has written a dire allegory: an eco-poet howls at the bottom of a mineshaft, where no one can hear him. Mine by Adam Ouston is published by Transit Lounge ($35). World.title: ASX edges higher as tech stocks jump; Virgin surges
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX edges higher as tech stocks jump; Virgin surges Staff writers Updated August 28, 2026 — 11:06am ,first published August 28, 2026 — 5:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket has advanced at the open after a solid night on Wall Street, with stocks jumping as Nvidia, Salesforce and others reported fatter profits than expected. The S&P/ASX 200 was up 19.5 points or 0.2 per cent to 9057.7 in early trade. The ASX lost 1 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was stronger at US71.95¢. Positive results from Nvidia and Salesforce helped allay concerns over AI stocks and drove Wall Street higher. Bloomberg Reporting season is drawing to a close and Virgin Australia surged by 9.5 per cent in early trade as it reported robust results, with underlying pre-tax earnings surging by more than 13 per cent to $753 million. Virgin will pay a dividend of 7.6¢ a share. Retail giant Harvey Norman slid 0.2 per cent as it reported that net profit increased 2 per cent to $528.5 million in the financial year.



Nvidia’s strong results pushed Wall Street’s Nasdaq higher overnight, and the positive sentiment flowed through to local technology stocks, with Xero jumping 5.9 per cent, WiseTech and Technology One each up 3.5 per cent and NEXTDC 3 per cent higher. Mining stocks are mixed with Fortescue up 0.4 per cent, BHP flat and Rio Tinto shedding 1 per cent in early trade. Gold stocks advanced with the price of the precious metal steady near $US4600 an ounce as investors weighed the outlook for US interest rates ahead of a key speech by Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh. Financial stocks are steady with National Australia Bank up 0.1 per cent, Westpac and Commonwealth Bank down 0.1 per cent and ANZ Bank 0.3 per cent lower. Energy stocks are higher with oil prices advancing overnight before steadying in early Asian trade. Woodside and Santos added 1.1 per cent each while refiner Ampol rose 0.9 per cent. Overnight, the S&P 500 rose 0.7 per cent and pulled closer to its all-time high set earlier this month. The Dow Jones added 105 points, or 0.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 1.6 per cent.



On Wall Street, Nvidia was the strongest force pulling the market higher, and the chip giant rallied 8.7 per cent after once again delivering stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. More importantly for Wall Street, it also gave forecasts for coming revenue growth that topped analysts’ estimates, suggesting demand remains strong for chips to power artificial-intelligence projects. “AI has reached its inflection point,” Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang said. “It’s doing useful work. Its tokens are productive and profitable.” Related Article Updated

Earnings season Qantas boss says air traffic delays at Sydney Airport ‘not OK’ That helped calm some of the worries that have built around AI stocks generally, which have been under pressure recently. After rocketing higher for years because of the frenzy around AI, stocks in the industry are confronting scepticism that they shot too high and that booming demand for AI chips may fade if the AI revolution does not produce as much profit as promised. Another big tech company, Salesforce, jumped 22.6 per cent after it said that AI helped it deliver one of its best quarters in history. It reported stronger profit than analysts expected, and chief executive Marc Benioff said it’s “seeing incredible demand for our AI and data products” and that it’s “turning AI into customer success at unprecedented scale”.



Salesforce, which helps companies to manage their customers’ data, also raised its forecast for revenue over the full year and announced an expanded partnership to pair Anthropic’s Claude chatbot with its platform. It’s notable because Salesforce’s stock struggled earlier on worries that competitors powered by AI could ultimately steal away customers from Salesforce and other software companies. Salesforce’s stock had its best day in six years. Elsewhere, though, trends were more mixed across big US companies, and the majority of stocks within the S&P 500 fell. HP sank 2.9 per cent even though it topped analysts’ expectations for profit and revenue in the latest quarter. Analysts pointed to worries about its sales of personal computers, as well as how higher prices for computer memory and other commodities are pressuring its profit margins. Best Buy and some other retailers sank amid continued worries that US shoppers could be stretched because of high inflation and discouragement about the economy. Best Buy fell 4.4 per cent even though it topped analysts’ expectations for both profit and revenue in the latest quarter. One potential winner from high inflation could be dollar stores, which could see higher-income households become new customers as they look for less expensive places to shop.



Dollar General rose 2.5 per cent after reporting a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. But rival Dollar Tree sank 3.9 per cent despite blowing past profit expectations. More attention may have been on its forecasted range for an important underlying measure of revenue, whose midpoint fell short of analysts’ expectations. In the bond market, Treasury yields ticked higher following a report suggesting that the US job market remains solid. Fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, an indication that layoffs could be remaining low. The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.67 per cent from 4.66 per cent late on Wednesday. Yields have been largely climbing through the summer on worries about high inflation, the US government’s gargantuan and growing debt and other factors. They got so high that the US Treasury Department made a surprise announcement last week to intervene in the bond market, though analysts say its effect could be limited. The next big event for the bond market will be a speech coming on Friday from Warsh. He has been adamant about giving financial markets fewer clues about what the Fed will do in future with interest rates to control inflation. But the pressure is on him to give clearer guidance.

World.title: ICAC Operation Rosny LIVE updates: Anita Perrottet questioned on disappearing messages as husband Charles prepares to front inquiry; Jean Nassif to give evidence next week
World.content:
The ICAC has heard that despite Wednesday’s evidence that Anita Perrottet had only heard of Jean Nassif through media reports, she appeared to send a detailed email advocating for his developments to a lobbying firm.

The email shown to the commission from Perrottet’s Macquarie Consulting company contained details about Nassif’s development issues, and used technical language about planning matters.

Anita Perrottet gives evidence before the ICAC on Friday. ICAC

Peggy Dwyer, SC: “Mrs Perrottet your evidence was that you knew nothing about Nassif apart from the media reports. I want you to think really carefully … in that email, Toplace was mentioned eight times. Nassif was mentioned multiple times. That’s an email sent by somebody with a detailed knowledge of what Jean Nassif wanted for Toplace and the projects.

“I don’t mean to embarrass you by that email. I’m suggesting you’ve been put in an impossible situation. Do you want to take some time to think about it before you answer the question: that was not the email that you sent on behalf of Macquarie Consulting? Was it?”

World.title: Guns, drugs and romance: GTA 6 explodes onto Netflix with a 27-minute trailer
World.content:
Updated TechnologyVideo games Guns, drugs and romance: GTA 6 explodes onto Netflix with a 27-minute trailer Tim Biggs Updated August 28, 2026 — 11:00am ,first published August 28, 2026 — 8:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

With a detonation of drugs, chaos, killings and hand-holding, Rockstar Games has given its first in-depth look at upcoming blockbuster Grand Theft Auto VI, releasing a 27-minute trailer composed entirely of in-game footage on Netflix. And while some elements are proving divisive, fans have been largely positive on the direction of what is expected to be the largest launch of an entertainment product in history. Set to launch on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S on November 19, the game, which has been estimated to have cost about $US2 billion ($2.8 billion) to develop, follows Lucia and Jason, a fugitive criminal couple getting into scrapes across Vice City and its surrounds. The trailer begins with the pair tensely navigating their way into a drug den to pick up for a client, only for a police raid to throw them into a bloody firefight. The GTA VI trailer has arrived. The protagonists and their romantic relationship features heavily in the footage, with some hints as to how their love affair will play out. It appears that while in the open world players can choose which character to control, can instantly switch to the other, or use their phones to call them in for back-up, to pull off a robbery or to hang out at the zoo. When they’re together, the player can have them hold hands, or quickly switch between who is driving a vehicle and who is passenger, whether they’re relaxing or shooting a shotgun out a window. In an interview with IGN, Rockstar North head of development Rob Nelson said the romance was optional, and players had the choice to play the characters as platonic partners. There’s no gameplay benefit to exploring the relationship, though the story will change. The trailer showed other ways of influencing the protagonists’ lives, similar to fan-favourite GTA entry San Andreas, including working out, eating and grooming.



Players will be able to customise Lucia and Jason and influence their relationship. Early looks at the game gave an ambiguous impression of the couple’s relationship, indicating that they could potentially turn against each other early on. But this trailer makes it clear they will be a unit for the large bulk of the game, and that whatever trouble they’re in (it sounds as though they could be working with police, or have some complicated secret agenda), they’re in it together. On online forums discussing the trailer, fans enthused about the look of the game and seemed excited by the prospect of managing a criminal couple’s relationship. Many expressed disappointment about Jason’s characterisation, however, specifically, his deep voice and monotone delivery. It will be interesting to see how he’s received once players can appreciate his arc through the whole game. As always, the massive game world is explorable in cars and other ground transport, or in planes, boats and helicopters. It has been 13 years since Grand Theft Auto V, a massive hit that topped bestseller charts for more than 10 years and made more than $14 billion in revenue, and US culture and politics has changed enormously in that time. So many commentators have wondered whether Rockstar could keep its satire sharp and relevant, or if the company may come off as out of touch given the protracted development cycle.



But the video may indicate that the funny stuff is taking a back seat. The opening scene’s drug raid is surprisingly grim, with police indiscriminately executing surrendering gang members and unarmed workers in their underwear. Later, while working as security for a coked-up VIP, Lucia is choked by a violent gatecrasher until she manages to embed a stiletto in his eye. The state of Leonida, a fictionalised Florida, goes far beyond city limits. If there are specific satirical jabs at the current state of affairs in the US, they’re not really hinted at in the trailer. There is a quick funny scene where a boy livestreaming on his phone animatedly asks his chat what he should do now that he’s been kidnapped, but in general, it appears to be familiar targets like America’s predatory commercialisation of food, guns and drugs that will get the gags. From a gameplay point of view, shooting, driving and interacting with the world appears to be a lot more fluid and seamless than before, which you’d expect given the previous game was two console generations ago. But most noticeable was how Rockstar’s characteristic focus on minuscule details has expanded along with the complexity and graphical fidelity of the scenes. The density of the areas and the level of animation is truly impressive; it’s a very expensive-looking game. Lucia and Jason are in some sort of bind together, but their relationship is sure to be tested at some point in the story.



We also saw a significant influence on the game from Red Dead Redemption 2 – the development team’s most recent game, released in 2018 – including dynamic safehouses, expanded conversation options and the ability to study and document wildlife. That game featured a much more grounded and emotional story than previous GTA editions, and was much slower with players able to take in the world and its many optional activities at their own pace. It’s unclear what the pace will be like here, but we did see many such activities, including scuba diving, parachuting, boat racing and visiting strip clubs. Editor's pick Video games Red Dead Redemption 2 review: a Wild West work of art Demand for Rockstar’s new game has been immense, with parent Take-Two already raking in more than $1 billion in pre-orders despite some players grumbling about the $130 price, some game features being locked behind the $160 Ultimate Edition, and the lack of an option to buy it on disc. Similarly, although some people were upset that the new video was exclusive to Netflix (it will be posted on YouTube on Friday at 11am), interest was high enough that the streaming service briefly crashed at 5am when the footage made its debut. World.title: Unemployed and unpaid: what the fate of sacked Qantas workers tells us
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAviation Opinion Unemployed and unpaid: what the fate of sacked Qantas workers tells us Chris Zappone Senior reporter, aviation August 28, 2026 — 11:00am

August 28, 2026 — 11:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

What do Qantas, labour law firm Maurice Blackburn or the Transport Workers’ Union have in common? None would tolerate a lengthy delay, with little explanation given, if they were in line to get a significant sum of compensation for an egregious, life-altering breach of their rights. Justice Michael Lee demanded an explanation from Maurice Blackburn when it asked for more time to distribute funds. Dominic Lorrimer But this isn’t the case for the 1822 illegally sacked Qantas workers who were turfed out of their jobs during the COVID-19 pandemic. They have been promised $35 million in penalty payments and $120 million from a compensation fund - both amounts paid up by Qantas in 2025. Six years after wrongly being forced out of work by the airline, five years after the move was ruled illegal, and almost two years after a major chunk of the compensation was first agreed, they still haven’t been paid.



And the wait goes on. Related Article Aviation ‘Chapter of Genesis’: Judge gets biblical over sacked Qantas workers It’s hard to imagine the other protagonists in this saga being forced to accept their fate as blindly as these workers. It took intervention from Justice Michael Lee of the Federal Court earlier this month to ensure the workers’ $35 million in penalty payments were decoupled from the $120 million compensation fund that has become mired in technicalities, allowing the smaller chunk of money to be paid out quickly. Maurice Blackburn had represented the TWU and its members in its case against Qantas, and then oversaw the administration of the employees’ compensation. After nailing the case, the firm has fumbled the administration.



When Maurice Blackburn informed Lee of a delay in the weeks preceding the July 31 deadline, he immediately ordered a hearing to ask why the firm hadn’t advised the court of the hitches as soon as possible? Why, in other words, did there appear to be so little urgency from the class action giant that brands itself as “fighting for fair”? Maurice Blackburn’s lawyers explained that the process got hung up both by a string of legally insufficient independent medical assessments of the fired workers and questions about how to repay Services Australia for treatment the employees had already accessed. There is a tension between the lawful requirement for accurate compensation based on a worker’s history, and a more timely resolution, but why not tell the judge about the issue and sort it out? As Lee said on August 6: “One can’t let the perfect be the enemy of the good.” Many of the 1800 sacked Qantas workers have taken a financial punch from their dismissal and not really recovered. A large proportion of them are doing so late in their careers when their options are constrained. Getting compensation isn’t just about the elegance of justice; the money is needed to inject some financial breathing space into their lives. On August 6, Lee told the sacked workers, “Your payment will be made within the next few business days into the bank account you previously provided to Maurice Blackburn.”



Related Article Aviation Alan Joyce has been writing his book. Here’s how five people illegally sacked by his airline have fared He appointed another firm, William Roberts Lawyers, in August to oversee the fine component of the case, such was Lee’s apparent level of faith in the larger firm. But even that has led to a further delay, albeit for a good cause. On Thursday, William Roberts Lawyers asked for another delay to the payments so that it could include more ex-workers, or their heirs. One ex-employee, Ryan Perrett, told the hearing that the money should be split equally among all affected workers, noting (in a very AI-era sentiment) that younger workers would get a bigger share, but they anyway will have “missed out on a larger opportunity to work further into the future”.



Payments now appear to be on track to come after September 1. The payout scheme’s long tail is emblematic of a broader reality. If people at the more modest end of the economy don’t see civil society working for them, politicians and business leaders can’t expect those same workers to uphold the status quo. That disjunct might be the bitter aftertaste of the largest corporate fine in Australia’s history. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion.
