World.title: Brilliant or boring? The verdict on Rachel Cusk’s new novel
World.content:
CultureBooksReview Brilliant or boring? The verdict on Rachel Cusk’s new novel Miranda Darling August 28, 2026 — 11:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Reading Rachel Cusk’s Life of M is a destabilising experience. The pages shadow you; the strange discomfort of their atmosphere lingers – as intended, surely, as most specifically intended. This is Cusk, after all, and her writing is no one’s comfort zone. Life of M has provoked much debate “in real life”, fed by the supposedly furious reactions of the famous actress whom “M” is allegedly based on, with entertainment channels thrilling about a feud between the writer and the Hollywood superstar. Outrage is performed, and it’s VERY EXCITING; more stories probe the line (maybe it’s more of a demilitarised zone) between what’s acceptable and what’s not when turning a famous life into fiction. The actress’ friends are said to be incandescent; others call out Cusk’s novel as a “cheap publicity stunt”, as if this were a brand-new form of intrusion, an unprecedented liberty taken. In other words, it’s difficult to read Life of M on the page alone, to experience it without the subsonic thrumming of this parallel storyline creating and/or revealing a whole other dimension to the novel. Rachel Cusk’s new novel has attracted attention well beyond the page. It took me a while to finish. After an enthusiastic dive into the familiar spartan beauty of Cusk’s sentences I found myself reacting with a mix of frustration, incredulity, boredom and confusion. I resisted reading for a few days while I unravelled my reluctance. Then I realised that the interesting dance was taking place off the page, that the novel was a commentary and a mirror, a performance, a provocation and a participation, all at once. We are warned in the very first paragraph: “Would you just make it up? she said.” Many scenes do feel “made up” in the sense that they feel clichéd, like the work of a lazy writer skimming the well-worn surface of things – the fashion model in the bookstore stood out as a clanger. Other scenes have descriptions of tables and glass tumblers and flowers that have a flatness to them, a banality, almost a Dick-and-Jane quality: “They are filled with books but also with other things, perhaps put there in haste to clear the room: [a list follows].”



The reminder that Cusk’s writing can be electrifying bursts in occasionally. Describing an art exhibition that M attends, there is a sudden rush of blood and life in the writing. The warning is there: Cusk is a fantastic, whip-smart writer who doesn’t ask to be liked, and we underestimate her at our peril. It remains, though, that Life of M presents more surface: the occasional descriptions of ugliness as some form of antidote fail to fragment the power of “seems”. The theatre director who chooses to pay no attention to his appearance as a statement of his power opens a small and interesting thematic door that the narrator fails to walk through. Indeed, in their brittle self-regard, the narrator resembles M to the point that we almost have a conflation. (This resonates if the narrator is indeed “making it all up”.) I found myself reacting with a mix of frustration, incredulity, boredom and confusion. I resisted reading for a few days while I unravelled my reluctance. Complicity runs through the work. The novel begins with first-person narration, and the ground seems solid. Early references to “we” appear initially to refer to the narrator and a partner; the use of the first-person plural then becomes increasingly claustrophobic until it becomes clear we are now dealing with a single entity of sorts that could very well include us, the “we” retaining the intimacy afforded by “I” yet adding a layer of reader inclusion. “We” unfixes the point of view. It can be read as a self-aggrandising royal “we” as a pretentious affectation, or a distancing from the earlier authorial “I”; “we” might be a comment on how completely we give over our identities to a partner that even childhoods blur into a shared space; it could suggest a mild psychosis, or offer a comment on the ubiquitous reach of non-binary pronouns. Very possibly and likely, all of the above and more are in play. Related Article Opinion

Literature Is Rachel Cusk’s new novel a ruthless betrayal of Natalie Portman? Jane Sullivan Books columnist and reviewer The novel provokes and performs a destabilisation of “truth” that goes beyond an unreliable narrator. It pulls us as readers into a co-creation that is fed by our own half-knowledge and dark assumptions. It’s all through the book: “People begin to see her, as though she were an image developing out of their own knowledge. She sometimes wonders whether it is she who needs this process to occur.”





Life of M by Rachel Cusk is published by Faber ($33) on September 1. The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: Another sorry from Christopher Luxon after beneficiaries miss out
World.content:
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon has apologised after people's benefits were wrongly suspended because officials were overwhelmed with paperwork.

But he's standing by his statement to Parliament that had not happened, saying it was correct at the time.

RNZ on Thursday revealed people had their benefit payments wrongly suspended following a law change that was rushed through Parliament last year.

The new law requires some beneficiaries to re-confirm their circumstances at least once every 52 weeks, to check whether they are still eligible.

The Ministry of Social Development (MSD) said processing delays caused by a high volume of people confirming their circumstances meant some of their paperwork was not checked in time, so their benefit payments stopped.

That same law change had also caused a separate issue: thousands of pensioners missed out on their Winter Energy Payment, because that payment was incorrectly included in the legislation.

Louise Upston. RNZ / Mark Papalii

Luxon and the Social Development Minister Louise Upston apologised for the missing Winter Energy Payments last week.

On Friday Luxon also said sorry for the second problem.

"There's clearly an issue, our job is to fix it ... I apologise for it, I'm sorry that it's happened," he said.

"It's really disappointing to see that there are further issues there."

Luxon said he was focused on ensuring people got the money they were owed, and that the underlying problem was fixed.

MSD said everyone had been paid back, and there were no longer processing delays.

Luxon last week told Parliament he was confident that no beneficiaries had lost payments due to processing delays.

"My statement was correct at the time," he said on Friday, adding that he had only found out about the problem on Friday morning.

Meanwhile Social Development Minister Louise Upston refused to comment on her statements in Parliament.

On Tuesday she was asked whether benefits had wrongly been suspended due to processing delays.

Upston said no, but changed her answer to "possibly" after multiple further questions.

RNZ asked whether Upston would clarify her statements.

World.title: Flynn McBride, 20, named as man killed in crash south of Whangārei
World.content:
Police have named a person who died following a single-vehicle crash in Northland, south of Whangārei last Friday.

He was Flynn Joseph McBride, 20, of Dargaville.

Emergency services attended the crash on Maungakaramea Road, Maungakaramea on 21 August.

Police said enquiries into the circumstances of the crash remained ongoing.

In a public social media post on McBride's page, his family said he was a "beloved son, brother, grandson, nephew, partner, friend and workmate, and his loss has left an enormous hole in the lives of everyone who knew and loved him."

"Flynn lived his life doing the things he loved, surrounded by the people who meant so much to him. On the day he passed, he spent his time doing something he loved - fishing. We take comfort in knowing that he was doing something that made him happy.

"Flynn had a huge personality and touched so many people's lives. Whether you knew him through family friends, work, the car scene or simply crossed paths with him, we know there are many people who will be feeling this loss."

His funeral would be held on Friday, August 28 at Sacred Heart Catholic Parish. Corner of Hokianga Rd and Charlotte St, Dargaville.

World.title: Car seen 'bolting up' street before gunshots heard in Wattle Downs suspected double homicide
World.content:
A man who lives near a South Auckland home where a woman and a man were found dead on Thursday says he saw a car "bolting up the street" before hearing gunshots.

Police say they are speaking with a 30-year-old male - who is in their custody - in relation to the double homicide.

It comes after police continued their hunt for those responsible.

Detective Inspector Tofilau Faamanuia Va'aelua of Counties Manukau CIB said police are working to determine if the 30-year-old was involved.

"Police will provide further updates as they are available."

A neighbour, who only wished to use his first name Robbie, said he was outside having a cigarette when the incident unfolded.

"We hear a car come bolting up the street and he stopped in front of that house there," he said.

"He slammed on the brakes, got out ran up the drive and all we hear after that is 'pop, pop, pop, pop'."

Robbie said he then heard the car driving away and then the sound of a woman screaming.

He said when police officers arrived, they surrounded the house and asked its occupants to come out and identify themselves.

"This was going on for 20 minutes, and nobody was coming out."

He said the two people who died had only moved to the street last week, and he briefly spoke to them for the first time on Wednesday.

He said he was in shock about what happened to them.

Early on Friday morning, two police officers with rifles were outside the cordoned-off home.

Police at the scene on Friday morning. RNZ / Jessica Hopkins

Police forensic and crime scene officers were also seen putting on shoe covers and entering the home just before 6.30am.

Emergency services responded to reports of a woman unresponsive at an address on Gambare Place about 1.45pm on Thusday.

The woman was pronounced dead at the scene and, during a search of the property, police found a man who was also pronounced dead.

Va'aelua said the offender or offenders fled the scene prior to officers arriving.

On Thursday evening, armed police stood guard in front of the house, as neighbours looked on.

RNZ / Jessica Hopkins

Dianna Kereopa-Turner had lived in the street her whole life. She told RNZ she had just returned home when "havoc started going on" outside.

"We thought it was our nail gun for our sleepout that we're building going off ... and then it was quite loud," Kereopa-Turner said.

"But no, it was shooting. All we heard was gun. Then my sister came out of her room and said 'somebody out there's shooting', so we gathered in whoever was loose around the house and stayed inside."

She said the victims had only just moved in to the street: "It's sad to know that whatever trouble was following them, obviously followed them right to the doorstep, and unfortunately it happened on this street where there's a lot of kids and a lot of elderly people."

Cordons in place around the house. RNZ / Erin Johnson

Many residents had been unable to return to their homes on Gambare Place and adjoining Volante Avenue while police cordons closed the roads on Thursday afternoon, with armed police stationed at the cordons.

Another Gambare Place resident, Bobbie, said she had been at the doctors and tried to return home around 2.45pm.

"The street was already closed off, so I thought, 'oh better shoot over to the school and pick up my niece', got over there and it was locked down as well."

Bobbie said they were allowed to go home just after 5pm.

She said, once home, she talked with neighbours and some were quite shocked.

While the cordon was in place, police were seen working behind a white tarpaulin on Volante Avenue. Police later confirmed staff had moved the victims to a safe location, away from the scene, to render first aid, while other staff continued working to clear the scene and make it safe.

Va'aelua said the incident appeared to be isolated, but police were not able to "rule anything out", and were now determining the exact circumstances of the incident.

"This is an awful set of events and no doubt unsettling for everyone involved and the wider community."

World.title: 'Major milestone' as Dunedin Hospital outpatient building officially opens
World.content:
Thousands more scans, day surgeries, and specialist appointments will soon be possible in Dunedin each year as its long awaited outpatient building is officially opened.

The new Dunedin Hospital project has faced years of setbacks and cost overruns with a scaled back inpatient building announced in January last year following protests over potential cuts.

But the official opening of the outpatient building on Friday marked a major milestone with a pre-dawn blessing and the name Whare Mātūtū gifted by mana whenua representatives.

The new Dunedin Hospital outpatient building will be opened to the public in October. Supplied / Health New Zealand

'Once-in-a-generation investment'

Health New Zealand chief executive Dr Dale Bramley. Supplied / Te Whatu Ora

Health New Zealand chief executive Dr Dale Bramley said it was one of the largest health infrastructure projects in the country's history.

"This is a once-in-a-generation investment in healthcare, education, and research that will benefit patients, whānau, staff, and communities throughout Otago and Southland for decades to come," he said.

Sprawling across five storeys and 15,000 spare metres, Bramley said the outpatients building was built within its budget - about $440 million - and would begin to provide clinical care to the public from October.

Once fully open, it was expected to support about 1700 more day surgeries, 13,300 additional medical imaging appointments, and 2700 additional medical day stay appointments each year.

Health New Zealand southern group director of operations Craig Ashton says the exact opening date will be shared with the public soon. RNZ / Tess Brunton

Health New Zealand southern group director of operations Craig Ashton said a significant amount of work was underway to install equipment, train staff, commission the building and prepare to welcome patients.

Some of those attending the opening. RNZ / Tess Brunton

This moment had been years in the making but the improvements would help them better respond to the growing demand for healthcare services across the southern region, he said.

"This building will enable us to deliver care in a modern, purpose-built facility, providing greater capacity, improved patient flow, and enhanced clinical facilities that support contemporary models of care.

One of the day surgery rooms. RNZ / Tess Brunton

It would bring specialist outpatient and diagnostic services under the same roof, offering children's and women's health, radiology and imaging services, orthopaedics, ophthalmology, respiratory medicine, physiotherapy, hand therapy, day surgery, and procedure rooms.

"Over time, the additional capacity will support improved access to specialist appointments, diagnostic imaging, elective procedures, and cancer care, benefiting patients across the Southern district."

Other features of the building included co-located radiology and imaging services, coordinated clinics planned centrally and shared across services, and larger purpose-build day surgery theatres and procedure rooms.

There would also be self-service patient check-in, digital wayfinding and queue management as well as reducing the reliance on paper records with electronic referrals, bookings and prescribing, and a South Island regional clinical portal to share electronic records.

Bramley said the digital infrastructure would mean clinicians have faster access to the information they need to deliver care and it would improve navigation, communiation and reduce paperwork for patients.

The outpatient building is fully electric and targeting a five-star Green Star rating.

Simeon Brown speaking at the opening. RNZ / Tess Brunton

Health Minister Simeon Brown said the new outpatient building was a critical investment in modernising healthcare for more than 350,000 people across the southern region.

"It has been purpose-built to support modern models of care, greater use of digital technology and more efficient clinical services, improving both the patient experience and the way our staff work," he said.

Technology was a big focus in the building with a digital network built on more than 150 kilometres of cabling and more than 300 wifi access points, he said.

"This is the digital backbone of a modern hospital, and it is already shaping how we build elsewhere.

"The standards and approach developed here have informed the Nelson and Whangārei redevelopments, reducing duplication and delivering greater consistency across the health system."

RNZ / Tess Brunton

About 3000 people have worked on the new Dunedin Hospital.

Some of the outpatient services would not relocate to the new building until early 2027 with more staff being recruited.

"Every milestone of the New Dunedin Hospital project brings us closer to a modern, fit-for-purpose hospital for the region," he said.

The MRI machine at the new outpatient building. RNZ / Tess Brunton

The exact opening date would be shared before the first patients walked through the doors.

The scaled-back inpatient building, which was an 11-storey, 72,000 square metre facility with an expanded emergency department, and 351 beds with the ability to expand to 404 beds over time - was on track to open in 2031.

An overhead bridge would link the two buildings.

World.title: Pacific maritime centre questions Japan's shipping emissions proposal
World.content:
A Pacific maritime research and policy centre is raising concerns about a Japanese government proposal to the United Nations agency responsible for regulating international shipping.

The Micronesian Center for Sustainable Transport (MCST) in Majuro, the Marshall Islands, released a statement on Japan's revised proposal submitted to the International Maritime Orgainsation (IMO) regarding the decarbonisaiton of the global shipping industry.

The centre said that Japan's submission ahead of the 85th session of the IMO's Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC85) meeting in November proposes "unambitious greenhouse-gas fuel-intensity reduction targets".

It said the proposal also "moves away from a central global carbon fund towards more flexible offsetting, which would also see profit-oriented shipping companies decide which projects globally to invest in".

The MCST said that decision should be made by IMO member states.

IMO Headquarters, London. RNZ Pacific / Kelvin Anthony

The international shipping industry accounts for about 2 to 3 percent of global carbon emissions, with an estimated 911 million tonnes of greenhouse gases emitted in 2023.

Pacific Island countries are among the most shipping-dependent in the world, relying on maritime transport for the vast majority of their food, fuel and essential supplies.

But Pacific economies also face some of the highest shipping costs and most severe impacts of climate change, the centre said.

Its co-director Maria Sahib said the proposed changes would weaken the ambition of the IMO's Net-Zero Framework (NZF) and create significant challenges for Pacific Small Island Developing States (SIDS).

Sahib said the centre was also concerned that moving away from a centrally managed fund and mandatory contribution system for emissions could make support for vulnerable states less predictable.

She said finance was fundamental for the Pacific to achieve a just and equitable maritime transition.

"We need predictable and accessible resources to ensure our countries can decarbonise their maritime sectors while strengthening resilience," she said.

Japan is one of the world's largest ship-owning nations by tonnage. Japanese officials noted in their submission that the revised draft amendments "do not represent the preferences of Japan", according to the maritime platform ENGINE.

The officials said the amendments were intended only as a basis for discussion aimed at reaching a compromise acceptable to all IMO member states.

Sahib said, as the MEPC85 approaches, the Pacific would continue working collectively, through the 6PAC+ group, to ensure that the voices and priorities of SIDS remained central to the IMO's climate negotiations.

The 6PAC+ alliance has maintained this position through successive IMO negotiations, including MEPC82 and MEPC83, where Pacific leaders and delegations pressed for a strong global emissions-pricing mechanism and a transition consistent with the 1.5 degrees Celsius temperature goal.

"The 6PAC+ has demonstrated what Pacific unity can achieve at the IMO," she said.

"We will continue to work together for a framework that delivers ambition, integrity and equity.

"The Pacific cannot support a transition that shifts the costs to those least responsible and least able to absorb them."

World.title: Queenstown residents evacuated as flooding, slips threaten homes
World.content:
Forty-five people were evacuated in Queenstown overnight due to flooding as a significant winter storm battered the South Island.

Fire and Emergency said some properties were evacuated around Fernhill because of concerns about slips and land instability.

Fernhill resident Debra Clarke said her family evacuated last night after water came gushing around her property like a river flooding her home.

There is silt through the house and her freshly landscaped gardens has been ripped up, she said.

Clarke said she had never seen anything like this in 36 years of living in the home.

Queenstown Lakes mayor John Glover said 45 people were evacuated from their homes overnight because of flooding.

People were evacuated from Gorge Road, Fernhill and the Qbox campground in Queenstown and moved into temporary accommodation.

Surface flooding on a road in Queenstown on Friday. RNZ / Katie Todd

Glover said nine homes had been affected by flooding and building inspections would be carried out.

Firefighters went to about 16 flooding jobs during the night across Queenstown, Frankton, Arrrowtown, Wanaka and Lake Hāwea.

In some cases, water went into homes.

Fire and Emergency said there were many other calls about flooded roads and sections that firefighters did not attend.

The South Island has been hit with a massive winter storm that brought heavy rain, flooding, rockfall, slips and snow.

More than 300 millimetres of rain had fallen in Franz Josef while more than 20 centimetres of snow fell in some parts of the South Island on Thursday.

Queenstown Lakes District Council said its emergency operations centre had been busy overnight responding to problems caused by heavy rain.

Surface flooding at the Queenstown Events Centre. Facebook / Queenstown Lakes District Council

It had set up a civil defence welfare hub in Queenstown overnight to support people.

In a social media post, it said multiple slips, washouts, rockfalls, and surface flooding were affecting the roading network, particularly on Haast Pass Road, Luggate Hill, Tarras Road, and Kingston Road.

"Expect delays, traffic management, and ongoing disruptions throughout the day," the post said.

RNZ / Katie Todd

The council was asking people to avoid unnecessary travel and take extra care on the roads.

Surface flooding, debris, and other hazards might still pose some risks, it said.

The Mountain Safety Council has warned of high avalanche danger across the Southern Alps.

The council said naturally triggered avalanches were likely and human-triggered avalanches are very likely across the Arthur's Pass, Aoraki /Mt Cook, Ohau, Queenstown, Wanaka, and Aspiring regions.

Highway closures

State Highway 6 between Makarora and Lake Hāwea has been closed due to a slip on Friday morning.

Motorists were urged to avoid the area or delay their trip.

The Transport Agency said slips, rockfalls and treefalls were a continuing concern.

State Highway 94 to Milford Sound remains closed from the Lower Hollyford Road intersection to Donne River due to the avalanche risk.

It was not expected to reopen until Saturday.

The Crown Range Road was closed on Friday morning between Eastburn Road and Cardrona.

World.title: Search underway after hiker swept down river in Selwyn
World.content:
A search is underway after a man was swept down a river while hiking the Cass-Lagoon Saddle track in Selwyn on Thursday.

The man was attempting to cross the river when he fell and was swept downstream, Christchurch Police Search and Rescue's Detective Cam Ellis said.

"The man's friend was able to make it back to State Highway 73 [West Coast Road], where a concerned passerby has stopped to help and contacted police."

A search of the river and surrounding areas was not successful in finding the man on Thursday and teams continued into the night.

Another search began Friday morning though Ellis said conditions were hazardous.

Police and Land Search and Rescue teams are working through snow, flooded rivers and an alpine environment, he said.

The man's friend was taken to Christchurch Hospital on Thursday with minor injuries.

World.title: Nepal flood: NZ pledges $2 million in humanitarian assistance, search for Kiwis ongoing
World.content:
An immigration checkpoint has reportedly been swept away in Nepal's flash flooding, as family of missing New Zealanders appeal for any information on people in the area.

Five New Zealanders have been reported missing following the flash flood and landslide at the Nepal-China border that has killed more than 380 people, with 1400 missing.

Rajeev Reddy, whose sister Suhasini is one of five missing Kiwis, said he is trying to work out the level of the damage around the immigration checkpoint between Nepal and Tibet, and if anyone was able to make it to higher ground.

"We have confirmed that Suhasini did not cross the border," he wrote on Facebook. "We therefore believe she may have been near the immigration/checkpoint area when the flooding hit."

Former Honorary Consul of Nepal to New Zealand Dinesh Khadka said the checkpoint was completely swept away in the flooding, and nobody has made contact with anyone who was in the area.

A member of the security forces and his sniffer dog search for survivors. PRAKASH MATHEMA / AFP

He said there's no further information on the five missing New Zealanders.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade (MFAT) said it is still waiting for official information from authorities on the ground, as they work to establish the whereabouts of the missing.

"The widespread and significant destruction is likely to mean verified information will take some time to emerge," a spokesperson said.

Consular staff are now on the ground in Kathmandu, working with authorities and partners to urgently gather information and support the affected families.

New Zealand has pledged a $2 million humanitarian assistance package for Nepal, to support the Nepal Red Cross deliver emergency assistance including shelter, water and sanitation, MFAT said.

"Funding will also be made available to other international humanitarian partners with the capacity to provide essential relief and early recover assistance."

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon. RNZ / Nick Monro

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said New Zealand is offering consular support in Nepal and it's happy to "surge" that with more resources.

He did not have any further information about the five New Zealanders missing "apart from to say that we've got consular support in there engaging with authorities".

Luxon also acknowledged thousands of Nepalese people in New Zealand.

"Having spoken to some members of the Nepalese community this morning, you know, there are many families here in New Zealand that are going through high levels of anxiety, understandably, because they're losing, they've lost loved ones at home as well."

Luxon said it was a devastating situation.

Here's what we know about those who are missing following the disaster:

Local residents inspect houses lying deluged in sludge after flash floods at Devighat, Bidur Municipality in Nepal's Nuwakot district. PRABIN RANABHAT / AFP

Hamilton couple was celebrating 50th birthday in Nepal

The son of a Hamilton couple missing following the Nepal flash flood is holding onto hope his parents left the area in the hours before the landslide struck.

Mihir Patel and Kinnari Patel, who own the Best Value Urlich Ave Dairy in Hamilton, were also among the missing New Zealanders.

Their eldest son, Drishya Patel, told RNZ the couple were visiting Nepal to celebrate his mother's upcoming 50th birthday. The couple had been gone for about a week, he said.

"They're just on a trip to go visit some of the mountains in Nepal. It's like a pilgrimage of sorts."

Mihir Patel and Kinnari Patel Supplied

Drishya Patel spoke to his father the day before the flash flood. He said the couple's trip was going "really good".

"They were having a good time."

He last got a message from his mother on WhatsApp about 5.30am local time from Timure.

"Leaving for Kerung," the message said.

The earthquake that triggered the floods occurred at 8.37am local time.

Drishya Patel said he was "shocked" when he first heard the news of the landslide. The family has heard nothing from the couple since.

He hoped that the couple left when they sent the message, about three hours beforehand.

"As long as like they actually did leave when my mum sent me that message, I'm hopeful. These guys tend to run things on time, these tour guides," he said.

"But again, haven't heard anything confirming."

He had spoken with MFAT but "they don't know anything either".

"I don't think I've processed it… realisations slowly setting in as every hour passes, and I don't hear anything, and no one knows anything."

Police personnel rescue stranded residents from a house buried in sludge after flash floods at Trishuli in Nepal's Nuwakot district on August 27, 2026. ARUN SANKAR / AFP

Mother of two missing

Rajeev Reddy earlier told RNZ his sister Suhasini Reddy had been living in Australia for the last four years.

Suhasini Reddy was hiking with a group of friends from Australia with the Kailash Journeys Guides, he said. The floods occurred on day four of the 15-day trip.

He last spoke to his sister the night before the floods, while she was in Kathmandu.

"She was all good, excited," he said.

"She had this trip planned for a while."

Before heading on the trip, Suhasini Reddy visited her parents in India where she left her youngest son. Her other son is with family in Australia.

Rajeev Reddy said the family were desperate for information.

"We actually don't know what's happening ... we're just saying that she'll be okay," he said.

The family appealed for anyone with information about her whereabouts to contact them.

Another missing Kiwi was on pilgrimage

Another New Zealander, Dejan Kuzmic was travelling on the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra, a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, when the disaster struck.

Nepal's Tourist Police confirmed Kuzmic's name to RNZ on Thursday morning.

He was part of the Isha Foundation's Sacred Walks pilgrimage group, which was travelling towards Mount Kailash, revered by Hindus as the abode of Lord Shiva.

An aerial view shows houses lying deluged in sludge after flash floods at Devighat, Bidur Municipality in Nepal's Nuwakot district. PRABIN RANABHAT / AFP

RNZ has also spoken to a family friend, who confirmed the family had been unable to contact Kuzmic since the floods.

"He was part of the Isha Foundation's walk group S3 and was at the border crossing, which was hit quite heavily within a reasonable time, which makes us believe he may have been involved," said Seyed Sepehr Hosseini, whose mother attends a meditation group with Kuzmic.

Hosseini contacted the Isha Foundation, which told him Kuzmic's emergency contacts had been notified.

He also contacted MFAT which said it had opened a consular case for Kuzmic.

Mount Kailash is revered by Hindus as the abode of Lord Shiva, while nearby Lake Mansarovar is also considered sacred.

India's official Kailash Mansarovar Yatra portal describes the pilgrimage as having deep religious and cultural significance.

World.title: Hockeyroos defeated in World Cup semifinal
World.content:
The Hockeyroos have missed out on their dream of making another World Cup final after their improbable run to the semis was sunk by a late goal in a 1-0 defeat to Argentina.

Australia's women's hockey team, hoping to make it to the final for the first time in 12 years on Thursday (Friday AEST), were sunk by a fourth-quarter penalty corner from Julieta ⁠Jankunas in the 47th minute of their last-four clash in Wavre, Belgium.

The Australians had enjoyed an almost unprecedented run to this stage, being the first side in 40 years to make it to the semis by winning just one match, having also lost one and drawn three at the tournament co-hosted by the Netherlands and Belgium.

The Hockeyroos' resilience, in evidence throughout the competition, served them well as they kept battling into the dying seconds but they were eventually to fall short in their bid to win the World Cup for a third time.

Argentina will now meet the Netherlands in Saturday's (Sunday AEST) final after the Dutch had earlier beaten their co-hosts Belgium ​1-0 in a home tie in Amstelveen to proceed to their eighth successive final.

It will be a repeat of the 2022 final when the Dutch beat Argentina ‌3-1 in ‌Spain.

The all-conquering Dutch, who are also European and Olympic champions, will be hot favourites to take a fourth successive ​title and a record-extending 10th overall.

Frederique Matla's ‌28th-minute goal ‌from ⁠a quick counter-attack saw the Dutch through, but Belgium felt they had equalised five minutes from the end through Famke van Heel.

But the goal was disallowed by ‌VAR after what was ruled an obstruction by a Belgian ​teammate in ‌the circle, much to their frustration.

AAP

World.title: New captain and changes in scrum as Wallabies name side to face Argentina
World.content:
The Wallabies have named an all-new starting front row for the first Test against Argentina, with stalwart Allan Alaalatoa taking over the captaincy.

Australia has two Tests against Los Pumas in Argentina, with the first match being played on Sunday morning AEST.

Wallabies coach Les Kiss has kept the same starting backline that soundly defeated Japan in Townsville earlier this month, while Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii is returning from injury and will come off the bench.

Up front, Isaac Kailea has his first start in two years at loosehead prop, while Brandon Paenga-Amosa starts at hooker and Alaalatoa at tighthead.

Usual captain Harry Wilson has been rotated out of the side, as Kiss cycles through his stocks ahead of next year's home World Cup.

Rob Valetini lines up at number eight in place of Wilson, with Tom Hooper starting for the first time this year at blindside flanker. Queensland Reds star Fraser McReight starts at openside flanker, after coming off the bench in Townsville against Japan.

Argentina has named the same starting side that was defeated by world champions South Africa earlier this month.

Los Pumas enter this two-Test series against the Wallabies with several key players unavailable after facing the Wallabies in 2025.

Captain Julián Montoya, flanker Marcos Kremer and backs Mateo Carreras, Santiago Chocobares, Bautista Delguy are all unavailable.

Juan Martin Gonzalez, Juan Cruz Mallia and Pedro Rubiolo, who also faced the Wallabies in 2025, are injured.

The Wallabies are on a three-Test winning streak after two wins over Japan earlier this month, and a thumping 57-10 win over Italy in Perth in July.

Argentina has played four Tests in 2026, all at home, with just one win.

Los Pumas were defeated by Scotland and England, but defeated Wales during July's Nations Championship.

The South Americans then lost a standalone Test match to South Africa, pushing the world champions to a 17-10 defeat.

The Wallabies and Los Pumas each claimed a victory in the two matches played on Australian soil during last year's Rugby Championship.

In 2024, both nations also traded victories in the two matches played in Argentina.

WALLABIES (15-1): 15-Tom Wright, 14-Max Jorgensen, 13-Isaac Henry, 12-Hunter Paisami, 11-Harry Potter, 10-Carter Gordon, 9-Ryan Lonergan, 8-Rob Valetini, 7-Fraser McReight, 6-Tom Hooper, 5-Jeremy Williams, 4-Josh Canham, 3-Allan Alaalatoa (captain), 2-Brandon Paenga-Amosa, 1-Isaac Kailea

Replacements: 16-Billy Pollard, 17-Angus Bell, 18-Massimo de Lutiis, 19-Lachlan Shaw, 20-Charlie Cale, 21-Tate McDermott, ⁠22-Ben Donaldson, 23-Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii.

ARGENTINA (15-1): 15-Geronimo Prisciantelli, 14-Rodrigo Isgro, 13-Lucio Cinti, 12-Faustino Sanchez Valarolo, 11-Ignacio Mendy, 10-Santiago Carreras, 9-Simon Benitez Cruz, 8-Joaquin Moro, 7-Benjamin Grondona, 6-Pablo Matera (captain), 5-Tomas Lavanini, 4-Guido Petti, 3-Francisco Moreno, 2-Ignacio Ruiz, 1-Boris Wenger

Replacements: 16-Leonel Oviedo, 17-Rodrigo Martinez, 18-Tomas Rapetti, 19-Efraín Elias, 20-Juan Penoucos, 21-Agustín Moyano, 22-Nicolas Roger, 23-Matias Moroni

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the first Test between the Wallabies and Argentina from 4am on Sunday, August 30.

World.title: 'I'm only human': Fremantle star Jackson dreaming of Dockers' maiden flag
World.content:
Luke Jackson has already been to the top of the AFL mountain.

In just his second season, the ruckman was part of the Melbourne side that ended a 57-year premiership drought.

He has not forgotten what that was like, and is desperate to deliver Fremantle's first-ever AFL crown.

Loading Instagram content

"I'm a WA boy, grew up here. I supported Freo when I was a kid," Jackson said as the Dockers started preparations for a qualifying final against Hawthorn next Thursday night.

"To be in that first group that hopefully does it, yeah, you'll be remembered forever.

"I was in and around Freo my whole life so I'm very determined to get there.

"I know it's going to be a lot of hard work, but if anyone can do it, it's the people at this club."

Luke Jackson has already won one premiership, with Melbourne in 2021. Can he land another? (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

Fremantle has already produced a historic season, winning a club-record 14 consecutive games on the way to recording more wins in a single season than ever before.

The Dockers finished two games clear of Sydney at the top of the ladder, earning two home finals and the double-chance.

With almost no injury concerns, and having beaten every side in the competition, Fremantle are rightfully among the favourites for the premiership.

Jackson has allowed himself to imagine lifting the cup, despite coach Justin Longmuir's best efforts to keep the playing squad focused on the task at hand.

Luke Jackson has been one of the best players in the AFL this season. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Janelle St Pierre)

"I personally let myself dream a little bit. I'm only human," he said.

"You definitely think about those things.

"JL (Longmuir) has been amazing. Ever since I've been at Freo, that's probably been his biggest strength, I reckon, is helping us stay in the moment.

Justin Longmuir has enjoyed his best season as an AFL coach, putting Fremantle in pole position to win its first flag. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

"He is very process-driven and yeah, makes it very clear for us week to week. We know the job this week and then obviously next week heading into Thursday."

All Australian cherished

Jackson produced an incredible 2025 which saw him win 17 Brownlow Medal votes, but he was overlooked for the All Australian side.

He took his game to another level in 2026, in which he produced career highs in disposals, goals, hit outs, tackles, clearances and contested possessions.

Luke Jackson has had a stellar season, culminating in his first All Australian blazer. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

He was also named in the All Australian side for the first time, alongside teammates Josh Treacy, Shai Bolton, Murphy Reid and Jordan Clark.

"You obviously don't play to get All Australians, but to be recognised by high-level people in the game and be up there with the best players, it's something I cherish," Jackson said.

Luke Jackson is keeping his eye firmly on the prize. (AAP: Richard Wainwright)

But while he's happy to be recognised for his performance this year, Jackson has his eye on a bigger prize.

"What everyone plays for, what everyone wants, is obviously the flag. And at Freo, we're very determined to be that first group that can do it [for the club]," he said.

"I think those things just come along the way, the All Australians and stuff like that, when you put in the work and play well. But the main goal is the premiership."

Jackson was named in the AA team alongside his former mentor and Melbourne great, Max Gawn, who claimed a record ninth blazer.

Loading Instagram content

For Jackson, it is something to aspire to.

Hird has chance to finally deliver true unity Essendon seeks James Hird may not have received his dream outcome, but still has the ability to lend his beloved club a big hand if he chooses to do so.

"I had the privilege of playing with Maxie early on, my first three years at Melbourne," he said.

"He taught me heaps as well in that ruck position and to see him still going as strong as he is now, it's definitely something you look up to.

"It's the consistency with Maxie I think is unreal. He might have had his best season yet.

"Personally, I look up to him and hopefully I can keep playing consistent footy like that in the years to come."

For now though, Jackson's focus is simple — delivering a historic premiership to the Purple Army.

World.title: Two world records broken within an hour, Aussie soars to high jump win
World.content:
Brazil's Alison dos Santos and American Masai Russell have both shattered world records in the hurdles at the Zurich Diamond League, producing a stunning night of athletics in Switzerland.

Dos Santos broke the men's 400 metres hurdles mark on Thursday, local time, pulling away over the final 100m to clock 45.80 seconds and better Karsten Warholm's previous world record of 45.94, set at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021.

Warholm finished second in 46.69.

"The crowd and the energy were perfect. I think this night was amazing for me, for those who came to watch; I did it for everybody," dos Santos said, as reported by BBC Sport.

"I hope that Brazil stopped to watch this as much as the people here in the stadium. This has been an incredible night. I have no words to explain what happened other than I just broke the world record.

"I was looking for my coach since I crossed the finish line. I was the one running, but he is the one who made this possible, someone who believed in me when I was younger.

"He helped me to develop both as an athlete and as a person, too. He's like an older brother, like a dad to me."

Olympic champion Russell set a world record of her own in the women's 100m hurdles, powering over the final barrier to clock 12.09 and erase the previous mark of 12.12 set by Nigeria's Tobi Amusan in 2022.

The 26-year-old Dos Santos has long been one of the few men capable of challenging Warholm's supremacy in the event, winning world gold in 2022 and silver in 2025, while claiming Olympic bronze in both Tokyo and Paris.

On a night when much of the build-up focused on a potential assault on the women's 800m world record, Dos Santos delivered an early headline performance, surging clear of Warholm off the final bend to extend his perfect record against the Norwegian this season to five victories from five races.

Meanwhile, Australian Nicola Olyslagers has soared back to her world champion best to win the women's high jump.

After a disappointing season in which she lost her Commonwealth title to teammate Eleanor Patterson, Olyslagers produced her best form with a season's best 2.02 metres to win by 2 centimetres from Ukrainian Iryna Gerashchenko.

Patterson and Ukraine's Olympic champion Yaroslava Mahuchikh both cleared 1.96m and settled for fourth and joint-sixth places, respectively.

Olyslagers revealed afterwards her victory had been down to ditching a new run-up, which she finally decided at the weekend was not working.

"It took me some time to reflect," she said after another disappointing outing in Poland at the weekend. "I decided it does not work, so within four days, I had to try to relearn in my head what I did last year to jump my lifetime best 2.04m here.

"When I felt the track, I knew it was the same feeling as last year in the street meet. After I cleared two metres at the first attempt, I knew I was in shape. It was amazing."

Among other excellent Australian performances, Cam Myers got involved in the shake-up in the 3000m, clocking 7:27.97, but ending up pipped in the denouement by American duo Parker Wolfe (meeting record 7:27.43) and Graham Blanks (7:27.92).

Jess Hull, fifth in 1:58.24, tested her speed out in a lightning 800m won by Swiss heroine Audrey Werro, who clocked a world-leading 1:53.70.

Torrie Lewis was second in a non-Diamond League 200m, clocking just outside her season's best in 22.66 seconds behind Swiss winner Fabienne Hoenke (22.53).

Saint Lucia's Olympic champion Julien Alfred also served notice ahead of next month's World Athletics Ultimate Championships, winning the women's 100m in a national record 10.70 seconds.

American Melissa Jefferson-Wooden matched Alfred's time, with the result decided by photo finish, while Sha'Carri Richardson was third in 10.97.

Kenya's Emmanuel Wanyonyi won the men's 800m in 1:41.76 — the fastest time in the world this season — for his second successive Diamond League victory.

He edged Djamel Sedjati of Algeria, who finished in 1:41.83.

Reuters/ABC.A/P

World.title: De Minaur gets qualifier in first round as US Open draw announced
World.content:
Alex de Minaur appears to have been given a kind draw for the year's final grand slam, but Australia's perennial hope will face a precociously formidable obstacle if he wants to make it to the quarterfinals for the third straight year.

The world number six will face a qualifier in the opening round, with the final rounds of qualifying still to be played.

Should De Minaur get through a qualifier in the first round, he could be set up for clashes with Dutchman Botic van de Zandschulp in the second round, and a potential third-round duel with 31st seed Belgian Zizou Bergs.

Demon heading home for Davis Cup tie Alex de Minaur will return to Australia off the back of his US Open campaign to lead the Aussie charge in a Davis Cup clash in Brisbane.

Should de Minaur make it past round three, he is in line for a potential fourth-round clash with world number 13 Rafael Jódar, the brilliant 19-year-old Spaniard who crushed de Minaur in their only meeting at the Madrid Open on clay in April and who has since made giant strides on hard courts too.

The winner of that match would meet number one Alexander Zverev in the quarterfinal, assuming this year's French Open champion wins his opening four matches at Flushing Meadows in New York.

Jódar will meet another Australian, Thanasi Kokkinakis, who is battling back from injuries and is on a protected ranking, in the first round.

Others among the 13-strong Aussie contingent — which could be increased as three more were seeking qualification in Thursday's final round — had tough draws, with Rinky Hijikata first up against Canadian third seed Felix Auger-Aliassime and James Duckworth facing Italian 30th seed Matteo Arnaldi.

Novak Djokovic, down to number five in the rankings, launches his bid for a record-setting 25th slam singles crown against Argentina's tough world number 48 Mariano Navone.

Newly restored as Australian women's number one, Daria Kasatkina has been handed a bit of a horror run, with former world number two Paula Badosa, now down to 83rd in the rankings after injury woes, representing a dangerous first-round barrier.

If Kasatkina negotiates that, she will likely face former champion Coco Gauff in the second round.

Maya Joint will have her hands full again with Liudmila Samsonova, the big-hitting Russian who defeated her at the Canadian Open earlier in the month and at Wimbledon last year.

Defending champion and world number one Aryna Sabalenka, who has been ailing, opens against Colombia's Camila Osorio.
