World.title: How the 'world champion persona' didn't come overnight for Matt Hauser
World.content:
Matt Hauser has delivered Australia back to the top of world triathlon.

His sensational victory on home soil at Wollongong ended a 15-year title drought for Australia.

But he knows that the race that matters is not for another two years, when he takes to the start line in Los Angeles at the 2028 Olympic Games.

Heading into the next leg of the World Triathlon Championship Series in Weihai on August 29, Hauser sits in third place in the standings.

Only Brazil's Miguel Hidalgo and Portugal's Vasco Vilaça are ahead of him, having completed four races to the Australian's three.

But Hauser has won each of those three events, recording race victories in Yokohama, Hamburg and London.

Matt Hauser (left) ran clear of Brazil's world championship series leader Miguel Hidalgo in Yokohama. (Getty Images: Nobuo Yano)

His current success makes him the number one target for the entire field, something that still takes some getting used to.

"It's a bit of a pinch me moment, honestly," Hauser told ABC Sport at the AusTriathlon Performance Hub at Miami on Queensland's Gold Coast.

"It just feels quite surreal to now be at the top of my game and I keep kind of pinching myself, knowing that this won't last forever, so I really need to take a step back and realise that I'm one of the best, if not the best in the world at the moment in my sport, and I need to try and capitalise on that and make sure the opportunities that I have I made the most of."

Hauser's climb to the top of the world is far from an overnight success story though — the ascendancy to the summit in sport's as gruelling as triathlon are rarely straightforward.

"It doesn't feel like a big sudden jump though, to be honest," Hauser says.

"It feels like a lot of smaller goals and processes have added up to accumulate to this world champion persona, I guess.

"For me to be in this position now is just a credit to the support I've had around me, to Dan Atkins, who I've been coached under for 10 years now.

"The relationship that we've kind of developed and the systems we've put in place to create daily performance environments right here on the Gold Coast has been super important."

Matt Hauser was the first Australian male world triathlon champion in 20 years. (AAP: Dean Lewins)

Hauser has taken charge of the triathlon scene in the time immediately after the Paris Olympics.

And it's been of huge inspiration to the next crop of Australia's triathlon talent that is coming through.

"Looking back at Australia's history in triathlon, it's so rich, and now we're definitely stepping up our game," 19-year-old rising star Aspen Anderson told ABC Sport.

Why this future star has 'goosebumps' over triathlon's future As AusTriathlon launches its High Performance Hub on the Gold Coast, one of the sport's rising stars is dreaming of success at Brisbane 2032.

"Matt's definitely led the way in that aspect. And I think it's really cool to see him paving the way for some of us.

"It's really exciting. You can kind of look at them and say, well, yeah, if they can do it, then I can do it too."

While gold medallist Alex Yee has been off running marathons (Yee set the second fastest time ever by a British man after Mo Farah with a 2:06:38) and silver medallist Hayden Wilde has dabbled in longer-distance triathlons as part of the T100 series, Hauser has been honing his race craft on the world series.

On the women's side, Olympic champion Cassandre Beaugrand has shown her running prowess by setting French records in the 3,000m and 5,000m on the track and in a 10km road race, also competing at athletics' highest level, the Diamond League.

"It's very inspiring to see those guys go off and do what they do outside of the sport," Hauser said.

"Ultimately, it props the sport up to a new level as well, getting that recognition that we are world-class athletes in most of the three disciplines.

"For me, I guess it's just about making sure that I'm perfecting my skills in triathlon. I think the sport has grown and developed so much even in the past two years since those guys have gone off and done other things … the sport has always changed and is developing."

Matt Hauser has been able to lay down an awesome pace on the bike to put pain into the legs of his opponents. (Getty Images: picture alliance/Philipp Szyza)

Balancing three very different sports is a challenge that triathletes have to juggle with every year.

Go too hard on the upper-body dominant swimming training and the extra weight will hurt on the bike and run legs.

Become too strong on the run and swim speed can be sacrificed — the old adage that you can't win the race in the swim but you can definitely lose it is drummed into triathletes from the first moment they pull on a pair of goggles.

Finding the right balance is tough, but it is crucial to how Hauser has developed his craft as an elite triathlete.

For a while, it felt like triathlon was developing into a sport for runners, where races would largely be contested as a pack through the swim and bike before the runners blew the legs off the rest to claim victory.

That has, however, been changing somewhat in recent years, with Hauser taking the charge right from the gun, powering into a lead through the swim and bike to erase the advantages of the runners in the back end of the race.

Matt Hauser claimed yet another victory at Hamburg, his third in a row. (Getty Images: picture alliance/Philipp Szyza)

It's not dissimilar to how British two-time Olympic champion Alistair Brownlee and his three-time Olympic medallist brother Jonathan would race at their peak.

"The dynamics change from year to year," Hauser explained.

"The Brownlees coined their swim-bike breakaways and were able to produce amazing runs off the back of that and split the race apart from the start.

"Then you had the likes of [three time World Series champion Spaniard] Mario Mola and [Australia's Tokyo Olympian] Jake Burtwistle and those stronger runners coming from behind and those packs really being quite large and condensed.

"Now we're kind of seeing the front pack and the breakaways kind of come to fruition again, so I think it all comes and goes in waves.

"The way the races have kind of panned out the last couple of years … for me to drive at the front pack and maybe limit the strengths of those stronger runners and the pack behind has been really crucial to me succeeding.

"There's a lot of momentum now and there's a lot of belief that you don't have to be like one of the best runners to win a race now."

Hauser will be hoping that his brand of racing will take him to success in LA.

Australia has only ever won a single gold in triathlon at the Olympics, when Emma Snowsill triumphed in Beijing.

Emma Snowsill won Australia's only Olympic gold medal in triathlon. (Getty Images: PA Images/John Walton)

Michellie Jones, Loretta Harrop, Emma Moffatt and Erin Densham have all won medals for Australia at the Games.

However, no Australian man has ever stood on the podium at the Olympics.

"I think the Olympics is always in the back of my mind," Hauser said.

"When I'm executing at world championship races, other races, training day to day, I think it's always in the back of my mind and I know that the process for me to be at a peak in two years time is gaining experience in these few years leading up.

"Only a few years ago I was able to perform but not consistently enough to call myself a front runner.

"So now, to be at the stage where I'm performing consistently, I'm at the top end of races.

"I need to make that normal in my own mind and so when it comes to two years time and executing in LA, I just have to execute what I've been doing the last few years.

"So definitely it is in the back of my mind always, trying to peak for one race every four years.

"But I know the process along the way is just as important, to make sure I've got enough notches in the belt to when that day comes, I can execute on the day, whether it be an excellent performance or an average performance, I know that I'm still going to perform in a high quality."

The World Triathlon Championship Series is set to take place in Weihai, China, on August 29, with the series final in Pontevedra, Spain, on September 23.

World.title: Breaking down the brilliance of Nick Daicos, and how to stop it
World.content:
Sit long enough in the outer of a footy game and the hot takes will start flying fast. Sometimes they start out innocuous, like about how much they should just kick the bloody thing.

But usually things get interesting as the game gets deeper. Opinions on the state of the world — both footy and real — usually proliferate conversation in the lulls of the action.

Differing views of one player tend to come up perhaps more than any other footy-based topic — the player in Collingwood's number 35 guernsey.

"I am on record as saying that Daicos is the best player in the comp," Geelong coach Chris Scott told the media ahead of their game against Collingwood last month.

At just 23 years old, Nick Daicos has achieved more than most players do across an entire career. Daicos is already a premiership-winning four-time All Australian. This year Daicos has already won the Coaches Association and Players' Association MVPs (his second of each), and is a heavy favourite for Collingwood's Copeland Trophy.

Despite starting this year off slowly, he has already been deemed by many to be the presumptive Brownlow Medallist and a chance to break the all-time record for votes under the current system.

Both Collingwood and Daicos have kicked into another gear after the bye, entrenching themselves in the finals race for yet another season.

"He's that diligent and professional in his game, and his desire to win," Collingwood coach Craig McRae told the media last week.

"His game's gone to another level. He takes us to places that we want to get to."

More importantly, Nick Daicos may be the single most exciting player to watch in football. If you had to recommend the highlights of one current player to watch for anyone new to the sport, Daicos is probably the choice.

Yet Daicos has not been above criticism from some corners of footy fandom. Some armchair critics deride the "soft" ball that he wins. Others poke at other parts of his game, or compare him to greats of eras past. At the same time, those in black and white are already calling for Daicos to be considered on track to be one of the greatest ever.

This weekend sees Daicos come head-to-head with another player often tabbed as the best player in the game; the Bulldogs' Marcus Bontempelli. For each player and their sides, they could be playing the last game of 2026 unless they can demonstrate something special.

Form and function

The famed architect Frank Lloyd Wright said that form and function are in union, not separate concepts.

Most football players follow this conceptual framework. If Errol Gulden is like the Opera House, Sam Collins is more like Scrivener Dam. Both fit their form to the function required.

There are few more aesthetically striking players from a footballing perspective than Nick Daicos across the history of the game. Some may opt for a Gary Ablett or Andrew McLeod. Generations earlier would have named Haydn Bunton and John Coleman. A select few might even nominate the elder Daicos, Peter. In style if not impact, Daicos is already in illustrious company.

Daicos glides over the turf, with his feet seemingly barely touching the surface. Defenders often fall by the wayside, not through contact but instead from movement, endurance and pure speed. If Daicos gets a centimetre of spare grass ahead of him, he'll take a kilometre.

To co-opt the language of the young, his bag is deep.

Daicos's visual appeal — the form — matches his function on the field. Daicos's job is to attack at all costs and to drive the ball forward.

Collingwood looks to get Daicos the ball at ground level at every opportunity they can. In open play, they look to feed him via hand, whether it's peeling around the man on the mark or as a floating target around the ground. Daicos's running ability means that he is usually able to create separation from any trailing opponent. Every Pie looks to handball it to Daicos more than any other teammate.

No player in the league is involved in a larger share of his team's scores. Daicos is involved in nearly two-fifths of his team's scores, part of the build-up on almost 30 per cent of scores and finishing the job another 8 per cent of the time.

When Daicos gets the ball, his use, as mentioned above, is utterly spellbinding at times. He is able to consistently hit kicks few others in the league can dream of, often drilling kicks off balance or with little space. It's this ability that forces opponents into hives.

But it's also something that has gotten him into trouble in the past.

Dialling down the risk

Daicos's purple patch coincided with the star doing something that ran slightly counter to his modus operandi. For about a month or so in the middle of the season, Daicos dialled down the risk when using the ball via foot, focusing on finding the percentage target instead of hitting home runs with every kick.

Early in the year, Daicos was often attempting the nearly impossible, often with poor results. Collingwood's attack suffered as a result.

Daicos shifted his approach to be a little less expansive. With about the same volume of touches, he's clearing the ball more but gaining fewer metres and kicking inside 50 less often.

In the first half of the year, Daicos turned the ball over more than he has historically, and more than expected given the difficulty of his kicks. After the break, Daicos has been able to keep the ball in black and white hands more often.

This change is most noticeable when Daicos has gone inside 50. As the number of entries has dropped, the production has increased. In the first half of the year, Daicos's kicks inside 50 resulted in 1.1 points per kick on average — below the league-wide average. Between rounds 13 and 18, this number more than doubled, setting the league-wide pace.

In the past month, Daicos has dialled the risk back up, harming his ability to retain the ball in the process. But the results are much more successful than earlier in the season, and Collingwood have kept their heads above water in the process.

Stopping Nick

One of the key questions for teams facing Collingwood is how to stop Daicos, or at least quell his influence.

The first tactic that often comes up is that of tagging. According to the man himself, tagging isn't something that concerns either Collingwood or himself.

"I think there's so many ways you can get around a tag," Daicos explained to the media last year.

"But to be honest, it's probably something that the media talks about more than us. I think everyone out there … has an opponent. So it's something that we don't really focus on."

Even if the tagger is over-hyped by the media, it's undeniable that some sides have tried throwing a negating option at the Pies star. The variety of options has varied from a purely defensive run-with option to a stoppage-only match-up, with different levels in between.

The traditional wisdom for tagging an outside player (even one that goes in at stoppages) is pretty simple — apply physical pressure early, keep in direct contact, act as a "caravan" trailing the player.

In years past the most important objective would be to push a player like Daicos away from goal and not let them get goal side under any circumstance.

For Daicos, that guidance is flawed from the outset. His speed and agility make tracking him from behind a fool's errand, turning opponents into spectators.

Instead, opposition sides have increasingly been trying to prevent him from getting goal side. Teams have tried to send multiple players in to pressure and limit his ability to use the ball. Daicos struggles more — as all players do — when he is denied options ahead or sees pressure. Despite Collingwood being adept at getting Daicos free from his direct opponent, being willing to defend with multiple players has had some success.

The other, more radical tactic has been to attack his weaknesses.

Flawed excellence

It goes without saying that no football player is perfect.

It makes sense that the weaknesses for the most aesthetically appealing player are the more invisible parts of football. Beyond his propensity to perhaps bite off too much with his ball use, the least impressive parts of Daicos's game are also the hardest to measure and evaluate.

Despite Daicos's speed and endurance, the defensive side of his game can often be exploited. Sometimes Daicos can be caught out looking to win the ball at contests, without providing appropriate defensive protection on lost hit-outs. This can be a risky move, but early success can shift his focus on ball-winning.

This is the most common tactic of the Bulldogs when opposing Daicos and the Pies, as demonstrated in round 12 this year. In that hard-fought Dogs win, Daicos racked up the ball but the likes of Ed Richards and Bontempelli did huge amounts of damage on their own. The Dogs won the clearance battle, but did damage on the scoreboard via intercept scoring, attacking the weak Pies transition defence.

Blessed with a deep midfield group, the Dogs have usually decided to play their natural game when coming up against the Pies, including falling into broader team structures. That game at stoppage includes a pretty disciplined defensive set-up that can turn on a dime into attack when required.

Away from the contest, Daicos often acts as a free radical, looking to generate time and space to counter-attack on his own. He appears to have licence to anticipate turnovers and move before a clear ball is won. This requires a high level of understanding of how footy is played and the cues behind the game. This often results in some of his (and Collingwood's) most stunning highlights.

But when it backfires, it can leave Collingwood exposed. There aren't numbers or indicators that track off-ball positioning, but it often shows up in team-wide trends. This year Collingwood has struggled at defending the whole field, conceding at high rates from defensive 50 and the defensive half.

The Pies have slowly declined in their ability to defend transition as they have increasingly reworked their midfield around Daicos. While their strong, all-ground defence helped carry them to the 2023 flag, it has often been left wanting this year. This may be hurt by the absence of Darcy Moore and a rotating cast down back, but has not been helped by an overly attacking perspective on their own counter-attack.

Instead of prioritising winning through stopping other sides from scoring more than them, the Magpies appear to instead be focusing on scoring more than their opposition.

While individual defensive numbers such as tackles should be taken with a grain of salt, it's rare for a player to be around the ball as much as Daicos without laying physical pressure on the ball.

It's hard to unpick how much of these perceived defensive issues are from his own ability, and how many are dictated by the role he has to play for Collingwood to keep their attack above water. Daicos is far from the only attacking weapon to spend less energy on defence. Regardless, it's a side of his game often ignored when looking at disposal counts, metres gained, score involvements and goals kicked.

For some, it's what stops him being considered in the same tier as players such as Marcus Bontempelli.

Daicos's other flaws are significantly smaller, and mostly relate to where he lacks relative to other dynamic top midfielders.

Most obviously, Daicos has been notably non-competitive in the air. Unlike many taller midfielders, he does not win one-out marking battles and took until his 82nd game to take his first contested mark.

Perhaps this is part of why he also hasn't been a regularly damaging target inside 50, taking opponents deep to exploit defensive mismatches.

These skills may develop with greater maturity, and make him even harder to stop.

Can Daicos drag the Pies deep?

Friday night's game shapes as the first test on whether Daicos can drag Collingwood to further September glory. The fate of Collingwood this year likely relies on how much they can get out of the rest of their side, rather than anything more they can extract from their best player. That task will be far harder without Scott Pendlebury to call on.

Perhaps the biggest wish for Pies fans is that there could be more than one Nick Daicos, and more than one ball for him to use. Despite leading the league in disposals, Daicos still only gets about 10 per cent of the Magpies' touches. Despite leading the league in score involvement percentage, most Collingwood scores still happen without him.

As good as he is, the path to further success may paradoxically involve using him less often — developing other paths to goal, other threats to draw attention away.

The answer to the puzzle, despite his individual brilliance, might be infuriatingly out of his hands.

World.title: UEFA planning criminal claim against FIFA boss over World Cup proposal
World.content:
European football's governing body, UEFA, is preparing a criminal complaint against the embattled president of world association FIFA, Gianni Infantino, over his failed plan to sell commercial stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

In an explosive escalation between football's two most powerful entities, UEFA has applied to US federal courts in New York and Florida, demanding the release of information over the widely derided "FIFA Forward Enterprise" proposal.

The application document, seen by the ABC, reveals UEFA intends to "bring criminal claims in Switzerland against Infantino and possibly other FIFA officials and advisers for criminal mismanagement under Article 158 of the Swiss Criminal Code". FIFA is based in Switzerland.

The court filings also claim that Infantino and a "small group of advisers" spent over a year secretly preparing the controversial privatisation scheme.

"The secretive structuring, valuation, financing, and marketing inflicted direct and concrete injury on FIFA reputation, governance authority, and commercial relationships to the detriment of FIFA as well as its 211 members, including UEFA's 55 member associations," the document claims.

UEFA's lawyers further allege that the stakes in the World Cup offered to private backers were "absurdly low" and not independently evaluated.

"Under the terms Infantino announced, those investors stood to acquire a permanent financial interest in FIFA's commercial arm for $US4.2 billion ($5.84 billion), implying an absurdly low enterprise value of only approximately $US20 billion, a figure that was neither the product of an open, competitive auction, nor tested by any independent valuer," the document says.

"Infantino pushed the plan through internal FIFA approval only days earlier at a hastily convened meeting where a limited number of FIFA management officials and employees--some of whom had never heard of the plan--were given mere hours to sign off on an unprecedented multi-billion dollar scheme.

" In truth, it was a vehicle for Infantino and that small circle to acquire a permanent stake in and otherwise profit from FIFA most valuable assets to the detriment of FIFA, its members, and other parties within the football family. "

The FIFA Forward proposal was announced by Infantino on July 28, naming Thrive Eternal, an investment vehicle affiliated with Thrive Capital, as a prospective backer.

Thrive Capital is run by billionaire Joshua Kushner, the brother of Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner. Mr Trump has repeatedly claimed that he and Infantino are "good friends".

The move sparked immediate infighting within global football. UEFA declared its member nations, which include England, France, Spain and Germany, would boycott the next World Cup if the privatisation project was not scrapped.

Infantino eventually backflipped on the proposal, conceding that it "created divisions" and was no longer viable.

On Thursday, UEFA member nations issued a fiery joint press release demanding an independent probe into the formation of the scheme.

"FIFA cannot investigate itself and expect the football community simply to accept its conclusions," the statement read.

"The consequences of this crisis go beyond governance. The trust required to exercise the office of FIFA president has been broken and cannot be restored by withdrawing one proposal, issuing assurances or promising reform after the event. World football now needs new leadership capable of rebuilding that trust."

FIFA has been contacted for comment.

Tech.title: The GTA VI ‘extended look’ is now streaming on YouTube
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Rockstar has officially published its “extended look” at Grand Theft Auto VI on YouTube and on its website, as promised. The in-depth preview, which “entirely” features footage captured from the PS5 version of the game, initially premiered on Netflix at 3PM ET. But because Rockstar allowed creators to post reaction videos, you’ve technically been able to watch the video on YouTube before the studio’s official upload.

Related The biggest video game of all time looks like a movie

The nearly 27-minute preview largely focuses more on atmosphere, protagonists Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, and highlighting locations in the game instead of diving deep on specific game mechanics. It feels more like slices of a movie than a video game trailer. But there are a few sections showing off playable shootouts and police car chases as well as activities like shooting a basketball and scuba diving. Other outlets that got previews from Rockstar have more details on gameplay that weren’t included in the video.

GTA VI is set to release on November 19th at a starting price of $79.99.

Tech.title: The biggest video game of all time looks like a movie
Tech.content:
I think I know why Rockstar Games debuted its “extended look” of Grand Theft Auto VI on Netflix instead of immediately dropping it for free on YouTube. Unlike most video game trailers, the almost 27-minute preview of GTA VI felt more like a slice of a prestige crime drama than any video game trailer that I’ve ever seen. To make a new game that lasts another decade or more and potentially rivals the success of its predecessor, Rockstar is clearly trying to further blur the lines between Hollywood and video games.

The line between games and movies has been getting consistently fuzzier. Look no further than this year’s James Bond game, 007 First Light, which has the snappy pacing, acting, and cinematography of a great action film. And TV shows and movies are increasingly pulling from video games for inspiration, to say nothing of entire TV and movie franchises being built around successful video games. Now, a video game trailer has wedged between prestige TV and streaming hit movies — after watching the GTA VI preview, Netflix is suggesting I watch Breaking Bad next.

Rockstar is keeping GTA VI’s plot details close to its chest, but the video gives the broad strokes: GTA VI is about protagonists Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos working together in Vice City. Across the tightly-edited video, which jumps between cutscenes and moments of actual gameplay, Jason and Lucia do a lot of GTA-style crimes: they evade cops in gunfights, pull off high-stakes robberies, and shoot a lot of people. But they also have moments of chatting leisurely in the car or even bickering about what clothes to wear.

The video also isn’t just an uninterrupted vertical section of gameplay, like video game deep dives often are. Instead, it artistically cuts between different sections, storylines, and characters to paint a picture of what to expect. I didn’t always know what was going on, but by the end of the video, I had a sense of who these people were and the city that they live in. It felt, well, like parts of a movie.

GTA VI will still be very much a video game. Rockstar invited a handful of outlets to preview GTA VI, and their coverage dives into things like the expansive map, the six-star Wanted system, escalating requirements to steal cars, and reactive NPCs. Those will almost certainly make for a vast sandbox to play in, building on the already immersive worlds of previous Rockstar games like GTA V and Red Dead Redemption 2. For GTA VI’s extended look, Rockstar instead opted to show setup, action, and dialogue scenes, leaning on story and atmosphere over gameplay mechanics. It’s a cinematic choice.

Maybe I’m thinking too deeply about a video game trailer. Yes, I know that part of this Netflix video is all just marketing hype — and Netflix probably saw it as a way to get new subscribers. And the trailer isn’t only available on Netflix; Rockstar let creators share reaction videos and is publishing the extended look on its YouTube channel and its own website at 9PM ET.

But expectations are high for GTA VI. 13-year-old GTA V has sold more than 230 million copies, making it one of the top-selling games of all time. Rockstar’s previous two trailers for GTA VI have racked up hundreds of millions of views. GTA Online is a big cash cow in its own right, too. But Rockstar can always do more with a game many years in the making that might be fighting for time with the Netflix library. If Thursday’s preview was any indication, all those titles might get real competition when GTA VI launches on November 19th.

Tech.title: Meta addresses ‘pervert glasses’ reputation with a privacy fix and a new marketing campaign
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Meta is updating its AI-powered smart glasses to close a loophole that allowed wearers to keep recording after covering the front-facing LED. Alex Himel, Meta’s vice president of augmented reality, writes in a post on Threads that “the camera will now stop working if the light is covered during a recording.”

The company’s line of smart glasses already disables their built-in cameras if someone covers the LED capture light, which blinks to alert others that you’re recording or taking a picture. However, some wearers found that they can bypass these restrictions by covering the LED light after they started recording. This latest fix comes a little over a month after Meta updated its glasses to turn off its camera when wearers physically tamper with the capture light.

Meta put this billboard up in Los Angeles. Image: Meta

“We’re going to keep rolling out updates like this to make sure the capture LED can reliably alert bystanders when photos or videos are being captured for someone’s gallery,” Himel writes. “Only a tiny minority of people try to get around these protections, and the fact they have to go to these lengths shows our efforts are working.”

But now, Meta is trying to spread “awareness” about its LED capture light by launching its own campaign in communities “where glasses sales have been popular,” Meta spokesperson Albert Aydin tells The Verge. One billboard, which is currently up in Los Angeles, shows Meta’s smart glasses alongside a caption that says, “The camera lets you capture the moment. The light lets everyone around you know when you do.” A video shared by Meta similarly says that the capture LED “signals when the glasses are capturing photos and videos,” and that “no light” means “no capture.”

Tech.title: GTA VI: all the news on Rockstar’s next entry in the Grand Theft Auto series
Tech.content:
It’s been over a decade and two console generations since GTA V came out, and its sequel is still a work in progress. GTA VI has faced multiple delays, with developer Rockstar Games bumping back its predicted release date twice, eventually shifting to November 19th, 2026, a full year after its originally planned fall 2025 release window. Early official glimpses offered a look at the game’s protagonists, Jason and Lucia, who players will navigate around Vice City as outlaws on the run after a job goes south.

Rockstar Games has also responded to “CyberLeek” posts that showed sequences of the game, calling them heartbreaking and saying, “…this is obviously not how we intended for you to see the game after all this time.” At about the same time, the leakers released yet another clip.

Now a half-hour “extended look” has arrived full of gameplay slices and cutscenes that’s available for viewing on Netflix, as well as all over other social media channels in reaction videos before it hits YouTube at 9PM — here are some of our first impressions.

Tech.title: GTA VI looks just as great as we could hope for
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Netflix and Rockstar Games finally debuted their “extended look” at Grand Theft Auto VI. It showed that the new game looks to keep much of the spirit of GTA — exploration, driving, crimes, shooting, and cinematic story scenes. But everything just looks much better than previous entries, with impressive graphics, densely-packed rooms, and detailed environments. The footage was captured on PS5, according to the end of the video.

A key focus of the game seems to be how protagonists Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos work together. In one scene, it appears you play as Duval as he hangs out of the window of a car that Caminos is driving so he can shoot at police chasing after them. Later, though, it looks like the player controls Caminos as the driver while Duval and another character keep shooting the police.

Another part of the video shows a mission where Duval and Caminos are split up. As enemies barge into an upper floor of a building, Duval, who is a security detail for the mission, takes them on by hiding behind cover and shooting at them. Caminos, who is on a different floor, sneaks around on foot to try and evade detection. At one point, while she is struggling on the ground against an enemy, you can see button prompts to press to escape their grasp.

Much of the video included tightly-edited scenes and cutscenes from the game, but there were a few other brief glimpses of gameplay, like a weapon wheel menu and activities driving a boat, playing basketball, underwater diving, racing on a track, and parachuting.

Previous Next



















1 / 11 Image: Rockstar Games

The game appears to be quite large. As part of a preview by The New York Times, Rockstar North co-studio head Rob Nelson said that a February playthrough of the game took 80 hours, including both the main story and some optional content. The map is three times as big as the playable map of Red Dead Redemption 2, Rockstar tells the NYT.

You’ll be able to switch between the two protagonists at “any time,” though you can also choose to have one character tag along while you’re running around the world or experience things as just one of them, according to IGN, which also got a preview of the game. Duval and Caminos also don’t necessarily have to be a romantic couple; that’s up to the player. (There’s a specific mechanic for holding hands.)

Snapmatic, GTA’s take on Instagram, returns in GTA VI, though you can’t actually post on it “due to Jason and Lucia being a couple on the run and not wanting to leave a digital footprint,” according to IGN.

The six-star wanted system is also officially back, and police can remember what you look like, meaning you may need to change outfits to lose them, IGN says. If you want to steal a parked car to get away from a sticky situation, you might want to look for an older car: more expensive cars will be harder to steal and you may need certain equipment to break into certain cars.

The deep dive follows several apparent video leaks of the game from a person or group identifying themselves as “CyberLeek,” which Rockstar said were “heartbreaking.”

Update, August 27th: Added details from IGN and the NYT’s previews.

Tech.title: Google’s AI note-taking app now allows you to interact with books
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google’s AI note-taking app, Gemini Notebook, can now pull information from the books you’ve purchased. The new “Expert Intelligence” feature allows you to bring titles from Google Play Books directly into Gemini Notebook, which means you can ask questions about the material, as well as generate plans, infographics, AI podcasts, and more based on their contents.

During a briefing with The Verge, Google Labs editorial director Steven Johnson showed how you can use the tool to generate a recipe book using the information in Michael Pollan’s Food Rules. In another example, Gemini Notebook applied the knowledge from Kim Scott’s management-focused Radical Candor to answer a question about handling a difficult conversation with an employee. You’ll also be able to view the full text of the book directly in Notebook.

To start, more than 100,000 books from publishers like Penguin Random House, Johns Hopkins University Press, Macmillan Publishers, O’Reilly Media, and others will support Expert Intelligence. Google also worked with 15 authors, including Pollan, Scott, Steven Pinker, and Jennifer Wallace, to create “Featured Notebooks” that each author customizes with additional source material, intro letters, and more. Titles that support the feature will have “Gemini Notebook” listed under the “Tools” badge in Google Play Books.

“I’m really interested in the idea of building a collection of people whose work you really value, and kind of creating your own dream team of advisors that are just available to you wherever you go,” Johnson says.

Additionally, Google built protections into Gemini Notebook to prevent other users from accessing material from books they haven’t purchased. If you share a Notebook that includes a purchased book, a user who doesn’t own the title will see it listed as a source, but they won’t be able to view the full text or information related to it. Clicking the source will direct users to Google Play Books, where they can purchase it.

“We want to be able to create a space where users can bring whatever knowledge, whatever expertise they think is going to be most relevant and do it in a way that creates new revenue possibilities for authors and publishers as well,” Johnson says.

Google will eventually bring this feature to AI Mode in Search and the Gemini app, both of which can already pull information from Gemini Notebook. The company also has plans to expand Expert Intelligence to support scholarly articles, magazine articles, and newspapers, according to Johnson.

Tech.title: Google tells Android app developers to cool it on memory use, or else
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer with over a decade of experience writing about consumer tech. She has a special interest in mobile photography and telecom. Previously, she worked at DPReview.

Google will start policing memory-hungry Android apps as a direct response to the RAM crisis. Spotted by TechCrunch, the company yesterday published a memo addressing the Play Store’s role in enforcing new memory-usage restrictions. The post emphasizes the importance of meeting new memory usage limits for apps, in order “to help developers navigate industry-wide hardware constraints and Android’s broader memory limits,” it says. And failing to meet the new memory restrictions will come with consequences.

The memory limitations were first introduced with Android 17, appearing first on Pixel phones. It’s probably no coincidence that the base configurations of the Pixel 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL come with less RAM than last year’s models. As Android 17 rolls out to the wider ecosystem, Google warns developers that they’ll need to play nice with a much bigger range of devices: “Over the coming year, an increasing number of manufacturers will leverage the Android per-app memory limits across their portfolio of device RAM configurations from 4GB to 16GB+ devices.”

Google has a pretty clear directive if apps misbehave: “If your app exceeds these limits, it will be slowed down and may be terminated.” But yesterday’s post hints at even bigger… ramifications (I’m so sorry): “Apps and games that do not meet these thresholds may see reduced app visibility and publishing capabilities on Google Play. Additional details will be provided later this year.” Google says it will start enforcing the memory limits in February 2027, so app makers have some time to figure it out, but dang. That’s potentially pretty serious.

The memory shortage has had a well-documented impact on hardware, and it seems that it’s time for software developers to feel the squeeze, too. And Google isn’t playing around — it seems to be putting some real teeth behind its new memory policies.

Tech.title: Speedo’s new smart goggles module can track all four swim strokes
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Speedo is launching a removable smart module for its Vanquisher goggles that can analyze a swimmer’s performance across all four swim strokes: freestyle, backstroke, breaststroke, and butterfly. The new Speedo iQ system uses swim-specific sensors to analyze head movement in the water, time breaths, and track distance per stroke.

Unlike other smart goggles, such as those from Form, Speedo’s iQ system doesn’t come with a built-in display. Instead, the Speedo iQ module automatically transmits data to its accompanying app, allowing swimmers to see their performance when they get out of the water. Additionally, Speedo notes that you can simply transfer the module to another pair of Vanquisher goggles if they need to be replaced.

Previous Next



1 / 3 Image: Speedo

The Speedo iQ system doesn’t require a subscription, and it’s also legal to use during World Aquatics competitions. The Vanquisher goggles with the iQ module included cost $189. They’re available to order now in a variety of colors.

Tech.title: Anthropic and OpenAI are joining the AI stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026
Tech.content:
AI hasn’t just changed how startups build; it’s broken how they sell, secure their data and customers, and scale it more rapidly than ever before. At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, the AI Stage is back to dig into the single hottest topic in the community for the past few years, presented by Google for Startups. Tech.title: Rivian’s CFO is leaving the company
Tech.content:
Rivian’s chief financial officer Claire McDonough is resigning her position at the end of October, the company announced in a regulatory filing Thursday.

The company said McDonough is stepping down to “pursue a new opportunity and relocate to the East Coast to be closer to her family.” McDonough has been hired as CFO at Massachusetts-based GE Vernova, according to the energy equipment manufacturer and her own post on LinkedIn.

Rivian said her resignation is “not the result of any disagreement.” The company is already searching for a replacement, and vice president of finance Derek Mulvey will serve as interim CFO once McDonough leaves her post.

Her departure comes as Rivian takes on some of its biggest projects to date, including scaling up production and sales of its R2 SUV, which started shipping to customers this summer.

McDonough was hired to the CFO spot in January 2021, replacing Ryan Green, at a critical and tumultuous time for Rivian. The EV maker, which was still a private company, had raised billions of dollars in its bid to bring three compelling electric vehicles — its flagship R1T truck and R1S SUV and a commercial delivery van — to market.

Rivian was plagued with delays and added costs, which was compounded by supply chain constraints. It was also burning through capital.

In her first year at Rivian, the company started production of its R1T truck and raised $12 billion in one of the biggest IPOs of the year. The company’s stock, which debuted at $78, has since fallen to $16.80, as of Thursday’s closing.

McDonough was a key figure in the company’s quest to improve its balance sheet, and specifically its cost of revenue. While she didn’t have any direct experience working in automotive — she held previous positions at JP Morgan and Fairway Market — McDonough was known for working closely with the design and engineering teams as well as founder and CEO RJ Scaringe to ensure future vehicles were modern and compelling without losing money on every sale, according to insiders who have spoken to TechCrunch in the past. Among her many responsibilities, McDonough led Rivian’s corporate and business development as well as a variety of other aspects of the business, including vehicle maintenance and repairs, facilities, and its charging network.

As CFO, she played a vital role in a technology joint venture with Volkswagen Group. Under that deal, which was finalized in November 2024, VW agreed to invest up to $5.8 billion into Rivian by 2027 in exchange for access to its electrical architecture and software know-how.

“Together, we launched the R1T, R1S, and our commercial van, drove technology innovation and partnerships, built our go-to-market operations, and positioned the company for global scale and profitability with the launch of R2,” McDonough wrote in a post on LinkedIn. “Being part of taking Rivian from an ambitious vision to a category-defining enterprise has been the highlight of my career.”

Tech.title: Bluesky adds an ‘algorithmic opt-out’ feature for those who don’t want to go viral
Tech.content:
In Brief

After adding support for longer videos just yesterday, open social network Bluesky on Thursday introduced a new algorithmic opt-out feature that allows users to stop their posts from appearing in the app’s main Discover feed.

That algorithmic feed can currently surface any post on Bluesky’s network, as posts on the network are public by default.

To be clear, this latest change isn’t a way to make posts private — Bluesky is still working on rolling out support for private data at the protocol level. Instead, the feature simply makes a user’s public posts less discoverable to people outside their existing personal network.

The company says it created the feature because not everyone using its social media site wants to go viral. Sometimes, people just want to post for their followers without having their words exposed to larger crowds.

To opt out of having posts shown in the Discover feed, users can toggle on a new option in the app’s Privacy and Security settings. The change can take up to an hour to fully take effect, the company says.

Image Credits:Bluesky

It’s also worth noting that Bluesky’s implementation of the feature extends beyond its own app.

Instead of just being a setting that applies only within Bluesky, the preference is recorded at the account level. That means the choice travels with the user, even if they’re posting from another app that is powered by the same underlying protocol that Bluesky uses, AT Proto.

However, while those other apps have access to this information, they still have to choose whether to respect it.

Tech.title: Buried in Meta’s $18B settlement is a legal pass on kids’ data
Tech.content:
In addition to paying out up to $18 billion and adding child safety measures, Meta’s settlement agreement with attorneys general from 29 states includes an interesting provision: The states have agreed not to sue Meta under existing child safety laws over its retention and use of children’s data.

That permission is being granted for the limited purpose of training and testing Meta’s age-assurance model and includes guardrails, but it’s a curious policy decision to make in a case centered on child safety, and one that could be difficult to properly enforce.

As specified in the settlement agreement, Meta must develop, train, and begin testing a model designed to detect which users on Meta’s platforms are under the age of 13. This must be done within a year of the document’s effective date. (While the agreement doesn’t specify that the model has to be AI-based, Meta’s current age-detection tools are powered by AI technology.)

Under U.S. child safety law, COPPA (Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act) typically requires that websites and apps limit the collection and retention of children’s personal information. Meta’s settlement agreement says that Meta shouldn’t need to violate COPPA to train or implement its age-assurance models. However, the agreement also says that the state AGs have agreed “fully, finally, and forever” not to bring any past, present, or future COPPA claims — or claims under similar state laws — related to Meta’s use of children’s data.

The agreement makes clear that Meta can’t use data from users under age 13 for ad targeting, marketing, or algorithmic optimization.

Meta’s request for legal protection, and the state AGs’ willingness to grant it, isn’t unreasonable, says Philip N. Yannella, a partner at law firm Blank Rome and co-chair of its Privacy, Security & Data Protection practice. “These kinds of data minimization guardrails are pretty typical for privacy compliance: e.g., verifying compliance with deletion requests,” he said, though he noted a caveat: COPPA is a federal law primarily enforced by the FTC, not the states, so it’s unclear whether the FTC, which isn’t a party to this settlement, has separately agreed to the same compromise.

It can be difficult for companies to keep data technically and organizationally isolated from the rest of their systems. Yet Meta is being asked to do just that — to isolate its understanding of children’s behavior signals and other data and use it solely for detecting and removing under-13 users. Fortunately, an independent auditor will be involved in monitoring Meta’s compliance with the settlement so we don’t only have to rely on Meta’s word.

Policing this limitation could be complicated. The data could hypothetically feed into other Meta systems over time, or could raise questions over whether the data, signals, or insights derived from it are being used elsewhere within the company. What’s not clear from the agreement is what data Meta will retain for training the model, how much behavioral information that may include, or how long it will retain the data. We also don’t know how these models will change in the future as Meta meets the settlement’s terms.

Barring state AGs from raising COPPA or similar state-law claims over this use of children’s data in the future could complicate the legal avenues states can pursue if questions arise around how Meta is using the data.

That doesn’t prevent them from pursuing legal claims, notes Joshua Wurtzel, a partner at Schlam Stone & Dolan LLP. “If Meta uses the data outside those lines, the release and covenant not to sue don’t apply,” he said. But those legal disputes could still be complicated, since they’d hinge on whether Meta’s use of the data fell within the settlement’s terms.

Peter Jackson, a Data & IP attorney at Greenberg Glusker LLP, agrees, saying the carve-out here could “disincentivize future enforcement actions.”

“The Settlement Agreement’s age-assurance measures bear all the hallmarks of a heavy, and perhaps hasty, negotiation,” he says.

The decision also touches on a broader question that’s been coming up across the AI industry lately, especially as more AI agents are being developed to help consumers with various tasks. The systems often require significant access to users’ personal data to work well. Similarly, Meta may need deep insight into children’s use of social media in order to identify which accounts belong to young people.

Tech.title: YouTube now lets creators tag Amazon products and earn commissions from purchases
Tech.content:
YouTube announced on Thursday that eligible creators in the U.S. can now tag Amazon products in their content and receive a cut of sales. Creators can link Amazon products in their shorts, long-form videos, and livestreams.

The update turns product recommendations into a more direct revenue stream for creators, and for Amazon, the move puts its massive online marketplace inside one of the most popular video platforms.

Although YouTube already runs a Shopping affiliate program with participating retailers, the addition of Amazon’s vast catalog essentially allows creators to recommend a variety of products through a native integration. By bringing Amazon into the Shopping Affiliate Program, creators no longer need to paste Associates links in the video’s description, then hope viewers copy the link when they make a purchase.

Instead, YouTube says Amazon will provide it with a curated catalog of highly requested and trending products that creators can tag in their videos. If a creator can’t find a specific product that they want to tag, they can request to add it by reaching out to YouTube Support.

The feature also includes auto-tagging support. If enabled, YouTube’s systems can automatically review a creator’s recent uploads to identify and tag eligible Amazon products.

YouTube notes that creators won’t see breakdowns for specific products or individual videos in their analytics, but that they’ll see their overall daily earnings in YouTube Studio. If a viewer ends up returning an item, that commission will be deducted from the creator’s balance.

While only eligible U.S. creators can currently tag Amazon products, those tags can be seen globally. YouTube says it may automatically match a tagged product with a trusted local merchant offer to allow creators to earn commissions on eligible international purchases. If a local merchant isn’t available, the tag will route viewers to the Amazon U.S. website, where commission will be earned if a purchase is finalized on the U.S. site.

To be eligible, creators must be enrolled in YouTube’s Partner and Shopping Affiliate programs, have an active Amazon Influencer or Associates account, and link it to their YouTube channel.

Tech.title: Barret Zoph, the Thinking Machines co-founder ousted before joining OpenAI, is now at Google
Tech.content:
In Brief

The game of musical chairs for AI executives continues. Barret Zoph, a co-founder of the AI startup Thinking Machines who left the company earlier this year to rejoin OpenAI, has found yet another job.

Zoph spent two years at OpenAI and left in October 2024 to co-found Thinking Machines with Mira Murati, who had left the AI lab the month prior. In January, Zoph and another Thinking Machines co-founder, Luke Metz, quite dramatically departed from the startup to return to OpenAI. It was later revealed that Zoph had been fired.

His return didn’t quite stick. Zoph spent only five months at OpenAI, where he was tasked with heading AI enterprise sales. He left the company in June. And now we know where he landed.

Zoph has taken a position as vice president of research at Google (which happens to be another company where he previously worked). “We look forward to Barret returning to Google and bringing his RL and post-training expertise to Gemini,” a Google spokesperson told the Wall Street Journal.

TechCrunch reached out to OpenAI and Google for more information.

It’s not always easy to divine why tech executives seem to be spending less time in their roles. The turnover rate in the AI industry is high, and it’s been especially high at OpenAI — a company that, despite readying itself for an IPO and being one of the most powerful presences in the tech world, has lost a lot of critical staff over the last eight months. The turnover of high-level executives — from the departure of its COO to the recent loss of one of its top data center execs — has left onlookers scratching their heads.

This story has been updated to include the fact that Zoph was fired from Thinking Machines.

Tech.title: ATF declares ‘major incident’ as ransomware gang claims hack
Tech.content:
In Brief

The U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, or ATF, says a cyberattack on one of its systems has been declared a “major incident,” a formal, legally defined classification that prompts a formal notification to lawmakers in Congress.

ATF said in a statement that it’s responding to the cyberattack on a stand-alone system that’s separate from the bureau’s network. An ATF spokesperson told reporters that the targeted computer system contained information such as the “targets of ATF investigations.”

TechCrunch has seen a claim of responsibility by the Qilin ransomware gang on its leak site, but it did not provide evidence for its claim, such as a sample of leaked data. Qilin is known for running a “ransomware-as-a-service” operation, in which it leases its hacking tools to other criminal affiliates for a cut of the profits. The gang has listed media giant Lee Enterprises and U.K. pathology lab giant Synnovis as targets.

Under federal law, “major incidents” include significant cyber incidents that are likely to cause demonstrable harm to U.S. national security or broader U.S. interests. Agencies are required to disclose major incidents to Congress within a week of their discovery.

The ATF joins several government agencies in recent years that have declared major incidents following a breach, including a 2023 ransomware attack on a system used by the U.S. Marshals Service, and a breach of an FBI system earlier this year that exposed phone numbers of targets under surveillance by federal agents.

Tech.title: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and 100 other companies call for action to defend against rogue AI
Tech.content:
Over a hundred tech companies — including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Microsoft — have signed an open letter urging both the private and public sectors to work together to defend themselves from AI-related cyber threats.

The letter — which was also signed by prominent cyber firms like CrowdStrike, Okta, and Fortinet, as well as prominent financial institutions and internet infrastructure firms — calls for the adoption of new forms of cyber defense, while also encouraging governments at the “local, national, and international levels” to collaborate on security.

“In the coming months, AI-enabled cyber attacks will become far more widespread and sophisticated as models around the world become increasingly capable,” the letter states. “The companies and public services our communities depend on — from hospitals to water treatment plants to the infrastructure that powers the internet — are at risk.”

The problem AI poses to traditional cybersecurity defenses has been thrust into the spotlight lately by a string of bizarre incidents in which AI agents have attacked companies.

The Hugging Face incident — in which one of OpenAI’s agents autonomously broke out of its sandboxed environment and attacked the tech company — has been followed by a trail of other reported break-ins involving agents developed by other AI companies, including Anthropic and Meta. These incidents have bolstered the argument that the field of cybersecurity has been fundamentally altered and that bold new commercial solutions are necessary to mitigate them.

The letter further suggests the mobilization of a “collective response,” one in which “new partnerships” are formed “to raise security standards and find new solutions to emerging cyber threats.”

Several of the AI companies that have signed the letter are still actively developing ever more advanced AI models, highlighting their conflicted position. At the same time, they are also offering programs to use frontier AI models for defensive purposes, including OpenAI’s Daybreak program, Anthropic’s Mythos, and Microsoft’s new cyber platform Perception.

Tech.title: 6 Takeaways From the GTA VI Extended Look
Tech.content:
It’s safe to say Grand Theft Auto VI is the most anticipated game ever. Thirteen years after the last entry in the series, rampant fervor and speculation about what features the game will include have ratcheted up. Today, Rockstar Games divulged more details through an exclusive livestream event on Netflix called Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look. The spectacle was a 26-minute-long collection of gameplay, cutscenes, and game mechanics.

And boy, does this sure look like a GTA game. The trailer featured Lucia and Jason, the two main characters, driving around Vice City, GTA’s fictional version of Miami. It highlighted all kinds of violence and shenanigans your characters can engage in, and it looks good doing it.

The livestream follows a week of gameplay leaks and story spoilers by the hacker group Cyberleek, which Rockstar called “heartbreaking.” A bevy of other details about the game emerged just a day before the event in a story published by the British magazine Dazed. The piece chronicles the extraordinary level of detail and effort Rockstar has put into GTA VI, including how players control the characters and the unprecedented realism that Rockstar put into its satirical sandbox version of Miami.

It’s bound to be a massive game; today’s reveal shows just how much of a monster it will be. Here are the big takeaways from the livestream.

It Sure Is Pretty

GTA VI is gorgeous. The cityscapes, nightclubs, and lush natural parks shown all seem vibrant and awash in color.

There is a noticeable difference between cutscenes and gameplay, though, as the gameplay clips looked a little flatter and more desaturated than the cinematic cutscenes. That’s kind of a nitpick, though it’s worth noting that in the very first scene—in the dark basement of a crack house—the lighting is so dim it washes out the features of several Black characters around the table.

Courtesy of Rockstar Games

You Play as 2 Characters Simultaneously

The player can control two characters, Jason and Lucia, a Bonnie-and-Clyde-esque couple who seem to be working out some lingering tension in their relationship as they go about their various criminal activities.

The voice acting for the main characters and other non-playable characters (NPCs) feels tightly written, though that’s based on the select clips Rockstar showed. According to Dazed, the relationship between the characters can change over time, and the player’s actions can affect how that plays out. Keep that in mind if you’re hoping for a particular ending.

GTA VI offers a plethora of options for changing the two main characters’ appearances. Eating too much or too little food affects their weight. Working out can make them swole. The Extended Look also showed off characters eating and working out in minigames. It was a feature in 2004’s GTA San Andreas and in a smaller way in GTA V. Now, that reactivity will be much more fully realized in GTA VI.
