Tech.title: Google Engineer Accused of Polymarket Insider Trading Says He Was Just Gambling
Tech.content:
Michele Spagnuolo, the Google engineer arrested in May by US authorities for alleged insider trading on Polymarket, is making a new bold bet. On Wednesday, his legal team filed a motion to dismiss the charges against him. Spagnuolo isn’t outright denying that he made money using internal information from Google. Instead, his legal team says that the wagers were not financial instruments subject to regulation by the United States’ Commodities Exchange Act but rather good old-fashioned international betting that the US has no authority over.

Spagnuolo, who has been placed on leave from Google, is accused of committing commodities fraud, wire fraud, and money laundering. Using the alias “AlphaRaccoon,” he allegedly made a series of wagers on Polymarket’s flagship platform that resulted in profits totaling over $1.2 million. According to the criminal complaint, “AlphaRaccoon” correctly wagered that the singer D4vd, who gained notoriety for his suspected connection to a grisly killing, would be Google’s most-searched person of the year in 2025. (D4vd was later charged with murder; he pleaded not guilty.)

You might not expect the lawyers defending someone accused of felonies to agree with state prosecutors, but the vicious legal infighting over prediction markets is creating strange alliances. Across the United States, state attorneys general and regulators are battling against both the federal government and prediction markets over whether event contracts should be considered “swaps” and therefore have to follow the Commodities Exchange Act, or instead be categorized as gambling, which is regulated by states.

Tech.title: Labor Day 2026 Deals Got Me a Complete Starter Tool Kit for Under $375
Tech.content:
Most people know that Labor Day is one of the best times of the year to buy tools (get it? Labor?), but if you’re a newly minted homeowner or DIY-er, the landscape can be intimidating. When I bought my first home, I owned only two screwdrivers, a pair of pliers, and a hammer; I had no clue what I was in for.

Now that I’ve been a homeowner for 17 years, I agree with WIRED reviewer Scott Gilbertson that unless you’re a professional tradesperson or really love large projects, you don’t need a garage full of specialty tools. Just the basics will do: a drill, a saw, a set of manual screwdrivers, and a stud finder, for example.

Luckily, early Labor Day deals are pretty decent this year. In fact, after examining all the major sales, I was able to find a rather encyclopedic house-repair kit for any new homeowner or DIY-er for under $375 (minus tax and shipping) with deals from Home Depot, Lowe’s, and Walmart. Any of these would also be great to stash away for a holiday gift.

Here’s what I chose:

Power-Tool Workhorses: Ryobi 4-Tool Kit for $199

Courtesy of Ryobi Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Ryobi ONE+ 18V Cordless 4-Tool Combo Kit $249 $199 (20% off) Home Depot

Look, you’re not going to take Ryobi tools to a jobsite or use them to build a house from scratch (a former WIRED editor once deemed them “the Kia of tools”), but if you’re just using them for basic, casual home use, they’ll do the job. Ryobi’s 18V ONE+ batteries (this set comes with one) are fully backward compatible with all Ryobi tools ever made, and this set has a three-year warranty. I live in a DeWalt household, so I don’t have a lot of firsthand experience with Ryobi, but my brother, a contractor, says the brand is great for the average DIY homeowner and offers a much broader range of tools than competitor Bauer from Harbor Freight.

This set packs a ½-inch drill/driver, an impact driver (which WIRED reviewer Scott Gilbertson said had a profound 'I can't believe I didn't own one sooner' impact on him, though his is Milwaukee), a circular saw, and an LED light. The impact driver packs 1,800 pounds of torque, which is pretty decent for a consumer-level tool. If you need a sander, there's also another kit with a sander plus drill/driver and circular saw, which may be worth a look if this set sells out.

The Hand-Tool Essentials: Workpro 408-Piece Set for $144

Courtesy of Workpro

Courtesy of Workpro Chevron Chevron Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Workpro 408-Piece General Household Home Repair Tool Kit $288 $144 (50% off) Walmart

I don't have this exact set, but I do have remnants of a similar one. Again, you're not going to bring these to a construction site, but this kit is a knockout deal for everything you get—pliers, screwdrivers, Allen keys, wrenches, sockets, bits, tape measure, knife, hammer, wire stripper … there's even a metal box in which to store everything. A lot of the “pieces” are doodads like screwdriver heads and drywall anchors, but it still contains pretty much any non-power tool you might need for light home repairs and even basic car maintenance. (There's no level, but you can always use an app on your phone for that.) However, note that this is a flash deal, so it's likely only live for a limited time.

Wall-Hanging Must-Have: Franklin Sensors Stud Finder for $22

Courtesy of Franklin Sensors Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Franklin Sensors Metal and Wood Stud Finder $22 Lowe's

No household repair kit is complete without a stud finder. (And if you're a dad, it will give you years of built-in dad jokes.) In fact, you can't—or, at least, shouldn't—hang anything even slightly heavy on your wall without one. I have a Franklin Sensors stud finder, though not this exact model, and it's done well to help my family hang pictures, shelves, mirrors, and pretty much everything else for the past decade or so. This is the best deal I could find, though it's not technically on sale. However, Lowe’s is having a sale on plenty of other tools, including outdoor furniture, appliances, and grills.

Tech.title: A Georgia Cop Used Flock to Track 2 Other Cops: His Ex and Her Friend
Tech.content:
In recent months, there has been a surge in reports of police officers misusing automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) sold by Flock Safety to stalk former romantic partners—but details about these incidents are often scarce.

WIRED has made this article free for all to read because it is primarily based on reporting from public records requests. Please consider subscribing to support our journalism.

Now, with documents obtained via a public records request, WIRED can reveal specific details about one extensive Flock-fueled surveillance campaign and the subsequent investigation and fallout.

Dustin Bozzo, who until this month worked as a patrolman in the Atlanta-area suburb of Alpharetta, Georgia, allegedly used Flock 56 times between March and May to search for the license plate of a former romantic partner—a fellow member of the Alpharetta Police Department. (Their relationship itself violated the city’s ban on workplace dating, documents show.) When Bozzo noticed that his ex’s car was often near that of another police officer, he began searching for that officer’s vehicle as well. He did so 29 times between March and May.

Lieutenant Jason Hiott of the Alpharetta Police Department tells WIRED that Bozzo was placed on paid leave on July 20 and resigned on August 5 following an internal investigation. He adds that an “ongoing criminal investigation” is underway in the department's Criminal Investigations Division.

Alpharetta police chief Trent Lindgren tells WIRED that the investigation will likely be finished soon, adding that the department holds itself to a “high standard,” and took “immediate action” when misuse was identified. Flock did not respond to a request for comment.

Bozzo did not respond to multiple requests for comment. He changed his Facebook profile picture and name after WIRED messaged him on the platform.

In the civilian world, a breakup may tempt people to check up on their former lovers by pulling up their social media profiles. But in the police world, many officers have instant access to Flock—a powerful, informative, and invasive tool for tracking people’s locations. Across the country, there have been at least 45 documented incidents of police officers misusing Flock in order to look up or track current or former romantic partners.

Tech.title: This Is How Anthropic Thinks AI Agents Should Navigate the Physical World
Tech.content:
Artificial intelligence agents might occasionally get confused and hack into other computers, but Anthropic thinks it has a way to unleash the little rascals into scientific labs and manufacturing facilities safely.

The AI company released details today of a new framework designed to help AI agents use physical systems like microscopes, liquid-handling equipment, quantum computing hardware, manufacturing machines, and robot arms.

The framework, called Model Hardware Standard, is a set of rules that specify how AI agents should—and should not—interact with all sorts of hardware. It reflects a growing belief that AI has the potential to revolutionize scientific research and industries like manufacturing–if it can venture into the physical world safely.

The company says it will work with trusted partners to determine how to maximize safety before making it generally available. Though there are potential misuse issues involved—developing biological weapons, for instance—the company says guardrails built into AI models themselves should prevent bad actors from taking advantage of the new standard for nefarious ends.

“The impetus is wanting to accelerate science,” says Alek Kemeny, a quantum physicist who co-led the development. “How do we close the loop between accelerating literature review and data analysis—and bring that power to the experimental world?”

Claude and other chatbots are already powerful tools for combing through large amounts of information in the form of scientific papers or experimental results to uncover new insights and ideas. AI agents are widely considered the next step after chatbots: They’re designed to take actions, often on ordinary computers, doing things like answering emails. They can potentially use other hardware, too—and Anthropic wants to make sure there are rules in place as they do.

Tech.title: Netflix Failed at Video Games. Now It’s Trying to Promote Them
Tech.content:
Later today, Netflix will stream a live event with Rockstar and Take-Two Interactive, the developer and publisher of the highly anticipated video game Grand Theft Auto VI. Called Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look, it’s the third official trailer for the game, which releases on November 19.

But unlike the two trailers before, this extended look will debut exclusively on Netflix, then be disseminated six hours later across other social platforms like YouTube. (Let’s be honest, people will rip the feed immediately and post it online.) Subscribers can watch the stream live on Netflix, starting August 27 at 3 pm Eastern (noon Pacific). WIRED will also have a roundup of the event's big takeaways.

This collaborative stunt follows a week of hacker leaks and gamer consternation on Rockstar’s decision not to ship the game with physical discs. The hackers initially said the leaks, which revealed GTA VI gameplay and story spoilers, were attempts to convince Rockstar to include physical discs. But the hackers quickly pivoted to collecting cryptocurrency in exchange for more leaks. Rockstar shared a statement on X saying the leaks had been “heartbreaking” for the team. It also wrote that the company is “excited for everyone to see the extended look.”

This marketing extravaganza is an unusual collaboration. Isn't GTA VI big enough for Rockstar to market it on its own? Also, why Netflix? The streaming giant hasn't nailed its attempts at incorporating gaming into its platform. The company introduced gaming in 2021 with big titles like GTA San Andreas on mobile, but they never really took off, as users didn’t play them. Netflix has wound down its focus on AAA games and recently shuttered two of its studios. While the platform might struggle to be a viable traditional gaming platform, it still wants in on that industry.

It’s not clear which company is paying for the privilege—either Netflix is paying Take-Two for the exclusive, or Take-Two is paying Netflix for access to the 325 million subscribers that use its service. Either way, Joost van Dreunen, a professor at NYU Stern School of Business who teaches about the business of video games and authors the blog Super Joost, says it's a good move for both companies.

Tech.title: OpenAI Is Developing a ‘Persistent’ AI Agent
Tech.content:
OpenAI is developing a proactive, highly persistent version of its flagship AI agent, Codex, WIRED has learned.

In recent days, OpenAI has started adding code for a new “Persistent mode” setting to its command line version of Codex, according to changes made to the product’s code base reviewed by WIRED. Changes to the Codex command line tool are made public by default, and new features tend to surface there before making their way to OpenAI’s other agent products, such as the Codex desktop app and ChatGPT Work.

Persistent mode has not been broadly rolled out or announced yet, but could be in the future. An OpenAI spokesperson confirmed to WIRED that the company is testing this feature, but said there are no immediate plans to launch it.

“OpenAI is a very bottom-up culture and many different things are explored on the open source repo which is a bit of our shared playground," said Thibault Sottiaux, OpenAI’s head of core products, in a statement to WIRED.

The feature appears to be OpenAI’s latest attempt to make AI agents that people will actually want to use. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta are racing to deliver general-purpose agent products that will help people automate tasks across their work and personal lives, such as filing expense reports or scheduling doctor’s appointments. So far, the people who use AI agents are largely software engineers, but Silicon Valley believes the tech could be a major line of business with a much broader customer base.

Persistent mode appears in Codex’s “reasoning effort” menu, in which users can select the level of computing power, tokens, and time they want to allow for an AI model to “think” before answering a prompt. It seems to be one of OpenAI’s most computationally intensive settings. When users have selected Persistent mode, OpenAI’s code base reads that Codex will “continue working until put to sleep.” That’s a stark contrast to currently available modes, which will stop working on a task after a few minutes or hours, even if it’s not complete.

In another file in the code base, OpenAI describes a feature within Persistent mode called “proactivity.” This appears to be a type of system prompt for agents in Persistent mode, which are told that their work is not done when they finish answering a user’s request. Instead, the agent is instructed to proactively create follow-up tasks for itself. The agent is capable of working on those tasks across sessions and using past user interactions and “knowledge of the user” to decide what to work on. It also has a tool to message the user without being asked but is told to send these sparingly.

The instructions also set limits for the agent, according to the file. The agent is told that Persistent mode does not expand what it is allowed to do and that altering anything outside the user’s own system requires the user's approval first—seemingly intended to limit how dangerous a persistent AI agent could be. The file sits in the shared core of Codex rather than in the code specific to the terminal, seeming to suggest the proactivity feature is intended for more than the command line tool.

Got a Tip? Are you a current or former AI lab employee who wants to talk about what’s happening? We’d like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact the reporter securely on Signal at mzeff.88.

In recently aired podcasts, interviews, and private investor meetings, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has described his desire to turn ChatGPT into a proactive, always-on AI agent. OpenAI hopes these changes will drive up adoption of the company’s most advanced AI models, which today are used by only a fraction of ChatGPT’s total user base.

Tech.title: What Meta’s All-New Social Media Guidelines Promise to Change for Teen Users
Tech.content:
The fallout of an $18 billion lawsuit against Meta, announced on Wednesday, is already here. A new announcement from Meta is designed to meet the terms of the settled lawsuit while helping to prevent teen social media addiction.

In its post, Meta outlined a series of changes to both Instagram and Facebook that will apply only to those under 18. Most of the changes were required as part of the lawsuit settlement, notably the creation of daily limits and night mode controls for teens, as well as the adoption of age-assurance measures to help prevent cheating the system. As part of the agreement, Meta has denied any wrongdoing.

There’s been worldwide pushback against teens and children using social media, including the EU restricting access to social apps for kids under 13, and Australia banning apps like Instagram for anyone under 16. But some advocates worry Meta’s changes won’t be enough to fully protect teens.

In an interview with Democracy Now on Thursday, attorney and co-director of the AI Now research institute, Amba Kak, said the changes don’t address the platform’s architecture, which is designed to addict teenagers with features like infinite scroll. “It’s the business model of surveillance advertising, where it is the optimization of engagement and attention at any cost,” Kak said. “And I think if we don’t get at those root cause fixes, we’re going to be stuck playing whack-a-mole.”

A representative from Meta didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Time limits for kids

Chief among the upcoming changes to Instagram and Facebook are time limitations for teens. A new default time limit will set the social media scrolling time to 2 hours a day for those under 18, and it can only be extended by parents.

An additional night mode will block most access to content such as feeds, stories, explore mode and reels between midnight and 6 a.m. and a school mode will mute notifications between 8 a.m. and 3 p.m.

Meta is also adding a feature to give 15-minute warnings to teens if they’ve been on the apps for an extended period of time, as well as 60-minute and 90-minute warnings they’re daily allotment is running down. To further reduce constant scrolling, autoplay for videos and clips will also be turned off by default, but like most features, it can be adjusted by parents.

Protection against toxic content

Meta is also implementing a number of changes intended to reduce toxicity and obsession with social media. By default, teens won’t see likes and reactions on posts, including their own. They’ll also be restricted from seeing certain content, such as cosmetic surgery and “extreme makeup” filters, although it’s not clear how far those limitations will extend (for example, a filter that adds dog ears).

Meta is adding age-appropriate content restrictions, but it remains vague on the details. While using movie ratings and parent feedback to build filters, the company fails to explain how this applies to social media posts or provide examples of blocked content.

In addition, teens will have the option to choose a non-algorithm version of their feeds that won’t be personalized by any Meta recommendations (which I also want for my own account).

Hazy tools for age verification

A new age-assurance strategy is also coming to Instagram and Facebook, but it’s unclear how it will work.

“We’re investing in even stronger technology to proactively catch accounts that may belong to under-13s,” Meta said on its blog. “We’re also strengthening the technology we use to identify accounts that may be between the ages of 13 and 17.”

Meta didn’t provide any details on how this tech would work, what it would look for or how it would flag accounts. I also asked about any appeals process for those incorrectly tagged, but Meta didn’t respond to my request.

It’s possible Meta will be using AI scan to profile context, account activity and visual cues to raise red flags, but there’s not much clarity otherwise.

Rolling out changes

The proposed changes were approved by a judge on Thursday, and Meta will roll out the first protections in the coming months, with the rest to follow afterward, although the exact timeline isn’t clear. As required by the agreement, Meta will also establish an independent social media research foundation to share “consented” user data in an effort to support teen well-being.

In its post, Meta said, “The fact is that teens move fluidly between dozens of apps a day. All platforms should empower parents and support teens by putting the same measures in place … we urge TikTok and YouTube to join us and state attorneys general in adopting this new standard.”

Other platforms have not responded to this call-out.

Tech.title: 1 in 6 VPNs Track Your Location, According to New Report From Proton
Tech.content:
Using a virtual private network is a surefire way to keep your information private when browsing the internet. But a new report from Proton, released on Wednesday, exposes some major holes in that concept.

A VPN is a tool that encrypts your internet behavior and hides your IP address and physical location, with the goal of keeping your identity and identifying information secure. But 64 of the VPN apps downloaded in the US, Proton found, are owned by Chinese companies and contain trackers that collect all sorts of user information, including device IDs, network information, device models and mobile carrier data.

And 25% of the apps in question were found to actively track your location.

Data from millions of VPN users is going to China

In June alone, these apps were downloaded over 13 million times.

Narrowing down the numbers further, Proton found that 31 of those Chinese-owned VPNs use shell companies registered in jurisdictions such as Singapore, Hong Kong and the UK to further hide their identities.

An authoritarian government like China’s could use this information to track a person’s location. So if a public official, someone in law enforcement, a journalist or even someone attending a protest was using one of these VPNs for safety, this flaw would expose them to potential threats.

It should be clear that China isn’t the only country where companies harvest the data these apps collect, but it’s near the top of the list. Israel, Russia and the Five Eyes countries — Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the UK and the US — all have companies collecting tracking data from millions of people.

Stronger privacy guardrails are needed

Transparency is a big issue here, with a load of bad VPN apps being readily available for download through Apple and Google. Proton’s report points out that both companies require developers to submit their own paperwork to verify their apps, with little verification (and no independent audits) being done on Apple’s or Google’s part. Apple and Google didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

This lack of guardrails in the verification process makes it hard to decipher which virtual private network apps protect your privacy and do what their policies promise and which are virtually doing the opposite.

“Proton’s report is yet another example of why it’s so important to know who’s behind your VPN and what data they’re collecting,” CNET Senior Writer Attila Tomaschek said. “It’s also another reminder that just because a VPN app is popular in Apple’s or Google’s app marketplaces, it doesn’t necessarily mean that the VPN app is safe to use.”

If you’re looking for a VPN, Tomaschek points to VPNs like Proton and ExpressVPN, which regularly rank near the top of CNET’s VPN recommendations. Each virtual private network is put through a rigorous testing process that includes a thorough examination of the app’s privacy policy, transparency reports, audits, corporate structure and legal jurisdiction.

When all else fails, avoid any VPN that is murky about any of those key principles. “Instead, opt for a trustworthy VPN that is crystal clear about where it’s based, who’s behind it and how it protects user privacy,” Tomaschek said.

Tech.title: Complaints Pile Up for Popular Meal Kit Services Amid Missing Ingredients and Poor Customer Service
Tech.content:
Weeks after fulfillment issues began at Marley Spoon following its former food supplier’s bankruptcy filing, customers are speaking out about their negative experiences with the Martha Stewart-backed meal kit brand.

(Full disclosure: CNET has tested Marley Spoon several times. We liked it so much, it landed on our list of the best services and earned an Editors’ Choice award before the fulfillment issues began.)

Sylvia Turcotte, who has been a Marley Spoon customer for over six years, told CNET that she and her husband have loved the brand’s offerings for years and would even mark certain recipes as “restaurant quality” when they were worthy and often served them to dinner guests.

Then, in July, issues began with her regular deliveries: melted ice, warm protein and questionable produce. In August, a box that was supposed to contain 27 ingredients was missing 21.

“Needless to say, I did not cook Marley [Spoon] that week,” Turcotte said. “What I do not understand is why the powers that be have not suspended the meal plan until they get their logistics straightened out. Instead, they are ruining their brand.”

Other Marley Spoon customers shared additional disappointing experiences, including receiving boxes missing protein and receiving no response from customer service when inquiring about damaged or incomplete boxes.

Marley Spoon’s transition

Marley Spoon’s transition to a new supplier has been rocky. Corin Cesaric/Zooey Liao/CNET

In April, Marley Spoon’s previous food supplier, FreshRealm, which also supplied Blue Apron, filed for bankruptcy. CNET later confirmed that Misfits Market would be taking over fulfillment for both brands.

Marley Spoon has offered customers credit toward their next order when a problem occurs.

Best Meal Kits, as Tested by CNET See at CNET

The transition has been rocky, with Misfits Market spokesperson Ken Shuman previously saying the company has “compressed what’s typically a 10- [to] 12-month transition into under 10 weeks,” and “an operational transition at that speed has real challenges, and the biggest one has been inventory.”

“Customers who experience missing items or other issues with their order are encouraged to contact Marley Spoon’s Customer Care team directly through the Help Center,” a spokesperson told CNET. “While credits may be automatically issued in some cases, the team will review the individual circumstances and determine the appropriate resolution, including a refund.”

When I inquired to customer service about a refund instead of credit for missing ingredients, I did not hear back on two occasions. The Marley Spoon customer service phone number directs you to the website or app.

However, Marley Spoon previously shared a statement regarding the fulfillment issues, which read in part, “We take this very seriously and are working around the clock to ensure our customers receive their boxes on time, with the correct, high-quality ingredients they expect from Marley Spoon.”

Stewart remains affiliated with the brand, with select recipes of hers featured every week, her team confirmed to CNET. However, they added that the “delivery and fulfillment operations are managed independently.”

While some loyal customers have said they want to help the brand weather the storm, others have told CNET they’ve decided to cut their losses and cancel their subscriptions entirely. When a subscription is canceled rather than paused, any accrued credits are lost.

“I love Marley Spoon,” Turcotte said. “I hope they can solve their issues.”

Blue Apron

Blue Apron faces similar challenges

Similar issues have plagued Blue Apron recently. In a previous statement to CNET, Blue Apron said in part that the company is “temporarily focusing our menu on what we’re confident we can deliver, adding quality checks before boxes ship, and making progress with our partners to fix what’s broken.”

On social media, after the company released a statement about the service disruptions, customers echoed complaints made about Marley Spoon, particularly about a lack of response from customer service.

“I’ve been a customer since 2012,” one commenter wrote. “[Blue Apron] has taught me how to cook, and I love it dearly. But these last two weeks have been challenging. This week we received a box of condiments, a bag of spinach, a card for a steak recipe (I’m a vegetarian) but no steak and not one complete recipe to cook.”



Blue Apron responded to the comment, saying it would reach out via direct message to handle the situation.

Tech.title: NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Telescope Is About to Start Its Cosmic Survey
Tech.content:
The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is ready for its trip to Florida so that it can get launched into space. NASA

After nearly a decade in development, NASA’s next big telescope is almost ready to travel into space. The agency has set Sunday as the launch date for the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. This places the project approximately eight months ahead of its original schedule and, according to NASA leadership, significantly under budget.

NASA is getting some assistance from SpaceX for this launch. The telescope is being taken into space by a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket, where it’ll separate and head to its final location while the SpaceX rocket returns to Earth.

With the launch just a few days away, the telescope should be pretty close to ready to go. That includes detailed inspections to verify it sustained no damage during transit. Engineers also loaded 290 gallons of hydrazine to fuel the telescope and conducted several dress rehearsals in preparation for the launch.

The destination for the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is the Sun-Earth L2 Lagrange point, located about 1 million miles from Earth on the far side of the sun. The region is a gravitational sweet spot that allows spacecraft to maintain a relatively stable position while orbiting the sun alongside Earth.

With its wider field of view, the Roman telescope promises to see quite a lot of the universe. NASA

How to watch the Nancy Grace Roman Telescope launch

The launch is set to take off from Launch Complex 39A at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Sunday at 7:26 a.m. ET/4:26 a.m. PT. NASA is livestreaming the event, with coverage beginning at 6:20 a.m. ET, and it’ll include a post-launch news conference starting at 9:30 a.m. ET with a media Q&A session.

NASA is streaming it across all its social platforms, including Facebook, Instagram, Twitch, YouTube and X. The agency says the launch is also watchable on NASA Plus, Amazon Prime and Discovery Plus. Netflix isn’t mentioned on NASA’s list, but it won’t hurt to check the day of the launch to see if it’s streaming there as well.

It’s quite an early launch for a Sunday, so if you’re a late sleeper or a churchgoer, you may have to wait until later to watch it back.

What is the Nancy Grace Roman Telescope looking for?

The telescope is named after astronomer Nancy Grace Roman, NASA’s first female executive and an instrumental voice in the planning and construction of the Hubble Space Telescope.

The two telescopes share more than just a connection to Roman. Both use 2.4-meter mirrors and can produce images with similar sharpness. But Roman is designed to see much more of the sky at once, capturing images at least 100 times larger than Hubble’s. The observatories also specialize in different wavelengths of light: Hubble observes ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared light, while Roman focuses on visible and infrared wavelengths.

The Roman Telescope can see as much of space in just two images as the Hubble does in over 400. NASA

NASA envisions Roman and Hubble working hand in hand. Roman will scan enormous swaths of the sky, uncovering objects and phenomena that can later be examined in greater detail by Hubble. By combining Roman’s panoramic surveys with Hubble’s more focused observations, astronomers hope to build a richer picture of the cosmos.

During its mission, Roman is expected to observe more than 100 billion stars and billions of galaxies, detect tens of thousands of supernovae and transmit nearly 1.4 terabytes of scientific data to Earth every day.

Tech.title: Human, Beware: The Secrets We Tell AI Chatbots Aren’t Private
Tech.content:
Are people oversharing sensitive information with AI? Short answer: yes.

A new survey called The AI Privacy Problem by DuckDuckGo Research said about a third of people are sharing secrets with chatbots that they don’t share with friends, family and medical professionals. The number rises to 56% among self-described AI enthusiasts. Researchers also found that 43% of parents reveal things to AI that they don’t tell the most trusted people in their lives, including their kids.

Though the survey didn’t specify what kind of personal information is shared with AI, past reports have shown that we often turn to chatbots for help with physical and mental health issues, financial advice, parenting questions and marital problems.

The problem isn’t about seeking help. The problem is losing control over what happens with the data after it’s shared in chats. Companies can use your private info to train their AI systems. Law enforcement can get it through subpoenas. And if you’re using AI chatbots at work, your employer can likely access your chat history, too.

AI companies try to convince people that chatbots are trusted confidantes, but that’s a false narrative, the DuckDuckGo report said.

“These messages all rest on one assumption: That these chats are private. In most cases, that just isn’t true,” researchers said.

In fact, the survey found that many respondents didn’t realize how their chatbot data could be used or accessed or that they didn’t know about settings to prevent their information from being recorded or stored. When it comes to protecting their data, nearly 40% of respondents had no trust in companies and nearly 50% had no trust in the US government.

Privacy risks of large language models

Many of us know that companies bombard us with targeted, personalized online ads. If you run a Google search for vacuums, you’ll see vacuum ads pop up on your screen. If you search for Mediterranean cruises, you’ll surely get cruise ads on YouTube (owned by Google). Companies also buy, sell and share our social media data to help guide their advertising.

But AI data-sharing goes well beyond being the focus of selling you products. If you provide sensitive information to a chatbot, it could be revealed or exposed. A researcher at Wake Forest University found that AI agents, which use LLM data to perform autonomous tasks, can sometimes leak data, either maliciously or unintentionally.

Your conversations with AI chatbots don’t disappear into the ether. Unless you opt out, the AI system will record and save them for future use, such as additional training for the AI model. Last year, hundreds of chats on Anthropic’s chatbot Claude appeared in Google search results.

One main concern with LLMs is data memorization, said AI expert Uttara Ananthakrishnan, assistant professor at the University of Washington’s Foster School of Business. “When someone asks the same question as someone else, it is possible that the LLM gives them exactly the same answer it gave someone else,” Ananthakrishnan told CNET. “The LLM might not know that the answer contains information that someone can use to identify someone else.”

Cops can use chat data

What you say in a “private” chat could also wind up in court or part of a police investigation. Companies with AI models such as Anthropic (Claude), Google (Gemini) and OpenAI (ChatGPT) are legally required to turn over chat data if subpoenaed by law enforcement or the US government. Only 25% of DuckDuckGo survey respondents knew this. As MemX, an AI memory agent, stated starkly in a blog post: “A conversation with a mainstream chatbot is a business record, not a confidential consultation.”



It’s already happened several times. ChatGPT transcripts were used during a double murder investigation in South Carolina earlier this year and in the Palisades arson case last year. A Snapchat AI conversation was used as evidence in a 2024 murder trial.

As OpenAI founder and CEO Sam Altman said on a podcast earlier this year, “If you go talk to ChatGPT about your most sensitive stuff and then there’s like a lawsuit or whatever, we could be required to produce that.”

Employers can use chat data

Free speech isn’t really free in the worker-employer relationship. Companies can fire you over your social media posts, and they can also access your AI accounts if you’re using them at work under certain circumstances, like if your access is based on the company’s enterprise account.

And putting company info in a private chat, even on your personal account, is a major no-no, although a survey earlier this year showed that two in five workers did just that.

Some big companies, such as Walmart, Delta, T-Mobile, Chevron and Starbucks, are even using AI to gauge worker positivity — or toxicity. These AI systems scan employee messaging platforms such as Slack or Teams, looking for clues in keywords and sentences, in what is called “emotion AI.”

Some companies also want workers to put their Slack messages in public channels so their AI systems can use those chats for further model training.

Chat data can be used for training

More than half of the DuckDuckGo survey respondents did not know (or were not sure) that their chatbot conversations were used for AI training. Nearly three in five were “uncomfortable” with that, and 30% were “very uncomfortable.”

Boiled down, AI training is the process of feeding massive amounts of data into an AI system so it can recognize patterns, make decisions and solve problems — basically, match or exceed what humans can do. That data can include published materials, video and audio recordings out in the world, as well as your chats.



A 2025 Stanford study showed that six companies fed user chat data back into their AI systems for further training — Amazon (Nova), Anthropic (Claude), Google (Gemini), Meta (Meta AI), Microsoft (Copilot) and OpenAI (ChatGPT). Not all of them have opt-out options.

AI chatbots provide a false sense of intimacy and perhaps confidentiality, said the University of Washington’s Ananthakrishnan.



“Users interact with these tools as sounding boards, sharing unfiltered thoughts, sensitive health queries, and vulnerable personal dilemmas that they would likely never type into Google,” Ananthakrishnan told CNET. “People are deeply uneasy about their most intimate, conversational thoughts being ingested into a system where they could inadvertently become public record.”

Use chatbots securely and privately

We aren’t advocating you run and hide from chatbots, but there are ways to maximize your privacy if and when you use them. Many chatbots have settings you can deploy that will prevent them from being stored on company servers to be used as an AI model training.

In an explainer, CNET reporter Blake Stimac gives a complete breakdown of how to turn off data sharing for Gemini, Claude, ChatGPT and Grok. With Meta, it’s more of a request than an opt-out.

There are also ways to keep your chatbot experiences as safe as possible: Treat chats as “public environments,” don’t overshare your mental state and regularly export your data to see what information the AI has stored about you.

For greater privacy, there are chatbots that run only offline and locally — in other words, not on any cloud servers. Those include Jan.ai, Ollama, LM Studio, PrivateGPT and GPT4All.

Tech.title: Adobe Photoshop Adds a Whole New AI Editing Mode
Tech.content:
Adobe is giving Photoshop users more AI tools for their work belt. A new feature called AI Assisted Editor lets you do a variety of things with your images using merely natural language prompts. It’s not replacing the traditional Pro Editor; it’s just another option.

Adobe also announced several other new features on Thursday — a light adjustment layer for more lighting controls, Instruct Edit with Masks for prompt-based editing, and Markup to let you visually communicate edits by drawing on an image.



Adobe has been busy with new AI wrinkles in the past several months. AI Assistant arrived in March to enable editing with conversational commands, and in June, the company added AI assistants to Photoshop, Premiere Pro, InDesign, Illustrator and Frame.io. Earlier this month, OpenAI and Adobe teamed up to integrate dozens of photo- and video-editing capabilities into ChatGPT.

AI Assisted Editor is currently being tested in the beta version of Photoshop, which costs $23 per month.

AI Assisted Editor keeps it simple

When you open Photoshop, you will see two editing interface options: AI Assisted and Pro Editor. AI Assisted is the new feature announced Thursday, and Pro Editor is Photoshop’s classic workspace offering manual control over layers, adjustments and editing tools.

Photoshop masters are likely comfortable with Pro Editor, but less-experienced users might gravitate toward AI Assisted for simpler editing.

If you go with AI Assisted, you can use a natural language prompt bar to request edits and changes. A vertical tool bar includes seven functions, including prompt to edit (using natural language prompts), remove background, generative expand (extend image dimensions), generative remove (eliminate unwanted objects), generative fill (add, replace, or remove content), generative upscale (increase image resolution) and AI markup (annotate images).



The Prompt to Edit function could be the biggest game changer. You can change out the image entirely with a natural language prompt. Maybe you’ve got an image of someone sitting on a beach, but want them in the mountains. A prompt of “Put this person on a hiking trail in the mountains” could do the trick.

More new Photoshop features

Adobe also announced three other new options for what the company called “more precise, sharper editing.” The light adjustment layer lets you toggle through several lighting controls — exposure, contrast, highlights, shadows, whites and blacks.

Photoshop’s Light Adjustment Layer lets you toggle between several adjustments.

With the Instruct Edit with Masks function, you can simply describe the edits you want in the masked areas — have the person smile, put the bird in flight, open the blue door — instead of having to mark every area on the image that you want to edit.

With the markup tool, you can draw on an image to tell the AI your changes. You might circle a building and tell the AI to make it brown, or maybe draw an arrow to where you want a certain object. Adobe says markup is a way of being more precise with the AI to avoid any ambiguity that might occur if you instead used text prompts.

Tech.title: The Powerful Stealth AI Model ‘Ox Alpha’ Is Now GLM-5.3-Flash, and You Can Use It
Tech.content:
The anonymous Ox Alpha AI model that popped up on OpenRouter, the unified AI platform, last week has been claimed by the Chinese company Z.ai. Now officially known as GLM-5.3-Flash, the model is both powerful and cheap, challenging the capabilities and cost of popular models from Anthropic and OpenAI.

When it was first teased, Ox Alpha became the most popular model for the week on OpenRouter and all of its traffic was served through Chinese-made AI chips. After it was confirmed to be the company behind the new model, Z.ai’s stock price soared, Bloomberg reports.

Ox Alpha was described as a “frontier model built for efficient coding, sustained agentic work, and real-world production use,” according to an OpenRouter post on X. In a follow-up post, the platform confirmed that the provider wouldn’t train on your prompts.

Z.ai’s GLM family are open-weight models, where core components are publicly released, allowing anyone to download and use them. (That’s different from open-source AI models, which make all pieces of the model available, including the source code, weights, and training data.) Weights for GLM-5.3-Flash are available on Hugging Face, another unified AI platform.

Being open-weight puts the GLM family in contrast to closed-weight models from big US developers like OpenAI and Anthropic. Open-weight models, which are popular among Chinese companies, have been the subject of heated debate in the US because of the potential that users will change or misuse them. But big American companies, including OpenAI, have come out in support of open ecosystems. Meta recently said it would release the weights of a previously closed model, Muse Spark 1.2.

Like other recent AI models, GLM-5.3-Flash has enhanced agentic capabilities, such as using a browser and a computer, allowing the model to navigate web pages and open and interact with desktop apps.

How can you access the GLM-5.3 Flash?

In an announcement post on X, Z.ai said the new model is available across all official platforms. The easiest and most direct way to access the model is to subscribe to one of Z.ai’s GLM coding plans, which start at $18 a month. The model will also provide 3x the usable quota of GLM-5.3.

Because GLM-5.3-Flash is open-weight, you can also download it and use it on your own hardware — no paying for subscription or API costs. Although it might require some hefty computing power to do so, as the model weights themselves tip the scales at more than 300GB.

Tech.title: Nokia’s 300 Charge Is the Cool Retro Phone You Won’t Be Using in the US
Tech.content:
Sometimes it’s best not to know what you’re missing.

For those of us who keep up with tech product announcements, it was hard not to notice a new, eye-catching gadget: the 300 Charge, a retro-styled phone from Nokia with an appealing blocky look (think earth-toned Lego bricks).

In addition to its old-school looks, the 300 Charge has a few interesting features. It can serve as a 10-watt powerbank for other devices, has an SD card slot and a headphone jack, and features an ultrabright LED torch for use as a flashlight, all for about $32. Yes, you read that price right.

The phone is like catnip for anyone who wants a cheap, stripped-down feature phone with a magnificent battery life, and it was prominently featured on tech sites including Gizmodo, Engadget and TechRadar.

But if you live in the US, the 300 Charge isn’t available to you. So far, it’s only for sale in the Philippines, and launch dates for other markets haven’t been announced.

Another big bummer: The phone is only compatible with 2G networks, and the last of those just shut down in the US (thanks, T-Mobile). Nor is it compatible with 3G networks, which most wireless carriers discontinued in 2022. There’s no indication that a 4G version that would work in the US might be available in the future.

Representatives from Nokia and its partner company HMD Global did not return a request for comment.

Going retro

So-called “dumb phones,” which go back to an era before smartphones, are currently in vogue, part of a kind of digital-detox awakening. Flip phones, like the reimagined Motorola Razr, the Light Phone and others, let you carry around a phone that’s less distracting and doesn’t demand excessive screen time — allowing you to focus more on core features like actual phone calls or T9-style texting.

Some of them look like they came straight out of the early 2000s, when my generation proudly sported them. Others resemble slightly smarter devices like the BlackBerry or Palm Treo, before we switched to screen-dominated smartphones.

And there seems to be a strong appetite for these types of phones, not just in foreign markets where low-cost, stripped-down phones are offered out of necessity.

Commodore, the ’80s brand associated with some of the first personal computers, recently launched a flip phone, the Callback 8020. The head of the group that bought the Commodore brand said the device sold almost 10,000 units at its launch and had a callback waitlist of 100,000, showing that retro feature phones are a hot commodity.

“People are not simply buying the past,” said Christian “Peri Fractic” Simpson, Commodore International’s president and CEO. “Retro phones like the Commodore Callback 8020 offer tactile buttons, personality, and a more deliberate relationship with technology.”

Simpson said the people buying these phones include Gen Zers who are discovering these devices for the first time. The audience also includes parents who want to limit their kids’ social media activity for safety reasons, and adults who want connectivity with fewer distractions.

Dumb phones also typically have longer battery life than smartphones, and because they lack apps flagged as addictive and have less responsive keypads, they can serve as a light form of digital detox, encouraging more intentional use.

The 2G loophole has closed

Long before the Callback 8020 was released, Simpson himself posted a video two years ago showing how an ancient Ericsson phone could operate on modern networks.

It did then, but that’s no longer possible.

And the Nokia 300 Charge won’t operate in the US for the same reasons.

“The Nokia 300 Charge cannot realistically be hacked for US use,” Simpson told CNET. “It supports only 2G GSM on 900/1,800MHz. Software cannot add the missing LTE bands, VoLTE support or carrier certification, so it should be treated as unusable on public US networks, even by most enthusiasts.”

That goes for other feature phones available overseas, such as Xiaomi devices, which have effectively been outlawed for sale in the US, even if they work with domestic carrier networks. Nokia’s 8110 “banana phone” and many Japanese flip phones also don’t work in the US.

Nokia and HMD have not said if they’re working on something like the Nokia 300 for American or European markets, but it seems like there’d be plenty of interest from those who want a break from their smartphone at a very low price.
